description: Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of a primary alkyl bromide with potassium thioacetate; converts the bromide to a thioacetate ester, generating potassium bromide as by‑product; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to reflux; no catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; metal‑sulfur hydrogen transfer. Cesium metal reduces hydrogen sulfide gas, yielding cesium sulfide and hydrogen gas. Usually performed in a sealed anhydrous conditions with gentle heating (100–200 °C) to promote gas–solid contact; no solvent or catalyst required.

Halogen exchange/fluorination of a silane with phosphorus pentafluoride; produces trifluorosilane, phosphorus trifluoride and hydrogen fluoride; a high‑temperature gas‑phase or sealed‑tube reaction under anhydrous conditions; the reaction is conducted in inert, dry vessels, often at 100–200 °C; no solvent is usually employed, and the HF generated is handled in suitable containment.

Condensation of chlorosulfuric acid with sulfuryl chloride to give pyrosulfuryl chloride and HCl; a halogen‑exchange/condensation process that forms the S–O–S “pyrosulfuryl” chloride; performed under anhydrous conditions, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, often in a dry inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or in the gas phase; HCl evolves as a gas.

Base‑acid catalyzed condensation/cyclization of dimethyl oxalate with 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde in the presence of piperidine and concentrated sulfuric acid to give anisindione; key steps are a Knoevenagel‑type condensation, intramolecular cyclization, decarboxylation and methanol elimination; typically performed under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) in the acidic medium, often neat or in a non‑polar solvent, with piperidine as the nucleophilic base and H₂SO₄ providing protonation and dehydration.

Simple double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation of lead(II) fluoride from lead(II) chloride and potassium fluoride; aqueous or alcoholic medium, often performed at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble PbF₂ precipitates, while KCl remains in solution.

Halogen‑exchange fluorination of tellurium tetrabromide with elemental fluorine to give tellurium tetrafluoride and bromine; a gas‑phase fluorination carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible vessel, sometimes with an inert carrier gas; no additional catalyst is required.

Type: enzymatic N‑acetyltransferase reaction. Purpose: synthesis of N‑acetyl‑L‑tyrosine. Key transformation: transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl‑CoA to the α‑amino group of L‑tyrosine, releasing CoA‑SH. Conditions: aqueous buffer, acetyl‑CoA, appropriate N‑acetyltransferase enzyme, pH 7–8, ambient temperature (≈25 °C).

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; exchanges anions between sodium nitrate and manganese(II) chloride to give sodium chloride and soluble manganese(II) nitrate; typically performed by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature, no special catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation reaction; peracetic acid oxidizes diallyl disulfide to the thiosulfinate allicin while being reduced to acetic acid; used to synthesize biologically active allicin generally carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen, without additional catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification; dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates formic acid to form an O‑acylurea intermediate which reacts with 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol to give isobutyl formate, producing N,N‑dicyclohexylurea as a by‑product; performed in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, typically at 0 °C to rt, sometimes with catalytic DMAP, under inert atmosphere.

Direct oxidative fluorination; used to prepare xenon hexafluoride, a powerful fluorinating reagent. Xenon difluoride is oxidized from Xe(II) to Xe(VI) by addition of four fluorine atoms from F2. Conducted in the gas phase in a sealed quartz tube at 200‑300 °C under F2 pressure; no solvent or catalyst required.

High‑temperature redox (thermite‑type) reaction; aluminum reduces perchlorate ion, releasing oxygen gas and forming potassium chloride and aluminum oxide; employed in propellant or oxygen‑generating formulations; requires ignition and high temperature (several hundred °C), conducted a solid mixture, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis; aqueous potassium hydroxide attacks cyclopentyl iodide, displacing iodide to give cyclopentanol and potassium iodide, with water as the solvent; usually refluxed in aqueous KOH ( KOH/ethanol mixture) to ensure complete conversion; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (ether formation). 1‑butanol and methanol condense in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to afford 1‑methoxybutane and water. Conducted at 130–150 °C with excess methanol as solvent; sulfuric acid acts as the catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to an alkene; HCl adds across the double bond of 2‑methoxypropene in a Markovnikov fashion, yielding 2‑chloro‑2‑methoxypropane; carried out in anhydrous non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often using gaseous HCl; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; used to exchange cations between magnesium selenate and sodium carbonate. In aqueous medium, magnesium selenate reacts with sodium carbonate, producing insoluble magnesium carbonate (MgCO₃) which precipitates, and soluble sodium selenate (Na₂SeO₄) remains in solution. Usually carried out at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction; vanadium(V) oxide is reduced by carbon to vanadium(III) oxide with evolution of carbon dioxide; carried out at high temperature (≈900–1200 °C) in a solid‑state furnace, inert atmosphere optional, solid reactants mixed and heated.

Ligand exchange/metal complexation: copper(II) acetate reacts with picolinic acid to form copper(II) picolinate and release acetic acid. Typically performed by refluxing a mixture of Cu(OAc)2 and picolinic acid in ethanol or methanol; the reaction proceeds via acid‑base exchange and coordination of picolinate ligands to the copper center.

Ketal formation (acetal protection): ethyl acetoacetate’s carbonyl group is protected by reaction with ethylene glycol in the presence of the Lewis acid catalyst indium trichloride. Water formed is removed (e.g., by Dean‑Stark or molecular sieves). The reaction is usually carried out in anhydrous toluene or dichloromethane under reflux.

Halogen displacement/disproportionation: potassium iodide reacts with iodine trichloride, reducing ICl3 to elemental iodine while the chloride is transferred to potassium, yielding KCl and liberating chlorine gas. The reaction occurs readily in aqueous or dilute organic solution at ambient temperature; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑amine condensation (amidation): decanoic acid reacts with ammonia to give decanamide and water. Direct condensation generally requires excess gaseous NH3 and elevated temperature (≈180–200 °C) under pressure, or can be performed via activation of the acid (e.g., as the acid chloride) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to a C–Se bond: sodium selenide attacks ethyl bromide in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, displacing bromide and yielding diethyl selenide with NaBr as by‑product. The reaction is typically carried out at room temperature to moderate reflux, under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of the selenide.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 1‑nitroadamantane to 1‑aminoadamantane. Purpose: convert nitro group to primary amine. Key transformation: –NO₂ → –₂ with formation of water; N–O bonds cleaved. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with Pd/C, Pt or Raney Ni in ethanol or methanol, 25–100 °C.

Acid–base neutralization forming a solid salt. Gaseous or aqueous hydrogen chloride reacts exothermically with ammonia, producing ammonium chloride. Typically performed by bubbling HCl gas into NH₃ gas (or mixing aqueous solutions) at room temperature; no solvent is required for the gas‑phase version, water serves as solvent in aqueous media.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 2,6‑dimethylphenyl azide to 2,6‑dimethylaniline with release of nitrogen gas. Purpose: generate aryl amine from azide. Key transformation: –N₃ → –NH₂, N₂ evolved. Conditions: H₂ (1–3 atm),/C catalyst, ethanol or THF solvent, ambient to mild heating.

Double displacement precipitation; purpose: isolate cadmium as the bright yellow sulfide precipitate and recycle sodium hydroxide; key transformation: Cd(OH)2 + Na2S → CdS (solid) + 2 NaOH (aq); typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, continuous stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Direct combination (high‑temperature synthesis) of boron tribromide with phosphine to form boron phosphide; serves to prepare BP as a refractory semiconductor; key transformation is Br‑H exchange and B‑P bond formation with liberation of HBr gas; typically carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor at 300–600 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent, catalyst generally not required.

Hydrolysis of platinum tetrafluoride; forms platinum dioxide and hydrogen fluoride. Solid PtF₄ is dissolved or suspended in water, often with mild heating, leading to conversion to PtO₂ precipitate and HF in solution. Reaction proceeds in aqueous medium; no catalyst necessary.

Metal‑acid redox reaction: europium metal reacts with hydroiodic acid to give hydrogen gas and europium(II) iodide. Purpose: preparation of EuI₂. Key transformation: Eu⁰ oxidized to Eu²⁺, 2 HI reduced to H₂. Conditions: aqueous conc. HI, 0–25 °C or gentle warming, no catalyst.

Acid‑base metathesis: dicalcium citrate reacts with hydrochloric acid to liberate citric acid and form calcium chloride. Purpose: recover citric acid or generate CaCl₂ solution. Key transformation: Ca²⁺ displaced by H⁺, yielding free citric acid and CaCl₂. Conditions: aqueous HCl (≈4 equiv), stirring at room temperature to reflux, aqueous medium.

Inverse‑electron‑demand Diels‑Alder reaction; 1,2,4,5‑tetrazine reacts with bicyclo[6.1.0]non‑4‑yne (a strained alkyne) to give a pyridazine and nitrogen gas. Purpose: click‑type ligation with a strained alkyne partner. Key transformation: [4+2] cycloaddition of the tetrazine across the alkyne, forming a dihydropyridazine that loses N₂ to generate the aromatic pyridazine ring. Typical conditions: MeCN or DMSO solution at room temperature to 37 °C; no metal catalyst required, though a small amount of acid (e.g., AcOH) can improve rate.

Acid‑carbonate reaction: lanthanum carbonate is protonated by excess hydrobromic acid producing carbon dioxide, water and lanthanum bromide. Purpose: generate soluble LaBr₃. Key transformation: CO₃²⁻ + 2 H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O; La³⁺ pairs with Br⁻. Conditions: aqueous HBr (excess), heating to evolve CO₂, aqueous solution.

Nitrosation of an acyl hydrazide to give an acyl azide; generates benzoyl azide, a precursor for Curtius rearrangement; carried out with freshly prepared nitrous acid (NaNO₂/HCl) at 0–5 °C in aqueous acidic medium; the –NHNH₂ group is converted to –N₃ with loss of water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl iodoacetate by sulfide ion from sodium sulfide, yielding ethyl thioglycolate and sodium iodide. Purpose: synthesize a thioester. Key transformation: I⁻ displaced by S²⁻ (as HS⁻/S²⁻) to form S‑CH₂COOEt. Conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or ethanol), ambient temperature, inert atmosphere optional.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; anions are exchanged between copper(II) nitrate and lead azide to form lead(II) nitrate (soluble) and copper(II) azide, which precipitates. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Heck cross‑coupling of an aryl chloride (chlorobenzene) with ethylene to form styrene; triethylamine serves as the base to scavenge the generated HCl; reaction proceeds via oxidative addition of Pd(0) to the C–Cl bond, insertion of ethylene, and β‑hydride elimination; common conditions include a Pd(0) source (e.g., Pd(OAc)2 with a phosphine ligand), TEA, and a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or NMP at 100–150 °C.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of basic lead carbonate to regenerate lead(II) oxide, releasing carbon dioxide and water vapor; the solid is heated in air or inert atmosphere at 300–500 °C; the reaction proceeds without solvent or catalyst; purpose is to recycle the carbonate back to PbO for further use.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; ammonium thiocyanate swaps its thiocyanate anion with bromide from mercury(II) bromide, producing soluble ammonium bromide and insoluble mercury(II) thiocyanate precipitate. Conducted in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride; LAH (1–2 equiv) in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C then reflux reduces 2‑methylcyclohexyl acetate to two alcohols—2‑methylcyclohexanol from the acyl fragment and ethanol from the original acetate alkoxy fragment; inert atmosphere, aqueous work‑up required.

Acid‑base deprotonation of an alcohol by alkali metal; metallic sodium reacts with 1‑decanol to generate sodium decylate (the decyl alkoxide) and hydrogen gas. Performed under anhydrous, inert conditions in dry ether or THF; no additional catalyst.

Acid chloride hydrolysis/neutralization; chloroacetyl chloride reacts with sodium bicarbonate, yielding chloroacetic acid, sodium chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Usually carried out in aqueous bicarbonate solution, often cooled (0 °C to 25 °C) to control CO₂ evolution; no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aluminum nitrate and calcium hydroxide exchange ions, forming soluble calcium nitrate and insoluble aluminum hydroxide precipitate. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; CHO → COOH; performed in aqueous alkaline medium (KMnO4, NaOH) under reflux; after oxidation the mixture is acidified to isolate the acid; water is the solvent.

Halogenation of isopropanol via phosphorus triiodide (Appel-type substitution); converts the hydroxyl group of isopropanol to an iodine, yielding isopropyl iodide and phosphorous acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of alcohol on PI3 forming alkyl iodide and H3PO3; performed at 0‑25 °C in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no added catalyst.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening; thiophenol attacks ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to afford 2‑phenylsulfanylethanol (a β‑mercapto alcohol). Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, often with a base (e.g., NaH or K₂CO₃) or mild acid catalyst to promote nucleophilicity; no metal catalyst needed.

Redox combustion reaction of ammonium nitrate with dodecane; purpose is to release energy and produce gaseous products; key transformation: ammonium nitrate acts as oxidizer for dodecane, yielding carbon dioxide, water vapor, and nitrogen gas; occurs at high ignition temperature, often initiated by spark or flame; no solvent; commonly used in solid rocket propellants; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement/complexation precipitation; purpose is synthesis of the fungicide Mancozeb, a mixed Zn‑Mn ethylenebis(dithiocarbamate) polymer. Sodium ethylenebis(dithiocarbamate) reacts with ZnCl₂ and MnCl₂ in aqueous solution, forming the insoluble metal‑dithiocarbamate complex and precipitating NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, stirring; no additional catalyst needed. Common solvent: water.

Oxidation of a 1,2,5‑oxadiazole to its N‑oxide (furoxan); H₂O₂ serves as oxidant in acetic acid, which also acts as solvent and proton source. Reaction is generally carried out at 0–25 °C to control exotherm, then warmed if needed. No catalyst is required. Purpose: preparation of the energetic heterocycle furoxan.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis); aqueous NaOH deprotonates alprenolol·HCl, liberating free‑base alprenolol and forming NaCl and water. Conducted at room temperature with stirring. After basification the free base is usually extracted into an organic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane. No catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous BaCl₂ and K₃PO₄ exchange anions to give insoluble barium phosphate precipitate and soluble KCl. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid barium phosphate is filtered and washed. No catalyst; solvent is water.

Partial acid‑base reaction; sulfuric acid protonates lithium acetate, generating acetic acid and lithium hydrogen sulfate (LiHSO₄). Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

N‑acylation (acetylation) of an amide; purpose is to introduce a second acetyl group on the nitrogen to give N‑acetylacetamide. The lone pair on the amide nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetic anhydride, displacing acetate and forming the N‑acylated product; acetic acid is released. Typically performed in pyridine or dichloromethane at reflux, with pyridine acting as base and solvent; no metal catalyst required.

Intramolecular Friedel‑Crafts acylation (cyclization) of 4‑phenylbutanoic acid to form 1‑tetralone. Anhydrous AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst, promoting formation of the acylium ion and subsequent electrophilic aromatic substitution onto the phenyl ring, closing a six‑membered ring. Reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions, often in dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, at low temperature (0 °C) followed by reflux. After quenching with ice/water, the product is isolated by extraction.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between silver nitrate and potassium thiosulfate forming soluble silver thiosulfate complex and potassium nitrate. Typically performed at room temperature in water; the silveriosulfate remains in solution (used in photographic fixing), while potassium nitrate stays dissolved. No special catalyst required.

Metalation‑carboxylation sequence; LDA deprotonates isoquinoline at C‑1 to give a lithio‑isoquinoline which then adds CO₂, followed by aqueous work‑up to afford isoquinoline‑1‑carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: THF, –78 °C to 0 °C, LDA generated in situ, CO₂ gas bubbled in, then quench with dilute acid. No additional catalyst.

Acid‑base protonation to liberate the β‑diketone; sodium acetylacetonate is treated with aqueous HCl, protonating the acac⁻ anion to give acetylacetone, NaCl and water; reaction performed at 0‑25 °C in water, followed by extraction of acetylacetone with an organic solvent such as ether.

Pechmann condensation (acid‑catalyzed coupling of a β‑keto ester with a phenol) to generate the coumarin scaffold scoparone with loss of ethanol. Carried out by heating ethyl acetoacetate and 2,3‑dimethoxyphenol neat or in excess conc. H₂SO₄ (80–100 °C). Sulfuric acid acts as both solvent and catalyst; no other reagents are needed.

Dehydrative cyclization (cyclodehydration) of o‑nitrobenzaldoxime to 2,1‑benzisoxazole using thionyl chloride as a dehydrating agent. Reaction is refluxed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine; pyridine often added to scavenge the released HCl. Gases (HCl, SO₂) evolve; no external catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed ether hydrolysis (cleavage) of tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether to give tetraethylene glycol and methanol. Conducted by refluxing the ether in aqueous HCl (typically 6 M) for several hours. Water is the solvent; the acid itself serves as the catalyst.

Protonolysis (acid‑base reaction); ethyl lithium, a strong organolithium base, is quenched with water, transferring a proton to the ethyl anion to form ethane gas while lithium hydroxide remains in solution; typically performed in anhydrous ether or THF at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) before warming to ambient.

Oxidative degradation (strong oxidant). Potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes the aliphatic chain of heptanoic acid completely to carbon dioxide and water; the acid is neutralized to potassium carbonate while Mn(VII) is reduced to manganese dioxide. Typical conditions: excess KMnO4, reflux or heating, aqueous NaOH or KOH as base; solid MnO2 precipitates.

Ligand exchange (salt metathesis) converting rhodium(III) acetate to rhodium(III) hydroxide in basic aqueous medium. Mix Rh(OAc)₃ with excess NaOH in water at room temperature; the product precipitates as Rh(OH)₃ and sodium acetate remains in solution. No additional catalyst needed.

Esterification via acyl chloride; ethanol reacts with 2‑furancarbonyl chloride to form ethyl furan‑2‑carboxylate and HCl; similar conditions to the methanol case—dry ethanol as solvent, 0 °C to rt, and a base (pyridine, TEA) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); purpose is to convert 4‑aminosalicylic acid into its phenyl ester (phenyl 4‑aminosalicylate) for increased lipophilicity or as a prodrug; key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid with phenol, releasing water; typical conditions involve reflux with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) in anhydrous toluene or benzene, often using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate; used to generate silver oxide from silver carbonate; key transformation is breakdown of Ag₂CO₃ into CO₂ gas and solid Ag₂O; typically carried out by heating the solid at 200–300 °C in a dry tube furnace; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; BeBr₂ reacts with water to form insoluble beryllium hydroxide precipitate and free HBr in solution; performed simply by dissolving BeBr₂ in water, usually at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (double‑displacement) to exchange acetate for bromide; purpose is preparation of thallium(I) bromide; key transformation replaces the acetate anion of TlOAc with bromide from HBr, forming acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water serves as solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Redox (oxidative digestion) reaction; elemental antimony is oxidized by hot, concentrated sulfuric acid to give antimony(III) sulfate, while the acid is reduced to sulfur dioxide gas and water. Typical conditions involve refluxing antimony in >90 % H2SO4 at temperatures around 250‑300 °C, often in a sealed or well‑ventilated apparatus to capture SO2. No external catalyst is needed; sulfuric acid serves as both oxidant and solvent.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction) to afford the hydrochloride salt of fadrozole; purpose is to increase the drug’s water solubility and stability; key transformation is protonation of the basic nitrogen(s) of fadrozole by HCl, yielding fadrozole·HCl; typically carried out by dissolving fadrozole in ethanol or isopropanol and adding aqueous or gaseous HCl at room temperature; solvent is an alcohol, and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base displacement reaction between strong acid and a phosphate salt; purpose is to produce phosphoric acid and precipitate calcium sulfate (gypsum); key transformation converts Ca₃(PO₄)₂ and H₂SO₄ into H₃PO₄ and CaSO·2H₂O; usually performed in aqueous medium with heating to accelerate dissolution and precipitation; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of zinc hydroxide; aqueous ZnCl₂ is mixed with NaOH. Zn²⁺ with OH⁻ to form insoluble Zn(OH)₂, while Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give NaCl in solution. Performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Hydrolytic cleavage of a hydroxamic acid; N‑hydroxypyridine‑2‑carboxamide is treated with water (often under acidic conditions such as 1 M HCl) and heated to reflux, leading to decomposition into pyridine‑2‑carboxylic acid and hydroxylamine. The reaction proceeds via protonation of the amide carbonyl followed by water attack and fragmentation.

Transmetallation (alkyl exchange) between a metal halide and a trialkylaluminum; purpose is synthesis of trimethylantimony, an organo‑antimony reagent; key transformation swaps chloride ligands on SbCl₃ with methyl groups from AlMe₃, producing Me₃Sb and AlCl₃; conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in dry, non‑coordinating solvents such as toluene or hexane; no additional catalyst is required.

Diels‑Alder [4+2] cycloaddition; synthesis of the strained bicyclic diene norbornadiene from acetylene (dienophile) and cyclopentadiene (diene). Key transformation: formation of two new C‑C σ bonds and a new six‑membered ring. Typically carried out under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, often at elevated temperature (150‑200 °C) or under 1–10 MPa pressure; Lewis‑acid catalysts (e.g., AlCl₃, BF₃·OEt₂) can be employed to increase rate.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (acetalization); conversion of 2‑chloroacetaldehyde and excess ethanol into the gem‑diethoxy chloroacetal (2‑chloro‑1,1‑diethoxyethane) with loss of water. Key transformation: nucleophilic addition of ethanol to the carbonyl followed by dehydration to give the acetal. Performed in anhydrous ethanol or a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., toluene) with a catalytic amount of a Brønsted acid (p‑TsOH, H₂SO₄) and removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) under reflux.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of terbium(III) oxalate; heating the solid oxalate causes decarboxylation to yield terbium(III) oxide together with carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide gases. Key transformation: breakdown of oxalate ligands to CO₂ and CO while the metal is oxidized to the oxide. Conducted by heating the dry salt under air or inert atmosphere at 400–600 °C; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Transmetallation (metal exchange) between dimethylzinc and mercuric sulfate; the organozinc transfers a methyl group to Hg(II), producing dimethylmercury and zinc sulfate. Key transformation: methyl ligand migration from Zn to Hg. Carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions in aprotic ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature (0 °C to ambient) to limit side reactions; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) is essential due to the moisture sensitivity of dimethylzinc and the toxicity of dimethylmercury.

Photocatalytic hydroxylation (heterogeneous oxidation) of phenanthrene using TiO₂ and hydrogen peroxide; under UV illumination the TiO₂ generates reactive •OH radicals that hydroxylate phenrene at the 1‑position, yielding 1‑hydroxyphenanthrene and water. Key transformation: addition of an OH group to an aromatic C‑H bond via radical pathway. Conducted as a suspension of TiO₂ (P25) in aqueous/acetone mixture with H₂O₂ (typically 30 %); reaction irradiated with UV light (λ ≈ 365 nm) at ambient temperature; no additional solvents required beyond the reaction medium.

SN2 alkylation of phenyl lithium with methyl iodide; purpose: production of toluene; key transformation: methyl iodide undergoes nucleophilic substitution by the phenyl anion, giving toluene and LiI; typical conditions: dry THF or Et₂O, −78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (neutralization) reaction; aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with ammonium hydrosulfide to generate ammonia gas, water, and sodium hydrosulfide. Key transformation: proton transfer from NH₄⁺ to OH⁻ and exchange of Na⁺ with NH₄⁺. Performed in water at room temperature; the liberated NH₃ can be distilled or vented, and the solution contains NaHS. No special catalyst is needed.

Redox precipitation in aqueous solution where potassium permanganate oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ while being reduced to MnO₂; K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl and Fe³⁺ hydrolyzes to iron(III) oxide‑hydroxide (Fe(OH)₃); reaction type is redox coupled with precipitation; typically performed in neutral to slightly alkaline water at room temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Metal‑mediated deprotonation of an alcohol to form an alkoxide; purpose is to obtain a nucleophilic ethoxyethoxide ion for subsequent alkylation or elimination steps. The reaction converts the hydroxyl group into a sodium alkoxide with evolution of hydrogen gas. Typical conditions: dry ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen), and stirring at ambient temperature. No catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (ether synthesis) of ethanol and methanol to give mixed ethyl‑methyl ether and water; a strong protic acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the alcohols, followed by nucleophilic attack of one alcohol on the protonated intermediate; reaction is performed at 120–150 °C with removal of water; the acid often serves as both catalyst and solvent or is used in an inert high‑boiling solvent; the purpose is formation of a mixed ether.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between aqueous nickel(II) chloride and ammonium fluoride forming insoluble nickel(II) fluoride precipitate and soluble ammonium chloride; proceeds at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required; the key transformation is exchange of anions and cations, allowing isolation of NiF₂ by filtration.

Redox oxidation in basic solution: persulfate (S₂O₈²⁻) oxidizes selenite (SeO₃²⁻) to selenate (SeO₄²⁻) while the persulfate itself is reduced to sulfate (SO₄²⁻); sodium hydroxide provides the alkaline medium and balances the generated protons, producing water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at 50–80 °C with stirring; no additional catalyst needed.

Dehydration (condensation) reaction to form an acid anhydride; adipic acid is dehydrated by phosphorus pentoxide, a strong dehydrating agent, typically under heating (100‑150 °C) in the absence of solvent or in a high‑boiling inert solvent; water is eliminated to give adipic anhydride.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; analogous to the sodium analogue, used to generate mercury(II) cyanide from mercuric chloride using potassium cyanide; HgCl2 + KCN in water produces KCl and Hg(CN)2 precipitate; carried out in aqueous medium, often with excess KCN, at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Base‑induced isomerization (Wohl‑Hepp rearrangement) of urea with potassium hydroxide; heating KOH and urea yields potassium cyanate (KOCN) together with release of ammonia and water; performed in the solid state or in a melt of KOH at 150–200 °C; no external catalyst required; the purpose is conversion of urea to cyanate salt.

SN2 substitution with aqueous ammonia; purpose is preparation of primary amine heptan‑1‑amine. 1‑bromoheptane is mixed with excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia (often in ethanol) and heated (reflux, 70‑80 °C). The reaction forms heptan‑1‑amine and ammonium bromide; excess ammonia suppresses elimination side‑reactions.

Transesterification of tert‑butyl benzoate with methanol; purpose is to exchange the tert‑butyl alkoxy group for a methyl group, forming methyl benzoate. Methanol acts as nucleophile, displacing tert‑butanol from the carbonyl. Usually catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a base (e.g., sodium methoxide) at reflux temperature (≈65 °C) in excess methanol; removal of the volatile tert‑butanol or methanol drives the equilibrium toward product.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (Schotten‑Baumann type) of menthol with isovaleroyl chloride; triethylamine acts as an HCl scavenger, forming triethylammonium chloride and driving formation of menthyl isovalerate; reaction is typically performed in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the key transformation is nucleophilic acyl substitution of the alcohol by the acid chloride, yielding the ester and a salt by‑product.

0.‑base carboxylation of a Grignard reagent; used to prepare carboxylic acids from alkyl bromides. The organomagnesium bromide adds to CO₂ to give a magnesium carboxylate which, after acidic work‑up, yields the corresponding carboxylic acid (octanoic acid) and MgBr₂. Typically performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature, with CO₂ gas bubbled through the solution; no catalyst required.

Simple acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Basic zinc oxide reacts with hydrogen iodide acid to give soluble zinc iodide and water. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no special solvent or catalyst needed.

Chemoselective reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol using sodium borohydride; purpose is to regenerate homovanillyl alcohol. Key transformation: R‑CHO → R‑CH₂OH, with formation of sodium borate. Usually run in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, using 1–1.5 equiv NaBH₄, quenching with water after completion.

Oxidative degradation of tartaric acid by concentrated nitric acid; an oxidative cleavage that converts the dihydroxy dicarboxylic acid into oxalic acid while releasing carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide gas. Conducted by refluxing tartaric acid in excess conc. HNO₃; the reaction is vigorous and generates NO₂, so it is performed in a fume hood without added catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed carbonate formation (transesterification of CO2 with ethanol). Purpose: synthesis of potassium ethyl carbonate. Key transformation: CO₂ + CH₃CH₂OH + KOH → KOCO₂CH₂CH₃ + H₂O. Typical conditions: ethanol solvent, KOH as base, temperature 0–80 °C, CO₂ pressure 1–30 bar. No extra catalyst needed.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (metathesis). Phosphoric acid protonates acetate ions from magnesium acetate, liberating acetic acid and precipitating magnesium hydrogen phosphate (MgHPO₄). The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution, often with mild heating to drive volatile acetic acid; no catalyst is required.

Oxidation of trimethylarsine by molecular oxygen (air oxidation). Each molecule of trimethylarsine is converted to its oxide, trimethylarsine oxide, with O₂ serving as the oxidant. The transformation occurs readily at ambient temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, sometimes under gentle stirring; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of ester (hexyl formate). Water attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, producing formic acid and hexanol. The reaction is typically performed in a refluxing aqueous acid medium (e., dilute HCl) or with acid‑resin catalysis; solvent can be a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., ethanol) to improve miscibility. No metal catalyst is required.

Base‑mediated double displacement/complexation; NaOH neutralizes Zn(NO3)2, precipitating Zn(OH)2 which dissolves in excess OH‑ to give sodium zincate (Na2[Zn(OH)4]) and NaNO carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no special solvents or catalysts required.

Chlorination of a metal oxide with thionyl chloride; SOCl₂ acts as a chlorinating/reducing agent converting CuO to CuCl2 while being reduced to CO and SO2 gases; typically performed under reflux in an inert atmosphere, often neat or in a dry non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) with gentle heating.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation) of 1,3‑butadiene with Br₂ to give the (E)‑1,4‑dibromo‑2‑butene; used to functionalize conjugated dienes via 1,4‑addition; key transformation is addition of two bromine atoms across the diene ending with a double bond between C‑2 and C‑3; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, protected from light.

Nucleophilic (SN2) of an alkyl halide by hydrosulfide; HS⁻ attacks 1‑chloroethane to afford ethanethiol and NaCl; conducted in aqueous alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol) at mild temperature (0 °C to reflux) without additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization; converts insoluble chromium(III) carbonate into soluble chromium(III) perchlorate while evolving carbon dioxide and water; key transformation: Cr2(CO3)3 + 6 HClO4 → 2 Cr(ClO4)3 + 3 CO2 + 3 H2O; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

N‑methylation (alkylation) of nordazepam using methyl p‑toluenesulfonate; the tosylate transfers a methyl group to the nitrogen of nordazepam, yielding diazepam and p‑toluenesulfonic acid; performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, often with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3) at rt to 50 °C.

Metal reduction (reductive precipitation). Sodium borohydride reduces Pd(II) in disodium tetrachloropalladate to metallic palladium (palladium black). Sodium chloride precipitates, boric acid and hydrogen are generated as by‑products. Typically carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acidic dissolution of zinc phosphate with hydrochloric acid; purpose is to generate zinc chloride and phosphoric acid from the insoluble phosphate. Zn₃(PO₄)₂ is reacted with excess HCl (typically 2‑6 M) under stirring and gentle heating (30‑70 °C): Zn₃(PO₄)₂ + 6 HCl → 3 ZnCl₂ + 2 H₃PO₄. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution; the resulting zinc chloride is soluble, and phosphoric acid remains in the liquid phase. No catalyst is needed.

Reductive amination of phenylacetone with methylamine; NaBH3CN reduces the imine formed in situ to give DL‑methamphetamine usually carried out in methanol or ethanol, buffered to pH 5‑6, at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with NaBH3CN as the selective reducing agent.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; benzoyl cyanide is hydrolyzed in aqueous strong acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) under reflux, converting the –CN group to a carboxylate to afford phenylglyoxylic acid while releasing ammonia; reaction times of 2–4 h at 80–100 °C are common, and the mixture is usually worked up by neutralization and extraction.

Formation of an acyl chloride from an ammonium carboxylate using thionyl chloride; SOCl₂ converts ammonium benzoate to benzoyl chloride, producing SO2 and NH4Cl as by‑products; reaction is performed under reflux in a dry solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, often with a catalytic amount of DMF, and the gases are vented.

Combustion reaction; complete oxidation of 2,3‑dimethylbutane by molecular oxygen to CO₂ and H₂O; exothermic, used for energy release; requires sufficient O₂ and ignition source; typically carried out at high temperature in the gas phase with air or pure O₂, no solvent or catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of benzyl chloride by acetate ion to give benzyl acetate (ester formation). Sodium acetate acts as the nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or DMF) at reflux temperature. By‑product is sodium chloride. Reaction proceeds cleanly because benzyl chloride is a primary halide.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between ammonium chloride and potassium dihydrogen phosphate; exchanges anions and cations to give potassium chloride and ammonium dirogen phosphate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst, stirring is sufficient.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; lead(II) sulfate reacts with barium nitrate to form insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble lead nitrate; carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at room temperature; precipitation driven by low solubility of BaSO₄; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; dissolves zinc hydroxide to form soluble zinc chloride; Zn(OH)2 + 2 HCl → ZnCl2 + 2 H2O; performed in aqueous HCl at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst or special solvent required.

Electrophilic methylation (SN2 O‑alkylation) of 8‑hydroxypsoralen using methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate; the hydroxyl oxygen attacks the methyl group, yielding 8‑methoxypsoralen and trifluoromethanesulfonic acid; conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, typically at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed, though a base can be added to scavenge the acid.

Double‑displacement metathesis between sodium malate and calcium nitrate; exchanges ions to produce calcium malate (often less soluble) and sodium nitrate; performed in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature; precipitation of calcium malate drives the reaction; no required.

Thermal disproportionation/decomposition of arsine; two molecules of AsH₃ combine to give diarsane (As₂H₄) and molecular hydrogen; occurs upon heating, often in the presence of a metal surface or catalyst such as copper or nickel; carried out in an inert gas stream to avoid oxidation; no solvent is used.

Nitrile hydrolysis; used to convert a nitrile functional group into a carboxylic acid while releasing ammonia. The carbon‑nitrogen triple bond of methoxyacetonitrile is cleaved by water, first forming the corresponding amide and then the methoxyacetic acid. Typically performed under reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 2 M H₂SO₄) or in aqueous base (NaOH) followed by acid work‑up Common solvent is water or a water‑ethanol mixture; acid or base serves as catalyst.

Type: alkaline hydrolysis (ring opening) of a benzoxazolinone. Purpose: regenerate anthranilic acid and obtain formate as a small‑molecule by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl of the oxazolinone, cleavage of the C–N bond, release of formate (as sodium formate) and formation of anthranilic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heat to reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–4 h, often in a MeOH/H₂O mixture. Reaction is quenched with acid to isolate anthranilic acid.

Precipitation/neutralization reaction; employed to remove ferric ions from solution as an insoluble hydroxide while producing soluble sodium nitrate. Hydroxide ions deprotonate water, generating OH⁻ that reacts with Fe³⁺ to form Fe(OH)₃ precipitate, and Na⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give NaNO₃ in solution. Conducted in aqueous at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring aids complete precipitation. No special catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction of phosphorus pentoxide; high‑temperature preparation of white phosphorus (P₄) from P₂O₅ using carbon as the reducing agent. Carbon is oxidized to CO₂ while P₂O₅ is reduced, yielding elemental phosphorus vapor that condenses as white phosphorus. Reaction is carried out in a sealed furnace or retort at 800–1200 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to prevent oxidation of P₄. No solvent; solid‑state reagents only.

The transformation is an SN2 nucleophilic substitution where ammonia displaces a chloride group in 2-(chloromethyl)pyridine, yielding 2-(aminomethyl)pyridine and ammonium chloride. The reaction typically occurs in aqueous ammonia under heating or pressurized conditions to facilitate the bimolecular substitution.

Oxidative decomposition of hydrazine sulfate by hypochlorite; analytical or waste‑treatment method that converts hydrazine to nitrogen gas while reducing hypochlorite to chloride. Hydrazine (N₂H₄) is oxidized to N₂, water is formed, and the sulfate counter‑ion is liberated as sulfuric acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution at near‑neutral to mildly alkaline pH, temperature 0–25 °C, with NaOCl as oxidant; stirring ensures complete reaction. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization to form lithium succinate; preparation of the lithium salt of succinic acid for use in polymer synthesis or electrolyte applications. Two equivalents of LiOH deprotonate the dicarboxylic acid, yielding lithium succinate and two equivalents of water. Conducted in water at room temperature or gentle heating; stoichiometric amounts ensure complete conversion. No catalyst required.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction; diagnostic conversion of acetaldehyde (or methyl ketones) to iodoform (CHI₃) and a carboxylate (formate) under basic conditions. Iodine reacts with NaOH to generate I₂⁻/I₃⁻ species that halogenate the methyl group three times; subsequent base‑induced cleavage yields iodoform precipitate and sodium formate, with water as by‑product. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH at 0–25 °C, iodine added dropwise; the characteristic yellow CHI₃ crystals precipitate, indicating reaction progress. No additional catalyst.

Oxidation (peracid oxidation) of 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde to 2,5‑furandicarboxylic acid; acetic acid and H₂O₂ generate peracetic acid in situ which oxidizes the aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid, releasing water. Typical conditions: 0 – 25 °C in glacial AcOH or AcOH/H₂O mixture, stirred under ambient pressure; no additional catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis/precipitation) reaction between aqueous cadmium sulfate and barium bromide; Ba²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form insoluble BaSO precipitate, while Cd²⁺ pairs with Br⁻ to give soluble CdBr₂. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: acid‑base precipitation. Purpose: conversion of a potassium zirconate to insoluble zirconium oxide and recovery of potassium chloride. Key transformation: protonation of the zirconate anion by HCl yields ZrO2 precipitate, K⁺ combines with Cl⁻ to give KCl in solution, and water is formed. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M) added to a suspension of the zirconate at room temperature or with mild heating while stirring. No catalyst required; solvent is water.

Wittig olefination (methylene Wittig reaction) of cyclopentanone with methylenetriphenylphosphorane, converting the carbonyl to a C=C double bond to afford cyclopentene and triphenylphosphine oxide as by‑product. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent (THF or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Transesterification of dimethyl phthalate with 2‑methoxyethanol catalyzed by zinc acetate. The methoxyethyl groups replace the methyl esters, producing dimethoxyethyl phthalate and methanol as a by‑product. Typically performed under reflux in excess 2‑methoxyethanol or a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or xylene, using catalytic Zn(OAc)₂; a Dean‑Stark trap may be employed to continuously remove methanol.

Oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid using Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4). Purpose: convert hex-3-en-1-ol into hex-3-enoic acid. Key transformation: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: dilute chromic acid generated in acetone, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, aqueous sulfuric acid present.

Base‑ or lipase‑catalyzed transesterification of glycerol with oleic acid methyl ester, yielding 2‑oleoylglycerol (mono‑acylglycerol) and methanol. Typical conditions: enzymatic catalysis with immobilized lipase (e.g., Novozyme ) ‑60 °C in solvent‑free or low‑polarity solvent (toluene, hexane); alternatively, NaOH/K₂CO₃ can be used as a base catalyst.

Knoevenagel condensation of 4‑nitrobenzaldehyde with malononitrile under aqueous NaOH; the base deprotonates malononitrile, which condenses with the aldehyde, eliminating water to form 4‑nitroylidene malononitrile. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in water or water/ethanol mixture; NaOH serves as the catalyst.

Oxidative conversion of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using a Fenton‑type system; FeCl3 acts as a catalyst that activates hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals, which oxidize phenoxyethanol to phenoxyacetaldehyde while Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) and water is formed. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media at ambient temperature; common solvents include water, acetonitrile or methanol; no additional catalyst required.

This is a complexation reaction where palladium(II) acetate reacts with triphenylphosphine to form bis(triphenylphosphine)palladium(II) acetate. It is commonly used in catalysis, such as in C-C bond-forming reactions. The reaction involves coordination of triphenylphosphine to palladium(II), with acetic acid typically released as a byproduct. The reaction is often conducted in solvents like benzene or toluene under an inert atmosphere to prevent palladium degradation.

Oxidative cleavage of a terminal alkene with hot, dilute potassium permanganate; the double bond of 2‑methyl‑2‑pentene is broken to give the carbonyl compounds acetone (from the more substituted carbon) and propanoic acid (from the less substituted carbon). Conducted in aqueous solution, heated (≈60–80 °C) under dilute KMnO4; water or dilute alkaline medium is the usual solvent; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Electrophilic quench of a vinyl Grignard reagent with molecular iodine to afford the vinyl halide iodoethene. Vinylmagnesium chloride (CH2=CH‑MgCl) reacts with I2 in anhydrous ether (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, delivering CH2=CH‑I and MgClI as by‑product. No additional catalyst; the reaction is performed under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Simple double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction: aqueous sodium iodide reacts with silver carbonate, exchanging ions to form insoluble silver iodide precipitate and soluble sodium carbonate. Performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring facilitates complete precipitation; no catalyst needed.

Type: Aminolysis of an acyl chloride to a secondary amide. Purpose: Prepare N‑methylformamide, a useful building block. Key transformation: Methylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of formyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming N‑methylformamide; HCl is generated. Typical conditions: A solution of methylamine (as a gas or 2 M solution in ether) is added dropwise to a cold (0 °C) solution of formyl chloride in dry dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; the mixture is stirred, allowing HCl to be scavenged by an added base such as triethylamine if desired. The product is isolated by evaporation of solvent and removal of residual amine.

Acid‑induced decomposition of sodium percarbonate with acetic acid (acid‑base reaction). Dilute acetic acid protonates the percarbonate, yielding hydrogen peroxide, carbon dioxide and sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; the acetic acid also acts as the solvent. No catalyst required.

Acyl transfer from acetic anhydride to a thiol (thiophenol) to produce the thioester phenyl acetate (thiophenyl acetate) and acetic acid. The reaction is a nucleophilic acyl substitution; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF with a mild base such as pyridine or triethylamine at 0 °C to room temperature to scavenge the generated acid. No metal catalyst required.

High‑temperature redox reaction of metallic chromium with dry hydrogen chloride gas, reducing the acid to hydrogen gas and forming chromium(II) chloride. Conducted in a furnace or flow tube at elevated temperatures (≈400–600 °C) under a stream of H; the solid CrCl2 is collected, and H2 is evolved. No solvent; reaction proceeds via direct metal–acid interaction.

Salt hydrolysis; generation of hypochlorous acid. Calcium hypochlorite dissolves in water, hydrolyzing to produce two equivalents of HOCl and calcium hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required. Used to obtain a bleaching/disinfecting HOCl solution.

Acid–base neutralization; the strong base NaOH neutralizes hexafluoroantimonyic acid to give water and the inorganic salt sodium hexafluoroantimonate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Redox metal–acid reaction; elemental lutetium is oxidized by acetic acid while the acid is reduced, producing hydrogen gas and lutetium(III) acetate. Conducted by refluxing lutetium metal in excess glacial acetic acid, often under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation by air.

Free‑radical halogenation; chlorine undergoes homolytic cleavage (initiated by UV light or heat) to replace a hydrogen atom of heptane, yielding 3‑chloroheptane and hydrogen chloride as a side product. Reaction is carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, under UV irradiation or at elevated temperature.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose: formation of a neutral salt (potassium sulfate) from strong acid and base; key transformation: proton transfer from H₂SO₄ to OH⁻ producing water and K₂SO₄; typical conditions: aqueous medium, controlled addition to manage exotherm; common solvent: water.

Single‑displacement (metal‑water) reaction; calcium metal reacts with water producing calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas; vigorous reaction often performed with finely divided calcium at room temperature or slightly heated; aqueous medium only, no added catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of an aryl chloride; converts 3‑chloro‑indole to indole with release of HCl; utilized to remove halogen atoms from heteroaromatic compounds; typical setup: Pd/C (10 % w/w) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in ethanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to 50 °C, reaction time 1–3 h.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); nitroacetyl chloride reacts with methylamine to give N‑methyl‑2‑nitroacetamide, with loss of HCl. Usually performed in a non‑protic solvent like dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, using a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamoylation) to synthesize the herbicide isoproturon; N,N‑dimethylcarbamoyl chloride acylates 4‑isopropylaniline, releasing HCl. The reaction is typically run in an aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to 25 °C with a tertiary amine base such as triethylamine or pyridine to neutralize HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis/cleavage of a vinyl ether; methyl vinyl ether reacts with water in the presence of sulfuric acid to yield acetaldehyde and methanol. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute H₂SO₄) at room temperature or with gentle heating; no additional catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Oxative of copper(II) oxalate by hydrogen peroxide producing copper(II) oxide, carbon dioxide and water; reaction type is redox decomposition used to prepare CuO; key transformation is peroxide oxidation of oxalate to CO₂ while peroxide is reduced to H₂O, leaving Cu²⁺ as CuO solid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at 50‑80 °C with stirring; no additional catalyst is required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; chloric acid is reduced to chlorine dioxide while hydrogen peroxide is oxidized to water and oxygen; carried out in cold dilute aqueous acid, slow addition of H2O2 to an ice‑bath solution of HClO3 to control gas evolution.

Acylation (amide formation) of an amino acid; acetyl chloride acylates the amine of DL‑leucine, with pyridine acting as base and HCl scavenger, yielding N‑acetyl‑DL‑leucine and pyridinium chloride; performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Nucleophilic (SN2) alkylation; cyanide ion displaces bromide on 3‑bromopropylamine to give 4‑aminobutyronitrile and sodium bromide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO) at 50–80 °C, often with a phase‑transfer catalyst to improve yield.

Esterification (formation of butamirate); the carboxylic acid 2‑phenylbutanoic acid condenses with the tertiary alcohol 2‑(dimethylamino)-2‑methyl‑1‑propanol, eliminating water to afford the ester butamirate; typical conditions use an acid catalyst (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or coupling reagent (DCC) in toluene or dichloromethane, with removal of water by azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark trap.

Transesterification; exchanges the alkoxy group of methyl furan‑2‑carboxylate with allyl alcohol to give allyl furan‑2‑carboxylate and methanol. Typically performed under reflux in anhydrous solvent (toluene, THF) with a catalytic amount of acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe); removal of methanol drives the equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a long‑chain fatty acid to the corresponding primary alcohol; the carboxyl group is reduced to a hydroxymethyl group while water is formed; typically carried out under high pressure hydrogen (50–100 bar) at 120–200 °C in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Raney nickel, Pd/C, or Cu–Cr‑oxide; solvents like isopropanol, ethanol, or water are employed to dissolve the substrate and transfer hydrogen; the reaction provides fatty alcohols for surfactant and polymer applications.

LiAlH₄ reduction of alkyl chloride; purpose is to replace the chloride with hydrogen, giving the alkane; key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbon bearing Cl, displacing Cl⁻ and forming octane; typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), LiAlH₄ (1.5–2 eq), reflux under nitrogen; by‑products LiCl and AlCl₃ are generated and are removed during aqueous quench.

Sulfide precipitation/decomposition; thioacetamide supplies sulfide that reacts with zinc acetate to precipitate ZnS while the acetate is protonated to acetic acid and the thioacetamide is converted to acetamide. Conducted in aqueous solution, often heated (80–100 °C); the solid ZnS is isolated by filtration.

Double displacement acid‑base reaction; hydrochloric acid converts praseodymium(III) acetate to praseodymium(III) chloride and releases acetic acid. Performed in water at ambient conditions; no catalyst required.

Gas‑phase redox oxidation; carbon monoxide is oxidized by oxygen difluoride to carbonyl fluoride (COF₂) while OF₂ is reduced to molecular oxygen. Requires high‑temperature, inert‑gas conditions (typically >300 °C) in a flow reactor; no solvent is used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis; water attacks 2‑fluoroethyl bromide, displacing bromide to form 2‑fluoroethanol and hydrobromic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or KOH) at reflux temperature, then acidified to liberate HBr if needed.

Acidic nitrile hydrolysis; converts 3,5‑dimethylbenzonitrile to 3,5‑dimethylbenzoic acid; reflux in concentrated aqueous HCl (often 6 M) for several hours; water is the solvent; ammonium chloride formed as the accompanying salt.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of alkyl halide; water attacks cyclopentylmethyl iodide, yielding cyclopentylmethanol and hydroiodic acid. Typically done in aqueous NaOH or under reflux in water; the reaction mixture is acidified to isolate the alcohol and HI.

Quaternary ammonium formation via nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – the tertiary amine N,N-dimethylallylamine attacks allyl chloride, displacing chloride and yielding diallyldimethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: excess allyl chloride, polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or acetone), reflux or ambient temperature, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Esterification (acyl substitution) with ethanol; produces ethyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate; Cl is replaced by OEt, generating HCl; performed by adding the acid chloride dropwise to dry ethanol at 0‑25 °C, employing a tertiary amine base such pyridine or triethylamine (1 equiv) to trap HCl; solvent is ethanol (or ethanol/THF); reaction typically completed within minutes to an hour.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a phosphoric acid ester – aqueous NaOH cleaves the P–O‑phenyl bond of dimethyl phenyl phosphate, producing sodium phenoxide and sodium dimethyl phosphate. Conducted in water or water/ethanol mixture, often at 50‑80 °C; reaction proceeds to completion with stirring.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; water attacks the methyl ester of 5‑methoxy‑5‑oxopentanoic acid to give pentanedioic acid (glutaric acid) and methanol; cleavage of the C‑O methyl bond; usually heated in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) at reflux; solvent = water or water/acetone mixture, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the diacid.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution to form a carbonate – phenol attacks phenyl chloroformate, displacing chloride as HCl and generating diphenyl carbonate. Reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or tetrahydrofuran at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the liberated HCl.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) – silver sulfite reacts with hydrochloric acid, precipitating insoluble silver chloride and forming sulfurous acid (H₂SO₃) in solution. Performed in aqueous medium at low temperature (0‑25 °C) to maximize AgCl precipitation; no special catalyst required.

Ester hydrolysis; aqueous hydrolysis of 2-(2‑hydroxyethoxy)ethyl acetate to yield diethylene glycol and acetic acid; typically performed under reflux in water with either dilute acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH) followed by acid work‑up; water is the solvent and the acid or base acts as catalyst.

Catalytic partial oxidation (selective oxidation) of a saturated hydrocarbon; butane is oxidized by oxygen to the ketone 2‑butanone with water as a by‑product; conducted in the gas phase at 300‑500 °C over metal‑oxide catalysts such as V₂O₅, MoO₃, or Cu‑based systems, sometimes with a steam diluent; no stoichiometric reagents other than O₂.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of chloride by cyanide – potassium cyanide displaces chloride of chloroacetic acid, giving cyanoacetic acid and potassium chloride. Conducted in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution, typically at 20‑60 °C, under basic conditions to keep CN⁻ available; excess KCN often used to drive the reaction.

Thermal decarboxylation of a β‑keto acid – 3‑oxopropanoic acid loses CO₂ upon heating, forming acetaldehyde. Reaction proceeds upon gentle heating (80‑150 °C) in inert solvent (e.g., toluene) or solvent‑free; sometimes acid or metal catalyst (e.g., copper) is employed to lower the decarboxylation temperature.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (alkene formation). Nonane is heated to 500–600 °C in the presence of a metal oxide or supported metal catalyst (e.g., Pt/Al₂O₃, Cr₂O₃, or Pd‑based catalysts), effecting removal of H₂ to form the terminal alkene non‑1‑ene. No solvent; reaction is carried out in the gas phase, sometimes with a carrier gas (N₂ or H₂) to control partial pressures.

Enolate alkylation (Williamson‑type C‑methylation). Potassium tert‑butoxide deprotonates dihydrotestosterone to form an enolate, which then attacks methyl triflate, a potent methylating agent, to install a methyl group and afford mesterolone. This transformation is used in the synthesis of anabolic steroids. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); the reaction is quenched with water after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) via Williamson ether synthesis. Purpose: Preparing ethers using bulky alkoxides. Transformation: tert-Butoxide attacks methyl iodide to form methyl tert-butyl ether. Conditions: Typically in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMSO).

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 methylation) of 1,2,4‑trihydroxybenzene; three phenolic hydroxyls are deprotonated by K₂CO₃ and alkylated with methyl iodide to give 1,2,4trimethoxybenzene, with KI as by‑product. Reaction is run in dry acetone or DMF under reflux (50‑80 °C) under nitrogen; excess K₂CO₃ serves as base and scavenges HI.

Complexation/acid dissolution of goethite with citric acid; used to produce soluble ferric citrate complexes for analytical or plating purposes. FeO(OH) reacts with citric acid, water is formed and Fe³⁺ is chelated by citrate anions (Fe(C₆H₅O₇)⁻). Reaction performed in water or dilute aqueous citric acid, often heated (50‑70 °C) to ensure complete complexation.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of urea; purpose is to produce isocyanic acid and ammonia as volatiles; key transformation: cleavage of the C–N bond in urea releasing NH3 and generating HNCO; typical conditions: heating solid urea to 150–200 °C under reduced pressure or in a stream of inert gas; no solvent; reaction often performed in sealed tube or flow reactor.

Fischer esterification of trichloroacetic acid with methanol to give methyl trichloroacetate; acid‑catalyzed condensation in which the carboxylic acid reacts with methanol and water is eliminated; typically performed by refluxing methanol (or methanol‑water mixture) with excess trichloroacetic acid, often using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; no external catalyst is required because the substrate is sufficiently acidic; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

High‑temperature redox (fluorination) reaction where elemental fluorine oxidizes barium oxide; fluorine is reduced to fluoride and barium oxide is oxidized to molecular oxygen, producing barium fluoride; carried out in a dry tube furnace at several hundred °C; no solvent; inert atmosphere aside from fluorine gas.

Catalytic hydrogenation (hydrogenolysis) of an alkyl azide; 3‑(azidomethyl)pyridine is reduced by H2 over Pd/C to the corresponding primary amine. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 5 % Pd/C (10–20 wt % loading), solvent such as EtOH or MeOH, temperature 25–40 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – Williamson ether synthesis. Methanol acts as the nucleophile, displacing chloride from benzyl chloride to give benzyl methyl ether, with liberation of hydrogen chloride. The reaction is employed to prepare benzylic ethers as protecting groups or intermediates. Conducted in excess methanol as solvent, often with a mild base (e.g., potassium carbonate) to scavenge HCl; temperatures range from reflux to 80 °C.

Two‑step conversion of 3‑aminobenzoic acid to 3‑aminobenzamide via an acid‑chloride intermediate; first, thionyl chloride reacts with the carboxylic acid to give the corresponding acid chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl (often in dry dichloromethane or toluene under reflux); second, the freshly formed acid chloride is treated with excess ammonia (aq. or gaseous) at 0–5 °C to give the amide, 3‑aminobenzamide; anhydrous conditions are required for the first step, then the reaction in aqueous ammonia yields the product.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation where ammonium oxalate reacts with calcium bromide; calcium oxalate precipitates out of solution while ammonium bromide remains soluble; performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature with stirring, then filtering and washing the insoluble calcium oxalate; no catalyst is needed.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between antimony trichloride and hydrofluoric acid; replaces chloride ligands with fluoride to give antimony trifluoride (SbF3) and releases hydrochloric acid gas; key transformation is ligand exchange driven by strong Sb‑F bond formation; performed at room temperature to 50 °C in aqueous or anhydrous HF; no catalyst; HCl is removed as gas.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction. Fluorine gas oxidizes metallic thallium to thallium(I) fluoride (TlF). It is a redox process, highly exothermic, usually performed in a dry, inert‑gas (N2 or Ar) environment at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control heat release. No solvent is required; the solid metal is exposed to a controlled flow of F2 in a fluorination apparatus.

Amide‑formation (condensation) using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI). Acetic acid is activated by CDI to form an imidazolide intermediate, which then reacts with the phenolic amine of 3‑aminophenol to give 3‑hydroxyacetanilide (an acetanilide derivative) and imidazole as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, THF, or DMF), 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; reaction time 1–12 h. No additional catalysts are needed.

Reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol with lithium aluminium hydride. 3‑Hexanone is reduced to 3‑hexanol via hydride transfer. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N2), at 0 °C initially then allowed to warm to rt or reflux. Excess LiAlH4 is quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of dimethylamine by ethyl methanesulfonate. The amine attacks the primary carbon of the sulfonate, yielding N,N‑dimethylethylamine and methanesulfonic acid (often retained as its conjugate base). Reaction is performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at rt to 40 °C. Excess amine or a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) is used to trap the acid and drive the reaction to completion.

Fluorination/acid‑base reaction converting alumina to aluminum fluoride using ammonium bifluoride; NH₄HF₂ supplies HF which attacks Al₂O₃, replacing oxide with fluoride to form AlF₃ while releasing NH₃ and H₂O; used to produce AlF₃ for ceramics or cryolite production; typically carried out in aqueous solution at 80‑120 °C under vigorous stirring, with excess bifluoride to ensure complete conversion; no external catalyst is needed.

Metal‑acid redox reaction; yttrium metal reacts with hydrochloric acid to afford yttrium(III) chloride and hydrogen gas; usually conducted in dilute HCl aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating.

Oxidative acid digestion of gallium(III) sulfide with nitric acid. Ga₂S₃ reacts with hot concentrated HNO₃, oxidizing sulfide to sulfur dioxide, producing water, and forming soluble gallium(III) nitrate. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous nitric acid (6–12 M) for 1–3 h; the reaction is exothermic and evolves SO₂ gas. The resulting solution is filtered to isolate the nitrate salt upon cooling.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion) of 2‑butanone oxime to 2‑butanamine. Molecular hydrogen reduces the oxime over palladium on carbon, cleaving the N‑O bond and yielding the primary amine plus water. Conducted in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) –80 °C; catalyst loading typically 5–10 wt % Pd/C. Reaction time ranges from  h to overnight depending on scale.

Halogenation/oxidative salt metathesis; used to convert magnesium antimonide to antimony tribromide and magnesium bromide; bromine oxidizes Sb³⁻ to SbBr₃ while Mg²⁺ forms MgBr₂; typically performed as a solid‑state reaction by heating the mixture to 200‑300 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Iron/HCl reduction (Bechamp reduction) of a nitroaromatic to an aniline; reduces the nitro group of 4‑nitro‑2‑methylaniline to a diamine while iron is oxidized to Fe³⁺; carried out in aqueous HCl with iron powder, refluxing at 80‑100 °C; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is needed.

N‑Methylation (SN2 alkylation) of a lactam nitrogen; the nitrogen of 4‑piperidone attacks methyl iodide to give N‑methyl‑4‑piperidone and HI; performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃) at 0‑50 °C to scavenge the generated HI; no metal catalyst is used.

Base‑mediated deprotonation of a phenolic ester; sodium hydride abstracts the phenolic proton of methylparaben in anhydrous THF, producing sodium methylparaben and hydrogen gas; reaction is run at 0 °C then allowed to warm to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: electrophilic aromatic substitution (para‑bromination of anisole). Purpose: synthesize 4‑bromoanisole, a useful building block. Key transformation: Br+ from the tribromide adds to the para position of the anisole ring, displacing a proton and yielding the brominated product while converting the tribromide to tetrabutylammonium bromide. Typical conditions: anisole is dissolved in dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, cooled to 0 °C, then tetrabutylammonium tribromide is added portionwise; the reaction proceeds at rt, often with a mild inorganic base (Na2CO3) to scavenge HBr.

Acyl‑chloride amidation; 4‑chlorobenzoyl chloride reacts with 3‑(4‑morpholinyl)propylamine to form the corresponding benzamide, releasing HCl; carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl, typically at 0 °C to rt; no metal catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2); sodium ethoxide attacks allyl bromide, displacing bromide to give allyl ethyl ether; performed in anhydrous ethanol or THF under reflux with a stoichiometric amount of sodium ethoxide; no additional catalyst is required.

Type: acid–carbonate reaction; purpose: to generate samarium fluoride and evolve CO₂, useful for preparing the fluoride salt; key transformation: samarium carbonate is protonated by hydrofluoric acid, yielding samarium fluoride, carbon dioxide, and water; typical conditions: dilute HF solution at room temperature or slight heating; solvent: aqueous HF; no catalyst required.

Acid‑induced decomposition of sodium thiosulfate: acetic acid protonates thiosulfate leading to breakdown into sulfur dioxide, elemental sulfur, water and formation of sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required.

Condensation of benzaldehyde with hydrazine to form (E)‑benzylidenehydrazine (a hydrazone); imine formation with loss of water; carried out in ethanol or methanol at room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., acetic acid) to promote dehydration.

Base‑promoted decomposition/neutralization of ammonium nitrite: barium hydroxide neutralizes ammonium ions producing ammonia and water while the nitrite remains as barium nitrite. Carried out in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Chlorination (halogenation) of terbium phosphide; produces terbium chloride and phosphorus trichloride. Chlorine gas attacks the Tb–P bonds, yielding TbCl₃ (solid) and volatile PCl₃. Reaction carried out at 300‑600 °C in a sealed tube or flow reactor under dry Cl₂; no solvent; inert atmosphere not required because Cl₂ is both reactant and carrier.

Oxidative decomposition (thermal oxidation); solid mercury(II) selenide is oxidized by oxygen to give mercury(II) oxide and volatile selenium dioxide; carried out at elevated temperatures (typically 400–600 °C) in a furnace with a flow of dry air or O₂; no solvent or catalyst required; provides a route to separate mercury and selenium oxides.
Simple acid‑base neutralization: lithium hydroxide reacts with ammonium nitrate to give ammonia gas, water and lithium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature; no catalyst.

Carbon‑dioxide‑evolving neutralization: difluoroacetic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ and water and forming sodium difluoroacetate. Performed in water, mild heating may accelerate gas evolution; no catalyst.

Oxidative coupling of diphenylhydrazine to azoxybenzene: molecular oxygen oxidizes diphenylhydrazine, removing hydrogen to afford azoxybenzene and water. Typically carried out in an organic solvent such as ethanol or acetonitrile under reflux with a metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl₂ or Fe(NO₃)₃); basic conditions may be employed.

Hydride reduction of 4‑chlorobutanal to 4‑chlorobutanol: lithium aluminium hydride delivers hydride to the aldehyde carbon, converting it into the primary alcohol. Reaction is performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation (partial reduction). Purpose: saturate the pyridine ring to give tetrahydroquinoline, a useful intermediate. Key transformation: addition of four equivalents of H₂ across the quinoline ring, reducing it to a tetrahydro derivative; no further functional groups are altered. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1‑5 atm, catalyst Pd/C (10 % wt) or Raney Ni, solvent ethanol or methanol, 25‑80 °C, 3‑6 h.

Esterification via diazomethane methylation; used to convert a carboxylic acid into its methyl ester while releasing nitrogen gas. The carboxylate anion attacks the electrophilic carbon of diazomethane, displacing N₂ and forming the ester. Typically performed in dry ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under an inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

SN2 alkylation (Williamson‑type ester synthesis). Acetate anion from potassium acetate attacks ethyl bromide, displacing bromide to afford ethyl acetate and potassium bromide. Conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often under reflux; the potassium bromide precipitates and is filtered off, leaving the ester in the solution.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) of benzoyl chloride by the amine; purpose is to protect the amine as N‑(3‑chloropropyl)benzamide; key transformation ClCH2CH2CH2NH2 + PhCOCl → PhCONHCH2CH2CH2Cl + HCl; typically performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl; no metal catalyst needed.

Lucas-type chlorination of an alcohol; converts isobutanol to the corresponding primary alkyl chloride (isobutyl chloride) with loss of water. Concentrated HCl protonates the hydroxyl group, and ZnCl₂ acts as a Lewis acid to facilitate nucleophilic substitution by chloride. Reaction is usually carried out at ambient temperature or with gentle reflux in aqueous medium; ZnCl₂ is the key additive.

Halogenation of an alcohol with phosphorus pentabromide; primary alcohol is transformed into a bromide (bromoethane) while generating hydrogen bromide and phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃) as by‑products. The PBr₅ activates the hydroxyl group, allowing bromide ion to displace it in an SN2 fashion. Conducted in anhydrous, aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Alkylation of a secondary amine; methyl iodide alkylates N‑methylisopropylamine to give N,N‑dimethylisopropylamine and hydrogen iodide. The amine nitrogen performs an SN2 attack on the methyl carbon, displacing iodide. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or acetonitrile) at reflux, often with an excess of the amine or with a base (such as NaHCO₃) to neutralize the generated HI.

NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; 2‑hexanone is reduced to the secondary alcohol 2‑hexanol by hydride delivery. Sodium borohydride supplies a nucleophilic hydride that adds to the carbonyl carbon, followed by protonation of the alkoxide. Reaction is carried out in methanol, ethanol, or a mixture of THF/water at 0 °C to room temperature; work‑up involves aqueous quench and neutralization.

Bamberger rearrangement (acid‑catalyzed); phenylhydroxylamine undergoes a para‑selective rearrangement in aqueous HCl to afford para‑aminophenol. Protonation of the N‑OH group initiates migration of the aromatic ring, leading to the para‑amino phenol after deprotonation. Conduct in aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically heated to 50–100 °C; no additional catalyst is required.

Transmetallation (halide exchange) between phenylmercuric bromide and copper(I) acetate producing copper(I) bromide and phenylmercuric acetate; typically performed in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid–base double displacement where sulfuric acid reacts with barium silicate to give soluble silicic acid and precipitate barium sulfate; carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating to complete precipitation.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification) of 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol with acetic acid using DCC, forming 4‑methoxybenzyl acetate and dicyclohexylurea; usually run in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with catalytic DMAP.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose is to neutralize a strong acid with a strong base to form a soluble salt; aqueous HCl reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide, yielding potassium chloride and water; typically carried out at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; no catalyst required.
