Acid‑base protonation (salt hydrolysis) of sodium catecholate with aqueous HCl; the catecholate anion is protonated to free catechol while sodium chloride forms. Typically carried out in dilute aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C; no special catalyst or organic solvent required.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of 2‑naphthol to 2‑hydroxy‑1,4‑naphthoquinone (juglone) using sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid. The acidic medium activates dichromate as an oxidant, effecting dehydrogenation to the quinone. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈1–2 M) with Na₂Cr₂O₇ at reflux (60–100 °C); common work‑up involves neutralization and extraction with an organic solvent such as dichloromethane.

Acid‑base neutralization; lithium hydroxide reacts with HBF₄ to afford LiBF₄ and water. Conducted in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature; straightforward stoichiometric reaction without catalyst.

Silyl‑ester formation (silylation) of benzoic acid with triethylsilyl chloride, using pyridine as a base. The reaction converts the carboxylic acid to triethylsilyl benzoate, generating pyridinium chloride as the only by‑product. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Chlorination of phenol with thionyl chloride; phenol is converted to chlorobenzene while thionyl chloride is reduced to sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride; reaction proceeds via formation of a phenyl chlorosulfite intermediate; usually performed under reflux in anhydrous pyridine or a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine acts as solvent and HCl scavenger); temperature 50‑80 °C; pyridine is essential to neutralize HCl.

Radical fluorination (halogen substitution). Elemental fluorine replaces the remaining hydrogen of pentafluoroethane to give perfluoroethane, with formation of hydrogen fluoride as a by‑product. Typically carried out in the gas phase at elevated temperature (300–500 °C) or under photochemical initiation; no solvent is used, and the reaction is highly exothermic and requires careful control and corrosion‑resistant equipment.

Nucleophilic substitution (transmetalation) of trimethyltin chloride with ethyl‑Li. Conducted in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere, yielding ethyltrimethylstannane and lithium chloride.

Thermal decarboxylation; 5‑methyl‑1H‑pyrazole‑3‑carboxylic acid loses CO₂ to give 5‑methyl‑1H‑pyrazole. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–C bond adjacent to the carboxyl group. Typical conditions: heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 150–200 °C for 1–3 h, sometimes with a catalytic amount of CuI or NaOAc to lower temperature. No reagents other than heat are required.

Selenium‑catalysed oxidative dehydrogenation (allylic oxidation). Phenylacetone is oxidised by tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) in the presence of catalytic SeO₂ to introduce a double bond between the α‑ and β‑carbons, yielding 1‑phenyl‑2‑propen‑1‑one (phenyl‑vinyl‑ketone). The reaction is usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, under reflux (room temperature to 60 °C) with a catalytic amount of SeO₂ (≈5 mol %). TBHP is used in stoichiometric excess as the terminal oxidant.

Hydrolysis of a silyl halide. Trimethylsilyl iodide reacts with water, cleaving the Si–I bond to give trimethylsilanol and hydrogen iodide. Usually carried out at ambient temperature with aqueous work‑up; no special solvent needed beyond the water phase.

Solid‑state redox metathesis. Aluminum metal reduces rhenium(V) chloride (ReCl₅) to rhenium(IV) chloride (ReCl₄) while being oxidised itself to aluminium chloride (AlCl₃). The reaction proceeds without solvent under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar elevated (≈300–400 °C) to promote diffusion of the solid reagents. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalysed transesterification. Ethyl acetate exchanges its ethoxy group with 1‑propanol, producing propyl acetate and ethanol. The equilibrium can be driven toward products by using excess 1‑propanol or by removing ethanol as it forms. Common conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, xylene) with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., 1–2 % H₂SO₄) or a base (e.g., NaOEt). Reaction times range from 1 to several hours depending on temperature (80–110 °C).

Acid–base neutralisation/complex formation. Citric acid protonates the hydroxide ligands of ferric hydroxide, generating water and the soluble ferric citrate complex. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the mixture is stirred until the solid dissolves completely. No external catalyst is needed; pH adjustment may be required to keep iron in solution.

Acid‑base complexation of zinc oxide with benzene‑1,2‑diol to give zinc catecholate and water. Performed by refluxing ZnO with catechol in ethanol (or other polar protic solvent); the basic oxide deprotonates the diol, forming the chelate and releasing H2O, often driven to completion by removal of water.

High‑temperature steam oxidation (metal‑steam reaction). Zinc metal reacts with water vapor form zinc oxide and release hydrogen gas. Conducted in a furnace or tubular reactor at temperatures above the zinc melting point (≈300–500 °C) under a flow of steam. No solvent or catalyst is used; the reaction is driven by heat and the continuous removal of hydrogen.

Acid–base reaction and isomerization (Wöhler synthesis); furnishes urea from ammonium sulfate and potassium cyanate; the salts generate ammonium cyanate in water which converts to urea, leaving potassium sulfate; carried out in aqueous medium, heated gently, no catalyst needed.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); used to convert 4‑chlorobutanoic acid into the corresponding ethyl ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol oxygen on the protonated carboxyl carbon followed by loss of water; typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of a strong acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; excess ethanol or a Dean–Stark trap is used to drive the equilibrium; common solvents are toluene or the alcohol itself.

Reduction of hexachloroplatinic acid (H₂PtCl₆) by synthesis gas; purpose is to precipitate metallic platinum and regenerate HCl; CO is oxidized to CO₂ and H₂ is oxidized to HCl while Pt(IV) is reduced to Pt(0); usually carried out in aqueous solution at 50–100 °C under a flow of CO/H₂ (often 1:1) gas mixture; no additional catalyst is required beyond the Pt salt; reaction is performed in a pressure‑resistant reactor.

Alkaline hydrolysis (nitrile hydrolysis) of benzonitrile; converts the nitrile to the benzoate salt with release of ammonia; key steps are nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the nitrile carbon, formation of an imidate intermediate, and subsequent hydrolysis to the carboxylate; generally refluxed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) for several hours; optionally a co‑solvent such as ethanol or methanol can be used to improve solubility.

Salt metathesis (halide exchange) between lithium chloride and sodium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (NaHMDS); produces lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (LiHMDS) and sodium chloride; performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is driven to completion by the low solubility of NaCl which precipitates and can be filtered off; no additional reagents are required.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation. Hydrogen sulfide gas is bubbled into an aqueous solution of cadmium nitrate, precipitating cadmium sulfide while forming nitric acid in solution. Conducted at room temperature under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of H₂S; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type SN2 substitution); purpose is to substitute chloride with iodide on a fluorochloromethane substrate. Key transformation: Cl⁻ is displaced by I⁻, giving fluoro(iodo)methane (CH2FI) and NaCl (CH2FCl + NaI → CH2FI + NaCl). Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, reflux, excess NaI; NaCl precipitates, driving the reaction forward; no catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation of thiourea (double SN2 substitution) with methyl iodide; yields N,N′‑dimethylthiourea and hydrogen iodide as by‑; nitrogen of thiourea attacks a methyl iodide molecule, displacing I⁻; typically carried out in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is often added to neutralize the formed HI; reaction time is 2–6 h depending on temperature.

Oxidation of 4‑methylpyridine to its N‑oxide using meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA); m‑CPBA is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid while the pyridine nitrogen is oxidized; reaction is a classic N‑oxide formation; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane; the mixture is stirred until consumption of m‑CPBA (typically 1–2 h), then work‑up removes the acid by washing with aqueous sodium bicarbonate.

Acid chloride formation via phosphorus pentachloride; used to convert 3‑methylbenzoic acid into 3‑methylbenzoyl chloride for further acylation; replaces the carboxyl OH with Cl, generating HCl and POCl₃ as by‑products; performed under anhydrous conditions, typically 0 °C to room temperature then reflux in dry dichloromethane, chloroform or carbon tetrachloride.

Simple double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; employed to prepare ammonium metaborate from inexpensive salts; exchanges K⁺ and NH₄⁺ ions to give potassium chloride and ammonium metaborate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required, product isolated by crystall or filtration.
Acid–base neutralization; cerium(III) hydroxide reacts with aqueous nitric acid to produce cerium(III) nitrate and water; performed in water, usually at room temperature with dilute HNO3.

Electrophilic epoxidation using dimethyl dioxirane; provides styrene oxide from styrene; transfers one oxygen atom from the dioxirane to the C=C bond, reducing the dioxirane to acetone; conducted at –20 °C to 0 °C in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, often with dimethyl dioxirane generated in situ from acetone and oxone; no additional catalyst needed.

Enzymatic methyl‑transfer reaction mediated by S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM); methylates daidzein to form glycitein, a natural isoflavone; SAM donates a methyl group to the aromatic substrate, yielding S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) with a specific O‑ or C‑methyltransferase enzyme, optionally Mg²⁺, at ~30 °C; no synthetic catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of sodium ethylxanthate; decomposes the xanthate to release ethylene, carbon disulfide and sodium sulfide; C–S bond cleavage furnishes gases and Na₂S solid; heated to 200‑300 °C under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of cobalt(II) oxalate; yields cobalt(II) oxide while evolving carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide; decarboxylation of the oxalate anion produces CO₂, CO and solid CoO; carried out by heating to 300‑500 °C in a furnace, either in air or under inert gas; no catalyst needed.

Condensation (Schiff‑base formation) of a ketone with thiosemicarbazide producing a thiosemicarbazone; used to generate chelating ligands or detect carbonyl groups. Key transformation: carbonyl C=O → C=N‑NHC(S)NH₂ with loss of water. Typically refluxed in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid; reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere.

Salt formation (acid–base neutralization) between morpholine (a secondary amine) and salicylic acid, yielding morpholine salicylate. The reaction is typically carried out in ethanol or aqueous ethanol, mild heating may be applied to ensure dissolution; no external catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (addition of H₂ across a C=C double bond). Purpose: converts the terminal alkene 3‑methylhept‑1‑ene to the saturated alkane 3‑methylheptane. Key transformation: C=C → C–C, adding two hydrogen atoms. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in an inert solvent (ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate) at 25–100 °C.

Williamson ether synthesis; alkylation of phenoxide with methyl chloride to give methyl phenyl ether (anisole); SN2 attack on primary halide; typically performed in dry acetone or DMF under reflux; sodium chloride precipitates as by‑product.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of the two benzylic chloride groups by azide ion, converting 3,3‑bis(chloromethyl)oxetane to 3,3‑bis(azidomethyl)oxetane. Useful for installing azide handles for click chemistry. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or NMP) with excess NaN₃, typically 50–80 °C under nitrogen; reaction is complete within several hours.

Fischer esterification of 1‑adamantyl alcohol with acetic acid, catalyzed by concentrated sulfuric acid, yielding 1‑adamantyl acetate and water. Purpose is to protect the hydroxyl group as an acetate ester. Performed by refluxing the alcohol in excess glacial acetic acid with a few drops of H₂SO₄, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium to products.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation reaction where ammonium hydroxide neutralizes gadolinium(III) nitrate, forming insoluble gadolinium trihydroxide and soluble ammonium nitrate (Gd(NO₃)₃ + 3 NH₄OH → Gd(OH)₃↓ + 3 NH₄NO₃). Used to isolate Gd(OH)₃ as a precursor for other Gd salts. Reaction is carried out at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed, while the ammonium nitrate remains in solution.

Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent: cyclopentylmagnesium chloride reacts with carbon dioxide to give the magnesium cyclopentanecarboxylate, which on acidic work‑up furnishes cyclopentanecarboxylic acid. A classic method to extend carbon chains by one carbon. Conducted in dry ether or THF at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under an atmosphere of CO₂ (dry ice or gas), followed by quenching with dilute HCl or NH₄Cl to liberate the free acid.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); purpose is introducing a nitro group, typically using H2SO4 and HNO3 as reagents; key transformation is nitro group attachment to the aromatic ring at the ortho position relative to bromine; reaction conditions include strong acid and heat; sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst and dehydrating agent.

Ammonolysis; purpose is converting an ester to an amide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack by ammonia on the ester carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release methanol; conditions often involve heating; common solvents include methanol or ethanol.

Diazotization of anthranilic acid with NaNO2/HCl followed by decarboxylative loss of CO2 and N2 to generate benzyne; reaction proceeds in cold aqueous acid to form the diazonium salt, then warming induces loss of N2/CO2 to give the reactive benzyne intermediate; commonly carried out in water with HCl as acid, no external catalyst.

Decomposition; purpose is releasing nitrogen gas (used in airbag systems); key transformation is thermal breakdown of lithium azide to metallic lithium and N2; conditions involve heat or shock; no solvent required.

Oxidative cleavage; purpose is converting a conjugated diene to a dicarboxylic acid derivative (mesaconic acid); key transformation is diol intermediate formation followed by cleavage by KMnO4 in basic conditions; reaction conditions involve aqueous KMnO4 and heat; potassium hydroxide and MnO2 are byproducts.

Type: Condensation (amidation) of a carboxylic acid with a primary amine; purpose: synthesize N‑methylpropanamide. Key transformation: conversion of the acid carbonyl into an amide bond with loss of water. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑protic solvent (toluene or benzene) with azeotropic removal of water or use of coupling reagents (DCC, EDC) and a base such as triethylamine; catalyst not required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne to an alkane; acetylenedicarboxylic acid is reduced by H₂ to succinic acid, saturating the carbon–carbon triple bond. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in ethanol, methanol or water at 25–80 °C; reaction proceeds to full reduction of the alkyne.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis) to free the amine. Purpose: liberate 2,2,2‑trifluoroethylamine from its hydrochloride salt. Key transformation: proton transfer from the ammonium ion to hydroxide, and chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution at ambient temperature, often with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Type: Double‑displacement/acid‑base reaction with gas evolution and precipitation. Purpose: generate insoluble magnesium carbonate and sodium sulfate while releasing CO₂. Key transformation: bicarbonate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O, the carbonate anion combines with Mg²⁺ to precipitate MgCO₃; Na⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give Na₂SO₄ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, mild heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde. Purpose: reduce benzenepropanal to the corresponding primary alcohol, 3‑phenylpropanol. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the C=O double bond to form a C‑O single bond. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), Pd/C (5–10 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF; room temperature to 50 °C; reaction under inert atmosphere.

Type: Precipitation (acid‑base) forming an insoluble metal cyanide. Purpose: produce silver cyanide as a solid. Key transformation: cyanide ion from HCN pairs with Ag⁺ from AgOH, releasing water. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, low temperature (0–25 °C) to keep HCN in solution; AgOH is generated in situ from Ag₂O and water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; yields tert‑butyl salicylate, often used as a UV‑absorbing ester or fragrance component; the ortho‑hydroxybenzoic acid condenses with tert‑butanol, forming the ester and water; reaction is carried out under reflux in a non‑polar solvent (toluene) with catalytic acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) and a Dean‑Stark apparatus; the phenolic OH can participate in hydrogen bonding, sometimes requiring a stronger acid or longer reaction time.

Type: Strong‑reducing‑agent reduction of an azo compound. Purpose: convert azobenzene (N=N) to hydrazobenzene (N‑N single bond). Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the azo nitrogen atoms, breaking the double bond and forming a hydrazo linkage. Typical conditions: dry diethyl ether as solvent, addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C under nitrogen or argon, followed by reflux for several hours; work‑up with aqueous acid to quench excess LiAlH₄.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; exchanges Na⁺ and K⁺ to give potassium hydroxide and sodium hexafluorosilicate. Typically carried out by dissolving the solids in water, stirring at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) of 1,5‑pentanediol to form tetrahydrofuran. Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as both acid catalyst and dehydrating agent; the diol is heated (≈150‑200 °C) in the acid (or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent) under reflux. Water is eliminated as by‑product.

Transesterification of dimethyl carbonate with isopropanol; the alcohol exchanges one methyl carbonate group to give mixed carbonate methyl propan‑2‑yl carbonate and methanol. Typically catalyzed by a basic catalyst (e.g., NaOMe, K2CO3) or under solvent‑free conditions, heated to 80–120 °C, often under reduced pressure or nitrogen flow to remove methanol and drive the equilibrium forward.

Fischer esterification of 3‑cyanopropanoic acid with ethanol to give ethyl 3‑cyanopropanoate. Reaction is acid‑catalyzed (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄ or HCl), refluxing ethanol (often excess) to drive equilibrium; water is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to improve yield. No special solvent beyond ethanol is needed.

Acylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol with acetic anhydride. The benzylic OH of 2‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol is converted to the acetate, giving 2‑hydroxybenzyl acetate and acetic acid. Commonly carried out in dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the generated acid.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the ammonium salt of picolinic acid (ammonium picolinate) with release of carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until gas evolution ceases. No catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to convert the 5‑chloropyrazine‑2‑carboxamide into the corresponding carboxylic acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon followed by loss of ammonia; typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (80‑100 °C) for 1–4 h, often in water or aqueous ethanol; after reaction the mixture is acidified to pH 1–2 to precipitate the 5‑chloropyrazine‑2‑carboxylic acid.

propan-2-yl 2,2,2-trichloroacetate + lithium aluminium hydride -> 2,2,2-trichloroethanol + propan-2-ol  
**Type:** Reduction reaction. **Purpose:** Converts an ester group to primary alcohols via cleavage. **Key transformations:** Lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) reduces the ester into two alcohols by breaking the ester bond. **Conditions:** Low-temperature inert atmosphere to prevent side reactions. **Solvents/catalysts:** LAH used in anhydrous ether solvents like THF.

High‑temperature solid‑state intermetallic synthesis; forms holmium bismuthide by direct combination of the elements; Ho + Bi → HoBi (or related stoichiometry); performed in a sealed tube or furnace at ≥600 °C under inert gas to prevent oxidation; no solvents or catalysts, only high temperature.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of isopropyl alcohol by copper(II) oxide, producing acetone, water, and reducing CuO to copper(I) oxide. Performed at elevated temperature (≈200‑300 °C) in the solid state or in a high‑boiling inert solvent; copper oxide serves as the oxidant, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑chlorododecane by ethylene glycol to form 2‑(dodecyloxy)ethanol. Reaction typically uses a base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) to generate the alkoxide of ethylene glycol and a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO; heated under reflux. Hydrochloric acid is liberated as by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of the conjugated double bonds in zearalenone to afford α‑zearalanol, a less estrogenic metabolite. Key transformation is the addition of H₂ across C=C (and possibly C=O) bonds. Typical conditions: H₂ gas at 1–5 atm, 5–10 % Pd/C as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to reflux temperature, reaction time 1–6 h under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); sodium hydroxide deprotonates dithiophosphoric acid to give the sodium dithiophosphate salt and water. Key transformation is proton transfer from the acidic –SH group to OH⁻. Performed in aqueous solution, usually at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring; excess NaOH ensures complete neutralization. No special catalyst required.

Type: acid‑salt (double‑displacement) reaction; essentially acidification of a metal oxalate. Purpose: convert insoluble cerium(III) oxalate into soluble cerium(III) nitrate while liberating free oxalic acid. Key transformation: protonation of oxalate ligands releases oxalic acid; nitrate anions replace oxalate around Ce³⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of concentrated HNO₃, gentle heating (30‑60 °C) to ensure dissolution, ambient pressure. Solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Ullmann ether synthesis (copper‑catalyzed C–O coupling); chlorobenzene reacts with phenol to form diphenyl ether, releasing HCl. Key transformation is the formation of a C–O bond via oxidative addition of aryl chloride to Cu(I) followed by reductive elimination. Typical conditions: CuCl (10–20 mol %), inorganic base such as K₂CO₃, polar aprotic solvent (e.g., 1,4‑dioxane, NMP), temperature 200–250 °C, sealed tube or inert atmosphere; reaction time 12–24 h.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base) reaction; phosphoric acid protonates acetate ions of magnesium acetate, producing acetic acid and magnesium phosphate precipitate. Key transformation is exchange of anions (PO₄³⁻ ↔ CH₃COO⁻). Performed in aqueous solution, often heated to 60–80 °C to drive off volatile acetic acid; stoichiometric amounts (2 eq H₃PO₄ : 3 eq Mg(OAc)₂) give quantitative conversion. No catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (nitration of benzene) using sodium nitrate and concentrated sulfuric acid to generate the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺). Key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen on benzene by a nitro group, producing nitrobenzene and sodium bisulfate as by‑product. Typical conditions: mix NaNO₃ with 95–98 % H₂SO₄ at 0–50 °C, add benzene slowly, maintain temperature below 50 °C to control rate, stir for 30 min to 2 h; reaction carried out in the acid medium without additional solvent.

Esterification via acyl chloride; purpose is to convert 2‑pentanol into its acetate ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on acetyl chloride forming 2‑pentyl acetate and pyridinium chloride; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere in a solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with pyridine acting as both base and solvent.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; purpose is synthesis of benzyl alcohol from benzoic acid; key transformation involves hydride transfer from calcium aluminum hydride (CaAlH₄) to the carbonyl carbon, reducing –COOH to –CH₂OH and generating calcium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide as by‑products; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under reflux and inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ester; purpose is cleavage of isoamyl acetate to give the corresponding alcohols; key transformation is addition of hydrogen across the C=O and C–O bonds producing isoamyl alcohol and ethanol; uses 5–10 % Pd/C as catalyst under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25‑80 °C in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, with stirring under inert gas.

Type: metathesis/neutralization reaction. Purpose: exchange of anions between ammonium chloride and cadmium hydroxide, producing soluble cadmium chloride and ammonia‑water complex. Key transformation: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ combine to form NH₃·H₂O (often written as NH₄OH) and Cd²⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give CdCl₂. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at room temperature, stirring until precipitation of Cd(OH)₂ dissolves. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

MnO2 oxidation; mild oxidation of veratryl (3,4‑dimethoxybenzyl) alcohol to veratraldehyde using powdered manganese dioxide as oxidant; generally carried out at room temperature in an inert solvent such as chloroform or dichloromethane with stirring until the solid is consumed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro aromatic; reduces the nitro group of 4‑nitropyridine to an amine to afford 4‑aminopyridine; key transformation NO₂ → NH₂; performed under H₂ (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5–10 wt %) in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to 80 °C.

Type: heterogeneous photocatalytic oxidation (air oxidation). Purpose: oxidative conversion cyclohexane to cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (full oxidation). Key transformation: abstraction of hydrogen from cyclohexane, subsequent oxygen insertion and sequential oxidation of cyclohexanol/ cyclohexanone to the carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: TiO₂ (anatase) powder as catalyst, UV irradiation (λ ≈ 350 nm), oxygen or air pressure (1–5 atm), reaction temperature 25‑80 °C, often in a solvent such as acetonitrile or under neat conditions with vigorous stirring. No additional catalyst needed beyond TiO₂.

Acid‑metal oxide reaction (acid digestion); purpose is conversion of barium aluminate to soluble metal chlorides; key transformation is protonation of the aluminate framework yielding AlCl₃ and BaCl₂ with water formed; typically performed by treating barium aluminate with excess aqueous HCl at room temperature or under reflux, in aqueous medium.

Redox solid‑state displacement reaction; zinc metal reduces manganese dioxide while being oxidized to zinc oxide and manganese(II) oxide. Typically carried out by intimate mixing of the powders and heating to several hundred °C in an inert or air atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Fischer esterification; forms ethyl 3‑methylbutanoate from 3‑methylbutanoic acid and ethanol. Conducted by refluxing the acid and ethanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (or another strong Brønsted acid); removal of the water by azeotropic distillation or a Dean–Stark trap drives the equilibrium to the ester. Key transformation: proton‑activated carbonyl attack by ethanol, followed by elimination of water to give the ester.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of a β‑chloro sulfonic acid; potassium hydroxide abstracts a proton and eliminates chloride, converting 2‑chloroethanesulfonic acid into vinylsulfonic acid while forming water and potassium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous KOH at 0–25 °C; the product is isolated by acidification and extraction.

Dehydrative coupling using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC); DCC activates formic acid to generate the mixed anhydride, which collapses to formic anhydride and dicyclohexylurea as the by‑product. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF; the reaction is inert to moisture but may include a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine to improve rate.

Oxidative decarboxylation of a formate salt; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the monoethanolamine formate to release carbon dioxide, regenerate free monoethanolamine, and produce water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess H₂O₂ may be added dropwise, and the reaction is often buffered to control pH.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; molecular hydrogen adds across the carbonyl of decanal in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Pt–O₂, or Raney Ni) to give 1‑decanol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature 25–80 °C, reaction time 1–6 h.

Thermal decomposition (acid‑base dissociation) of diammonium hydrogen phosphate; heating the salt causes it to split into gaseous ammonia and liquid phosphoric acid. Usually performed by gradual heating above 150 °C under reduced pressure to drive off NH₃; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization; formation of a quaternary ammonium salt. Trimethylamine is protonated by acetic acid to give trimethylammonium acetate. Typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; the salt can be isolated by solvent removal or precipitation.

Reduction reaction. Purpose: aldehyde to alcohol conversion. Key transformation: sodium borohydride reduces aldehyde group in 3-aminopropanal to primary alcohol. Conditions: typically in protic solvents (ethanol/methanol) at room temperature.

Solid‑state base‑mediated liberation of diethylamine from diethylammonium hydrogen sulfate using potassium carbonate. Purpose: generate the free amine for further synthesis. Key transformation: the ammonium salt is deprotonated; CO₂ is released from carbonate, forming K₂SO₄, water and free diethylamine gas. Typical conditions: dry heating (120–150 °C) of a mixture of the two salts, often in a sealed tube or under a nitrogen stream to sweep away the volatile amine. No solvent is required; the reaction proceeds heterogeneously.

Type: nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening (alkoxy addition). Purpose: synthesis of β‑aryl ether 2‑phenoxy‑1‑propanol. Key transformation: phenoxide (generated from phenol) attacks the less hindered carbon of glycidol, opening the epoxide to give a C–O bond and a secondary alcohol. Typical conditions: base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) or Lewis acid catalyst, aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, 0 °C to reflux (30‑80 °C) for 1‑4 h, then work‑up. Common catalysts: NaH (strong base) or BF₃·OEt₂Lewis acid) for acid‑catalyzed variant.

General type: gas‑phase redox oxidation; purpose: atmospheric conversion of toxic NO to NO2; key transformation: NO is oxidized to NO2 while ozone is reduced to O2; typical conditions: room temperature, atmospheric pressure, gas phase; common solvents/catalysts: none required.

Acid‑base neutralization producing a metal sulfate. Sulfuric acid protonates silver hydroxide, forming water and silver sulfate. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature; no special catalyst needed. The silver sulfate product may precipitate or remain in solution depending on concentration.

This is a catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenolysis of C–Br bonds) of a dibromocyclooctane using hydrogen gas and palladium on carbon. The Pd/C surface adsorbs H₂, generating atomic hydrogen that reduces the C–Br bonds to C–H, giving cyclooctane and HBr (often captured as the bromide salt in the medium). Conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature from room temperature to reflux, stirring under a hydrogen atmosphere.

Acylation (acetylation) of a primary amine; of an amide. Phenylglycinol reacts with acetic anhydride, the amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl of the anhydride, giving N‑(2‑hydroxy‑1‑phenylethyl)acetamide and one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine as base; reaction is often driven to completion by removal of generated acetic acid.

Acid‑base displacement with carbonate decomposition; preparation of bismuth triiodide. Bismuth subcarbonate reacts with excess hydroiodic acid; the carbonate is protonated to release CO₂ and water, while Bi³⁺ forms insoluble BiI₃. Usually performed in aqueous HI (6 M) under reflux; the mixture is kept anoxic to prevent oxidation of I⁻, and the BiI₃ precipitate is filtered and washed.

Transmetalation (organometallic exchange). Used to prepare the volatile organocadmium reagent dimethylcadmium from dimethylzinc. Key transformation: the methyl groups are transferred from zinc to cadmium while the metal oxides exchange, giving dimethylcadmium and zinc oxide precipitate. Typically performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at 50‑150 °C in dry ether or THF; solid CdO is added to a solution of Me₂Zn, and the mixture is stirred until completion, after which ZnO is filtered off.

Dehydration of a gem‑diol (equilibrium). Methanediol loses water to afford formaldehyde plus water. Heating or removal of water (e.g., reduced pressure) drives the equilibrium toward formaldehyde. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic media; no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation in acidic aqueous medium. Ferrous sulfate is oxidized to ferric sulfate by the strong oxidizer potassium chlorate, which itself is reduced to chlorite; sulfuric acid provides the acidic environment and supplies water. Reaction is carried out by dissolving the salts in water, adding dilute H₂SO₄, and heating gently (≈60‑80 °C) while stirring. No special catalyst is required; the process yields aqueous ferric sulfate and potassium chlorite solution, with water as a by‑product.

Halogen exchange (halogenation/substitution) of chloroform with hydroiodic acid. One chloro substituent of chloroform is replaced by iodine, producing dichloroiodomethane and releasing HCl. The reaction is usually conducted by refluxing chloroform with concentrated HI (often generated in situ from NaI and H₂SO₄) at 80‑100 °C. Anhydrous conditions are maintained; excess HI drives the reaction to completion.

Formation of a chloroformate (Fmoc‑Cl synthesis). The hydroxyl group of 9‑fluorenylmethanol reacts with phosgene to give 9‑fluorenylmethyl chloroformate, with concomitant release of HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, using a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to trap the generated HCl. The reaction is typically run dropwise for phosgene addition, and the product is isolated by aqueous work‑up and purification.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (or cracking) of a saturated hydrocarbon. 2‑Methylheptane loses a molecule of hydrogen to form the terminal alkene 2‑methylhept‑1‑ene. Performed at high temperature (500‑600 °C) in the presence of a metal oxide or metal‑based catalyst (e.g., Pt/Al₂O₃, Cr₂O₃, or V₂O₅) often in a flowing inert gas or steam. No solvent is used; the reaction is continuous‑flow and the alkene is separated from the hydrogen gas effluent.

Acidic protonolysis of a metal arsenide producing arsine gas. Magnesium arsenide reacts with hydrochloric acid, protonating the arsenide ion to liberate volatile AsH₃ while forming magnesium chloride. The reaction is carried out in dilute (≈3 M) HCl at 0‑25 °C in a closed system with proper gas‑scrubbing; vigorous evolution of a foul‑smelling, highly toxic gas occurs. No catalyst is required, but the setup must include adequate ventilation and safety controls.

Thermal decomposition reaction; production of ammonia and hydrogen bromide gases; ammonium bromide breaks into NH3 and HBr; requires heat, typically moderate temperatures; no solvents or catalysts needed.

Ox cyclic ketone with hydroxylamine to afford cyclohexanone oxime and water. Conducted in methanol, ethanol, or aqueous buffer at 0–50 °C, commonly under mildly acidic conditions (pH 4–6) or with a catalytic amount of pyridine/acetic acid. Oxime serves as an intermediate for Beckmann rearrangement or as a protected carbonyl.

Acid‑base reaction (carbonate acidification); purpose: convert holmium carbonate hydrate to holmium(III) chloride; key transformation: Ho₂(CO₃)₃·xH₂O + 6 HCl → 2 HoCl₃ + 3 CO₂ ↑ + (x+3) H₂O; conditions: add excess aqueous HCl to the carbonate, gentle heating to drive off CO₂, stir and filter the resulting HoCl₃ solution; solvent: water.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyridine ring; hydroxide ion replaces the chlorine atom to give 4‑hydroxypyridine and NaCl; usually performed in aqueous NaOH or water/ethanol mixture at reflux temperatures (≈80‑100 °C).

Base‑catalyzed transesterification with ethanol; purpose is to produce ethyl acetate and 1‑nonanol; key steps analogous to methanol transesterification; common conditions include using excess ethanol, catalytic NaOEt or K₂CO₃, reflux (78 °C) in ethanol solvent.

Acid–base proton transfer with a strong mineral acid: ammonium acetate reacts with sulfuric acid to give acetic acid and ammonium hydrogen sulfate (NH₄HSO₄). The reaction is performed in aqueous medium, often at 0–20 °C under controlled addition of sulfuric acid to avoid excessive heat. No catalyst is needed. The process converts the acetate salt into free acetic acid while forming the bisulfate salt of ammonium.

Nitrous‑acid mediated deamination of a primary aliphatic amine; in cold acidic solution NaNO₂ generates nitrous acid, which converts the amine to a diazonium‑like intermediate that rapidly loses N₂ and is hydrolyzed to the corresponding alcohol (1,3‑dimethylbutanol); reaction is carried out in an aqueous HCl/NaNO₂ mixture kept ≤5 °C during addition, then allowed to warm to evolve nitrogen gas.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; cobalt(II) carbonate reacts with silver nitrate to exchange anions, forming soluble cobalt(II) nitrate and insoluble silver carbonate precipitate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, followed by filtration of Ag₂CO₃.

Direct chlorination (oxidation) of phosphorus trichloride; chlorine gas adds to PCl₃ to give phosphorus pentachloride; performed in a dry, inert‑gas atmosphere, usually at 0‑25 °C, sometimes in a non‑reactive solvent such as CCl₄ or liquid PCl₃ itself.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a fluoro‑silicate salt; lithium hydroxide neutralizes fluorosilicic acid to produce lithium hexafluorosilicate and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution with stirring at room temperature, followed by evaporation or crystallization of Li₂SiF₆.

Disproportionation (redox) decomposition of sulfoxylic acid; H2SO2 spontaneously converts to hydrogen sulfide and sulfuric acid. 2 H2SO2 → H2S + H2SO4. Occurs upon heating or even at room temperature in aqueous solution; the acid is unstable, no solvent or catalyst is required beyond the reaction medium.

Esterification via acyl fluoride: nucleophilic acyl substitution of ethanol with propanoyl fluoride to give ethyl propionate and HF; typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to neutralize HF.

Carbene insertion / electrophilic methylation using diazomethane; the diazomethane carbene adds a methyl group to the 3‑position of 2ethylindole, with loss of nitrogen gas, affording 2,3‑dimethylindole. Performed in an inert solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde: reduction of 3‑methylbutanal to 3‑methylbutanol using H₂ gas and a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, typically at 1–5 atm and ambient temperature.

Palladium‑catalyzed Heck cross‑coupling (aryl‑alkenyl coupling): coupling of 4‑iodophenol with 4‑vinylphenol to afford 4,4′‑stilbenediol; the reaction uses Pd(OAc)₂ as catalyst, triethylamine as base to scavenge HI, and a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, dioxane, or NMP) at 100–120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Acidic oxidative decomposition of ferric ammonium oxalate: oxalate is oxidized by Fe³⁺ in concentrated H₂SO₄, producing CO₂ and H₂O while forming Fe₂(SO₄)₃ and (NH₄)₂SO₄; the mixture is heated gently (≈80‑100 °C) to complete gas evolution.

Phenolic acetylation: acetic anhydride reacts with 3‑iodophenol to give 3‑iodophenyl acetate; the reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane or pyridine, with catalytic DMAP or pyridine to accelerate acyl transfer and neutralize the generated acetic acid.

Ozonolysis of a conjugated diene: ozone adds across the double bonds of 2‑methyl‑1,3‑butadiene, cleaving them to form a mixture of carbonyl compounds (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, methacrolein, and methylglyoxal). The reaction is carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane; after ozone addition the reaction mixture is worked up reductively (e.g., Zn/AcOH) or oxidatively (H2O2) to give the aldehydes and ketones.

Crossed aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation between a phenolic aldehyde and an aromatic ketone; forms a conjugated α,β‑unsaturated ketone (hydroxychalcone) by C‑C bond formation between the aldehyde carbonyl carbon and the acetophenone α‑carbon, eliminating water; typically performed with a base such as NaOH or KOH (10–20 % w/v) in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, often under inert atmosphere; reaction mixture is quenched with dilute acid and the product isolated by filtration or chromatography.

Amide hydrolysis (deacetylation) of N‑acetyl‑L‑histidine to regenerate the free amino acid and acetic acid; the amide bond is cleaved by nucleophilic attack of water under either acidic conditions (e.g., 1–6 M HCl, reflux 2–6 h) or basic conditions (e.g., 1 M NaOH, 60–100 °C, 1–3 h); after completion the reaction is neutralized, and L‑histidine is recovered by crystallization or ion‑exchange.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction forming yttrium hydroxide and potassium bromide; YBr₃ solution is mixed with stoichiometric KOH (typically 1 M) at ambient temperature; Y(OH)₃ precipitates as a gelatinous solid which is filtered, washed, and dried; the potassium bromide remains dissolved in the filtrate.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine (2‑heptanamine) with methyl iodide via an SN2 pathway to give N‑methyl‑2‑heptanamine and hydrogen iodide; carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile, DMF or acetone, with a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, or triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HI; the mixture is stirred at 0 °C to room temperature for several hours, then worked up by aqueous extraction and purification by distillation or chromatography.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine (diethylamine) to afford N‑nitrosodiethylamine with concomitant formation of water; generated by reacting diethylamine with dinitrogen trioxide (or in situ NO⁺ from NaNO₂/HCl) in a cold aqueous acidic medium (0–5 °C, pH ≈ 3); the reaction proceeds through formation of the nitrosyl cation which attacks the amine nitrogen; product is extracted into an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) and purified; safety caution due to carcinogenicity of nitrosamines.

Acid‑catalyzed amide bond cleavage of aniracetam, yielding 4‑methoxybenzoic acid and 2‑pyrrolidone; performed by refluxing aniracetam in aqueous HCl (1–6 M) for 2–8 h; the amide carbonyl is protonated, water attacks, and the bond fragments to give the corresponding carboxylic acid and lactam; after cooling, the mixture is neutralized, and the two products are isolated by extraction (acidic aqueous layer for the benzoic acid, organic layer for pyrrolidone) and crystallization.

N‑alkylation of a diamine via SN2 substitution; ethyl bromide reacts with ethylenediamine to give mono‑ethylated ethylenediamine and HBr. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF) at reflux, using excess amine as both nucleophile and HBr scavenger to limit over‑alkylation.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂/HCl) converts pyrrolidin‑1‑amine into N‑nitrosopyrrolidine with loss of water. Conducted at 0–5 °C in aqueous acidic medium to prevent oxidation; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization/decarbonation; two equivalents of formic acid protonate thallium(I) carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming thallium(I) formate. Carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine via SN2; methyl iodide reacts with 2‑pyridinemethanamine to give N‑methyl‑2‑pyridinemethanamine and HI. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at reflux, with the amine in excess to absorb the generated HI.

Carbothermal reduction of calcium phosphate in the presence of silica; at ~1500 °C carbon reduces Ca₃(PO₄)₂ and SiO₂ to produce carbon monoxide, elemental white phosphorus (P₄), and calcium silicate slag (Ca₂SiO₄). Conducted in an electric furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent, high‑temperature solid‑state reaction.

Oxidation reaction (Jones-type oxidation). Potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes the phenolic group of 2‑naphthol to a quinone, converting the C‑OH to a C=O and forming 1,2‑naphthoquinone; potassium sulfate and water are by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous H2SO4, controlled temperature (0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation), reaction often run under reflux for 1–2 h. No special catalyst beyond the dichromate; water is the solvent.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde; methylmagnesium bromide adds to pentanal to form the corresponding alkoxide, which after aqueous work‑up yields hexan‑2‑ol. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen or argon; quench with dilute acid for protonation.

Nitrosation reaction; electrophilic nitrosation of N‑propylurea using nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate to install a nitroso group on the nitrogen, producing N‑nitroso‑N‑propylurea and tetrafluoroboric acid as the by‑product. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required beyond the nitrosonium salt.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation; copper(I) bromide together with the nitroxyl radical TEMPO catalyzes the oxidation of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) by molecular oxygen, converting the benzylic alcohol (and possibly the aldehyde) to the corresponding carbonyl functions to give 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde. The reaction is usually performed in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water), at 60–100 °C under an O₂ atmosphere (or air) with CuBr (5–10 mol %) and TEMPO (5–10 mol %). No stoichiometric oxidants are needed.

Condensation amidation; dimethylamine reacts with formic acid in a dehydration step to afford N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF) and water. Direct dehydration requires removal of water or an activating/dehydrating agent (e.g., excess formic acid, azeotropic distillation, or addition of a catalyst such as POCl₃ or thionyl chloride) and is typically conducted at elevated temperature (150–200 °C) under reduced pressure or with a Dean‑Stark trap. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the amine on the carbonyl of formic acid followed by elimination of water.

Acid‑base double displacement/precipitation; salicylic acid neutralizes bismuth subcarbonate in aqueous solution, releasing carbon dioxide and water while forming insoluble bismuth subsalicylate. The process is carried out in water with gentle heating (40–80 °C) and stirring, allowing the evolution of CO₂ gas; the product precipitates and is filtered. No external catalyst is required.

Alkaline hydrolysis of a halo‑silane; sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes dibromodichlorosilane, replacing the Si–Cl and Si–Br bonds with Si–O⁻Na⁺ to produce sodium silicate, while the halides are liberated as sodium chloride and sodium bromide and water is formed. The reaction is performed in aqueous NaOH (typically 1 M to 5 M) at ambient temperature or with mild heating (≤60 °C). No catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of an internal alkyne; diphenylacetylene undergoes Markovnikov addition of water in the presence of a strong acid (commonly HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ or a gold catalyst such as AuCl₃) to give the ketone benzophenone after tautomerisation of the enol intermediate. The reaction is conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid or another protic acid medium at 60–120 °C. The metal salt acts as a catalyst to activate the alkyne toward nucleophilic attack by water.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). The reaction converts the carbonyl of methyl tridecanoate into a tridecanal while the methoxy group leaves as methanol. Typically carried out under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at –78 °C with 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, then quenched with methanol or aqueous work‑up at low temperature to prevent over‑reduction to the alcohol.

Double displacement/precipitation in aqueous solution; copper(II) sulfide precipitates from copper(II) sulfate when hydrogen sulfide gas is bubbled through the solution, generating sulfuric acid in the filtrate. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Dehydrative chlorination of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride; converts 2‑propylpentanoic acid into 2‑propylpentanoyl chloride while releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl; oxalyl chloride acts as the chlorinating reagent, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate activation; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; excess oxalyl chloride and generated gases are removed by evaporation or gas venting.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming a fluorosilicate salt. Lithium carbonate reacts with hexafluorosilicic acid in aqueous solution, releasing carbon dioxide and water and generating lithium hexafluorosilicate (Li₂SiF₆). The reaction is performed in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; no special catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a (Z)‑alkene. Pd/C (10 % on carbon) mediates the addition of H₂ across the C=C bond of (Z)-2‑methylhex‑3‑ene, yielding the fully saturated alkane 2‑methylhexane. Standard conditions use H₂ gas at 1–5 atm, Pd/C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, and room temperature to gentle reflux.

Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis. Purpose: Amide bond cleavage. Key transformation: Amide functional group converted to carboxylic acid and amine. Conditions: Aqueous hydrochloric acid under reflux or elevated temperature.

Redox oxidation‑reduction in acidic medium. Sodium bromate oxidises Fe(II) sulfate to Fe(III) sulfate while being reduced to elemental bromine; sulfuric acid provides the acidic environment and forms sodium sulfate and water as by‑products. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄, often heated to reflux; stoichiometry as written gives 5 Fe³⁺, 1 Br₂, 1 Na₂SO₄ and water.

Transesterification (ester exchange) between isopropanol and methyl acetate. The alcohol attacks the carbonyl of methyl acetate, displacing methanol and forming isopropyl acetate. Reaction is catalysed by an acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOMe) and performed under reflux in excess isopropanol; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium to product.

Dehydrative cyclization of itaconic acid with N,N′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) to form itaconic anhydride, with imidazole as by‑product. Typical conditions: dissolve acid in dry THF or DMF, add CDI at 0 °C then warm to rt; reaction completed in 1–2 h, isolated by removal of volatiles and filtration of imidazole.

Syn-dihydroxylation of an alkene; oxidation of cyclohexene to a vicinal diol using osmium tetroxide. Purpose is to introduce two hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons with syn stereochemistry. Typically performed with catalytic OsO4 and a stoichiometric co‑oxidant such as N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) or hydrogen peroxide, in a mixture of tert‑butanol/water or acetone at 0 °C to room temperature.

Carbon monoxide reduction; technetium dioxide is reduced by CO gas at 600‑800 °C, producing metallic technetium and carbon dioxide; performed in a tube furnace under CO flow, no extra catalyst required.

O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of tert‑butyl alcohol with dimethyl sulfate. Base deprotonates the alcohol to give tert‑butoxide, which attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, forming tert‑butyl methyl ether and methyl sulfate (methyl hydrogen sulfate) as the leaving group. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, DMSO), 0–25 °C, inorganic base such as NaOH, K2CO3 or NaH, inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Peracid epoxidation of a polyunsaturated fatty acid; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the 8,9‑double bond of arachidonic acid to give 8,9‑epoxyeicosatrienoic acid while being reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, usually under nitrogen to avoid oxidation of the substrate.

High‑temperature solid‑state conversion of a metal halide to its oxide; sodium carbonate reacts with zirconium tetrachloride to afford zirconium dioxide, evolving carbon dioxide and forming sodium chloride as a by‑product. Performed by thoroughly mixing the solids and heating in a furnace (≥600 °C) under a dry inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid‑base protonation (salt hydrolysis); protonates the carboxylate anion of sodium 4‑methylpentanoate to regenerate the free acid, yielding 4‑methylpentanoic acid and NaCl; typically done by adding aqueous HCl (1 equiv) at 0–25 °C; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Oxidative coupling of a thiol to a disulfide; molecular iodine oxidizes benzyl mercaptan, forming benzyl disulfide while being reduced to hydrogen iodide. Typically run in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to room temperature; a mild base (e.g., pyridine) may be added to neutralize the generated HI.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to form a glycidyl ether; sodium phenoxide attacks the less hindered carbon of epichlorohydrin, displacing chloride and yielding phenyl glycidyl ether. Reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, or acetone) at 0–50 °C; no additional catalyst is required beyond the phenoxide nucleophile.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction between two inorganic salts; exchanges ammonium and lithium ions to give ammonium perchlorate (an oxidizer) and lithium nitrate. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.
Acid‑base neutralization; proton from tetrafluoroboric acid combines with hydroxide ion to form water, yielding sodium tetrafluoroborate; performed in aqueous medium at room temperature; no catalyst.

Synthesis of calcium thiocyanate by reacting elemental sulfur with calcium cyanide; sulfur inserts into the cyanide ion forming the thiocyanate anion (SCN⁻). Typically carried out by heating a solid mixture of Ca(CN)₂ and S (≈200–300 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation). 1‑Pentanol is oxidized by chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃) in aqueous sulfuric acid, often with acetone as co‑solvent, to give pentanoic acid. Reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature under stirring; CrO₃ acts as the oxidant; work‑up involves quenching with methanol or water.

Oxidative aromatic hydroxylation of meta‑xylene using hydrogen peroxide. In the presence of an acid or metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Ti‑silicalite, or H₂SO₄), H₂O₂ introduces a hydroxyl group onto the aromatic ring to afford 4‑hydroxy‑1,3‑dimethylbenzene and water as by‑product. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium at 50–80 °C; catalyst is required for reasonable rate.

Reductive alkylation to form N,N‑diethyltryptamine. LiAlH₄ reduces the nitrile group of indole‑3‑acetonitrile to the primary amine (tryptamine); the resulting amine is then alkylated twice with ethyl bromide in the presence of potassium carbonate as base, giving the di‑ethylated product. Reaction carried out in dry THF or ether under nitrogen, low temperature for the reduction (0 °C → reflux), followed by addition of EtBr and K₂CO₃ at ambient temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification: methanol exchanges the n‑butyl group of butylparaben for a methyl group, yielding methylparaben and n‑butanol; commonly run in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid under reflux.

Catalytic skeletal isomerisation (hydro‑isomerisation) of n‑hexane to 2‑methylpentane; C–C bond shift over a solid acid (e.g., HZSM‑5, USY) or Pt‑based catalyst under H2. Conditions typically 150–250 °C, 1–5 atm H2, liquid‑phase or vapor‑phase flow; no solvent required in the vapor phase.

Type: Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis to give a ketone. Purpose: synthesize 3‑acetylpyridine. Key transformation: –C≡N + 2 MeMgBr → –C(=O)CH3 after work‑up. Typical conditions: methylmagnesium bromide (2 equiv) in dry ether, addition at 0 °C to –20 °C, then stir at reflux, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up to hydrolyze the imine intermediate.

Reaction type: selective oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using hydrogen peroxide. Purpose: transform 1,3‑propanediol into 3‑hydroxypropionaldehyde while leaving the second hydroxyl group intact. Key transformation: catalytic oxidation (commonly with TEMPO/NaBr, or a metal catalyst such as Mo(VI) or W(VI) complexes) converts the terminal primary –CH₂OH to –CHO, producing water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂O₂ (30 % w/w), catalytic amount of TEMPO (5–10 mol %) and NaBr, buffered pH 8–9 (e.g., sodium bicarbonate), temperature 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation. Alternative metal‑catalyzed systems use Na₂WO₄ or Na₂MoO₄ with H₂O₂ under similar mild, aqueous conditions. The reaction is usually complete within 1–3 h, after which the product is extracted or purified by distillation.

Acid‑base double displacement (neutralization) between calcium dihydrogen phosphate and magnesium hydroxide. The basic Mg(OH)₂ reacts with the acidic calcium phosphate to exchange ions, producing calcium hydroxide and magnesium dihydrogen phosphate in aqueous solution. Performed at room temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 2,4‑dinitrophenol to 2,4‑diaminophenol; nitro groups are reduced to amines using H₂ gas over a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Pt, Raney Ni) in an alcoholic or aqueous solvent at elevated pressure (1–5 atm) and moderate temperature (25–80 °C); purpose is to convert an electron‑poor aromatic nitro compound into the corresponding aromatic diamine, with water formed as the only by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization of rubidium carbonate with tetrafluoroboric acid; the carbonate is protonated, liberating CO₂ and H₂O, while rubidium cations pair with tetrafluoroborate anions to give RbBF₄ salt; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.
Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide. FeO reacts with aqueous HBr, producing soluble FeBr₂ and water. Usually performed at room temperature in aqueous HBr solution with stirring; no catalyst.

Redox reaction of lithium manganate with concentrated HCl; acidic conditions reduce Mn(VI) (manganate) to Mn²⁺ forming MnCl₂, while chloride ions are oxidized to Cl₂ gas; Li⁺ combines with Cl⁻ to give LiCl; carried out in aqueous medium, usually at 0–25 °C to control Cl₂ evolution; no external catalyst.

N‑methylation (alkylation) of diethylenetriamine with dimethyl sulfate under basic conditions; NaOH deprotonates the amine, allowing successive SN2 attack of dimethyl sulfate to yield pentamethyldiethylenetriamine, sodium sulfate, and water; typically performed in a mixed water/organic solvent (e.g., water/acetone) at 0–25 °C; no catalyst other than the base.

Iron‑catalyzed C–O cross‑coupling (Ullmann‑type ether synthesis) of phenol with bromobenzene to give diphenyl ether; Fe(acac)₃ is the catalyst, 1,10‑phenanthroline acts as a ligand, and a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) is used; reaction run in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or NMP at 140–180 °C; purpose is to form an aryl ether bond.

Oxidative N‑hydroxylation of 2‑acetylaminofluorene using the hypervalent iodine oxidant iodobenzene diacetate (PhI(OAc)₂); the reagent transfers an acetoxy group that is displaced by water, converting the secondary amide to the N‑hydroxy derivative and generating acetic acid and iodobenzene as by‑products; typically carried out in dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature to 40 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; used to prepare scandium sulfide (Sc₂S₃) by high‑temperature solid‑state reaction of elemental scandium with sulfur; key transformation is Sc⁰ + S⁰ → Sc₂S₃; typically performed in an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at 900–1100 °C; no solvent or catalyst required, just finely powdered reagents pressed into a pellet or mixed in a crucible.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); converts molybdic acid to potassium molybdate, useful for preparing soluble molybdate salts; key transformation: H₂MoO₄ + 2 KOH → K₂MoO₄ + 2 H₂O; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; converts phosphoric acid and magnesium bromide into insoluble magnesium phosphate and gaseous hydrogen bromide, useful for precipitating phosphate salts; key transformation: 2 H₃PO₄ + 3 MgBr₂ → Mg₃(PO₄)₂↓ + 6 HBr↑; typically conducted in aqueous solution with heating to drive off HBr gas; water is the solvent, and the reaction may be performed under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / aminolysis of an α‑chloro amide; replaces the chloride with an amino group to give 2‑aminopropanamide, useful in the synthesis of β‑amino amides; key transformation: ClCH(CH₃)CONH₂ + NH₃ → H₂NCH(CH₃)CONH₂ + NH₄Cl; carried out in aqueous ammonia, often heated (reflux) to promote substitution; water acts as solvent, and excess ammonia drives the reaction forward; no external catalyst required.

Single‑displacement redox reaction (metal displacement); zinc reduces Cr(III) to Cr(II) while being oxidized to Zn(II), yielding zinc sulfate and chromium(II) sulfate; key transformation: Zn⁰ + Cr₂(SO₄)₃ → ZnSO₄ + 2 CrSO₄; performed in aqueous acidic or neutral solution, typically at ambient or mildly elevated temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed, but the system must be kept oxygen‑free to prevent oxidation of Cr(II) back to Cr(III).

Oxidation reaction; NaOCl oxidizes the thiol side chain of DL‑cysteine to the sulfonic acid (DL‑cysteic acid). Purpose is to convert cysteine to its over‑oxidized form for analytical or synthetic use. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, pH neutral to slightly basic; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen fluoride (hydrofluorination); used to install a fluorine atom at the tertiary carbon to give tert‑butyl fluoride, a useful fluorinated building block; Markovnikov addition of H and F across the C=C bond forming a C–F bond on the more substituted carbon; typically performed with liquid anhydrous HF or HF/pyridinium poly‑hydrogen fluoride (Olah’s reagent) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as SbF5, BF3·OEt2 or AlCl3, at 0–25 °C, HF itself serving as solvent or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent.

Intramolecular dehydration/chlorination (epichlorohydrin synthesis) from glycerol. HCl chlorinates glycerol to give a chlorohydrin intermediate, which undergoes base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation in the presence of K₂CO₃ to yield epichlorohydrin and CO₂. Conducted by heating glycerol with gaseous or aqueous HCl and solid K₂CO₃ at 120–150 °C, often under reflux; reaction mixture is essentially the glycerol melt, and K₂CO₃ acts as both base and CO₂ scavenger.

Cation exchange (acid‑base neutralization) between calcium 2,3‑dihydroxybutanedioate (calcium tartrate) and sodium hydroxide. Produces the disodium salt of the dihydroxybutanedioate (disodium tartrate) and precipitates calcium hydroxide. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is needed.

Simple acid‑base neutralization; iodoacetic acid reacts with potassium hydroxide to give potassium iodoacetate and water. Used to prepare the potassium salt of iodoacetic acid, a useful alkylating agent. Typically carried out in water or aqueous ethanol at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid-catalyzed ether cleavage with hydrogen iodide; protonated diisopropyl ether undergoes SN1‑type bond scission, the resulting secondary carbocation is trapped by iodide to give isopropyl iodide, while the other fragment is released as isopropyl alcohol; usually carried out by heating the ether with excess aqueous HI (48 % w/w) under reflux, sometimes in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol) to improve solubility.

Transfer‑hydrogen reduction of an aromatic nitro group to an amine (4‑bromo‑nitrobenzene to 4‑bromoaniline) using NaBH₄ with NiCl₂ as a catalytic precursor. NiCl₂ is reduced in situ to metallic nickel, which mediates the reduction; sodium borate is formed as a by‑product. Conducted in ethanol (or ethanol‑water) under reflux, with excess NaBH₄; catalytic amounts of NiCl₂ are employed, and the nickel metal precipitates out.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2‑phenylethanol to styrene. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the alcohol, facilitating loss of water and formation of the alkene via an E1 mechanism. Reaction is performed at elevated temperature (≈150‑180 °C) in the presence of excess sulfuric acid; the mixture is often heated under reflux or in a sealed tube, and water is removed as it forms. No additional solvent or catalyst beyond H₂SO₄ is required.

Type: Acid‑mediated oxidation/disproportionation; purpose: generates chlorine gas for laboratory or industrial use. Key transformation: hypochlorite (OCl⁻) is oxidized by chloride (Cl⁻) in acidic solution to elemental Cl₂, while water is formed and calcium chloride remains in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of calcium hypochlorite treated with excess concentrated HCl, kept cool (0‑5 °C) to limit side reactions; reaction proceeds spontaneously at ambient temperature. No special solvent beyond water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base precipitation; dysprosium(III) hydroxide is treated with phosphoric acid, producing dysprosium(III) phosphate as a solid precipitate and water. Usually carried out in aqueous medium with excess H3PO4, stirring at room temperature or slight heating to complete precipitation; the DyPO4 solid is filtered, washed, and dried.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl halide; purpose: converts 1‑bromobutane to the corresponding primary alcohol. Key transformation: water attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing bromide, displacing Br⁻ and forming 1‑butanol while releasing HBr. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous medium, often with a small amount of acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) to protonate the leaving group or with a phase‑transfer catalyst to enhance the rate. Solvent can be pure water or a water‑organic mixture (e.g., water/acetone). No metal catalyst required.

Type: Strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; purpose: converts the –COOH group of 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methylbenzoic acid into a benzylic –CH₂OH while leaving the phenolic –OH untouched. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, reducing the acid to an alcohol after work‑up. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C followed by reflux; excess LiAlH₄ is often used. Quench with water or dilute acid at the end. No additional catalyst needed.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base precipitation; purpose: isolates insoluble erbium(III) hydroxide while converting the organic acetate to a soluble sodium salt. Key transformation: Na⁺ exchanges with Er³⁺; acetate anion pairs with Na⁺ to give NaOAc in solution, and OH⁻ from NaOH combines with Er³⁺ to precipitate Er(OH)₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of both reagents mixed at room temperature with stirring; the hydroxide precipitates and is filtered. No special solvent or catalyst required.

Simple acid‑base neutralization; indium(III) hydroxide reacts with acetic acid to form indium(III) acetate and water; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient or reflux temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (SN2) of benzyl chloride with potassium fluoride to afford benzyl fluoride and potassium chloride. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, often at 80–120 °C; excess KF drives the reaction to completion and the inorganic KCl is filtered off.

Type: Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl fluoride (acyl‑fluorination) using thionyl fluoride; purpose: prepares the reactive 2,2‑difluoroacetyl fluoride for further acylation chemistry. Key transformation: thionyl fluoride activates the acid, forming the acyl‑F bond while releasing SO₂ and HF as gaseous by‑products. Typical conditions: dry, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), low to moderate temperature (0‑25 °C) in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, chloroform, or carbon tetrachloride; stoichiometric SOF₂ gas is bubbled through the solution. No additional catalyst is required.

N‑acetylation of 3‑aminophenol using acet chloride to afford 3‑hydroxyacetanilide and hydrogen chloride. Performed at 0 °C to 5 °C under anhydrous conditions, typically in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to neutralize HCl; the reaction mixture is usually dissolved in an inert solvent like dichloromethane or THF.

Oxidation/chemiluminescent reaction; purpose: forensic detection of blood by generating visible light; key transformation: deprotonated luminol is oxidized by permanganate in basic solution, producing nitrogen gas, water, MnO2 precipitate and 3‑aminophthalic acid whose excited form emits blue chemiluminescence; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution (0.1–0.2 M) at room temperature with KMnO4 added dropwise; solvent: water; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose: preparation of zinc nitrate salt; key transformation: nitric acid protonates zinc oxide, yielding Zn2+ combined with nitrate anion to form Zn(NO3)2 and water; typical conditions: aqueous solution with gentle heating to dissolve the oxide; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Halide metathesis (double displacement) to form palladium(II) fluoride; purpose: synthesis of PdF2; key transformation: chloride ligands on PdCl2 are exchanged for fluoride from KF, producing PdF2 and KCl; typical conditions: solid‑state reaction or molten KF at 300–400 °C under inert atmosphere, sometimes performed in dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) with excess KF; no catalyst required.

Disproportionation (self‑condensation) of a hydroperoxide; tert‑butyl hydroperoxide is converted into di‑tert‑butyl peroxide and water. Typically carried out by heating the peroxide neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent (toluene, xylene) at 80‑120 °C, often catalyzed by a trace of acid (H₂SO₄) or a transition‑metal ion (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺). No additional reagents are required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; purpose: production of cadmium fluoride; key transformation: fluoride ions from HF replace chloride on CdCl2, yielding insoluble CdF2 precipitate and HCl in solution; typical conditions: aqueous HF solution, 20–60 °C with stirring; solvent: water; no catalyst required (HF is corrosive, handle with care).

Halide exchange (metathesis) to synthesize rhodium(III) iodide; purpose: preparation of RhI3; key transformation: iodide ions from HI displace nitrate ligands on Rh(NO3)3, forming solid RhI3 and releasing nitric acid; typical conditions: aqueous solution of Rh(NO3)3 treated with excess HI, gentle heating (≈50–80 °C); solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Copper‑mediated cross‑coupling (Ullmann‑type) that installs a trifluoromethyl group onto an aryl iodide. Phenanthroline ligates Cu(I) catalyst, Bromo‑CF3‑Hg provides the CF3 source, and CuI catalyzes formation of the C–CF3 bond, yielding trifluoromethylbenzene and HgBr₂ as waste. Typically run under inert atmosphere at 80‑120 °C in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO.

Type: Esterification (acyl substitution) of an alcohol with an anhydride. Purpose: Protect the allylic hydroxyl as an acetate or introduce an allyl acetate functionality. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming allyl acetate and releasing acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, using a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to scavenge the generated acid; solvent often dichloromethane or chloroform. Common solvents/catalysts: Pyridine or DMAP as catalyst/base, DCm as solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis via SN2 alkylation. Potassium phenoxide attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give methyl phenyl ether (anisole) and potassium iodide. Performed in a dry polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or DMSO) at 0‑50 °C; no catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation (epoxidation) of carbamazepine to oxcarbazepine. Meta‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid (mCPBA) transfers an oxygen atom to the 10,11‑double bond of carbamazepine, forming the epoxide (oxcarbazepine) while being reduced to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in dichloromethane or chloroform at 0‑25 °C; stoichiometric mCPBA is used, often with a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to neutralize the acid by‑product.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of a primary amine (MDA) to the amine MDMA. Formaldehyde forms an iminium intermediate with the amine, which is reduced by formic acid, delivering a methyl group and generating CO₂ and water as by‑products. Carried out in methanol or ethanol at reflux (≈65 °C) under acidic conditions; excess formaldehyde and formic acid are typical.

Williamson ether synthesis; deprotonation of hexan‑3‑ol with NaH forms the alkoxide, which undergoes SN2 attack on methyl iodide to give 3‑methoxyhexane; typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; NaI is formed as by‑product.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; a strong oxidative oxidation that transforms the aldehydic carbonyl of nonanal into a carboxyl group, forming nonanoic acid; usually performed in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., dilute NaOH) with KMnO₄ at 0 °C to reflux, then acidifying the mixture to precipitate the acid.

Acid‑base neutralization of sodium ethoxide with acetic acid; produces ethanol and sodium acetate. Proton transfer from the carboxylic acid to the ethoxide ion forms ethanol, while Na+ forms the acetate salt. Conducted in ethanol solvent at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic addition of a primary amine to an isocyanate forming a substituted urea; methylamine attacks phenyl isocyanate to give N‑methyl‑N‑phenylurea; usually carried out at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2, THF) without catalyst; purpose: preparation of N‑aryl urea derivatives.

Acid‑base neutralization of ammonium dihydrogen phosphate with sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide deprotonates NH₄⁺, liberating NH₃ gas and forming water; the phosphate is converted to sodium dihydrogen phosphate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be used to drive off ammonia.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a secondary alkyl bromide with azide ion yielding an alkyl azide; purpose is introduction of an azide group for click chemistry or reduction to an amine. NaN₃ attacks the carbon, displacing bromide to give 2‑azidopropane and NaBr. Typical conditions: NaN₃ in DMF or DMSO at 60‑100 °C, under anhydrous conditions.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution) of difluoromethyl chloride with hydrogen iodide, converting the chloride to iodide to give difluoroiodomethane; HI provides I⁻ which attacks the carbon, releasing HCl; typically carried out in refluxing ethanol or acetic acid under anhydrous conditions.

Base‑catalyzed saponification; NaOH hydrolyzes heptan‑2‑yl acetate to heptan‑2‑ol and sodium acetate; ester C–O bond is cleaved under basic conditions; typically done in aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M) at reflux, followed by acidification of the reaction mixture to isolate the alcohol.

Thermal decomposition of diethylammonium chloride, a salt‑deprotonation process. Upon heating, the ammonium cation releases HCl gas and yields free diethylamine. Performed by heating the solid salt (≈150‑200 °C) under reduced pressure or in a vented apparatus to purge HCl; no solvent or catalyst required.

General type: oxime formation (nucleophilic addition of hydroxylamine to an aldehyde). Purpose: converts the carbonyl group of benzaldehyde into a protected oxime functionality, useful for subsequent transformations such as Beckmann rearrangement. Key transformation: C=O → C=NOH (benzaldehyde to benzaldehyde oxime). Typical conditions: benzaldehyde is mixed with hydroxylamine hydrochloride or free hydroxylamine in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol, methanol) or aqueous alcohol, often with a catalytic amount of weak acid (acetic acid) to promote condensation; temperature ranges from 0 °C to reflux for 1–4 h. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol or methanol; acetic acid as catalyst; reaction may be carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); removes the bromine from α‑bromo‑aldehyde to give the unchanged aldehyde.
