Transesterification (ester exchange) converting ethyl acetate and octanol (not shown) into ethanol and octyl acetate; used to synthesize higher alkyl acetates; key transformation is replacement of the ethoxy group by an octoxy group; typically catalyzed by acid (e.g., sulfuric acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe) at reflux in solvents such as toluene or methanol, with removal of ethanol to drive equilibrium.

Partial reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to obtain 2‑(pyridin‑2‑yl)acetaldehyde from the corresponding nitrile; key transformation is hydride delivery to the nitrile carbon forming an imine intermediate that hydrolyzes to the aldehyde; performed at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as THF or toluene under inert atmosphere; typically 1.0–1.5 equiv DIBAL‑H are used, followed by quench with aqueous acidic work‑up.

Redox reduction; used to convert MnO2 to lower‑valent MnO; MnO2 is reduced by H2 gas to MnO with formation of H2O; typically carried out at 500–800 °C in a flow of dry H2 under inert atmosphere; solid‑gas system, no solvent required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of D‑allulose (a ketohexose) to 5‑(hydroxymethyl)furfural (HMF); purpose is conversion of a renewable sugar into a versatile platform chemical; key transformation is loss of three molecules of water and formation of a furan ring; commonly carried out with concentrated H₂SO₄ (10–30 % v/v) at 80–120 °C; reaction is performed in water or biphasic systems (water/MTBE, DMSO, ionic liquids) to extract HMF and limit side reactions.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of cobalt(II) carbonate from cobalt(II) acetate and ammonium carbonate; purpose is to isolate the insoluble carbonate salt; key transformation is exchange of acetate and carbonate ligands producing solid CoCO₃ and soluble NH₄OAc; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; stirring until complete precipitation followed by filtration and washing; no special catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) oxidation; forms magnesium oxide from elemental magnesium and oxygen; 2 Mg + O2 → 2 MgO; achieved by igniting magnesium ribbon in air or pure O2 at high temperature; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Double‑replacement precipitation reaction between silver nitrate and nickel(II) thiocyanate; purpose is to obtain insoluble silver thiocyanate; key transformation is exchange of nitrate and thiocyanate anions forming solid AgSCN and soluble Ni(NO₃)₂; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; the mixture is stirred until a white precipitate of AgSCN forms, then filtered; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative nitration; converts guanidine carbonate to nitroguanidine by reacting with concentrated nitric acid. Key transformation is introduction of a nitro group on the guanidine nitrogen while the carbonate decomposes to CO₂ and water. Typically performed at 0–5 °C in aqueous medium to control exotherm; no additional catalyst required, using excess cold HNO₃ and careful temperature control.

Coordination complex formation (ligand substitution); aqueous ammonia displaces chloride ligands of ammonium tetrachloropalladate to give tetraamminepalladium(II) chloride and ammonium chloride. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; excess NH₃ (4 eq) drives formation of the [Pd(NH₃)₄]²⁺ complex. No external catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis to give a ketone; purpose is to construct a carbon‑carbon bond and generate a mixed aryl‑alkyl ketone; key transformation: phenylmagnesium bromide adds to the carbon of 2‑cyclohexylacetonitrile forming an imine magnesium complex, which upon acidic work‑up yields 1‑cyclohexyl‑2‑phenylethanone; typical conditions include dry ether or THF as solvent, low temperature (0 °C) during Grignard addition, followed by aqueous acid quench to complete hydrolysis.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a chloroformate; benzyl chloroformate reacts with water in the presence of sodium bicarbonate to yield benzyl alcohol, CO₂ and NaCl. The bicarbonate neutralizes the generated HCl and evolves CO₂ Conduct at room temperature or slight cooling in aqueous bicarbonate solution; water acts as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Alkaline oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; KMnO₄ oxidizes 2‑chloro‑3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to 2‑chloronicotinic acid, reducing Mn(VII) to MnO₂ precipitate and generating KOH and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH or KOH medium, reflux or gentle heating, stoichiometric KMnO₄; MnO₂ is removed by filtration. No extra catalyst.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) to form chloroquine; the diamine N,N‑diethyl‑1,3‑propanediamine attacks 4,7‑dichloroquinoline, displacing chloride and forming chloroquine with release of HCl. Usually performed in ethanol or isopropanol under reflux with a base (e.g., triethylamine or NaHCO₃) to trap HCl. No metal catalyst required.

Fischer esterification; formic acid reacts with sec‑butanol under acidic catalysis (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) to give sec‑butyl formate and water. Reaction is carried under reflux with excess alcohol or a Dean–Stark trap to remove water and drive equilibrium toward ester formation. Solvent can be the alcohol itself; acid catalyst is essential.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide ion replaces bromide on 2‑bromoacetonitrile to give malononitrile, a useful dicyano building block; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux temperature, often with excess NaCN and NaBr precipitated as a by‑product.

General type: Gas‑phase disproportionation (Boudouard reaction). Purpose: Often leads to coke formation or is used to produce carbon deposits; also important in catalyst deactivation studies. Key transformation: Two molecules of CO rearrange to give one molecule of CO₂ and elemental carbon. Typical conditions: High temperature (650–900 °C) in the gas phase; equilibrium strongly temperature‑dependent. Catalysts such as iron, nickel or copper may accelerate the reaction, but it also proceeds uncatalyzed. No solvent required.

General type: Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide (SN2‑type addition). Purpose: Synthesis of hydroxy‑ethyl‑sulfonate salts, useful as surfactants or intermediates. Key transformation: Bisulfite ion attacks the less‑hindred carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give sodium 2‑hydroxyethanesulfonate. Typical conditions: Aqueous or mixed water/ethanol solution, pH near neutral, temperature 0–25 °C (often cooled to control side reactions). No additional catalyst required.

General type: Catalytic partial hydrogenation (selective hydrogenation). Purpose: Removal of trace acetylene from ethylene streams in petrochemical processes (alkyne hydrogenation). Key transformation: One equivalent of H₂ adds across the C≡C triple bond of acetylene to give ethylene, stopping before over‑hydrogenation to ethane. Typical conditions: Gas‑phase reaction at 0–50 °C, low pressure (1–5 atm H₂/acetylene), Pd on carbon (5–10 % Pd) as catalyst; often a diluted feed in an inert carrier gas. No solvent.

General type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) with azide ion. Purpose: Introduction of the azide functional group for subsequent click chemistry or azide‑alkyne cycloaddition. Key transformation: Cesium azide furnishes N₃⁻, which displaces bromide from methyl bromide to give methyl azide and CsBr. Typical conditions: Polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile; temperature 0–25 °C to minimize side reactions; stoichiometric or slight excess of CsN₃; inert atmosphere optional.

General type: Combustion/oxidative degradation of a trialkylborane. Purpose: Complete oxidation of organoborane, often observed as a safety hazard; yields benign inorganic product. Key transformation: Trimethylborane reacts with molecular oxygen to give carbon dioxide (from the three methyl groups) and boric acid (B(OH)₃) as the final oxidation state of boron. Typical conditions: Exposure to air or pure O₂, usually at ambient temperature; the reaction is highly exothermic and can be flame‑driven. No solvent or catalyst required.

General type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: Preparation of cadmium selenide (CdSe), a semiconductor material, via an aqueous route. Key transformation: Cd²⁺ from cadmium chloride exchanges anions with Se²⁻ from sodium selenide, forming insoluble CdSe and soluble NaCl. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, stoichiometric amounts, often performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to prevent oxidation of Se²⁻; the mixture may be heated mildly (30–80 °C) to improve precipitation. No additional catalyst.

N‑alkylation of an aromatic amine (SN2 alkylation); 3‑aminopyridine acts as a nucleophile attacking methyl iodide, forming N‑methyl‑3‑aminopyridine and generating HI; reaction is promoted by a base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH, or triethylamine) to scavenge HI; commonly carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetonitrile at reflux or room temperature; catalytic or stoichiometric base is required to drive the reaction to completion.

Free radical halogenation; purpose is to substitute a hydrogen atom with chlorine. Initiated by UV light or heat, often in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst required. Key transformation: generation of a cyclopentyl radical followed by chlorine atom capture, forming 1‑chloro‑1‑methylcyclopentane and HCl.
Decomposition reaction. Converts plumbane (PbH₄) into lead and hydrogen gas. Typically occurs under heating. No catalyst required. Solvent not specified.

Neutralization reaction. Propionic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and sodium propionate. Occurs under ambient conditions. No catalyst needed; aqueous solvent.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; silicic acid protonates chloride ligands of ZrCl4, forming insoluble zirconium silicate (ZrSiO4) and liberating HCl; carried out in aqueous solution, often at ambient to mildly elevated temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Lithiation‑carboxylation sequence: 2‑bromothiophene undergoes metal‑halogen exchange with n‑butyllithium at –78 °C in dry THF under nitrogen, forming 2‑lithiothiophene. The organolithium intermediate is then bubbled with CO₂ (dry ice or gas) to give the lithium carboxylate, which on aqueous work‑up yields 2‑thiophenecarboxylic acid and LiBr. No additional catalyst; inert atmosphere and low temperature are essential.

Oxidation reaction. Dess-Martin periodinane oxidizes 2-methoxybenzyl alcohol to 2-methoxybenzaldehyde. Proceeds via a hypervalent iodine mechanism. Reaction conducted in dichloromethane solvent, typically at room temperature.

Dimerization/disproportionation of nitroxyl (HNO) to hyponitrous acid (H2N2O2); two molecules of nitroxyl combine, one acting as a reductant and the other as an oxidant, yielding the diacid. Typically performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to avoid side reactions; no external catalyst required.
Double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Silver perchlorate and rubidium bromide exchange ions, forming insoluble silver bromide precipitate. Occurs in aqueous solution; no catalyst required.

Transesterification. Purpose is ester interchange. Key transformation: methanol displaces tert-butanol via nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon. Conditions: mild heat, catalytic acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p-toluenesulfonic acid). Common solvents: toluene or methanol.
Photolysis-induced cleavage. 1,2-dichloroethane absorbs UV light to generate ethylene and chlorine gas. Photochemical process; occurs via homolytic bond cleavage. Conditions: UV irradiation.
Decomposition reaction. Iodine azide (IN₃) breaks down into elemental iodine and nitrogen gas. Produces 3 moles of N₂ per 2 moles of reactant. Likely triggered by heat; no catalyst.

Hydrogenolysis of an aryl chloride; purpose is to replace the chlorine atom with hydrogen to regenerate the parent heteroaromatic ring. Key transformation: C–Cl bond in 2‑chlorothiophene is reduced to C–H, producing thiophene and HCl. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm) over a palladium on carbon, Raney nickel, or platinum catalyst, often in ethanol or THF at 50–100 °C. The volatile HCl is removed or trapped in a basic scrubber.

Reductive hydride reduction; LiAlH4 serves as a strong hydride donor that reduces silicon tetrachloride to silane gas while forming lithium chloride and aluminum chloride salts. Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature in a sealed apparatus to contain the evolved SiH4.

Ligand exchange/complexation reaction forming tetrachloroauric acid (chloroauric acid) by adding excess concentrated hydrochloric acid to gold(III) chloride. The chloride ligands coordinate the Au³⁺ center to give the [AuCl₄]⁻ anion in aqueous solution; typically performed at room temperature or mild heating, in aqueous HCl, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification between formic acid and isopropyl alcohol; forms isopropyl formate and water; requires a strong Brønsted acid catalyst such as concentrated H2SO4 or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; performed under reflux with excess isopropanol or in an inert solvent (e.g., toluene) using a Dean‑Stark apparatus or azeotropic removal to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between nitrosyl chloride and silver fluoride; purpose is to prepare nitrosyl fluoride and precipitate silver chloride. Key transformation: Cl⁻ on NOCl is displaced by F⁻, giving NOF and AgCl(s). Typical conditions: dry, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0–25 °C; silver fluoride is added in stoichiometric amount, and the mixture is filtered to remove the insoluble AgCl.

Oxidation of sulfide to sulfate; purpose is to convert sulfide anion to its highest oxidation state. Sodium sulfide (Na2S) reacts with molecular oxygen to form sodium sulfate (Na2SO4), passing through sulfite intermediates under high‑temperature oxidative conditions. Typical industrial conditions: solid‑state roasting at 500–800 °C in a flowing O2 or air stream; sometimes catalyzed by metal oxides (e.g., Fe2O3) to enhance rate. No liquid solvent; reaction occurs in the gas‑solid phase.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to separate barium as an insoluble sulfate and generate chromium(II) chloride in solution. Key transformation: Ba²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form BaSO₄(s) while Cr²⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give CrCl₂(aq). Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of BaCl₂ and CrSO₄ mixed at ambient temperature, often with gentle; the BaSO₄ precipitate is filtered off and the filtrate contains CrCl₂.

General type: oxidative dehydrogenation/dehydration of a vicinal dihydroxy acid to an α‑keto acid. Purpose: convert (R)-2,3‑dihydroxypropanoic acid (glyceric acid) into pyruvic acid, a key metabolic intermediate. Key transformation: oxidation of the secondary alcohol at C‑2 to a carbonyl, accompanied by loss of water from the adjacent hydroxyl, yielding the α‑keto carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: mild oxidants (e.g., Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ with O₂, CuCl₂/H₂O₂, or enzymatic NAD⁺/NADH recycling) at ambient temperature, aqueous buffered medium (pH ≈ 7). For purely chemical oxidation, reagents such as pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt can be used, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Solid‑state metathesis (acid‑base) reaction: yttrium(III) nitrate is treated with sodium oxide at high temperature, causing exchange of anions to give yttrium(III) oxide and sodium nitrate; usually carried out by grinding the powders together and heating in a crucible at 600–900 °C; no solvent, solid‑state conditions.

Aminolysis of an ester (ammonolysis); purpose is to convert an ester into the corresponding amide and liberate the alcohol. Key transformation: the carbonyl carbon of ethyl lactate is attacked by NH₃, forming lactamide and releasing ethanol. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, reflux (≈80 °C) in a sealed tube or high‑pressure reactor; sometimes a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOH) is added to drive the equilibrium toward amide formation.

Redox halogen displacement; purpose is to produce sodium fluoride and elemental chlorine by oxidizing chloride with elemental fluorine. Key transformation: F₂ oxidizes Cl⁻ to Cl₂ while being reduced to F⁻, forming NaF. Typical conditions: dry fluorine gas passed over solid NaCl or a NaCl melt at 0–200 °C; reactions are conducted in fluorine‑compatible apparatus (e.g., nickel or Monel reactors) under inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions.

Double displacement (halide exchange) reaction; replaces chloride ligands on mercury(II) with bromide to give mercury(II) bromide and ammonium chloride; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water serves as solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl iodide with cyanide; purpose is to install a nitrile functional group; key transformation: the iodine atom is displaced by a cyanide ion to give 3‑cyanobutan‑2‑one with sodium iodide as by‑product; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or aqueous ethanol, 40–80 °C, stoichiometric NaCN.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis (double‑displacement); purpose is to synthesize scandium(III) oxide. A mixture of BaO and ScCl3 is heated to 800–1000 °C in an inert or reducing atmosphere, often using a flux (e.g., NaCl/KCl) to improve contact. The oxide ion transfers to scandium, producing Sc2O3, while BaCl2 forms a molten salt that can be removed by leaching. No liquid solvent in the reaction step; the molten BaCl2 acts as a medium, and no additional catalyst is required.

Esterification (acylation) of a secondary alcohol with trifluoroacetic anhydride; forms the corresponding trifluoroacetate ester (3‑pentyl trifluoroacetate) while producing trifluoroacetic acid as a by‑product; typically performed in a dry, aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, using a catalytic amount of a base such as pyridine or DMAP to neutralize the generated acid and promote acyl transfer.

Metathesis precipitation reaction; exchanges potassium ions for silver ions to form insoluble silver oxalate and soluble potassium bromide; performed in water, often at low to moderate temperature to maximize precipitation; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Thermal dehydrohalogenation (pyrolytic elimination) of acetyl chloride to give ketene gas and hydrogen chloride. The reaction is carried out by passing dry acetyl chloride vapour over a heated glass tube (≈200‑250 °C) under an inert atmosphere; the resulting ketene is collected or used in situ, while HCl is removed by a gas scrubber. No solvent; sometimes a basic trap (e.g., Na₂CO₃) is employed to capture HCl.

Oxidation (PCC oxidation); purpose: convert secondary alcohol to ketone; key transformation: 4‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑ol oxidized to 4‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑one; typical conditions: PCC (1.1–1.5 eq) in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, anhydrous; common solvent: CH₂Cl₂; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement precipitation (salt metathesis) reaction; ammonium ions exchange with cerium(III) to produce soluble ammonium nitrate and insoluble cerium(III) oxalate precipitate; conducted in aqueous solution, mild heating may be applied; no catalyst; water is the medium.

Reduction of an acyl chloride to a primary alcohol using sodium aluminum hydride (NaAlH4); NaAlH4 acts as a strong hydride donor, delivering H‑ to the carbonyl carbon and then further reducing the intermediate aldehyde to the alcohol. Typically carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required. Purpose: convert a carbonyl chloride (R‑COCl) into the corresponding primary alcohol (R‑CH2OH).

Type: thermal pyrolysis (fast pyrolysis) of cellulose. Purpose: produce levoglucosenone, a platform chemical, together with gaseous by‑products. Key transformation: depolymerization of β‑1,4‑glucan to levoglucosenone with simultaneous release of water, CO and CO₂. Conditions: 350–450 °C under nitrogen or other inert gas, short residence time, no solvent, often in a fluidized‑bed reactor.

formation of ethyl methanesulfonate from methanesulfonyl chloride, ethanol and pyridine; same sulfonate esterification mechanism as above; pyridine neutralizes HCl; conditions: 0 °C to rt, dry dichloromethane (or similar aprotic solvent), stoichiometric pyridine, inert atmosphere.

High‑temperature redox (fluorination) reaction; elemental fluorine oxidizes aluminum oxide, yielding aluminum fluoride and elemental oxygen; carried out in the gas phase or in molten aluminum oxide at temperatures above 1000 °C; inert atmosphere often used; no solvent or catalyst.

Grignard addition of methylmagnesium bromide to cyclopropanecarbaldehyde; nucleophilic addition to the aldehyde carbonyl followed by aqueous work‑up gives 1‑methylcyclopropan‑1‑ol; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of a secondary amine; methyl iodide methylates 4‑fluoroamphetamine in the presence of potassium carbonate base to give 4‑fluoromethamphetamine; typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetonitrile under reflux or at room temperature; K2CO3 acts as base; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base metathesis (halide exchange) reaction; thallium acetate reacts with hydroiodic acid to produce thallium iodide and acetic acid; usually carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑ethanol solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Gas absorption/acid–base reaction; carbon dioxide is absorbed by aqueous lithium hydroxide forming lithium carbonate and water; employed in CO₂ scrubbing or air purification; carried out at room temperature with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed aldol addition; purpose is C‑C bond formation to give the β‑hydroxyketone diacetone alcohol. Acetone is deprotonated by KOH to form an enolate which attacks a second acetone carbonyl; the resulting alkoxide is protonated to give 4‑hydroxy‑4‑methyl‑2‑pentanone. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic KOH (10–30 % w/w) at 0 °C to room temperature, often followed by gentle warming; solvent water/ethanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Carbodiimide‑mediated condensation (esterification) of salicylic acid to form the dimeric drug salsalate; DCC activates the carboxyl group as an O‑acylurea, and DMAP catalyzes nucleophilic attack by the phenolic OH of a second salicylic acid molecule. By‑product is dicyclohexylurea, which precipitates. Typical conditions: room temperature, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane or DMF as solvent, 1–2 equiv DCC, catalytic DMAP (0.1 equiv); reaction proceeds in 1–4 h.

Direct fluorination synthesis; produces silicon tetrafluoride gas; Si + 2 F2 → SiF4; fluorine gas passed over heated silicon (400–600 °C) in a fluorination furnace; gas‑phase, no solvent; no catalyst.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of methanol to formaldehyde using hydrogen peroxide; usually a metal catalyst (e.g., Fe‑ or Mo‑based, vanadium‑oxo, or a heteropolyacid) is required to activate H₂O₂. Key transformation is oxidation of the primary alcohol to the aldehyde with water as the only other product. Typical conditions: aqueous methanol (10–30 % methanol), catalyst 0.5–5 mol %, temperature 25–80 °C; solvent is the methanol/water mixture itself.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by cyanide ion to give a nitrile. KCN provides CN⁻ which displaces Br⁻ to afford 5‑chloropentanenitrile; KBr is formed as the inorganic salt. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone; excess KCN (1.5–2 equiv); temperature 0 °C to reflux (25–80 °C); reaction time 1–6 h; work‑up includes aqueous extraction and removal of inorganic salts.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated). Zinc dust removes a chlorine from trichloroacetonitrile, forming zinc chloride and dichloroacetonitrile. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous ether or THF, excess Zn, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt formation (neutralization) of the secondary amine of DL‑ephedrine with hydrochloric acid to give the hydrochloride salt. The amine is protonated, producing DL‑ephedrine·HCl as a solid, which is more water‑soluble. Typical conditions: dissolve DL‑ephedrine in ethanol or methanol, add aqueous HCl (1 equiv) at 0–25 °C, stir 0.5–2 h; the hydrochloride precipitates and is, washed with cold solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) – phenoxide anion acts as nucleophile displacing chloride on benzyl chloride to form phenylmethyl ether; purpose is formation of a benzylic ether. Typically performed in dry polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere; sodium phenoxide generated in situ from phenol and NaH or Na metal.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; formation of a symmetric carbonate. Phenyl chloroformate reacts with sodium phenoxide to give diphenyl carbonate and NaCl. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required. Useful for preparing carbonate linkages in polymer or pharmaceutical intermediates.

Hydride reduction of an aryl azide using lithium aluminium hydride. Purpose: obtain an aniline from phenyl azide without the need for hydrogen gas. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the azide, converting –N3 to –NH2 and liberating N2. Typical conditions: phenyl azide dissolved in dry diethyl ether or THF, LiAlH4 added at 0 °C, then the mixture is warmed to reflux under nitrogen. After completion, the reaction is quenched with dilute acid or water and the product is extracted.

Acyl transfer / esterification using methacrylic anhydride – tert‑butanol attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, yielding tert‑butyl methacrylate and methacrylic acid as by‑product. Used to prepare acid‑labile tert‑butyl esters. Commonly carried out at 0–25 °C in dichloromethane or THF with a base catalyst (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to scavenge the generated acid; reaction is kept dry and may be protected from light to avoid polymerisation of the methacrylate.

Acid‑carbonate neutralisation – barium carbonate reacts with hydroiodic acid to give soluble barium iodide and carbonic acid, which instantly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O This is an inorganic acid‑base reaction employed to evolve carbon dioxide or to remove carbonate impurities. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no special catalyst required.

Strong oxidative cleavage (KMnO₄ oxidation) – the benzylic primary alcohol of 3,4‑methylenedioxyphenethyl alcohol is oxidised by potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium to the corresponding phenylacetic acid derivative. Purpose: convert side‑chain alcohol to carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH or KOH, KMnO₄ added portionwise at 50–80 °C, reaction monitored until purple color disappears; work‑up with acid (H₂SO₄) to precipitate the acid. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of tin tetrahydride; SnH4 breaks down to elemental tin and hydrogen gas; involves homolytic cleavage of Sn–H bonds upon heating; carried out in an inert atmosphere (e.g., N2 or Ar) at elevated temperatures (≈200–300 °C), often in a sealed tube or flow reactor, no solvent or catalyst required.

Metal‑mediated reductive dehalogenation. 2‑Bromo‑1,3‑oxazole reacts with activated zinc metal in glacial acetic acid. The zinc reduces the C–Br bond, producing the parent heterocycle 1,3‑oxazole and zinc bromide in solution. Conditions are typically reflux or room temperature with stirring; no additional catalyst is needed.

C‑alkylation of diethyl malonate (malonate ester alkylation) – ethoxide deprotonates diethylonate, forming an enolate that attacks ethyl bromoacetate via SN2, giving diethyl 2‑(ethoxycarbonyl)malonate and sodium bromide. Used to extend carbon skeleton in synthesis of β‑ketoesters. Conducted in dry ethanol under reflux with excess NaOEt; inert atmosphere to avoid moisture; the reaction proceeds cleanly without further catalyst.

Acid‑base deprotonation of a carboxylic acid with a hydride – sodium hydride abstracts the acidic proton of propionic acid, releasing H₂ gas and forming sodium propionate. Serves to generate the carboxylate salt for subsequent reactions. Performed in aprotic, polar solvents such as THF or 0 °C to rt under inert nitrogen; excess NaH is avoided to control H₂ evolution; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange). Sodium methoxide attacks isopropyl acetate, displacing the isopropoxy group to give methyl acetate while forming sodium isopropoxide. Typically performed in anhydrous methanol (or neat methanol) at reflux or room temperature, often under nitrogen. No additional catalyst is required beyond the sodium methoxide.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 3‑chloro‑2‑methyl‑1‑propene with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give the allylic alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑propen‑1‑ol and NaCl; typically performed in water or a water/ethanol mixture at ambient to mild heating; no special catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction of a metal by dilute nitric acid. Silver metal is oxidized to silver nitrate while nitrate ion is reduced to nitric oxide gas; water is formed from protons. Conducted in aqueous dilute HNO₃ at ambient temperature or with mild heating. No special catalyst; the acid itself provides the oxidizing power.

Aerobic oxidative cyclization (C–H activation) to form an oxindole. Acetanilide undergoes copper(II) acetate/palladium(II) acetate dual‑catalyzed activation in the presence of molecular oxygen; the acetate ligands are liberated as acetic acid. Reaction is usually run in a polar aprotic solvent such as dimethyl sulfoxide or acetic acid, at 80–120 °C under an O₂ atmosphere. The copper and palladium salts act as catalysts; no additional reagents are needed.

Salt metathesis (ion‑exchange) to prepare a tetra‑n‑butylammonium hexafluorophosphate phase‑transfer salt. Mixing tetra‑n‑butylammonium chloride with ammonium hexafluorophosphate exchanges the anions, yielding ammonium chloride (uble in water) and the desired TBA·PF₆ which partitions into organic solvents. Usually performed in a biphasic water/acetone or/acetonitrile system, followed by removal of the aqueous layer and recrystallization of the product. No catalyst required.

Free‑radical halogenation of an alkane; bromine replaces a hydrogen atom of methylcyclohexane to give 1‑bromo‑1‑methylcyclohexane and hydrogen bromide. Initiated by UV light or a radical initiator (e.g., peroxides) at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, typically in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane. No additional catalyst is required beyond the radical initiator.

Microscopic enzymatic oxidation (P450‑mediated sulfoxidation) of malathion to malaoxon. In rat liver microsomes, NADPH‑dependent cytochrome P450 enzymes insert an oxygen atom into the phosphorothioate moiety, converting the thio‑ester to the corresponding oxon. Conducted at 37 °C in phosphate buffer (pH 7.) with NADPH‑regenerating system; microsomal protein provides the catalytic activity. No synthetic reagents besides the cofactor system.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction between potassium hydroxide and calcium adipate. Two equivalents of KOH exchange cations with calcium adipate, producing calcium hydroxide and potassium adipate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with heating to ensure complete dissolution and reaction. No catalyst is required.

Complexation / metathesis to form a hexafluoroplatinate: PtF4 reacts with KF (often in molten KF or in anhydrous HF) to generate potassium hexafluoroplatinate, K2[PtF6]. Typically carried out at 150‑250 °C in a sealed vessel; excess KF ensures complete conversion.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl halide with cyanide; bromomethane is displaced by CN⁻ to form acetonitrile and NaBr. Carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C‑reflux; excess NaCN is sometimes used to drive the reaction to completion.

Reaction type: cyclodehydration of an oxime (intramolecular heterocyclization) promoted by acetylation. Purpose: convert o‑nitrobenzaldoxime to 1,2‑benzisoxazole. Key transformation: acetic anhydride acetylates the oxime nitrogen, facilitating intramolecular attack of the nitro oxygen and loss of acetic acid to form the isoxazole ring. Typical conditions: heat neat or in excess acetic anhydride at 80–120 °C for 1–3 h under nitrogen. Solvent/catalyst: acetic anhydride acts as both reagent and solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) of halide by chloric acid. Iodide is oxidized to elemental iodine while chloric acid is reduced to chloride, producing water and sodium chloride. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; acid medium provides the oxidant, no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; silver nitrate reacts with potassium sulfite to exchange ions, forming soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble silver sulfite (Ag₂SO₃) which precipitates; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring.

Acid‑catalyzed peroxidation; hydrogen peroxide in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ adds a hydroperoxy group to tert‑butanol, yielding tert‑butyl hydroperoxide and water; reaction is run at 0–5 °C in a biphasic mixture of aqueous H₂O₂ and tert‑butanol, sulfuric acid acts as catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed heterocycle formation (cyclocondensation); o‑toluidine condenses with 2‑amino‑5‑methylbenzoic acid in methanesulfonic acid to give the quinazolin‑4(3H)-one skeleton (2‑methyl‑3‑(2‑methylphenyl)quinazolin‑4(3H)-one) via amide formation and cyclization; typically refluxed in neat methanesulfonic acid (120‑150 °C) under inert atmosphere.

Direct combination reaction. Synthesis of niobium nitride from elemental niobium and nitrogen gas. High-temperature solid-state reaction (e.g., >1000°C). No solvent or catalyst required; niobium metal reacts directly with nitrogen under heat.

Fischer esterification; converts 3‑bromopropanoic acid to methyl 3‑bromopropanoate. Key transformation: condensation of a carboxylic acid with methanol, loss of water. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH). Removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium. Common solvent: methanol itself or toluene if water removal is needed.

Metathesis/precipitation (acid‑base) reaction; silicic acid reacts with zirconium(IV) sulfate in aqueous solution, exchanging sulfate for silicate to produce insoluble zirconium silicate (ZrSiO₄) and regenerating sulfuric acid; performed by mixing aqueous solutions and heating mildly to promote precipitation.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol; 4‑octanol is converted to 4‑octanone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) as a mild oxidant; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under anhydrous conditions.

Gas‑phase catalytic conversion of syngas (CO + H2) to an olefin; a Fischer‑Tropsch type hydrogenation/deoxygenation. Purpose is to generate ethylene as a building block from simple gases. Key transformation: 2 CO + 4 H2 → C2H4 + 2 H2O (reduction of CO and removal of oxygen as water). Typical conditions: 20–40 bar pressure, 200–350 °C, iron or cobalt based catalyst (often with alkali or Mn promoters), gas‑phase reactor. No solvent; reaction run in a tubular or fixed‑bed reactor under inert carrier gas.

Hydride reduction of a dinitrile to a diamine. Lithium aluminium hydride reduces each –C≡N group to –CH2NH2, delivering 1,4‑butanediamine. Purpose is the synthesis ofiphatic diamines for polymers or cheating agents. Typical conditions: LAH (1–3 equiv) in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C → reflux under nitrogen; reaction quenched cautiously with water or dilute acid. No additional catalyst; solvent is anhydrous ether.

Catalytic reductive amination of acetophenone to 1‑phenylethylamine using ammonium formate; purpose: preparation of benzylic primary amine; key transformations: acetophenone + NH₃ (from ammonium formate) → imine, reduction to 1‑phenylethylamine; formate → CO₂ + H₂O; typical conditions: Pd/C (5 % Pd), ethanol or methanol, 80‑100 °C, excess ammonium formate; catalyst: palladium on carbon.

Thermal decomposition of thiosulfuric acid: general type decomposition of an unstable acid; purpose is none (it is a breakdown pathway); key transformation is breakdown of H₂S₂O₃ into sulfur dioxide, elemental sulfur, and water; occurs spontaneously on standing or upon gentle heating; no solvent or catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (oxidative halogenation) of phenol using sodium hypochlorite as an in‑situ source of Cl2. The reaction installs three chlorine atoms at the ortho and para positions to give 2,4,6‑trichlorophenol. Purpose is preparation of a chlorophenol pesticide/intermediate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOCl (≈10 % w/v), pH alkaline (≈8–9) with NaOH, temperature 0–25 °C to limit over‑reaction, stirring for 1–2 h. No metal catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid in mixed acid. The nitronium ion generated from HNO3/H2SO4 attacks the 3‑position, yielding 4‑hydroxy‑3‑nitrobenzoic acid. Purpose is introduction of a nitro group for further reduction or dye synthesis. Typical conditions: chilled (0–5 °C) mixture of concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3, addition of substrate, then gradual warming to ≤30 °C; reaction time 30 min–1 h. Solvent is the acid medium itself; no additional catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated Steglich esterification to form caffe acid phenethyl ester (CAPE). DCC activates the carboxyl of caffeic acid to an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate; DMAP catalyzes acyl transfer to phenethyl alcohol, affording the ester and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Purpose is synthesis of a bioactive phenolic ester. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or DMF) at 0 °C → rt, under nitrogen, 0.1–0.2 equiv DCC, 0.05 equiv DMAP, reaction 12–24 h. No metal catalyst; DCC and DMAP are the reagents.

Metathesis (double displacement) precipitation reaction; exchanges carbonate and nitrate ions, forming insoluble silver carbonate and soluble ferrous nitrate; FeCO3 + 2 AgNO3 → Ag2CO3 (s) + Fe(NO3)2 (aq); conducted in aqueous medium, usually at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst required.

Acidic oxidative decomposition of ferrous oxalate with potassium permanganate. KMnO4 oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ (forming ferric sulfate) and reduces Mn(VII) to Mn2+ (manganese(II) sulfate); oxalate is oxidized to CO2, and water is formed. Purpose is quantitative determination of oxalate or preparation of Fe(III) salts. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of H2SO4 (conc.), fine ferrous oxalate added, then KMnO4 solution (excess) at reflux (≈80–100 °C) until the purple color disappears. Reaction carried out in a beaker or reflux flask; no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive amination) of a nitrile to a primary amine, yielding 1,4‑diaminobutane. Performed under H₂ pressure (50‑100 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt, in ethanol or methanol at 100‑150 °C. No additional reagents required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of a tertiary alkyl halide with acetate ion to form an ester. The purpose is the preparation of tert‑butyl acetate from tert‑butyl bromide. Key transformation: tert‑butyl bromide → tert‑butyl acetate while potassium bromide is formed. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, using excess potassium acetate; reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions to avoid competing hydrolysis.

Acid–carbonate reaction; terbium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to give terbium(III) chloride, carbon dioxide and water; protonation of carbonate leads to CO₂ evolution while Tb³⁺ pairs with Cl⁻; carried out in aqueous HCl at room temperature or with mild heating; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Reimer–Tiemann ortho‑formylation of a phenol. Hydroxide generates dichlorocarbene from chloroform, which inserts into the ortho position of 4‑methoxyphenol, yielding 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methoxybenzaldehyde (vanillin precursor). Conditions: aqueous NaOH (≈3 equiv), temperature 0 °C to reflux, water/ethanol as solvent; reaction is quenched with acid after completion.

Acid‑base neutralization coupled with decarboxylation of a bicarbonate component. The reaction neutralizes acetic acid with sodium sesquicarbonate, producing sodium acetate, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Key transformation: AcOH + Na₂CO₃·NaHCO₃ → NaOAc + CO₂↑ + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring until gas evolution ceases. No special solvent beyond water; reaction is exothermic.

Fenton‑type oxidative cleavage (hydrogen peroxide/Fe2+). Fe2+ catalyzes the decomposition of H2O2, generating hydroxyl radicals that cleave the C=C of 4‑vinylsyringol to afford 4‑hydroxy‑3,5‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde. Typical conditions: aqueous H2O2 (30 %) with FeSO4 (0.1 M) at pH 3–4, room temperature to 40 °C; water is the reaction medium.

Free‑radical chlorination at a primary carbon; chlorine gas abstracts a hydrogen from the terminal (C‑1) position of 2‑methylhexane, forming 1‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane; initiated by UV light or a radical initiator (e.g., peroxides) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, typically at ambient temperature or mild heating; yields a mixture of isomers, with the specified product isolated by distillation or chromatography.

Acid‑catalyzed decomposition of dazomet; provides methyl isothiocyanate under acidic conditions. In aqueous HCl (1–2 M) the protonated dazomet undergoes ring opening to give methyl isothiocyanate, dimethylammonium chloride, and carbon disulfide. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and the acid itself serves as the catalyst.

Redox oxidation; oxidizes Te(IV) to Te(VI). H2TeO3 is treated with H2O2 in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C, to afford H6TeO6 (telluric acid) and water. Reaction is acid‑free; water is the solvent and H2O2 acts as oxidant.

Oxidative decomposition of hydroxylamine by peracetic acid. Peracetic acid oxidizes hydroxylamine, producing nitrogen gas, acetic acid and water. Conducted in aqueous solution typically at room temperature; excess peracetic acid ensures complete conversion; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑base reaction forming an acidic ammonium salt. Sulfur trioxide dissolves in water to give sulfuric acid; partial neutralization by ammonia yields ammonium hydrogen sulfate (NH₄HSO₄). Key transformation: SO₃ + H₂O + NH₃ → NH₄HSO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, low temperature (0–5 °C) to avoid formation of the fully neutralized salt; stirring under an inert atmosphere is common; no solvent other than water is needed.

Alkaline hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) of a thioether. Aqueous NaOH cleaves allyl sec‑butyl sulfide, producing allyl alcohol and sec‑butyl mercaptan. Key transformation: R‑S‑R' + OH⁻ → R‑OH + R'‑SH, with the allylic carbon undergoing SN2 attack. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating to reflux (≈80–100 °C) for several hours; reaction may be performed in a water/ethanol mixture to improve solubility; no additional catalyst required.

Oxative dehydrogenation (aromatization); nitric acid acts as a strong oxidant converting 1,4‑dihydropyridine to aromatic pyridine while being reduced to nitrogen dioxide and water; typically performed by refluxing the substrate in concentrated HNO₃ without added solvent or catalyst.
Direct halogenation redox reaction; PH3 is exposed to Br2 vapor, often dissolved in CCl4 or performed in a sealed tube at low temperature, producing PBr3 and HBr gas; no catalyst.

Acid‑base reaction; hydrolysis of NaAlH4 by ethanol produces sodium ethoxide, aluminum ethoxide and H₂ gas. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of excess ethanol; no catalyst required.

Acid‑metal reaction (hydrogen evolution); elemental germanium reacts with hydrogen iodide, producing germanium diiodide and hydrogen gas; carried out in anhydrous HI under reflux or gentle heating, inert atmosphere, no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; magnesium sulfate exchanges its sulfate anion with benzoate from sodium benzoate, yielding soluble sodium sulfate and sparinglyzoate precipitate; performed in water at ambient to mild heating, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamate/urethane formation). Alkyl chloroformate reacts with aniline to produce the corresponding phenyl carbamate and HCl. Key step: the amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride and forming an N‑CO‑O linkage. Typical procedure: aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF), 0 °C to rt, with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine, pyridine) to capture HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization; aqueous ammonia reacts with nitric acid yielding ammonium nitrate and water; carried out in water at room temperature, commonly used for fertilizer production; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative intramolecular lactonization; sodium hypochlorite oxidizes 1,4‑butanediol, promoting cyclization to γ‑butyrolactone with concomitant formation of chloride by‑products; generally run in aqueous NaOCl (often generated from NaCl/NaOH) at 0–25 °C, pH controlled, no additional catalyst.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed Fischer ether synthesis (dehydrative condensation of two alcohols). Purpose: prepare methyl ethyl ether (ethyl methyl ether). Key transformation: protonated ethanol attacks methanol (or vice‑versa) followed by loss of water to give CH3OCH2CH3. Typical conditions: excess concentrated H2SO4 as catalyst, temperature 130–150 °C, removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark apparatus) to drive equilibrium toward ether formation.

Conversion of pentafluoroethanol to pentafluoroethyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); an SN2‑type substitution where the alcohol is transformed into the corresponding alkyl chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl; performed in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) under reflux or cooling, often with a base such as pyridine to trap HCl.

Carbonylative cyclization to a cyclic carbonate – Triphosgene reacts with 1,2‑ethanediol in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl. The reaction proceeds at 0 °C to room temperature, forming ethylene carbonate and releasing hydrogen chloride, which is neutralized by the base. No metal catalyst is required.

Redox metathesis (metallothermic reduction); aluminum reduces Cr(III) bromide to Cr(II) bromide while being oxidized to AlBr₃; conducted at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in the solid state or molten halide flux (e.g., NaCl/KCl), under inert atmosphere; no external catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation. Aqueous terbium(III) chloride reacts with phosphoric acid, yielding insoluble terbium(III) phosphate (TbPO₄) and hydrochloric acid. The reaction is carried out by slowly adding concentrated H₃PO₄ to a TbCl₃ solution while stirring, often with mild heating (40‑60 °C) to improve crystallization; the solid is filtered and washed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein reaction) on a primary alkyl halide; sodium iodide replaces the chloride of ethyl chloride to afford ethyl iodide and NaCl; performed in dry acetone or another polar aprotic solvent under reflux; precipitation of NaCl shifts the reaction forward; no catalyst needed.

Aminolysis of cyclic carbonate (ring‑opening) with decarboxyl; diethylamine attacks ethylene carbonate, opening the ring to give 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol and releasing CO₂; typically performed by refluxing the amine and carbonate neat or in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene, often with excess amine; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis/precipitation in water; purpose is to convert lutetium sulfate to the chloride salt while precipitating insoluble barium sulfate; key transformation: Lu₂(SO₄)₃ + 3 BaCl₂ → 3 BaSO₄(s) + 2 LuCl₃(aq); typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring, filtration to isolate BaSO₄.

Complete reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline using sodium amalgam in aqueous hydrochloric acid (Bechamp‑type reduction). Sodium metal dissolved in mercury provides electrons, while HCl supplies protons, yielding aniline, water and NaCl. Typically performed at 0–25 °C with vigorous stirring.

Williamson ether synthesis; purpose: form an aryl–alkyl ether; key transformation: phenoxide ion attacks primary bromobutane via SN2 to give phenyl n‑butyl ether and sodium bromide; typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, DMSO) under reflux; sodium phenoxide generated in situ serves as nucleophile.

Acyl chloride esterification; purpose: prepare an ester; key transformation: acetyl chloride reacts with 3‑hexen‑1‑ol to afford 3‑hexenyl acetate (with release of HCl that is scavenged by a base); typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C) to room temperature in dichloromethane or ether, using pyridine or triethylamine as HCl trap.

Redox oxidation of carbon monoxide; purpose: oxidize CO to CO₂ while reducing osmium(VIII) to osmium(IV); key transformation: two CO molecules are oxidized to CO₂ and OsO₄ is reduced to OsO₂; typical conditions: gas‑phase reaction at elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) under inert atmosphere; generally performed without solvent.

Oxymercuration‑reduction of isobutylene; Hg(OAc)₂ adds to the double bond forming a mercurinium ion, water attacks to give an organomercury intermediate, which is reduced (e.g., NaBH₄) to tert‑butyl alcohol; conducted in acetone‑water at 0‑25 °C, Hg(OAc)₂ as catalyst, followed by aqueous NaBH₄ work‑up.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; ethyl acetate exchanges its ethoxy group with methanol to produce methyl acetate and ethanol; generally run in excess methanol at reflux (≈65 °C) using catalytic amounts of sodium methoxide or sulfuric acid; solvent is often methanol itself.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: generate sodium nitrite solution from nitrous acid. Key transformation: proton from HNO₂ transfers to hydroxide, forming water and the nitrite anion paired with Na⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, temperature kept below ~5 °C because HNO₂ is unstable and can decompose; stoichiometric amounts of NaOH are added slowly. No catalyst needed.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; purpose: produce silver sulfide; key transformation: elemental silver reacts with elemental sulfur to form Ag₂S; typical conditions: heating a solid mixture of Ag and S (≈200–300 °C) or bubbling H₂S through an aqueous AgNO₃ solution to precipitate Ag₂S.

Type: reductive metal displacement (single‑electron reduction); purpose: produce metallic ytterbium; key transformation: YbCl3 + 3 Li → Yb(s) + 3 LiCl; typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free atmosphere, aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, low temperature then gentle warming; no catalyst.

Ozonolytic oxidative cleavage; purpose: convert the furan ring to a dicarboxylic acid; key transformation: ozone adds across the double bonds of 2‑methylfuran; subsequent reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) yields 2‑methylsuccinic acid; typical conditions: O₃ bubbled through the substrate in CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C, followed by reductive quench at low temperature.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange anions between copper(II) sulfate and sodium benzoate to form copper(II) benzoate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Key transformation: Cu²⁺ pairs with benzoate anion, Na⁺ pairs with sulfate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring promotes ion exchange. No specific catalyst; water is the solvent and the reaction proceeds spontaneously due to low solubility of copper(II) benzoate.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) acid‑salt exchange; purpose: isolate insoluble beryllium oxalate and generate sulfuric acid; key transformation: BeSO₄ reacts with oxalic acid to form solid BeC₂O₄ (beryllium oxalate) and H₂SO₄ remains in solution; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; filtration separates the precipitated beryllium oxalate.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose is to convert the strong acid trichloroacetic acid into its water‑soluble salt. The carboxyl proton is abstracted by hydroxide, forming water and sodium trichloroacetate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; often no additional reagents or solvents are required.

Halide exchange (salt metathesis) of phenylmercury bromide with potassium iodide to produce phenylmercury iodide and potassium bromide. As with the chloride analogue, the reaction is a straightforward double‑displacement carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑acetone solution at ambient temperature, without need for a catalyst.

Silyl‑ester transesterification (protecting‑group removal); purpose is to exchange the triethylsilyl group for a methyl ester, yielding methyl benzoate and triethylsilanol. Methanol attacks the Si–O bond of triethylsilyl benzoate, displacing the silyl group. Commonly carried out by refluxing the silyl ester in excess methanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or base; solvent is the methanol itself.

High‑temperature solid‑state pyrolysis to synthesize boron nitride; purpose is to generate BN as a ceramic material while releasing small gases. Upon heating, urea decomposes to ammonia, carbon dioxide and water, and the nitrogen and carbon residues react with boric acid to form crystalline boron nitride. Usually performed in a tubular furnace at 800–1000 °C under inert (N₂ or Ar) atmosphere; no solvent, solid reactants mixed and heated directly.

Acid–base neutralization. Calcium hydroxide neutralizes hexafluorophosphoric acid to form calcium hexafluorophosphate and water. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature by adding Ca(OH)₂ to an aqueous solution of HPF₆; no catalyst needed.

Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of a ketone; perbenzoic acid acts as the peracid oxidant. Acetophenone is rearranged to phenyl acetate while the peracid is reduced to benzoic acid. Typical conditions: 1–1.5 eq perbenzoic acid, 0 °C to room temperature, dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, inert atmosphere; reaction is usually run under anhydrous conditions.
Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using sodium borohydride. Performed in methanol, ethanol, or a mixed solvent at 0 °C to rt. No catalyst; NaBH₄ provides the hydride source.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; purpose is to oxidize thiocyanate to the dimeric oxidant thiocyanogen while reducing iodine to iodide. I₂ accepts electrons from two SCN⁻ ions, producing 2 KI and (SCN)₂. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at room temperature; the reaction proceeds readily in water without added catalyst, though the mixture may be buffered to control pH.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride; 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoic acid reacts with excess SOCl2 to give 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoyl chloride, with evolution of SO2 and HCl gases; performed under reflux in dry dichloromethane or neat SOCl2, often with a catalytic drop of DMF or pyridine to speed the reaction and scavenge HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to reduce the C2=C3 double bond of the isoflavone daidzein to give the dihydro‑isoflavone (4′,7‑dihydroxy‑3,4‑dihydroisoflavone). Molecular hydrogen is activated on palladium on carbon (Pd/C), delivering hydrogen atoms to the unsaturated bond. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C (5–10 wt % Pd), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time from minutes to a few hours.

Esterification via acyl‑anhydride: tert‑butanol reacts with phenylacetic anhydride to afford tert‑butyl phenylacetate and phenylacetic acid. This acyl‑substitution proceeds under mild heating (60–110 °C) in an inert solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, toluene) and is commonly catalyzed by a nucleophilic base such pyridine or DMAP. The transformation installs a tert‑butyl phenylacetate ester and generates phenylacetic acid as the co‑product.

Ester aminolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Ammonia attacks the carbonyl of ethyl isobutyrate to give isobutyramide and ethanol as the leaving alcohol. Typically performed by refluxing the ester with excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia, often in an alcohol or water solvent; no special catalyst required, though a basic medium can aid the reaction.

Type: Thermal decomposition (self‑decomposition) of a peracid. Purpose: Decompose trifluoroperacetic acid, releasing oxygen gas. Key transformation: CF3C(O)OOH → CF3C(O)OH + O2. Conditions: Mild heating (room temperature to 60 °C) accelerates the reaction; can be catalyzed by trace transition metals (e.g., Fe²⁺). Solvent: Often neat or in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane.

High‑temperature hydrogen reduction of a metal oxide; Gd₂O₃ (represented as gadolinium(III) oxide) is reduced by H₂ gas to metallic gadolinium while producing water vapor. Typically performed at 1200–1400 °C under a flowing H₂ atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent. This is a metal‑oxide reduction process used to obtain the pure metal.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) to assemble Meclizine. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the secondary amine of N‑(4‑chlorobenzyl)piperazine, which then displaces chloride of 2‑pyridylmethyl chloride to form the tertiary amine Meclizine, with KCl as by‑product. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, MeCN, or acetone) at reflux or 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Acyl chloride esterification (acylation of an alcohol). Isobutanol attacks formyl chloride, forming isobutyl formate and releasing HCl. The reaction is usually run at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, with a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to trap the generated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Hydrolysis of morpholine‑borane complex; a water‑mediated hydrolysis that cleaves B–H bonds, oxidizing boron to boric acid while releasing hydrogen gas and regenerating free morpholine; typically carried out in aqueous solution, often with mild heating (50‑80 °C), no catalyst required.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl nicotinate with ethanol to give ethyl nicotinate and methanol. The ester exchange proceeds via a tetrahedral intermediate. Standard conditions employ excess ethanol, catalytic amount of NaOEt or sulfuric acid, and reflux (≈78 °C) for several hours; the reaction mixture is often azeotropically distilled to remove methanol and drive equilibrium toward product.

Acid‑base salt formation; purpose is to convert the basic guanfacine into its hydrochloride salt for improved water solubility and handling; key transformation is protonation of the guanfacine amine nitrogen by HCl to give guanfacine·HCl; typically performed in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water at ambient temperature with stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed depolymerization/hydrolysis of a phenol‑formaldehyde resin; purpose is to break the polymer network and regenerate formaldehyde while forming sodium phenolate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the methylene bridges linking phenolic units, releasing formaldehyde and generating phenolate anion; usually carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, heated to 50–100 °C under reflux; NaOH serves both as base and as the source of sodium phenolate; no extra catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between aluminum sulfate and phosphoric acid; Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 2 H₃, H₃PO₄ → 2 AlPO₄ (precipitate) + 3 H₂SO₄; performed in aqueous solution with excess phosphoric acid and gentle heating to drive precipitation; no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed phenol‑formaldehyde condensation (methylene bridge formation) to give a symmetric bisphenol; purpose is to synthesize 4,4'‑methylenebis(2,6‑dimethylphenol), an industrial bisphenol used in resins; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the phenoxide ion (generated from 2,6‑dimethylphenol and NaOH) on formaldehyde, followed by condensation of two phenoxide equivalents with one formaldehyde to form the methylene‑linked dimer; reaction is conducted in aqueous NaOH solution at 60–80 °C, often with vigorous stirring; NaOH acts as both base and catalyst; no additional reagents required.

Gas‑phase nitridation (chemical vapor deposition) of titanium tetrachloride; purpose is to produce titanium nitride (TiN) as a hard, conductive coating; key transformation is the reaction of TiCl₄ with ammonia and hydrogen to form solid TiN while liberating hydrogen chloride gas; typically carried out at high temperature (800–1200 °C) in a flowing mixture of NH₃ and H₂ under reduced pressure; TiCl₄ is delivered as a vapor; H₂ serves as a reducing agent; the process is catalytic in the sense that surface TiCl₄ reacts continuously to grow TiN.

Acid‑base proton transfer forming pyridinium salt; purpose: prepare pyridinium trifluoromethanesulfonate for use as a mild acid or ion‑pairing reagent; key transformation: CF₃SO₃H protonates pyridine to give pyridinium⁺ CF₃SO₃⁻; typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, no catalyst.

Acidic hydrolysis (cleavage) of an amide to regenerate the parent acid and amine. N‑Phenylhexanamide is protonated in aqueous HCl, water attacks the carbonyl, and the C–N bond is broken to give hexanoic acid and free aniline. Typically refluxed in 6 M HCl or concentrated HCl aqueous solution for several hours at 100–120 °C. Solvent is aqueous HCl; no additional catalyst needed.

Strong oxidative conversion of a benzylic halide to a carboxylic acid using aqueous potassium permanganate; purpose is to oxidize benzyl chloride completely benzoic acid; key transformation involves MnO₄⁻ oxidizing the benzylic carbon, cleaving the C–Cl bond and further oxidizing the resulting benzyl alcohol/aldehyde intermediate to the acid; reaction is typically performed in warm aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or KOH) with excess KMnO₄, followed by acidic work‑up; MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate; side products include KCl and water.

Haloform (bromoform) reaction of methyl isobutyl ketone; basecatalyzed oxidative cleavage of a methyl ketone that yields sodium isobutyrate and bromoform (CHBr3); involves NaOH and Br2 in aqueous medium, added at 0 °C then refluxed; water or water/acetone is the common solvent, no special catalyst.

Basic hydrolysis of an acid chloride; water (or aqueous NaOH) attacks the acyl chloride to yield the corresponding carboxylic acid and sodium chloride; carried out in aqueous NaOH solution (often ice‑cold to control exotherm), followed by acidification of the mixture to isolate the acid.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (sulfonylation). Purpose: convert an alcohol into a good leaving‑group mesylate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl oxygen of butanol attacks the sulfur of methanesulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming butyl methanesulfonate while releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) present to scavenge the generated HCl.

Selenium dioxide oxidation (allylic oxidation) of 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene; SeO2 oxidizes the benzylic/allylic C‑H at the 2‑position to a carbonyl, giving the corresponding ketone; performed by refluxing the substrate with stoichiometric SeO2 in 1,4‑dioxane or ethanol, sometimes with TBHP as co‑oxidant; no additional catalyst beyond SeO2.

General type: Fischer esterification (condensation of a polyol with a carboxylic acid). Purpose: Synthesize pentaerythritol tetraacrylate, a multifunctional monomer used in UV‑curable coatings and adhesives. Key transformation: The four hydroxyl groups of pentaerythritol react with four equivalents of acrylic acid, each forming an ester linkage and releasing water, giving the tetra‑acrylate product. Typical conditions: Acid catalysis (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sulfuric acid) at 80–120 °C, removal of the generated water by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark apparatus) or by using a Dean‑Stark trap with toluene or benzene as solvent. Reaction time 4–12 h depending on scale. Common solvent/catalyst: Toluene (or xylene) as azeotropic solvent; p‑TsOH as catalyst; molecular sieves can also be employed to scavenge water.

General type: Direct fluorination (oxidative fluorination of a metal oxide). Purpose: Convert osmium tetroxide to the highly oxidized volatile osmium hexafluoride, a reagent for further fluorination chemistry. Key transformation: Fluorine gas oxidizes OsO₄, inserting six fluorine atoms and releasing two equivalents of O₂, yielding OsF₆. Typical conditions: Excess F₂ at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in a metal‑free, pressure‑rated reactor (e.g., nickel or Monel vessel) to control the vigorous reaction; reaction is usually carried out under static vacuum or inert carrier gas (Ar). No solvents are used because both reactants and product are gases or volatile solids. Common solvent/catalyst: None; the reaction proceeds without a catalyst, but the apparatus must be constructed of fluorine‑compatible materials.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of benzyl isothiocyanate; alkaline hydrolysis where hydroxide attacks the electrophilic carbon of the –N=C=S moiety, producing benzyl amine and carbonyl sulfide; performed in aqueous NaOH (0.5–2 M) at ambient temperature to reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst needed.

General type: Radical recombination (gas‑phase radical termination). Purpose: Form ethyl nitrate, an atmospheric nitrate ester, from reactive radicals. Key transformation: An ethoxy radical (·OCH₂CH₃) combines with a nitrogen dioxide radical (·NO₂) to give the covalent nitrate ester ethyl nitrate (CH₃CH₂ONO₂). This is a termination step in atmospheric oxidation mechanisms. Typical conditions: Ambient temperature and pressure in the gas phase; radicals are generated by photolysis of precursors (e.g., ethanol + OH·) and by NO₂ from combustion sources. No solvents; the reaction occurs in the troposphere or in controlled flow reactors. Common catalyst/solvent: None; the reaction is purely radical and diffusion‑controlled.

General type: Electrophilic addition of halogen (halogenation of an alkene). Purpose: Saturate the carbon‑carbon double bond of 1‑heptene with two chlorine atoms, producing the vicinal dichloride. Key transformation: Chlorine molecule undergoes heterolytic cleavage to form a cyclic chloronium ion across the C=C bond; nucleophilic attack of chloride on the more substituted carbon gives 1,2‑dichloroheptane. Typical conditions: Reaction at 0 °C to room temperature to avoid side reactions, in an inert, non‑polar organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane). Stoichiometric Cl₂ (1 equiv) is added dropwise with stirring. Common solvent/catalyst: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) or dichloromethane as solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidative decomposition (oxygen‑release) reaction; used as a bleaching or oxidizing agent; hydrogen peroxide and sodium perborate break down to water, molecular oxygen and sodium borate; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating (0‑50 °C), pH neutral to slightly basic; no catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; converts bismuth(III) chloride to bismuth tribromide while producing hydrochloric acid; key transformation is substitution of chloride ligands by bromide on Bi³⁺; usually performed in refluxing solvent such as acetonitrile or water under an inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Redox reaction of ammonia with nitrous acid; aqueous nitrosation/disproportionation that converts NH3 and HNO2 into nitrogen gas and water; typically carried out at low temperature (0‑10 °C) in aqueous solution generated in situ from NaNO2/HCl; no catalyst required.

Appel‑type halogenation (alcohol to alkyl iodide) reaction; iodine and red phosphorus generate HI which converts isopropyl alcohol to isopropyl iodide; key transformation is substitution of the hydroxyl group by iodine; performed in dry dichloromethane or THF under reflux with an inert atmosphere; red phosphorus acts as stoichiometric reagent, no metal catalyst needed.

Acid–base deprotonation (phenoxide formation). Potassium hydride removes the phenolic proton to afford potassium phenoxide and H₂. Reaction is carried out in dry ether or THF, often under nitrogen, at 0 °C to rt; the solid KH acts as the sole base, no catalyst required.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (acid‑base neutralization) of sodium carbonate with hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to convert the carbonate to soluble sodium fluoride while releasing CO2. Key transformation: Na2CO3 + 2 HF → 2 NaF + H2CO3 → 2 NaF + CO2 + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous HF solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Thermal dehydration (amide formation) of ammonium acetate; intramolecular condensation eliminates water to give acetamide; key transformation is loss of a water molecule from the ammonium salt; achieved by heating neat ammonium acetate at 150‑170 °C under reduced pressure or with gentle stream of inert gas; no solvent or catalyst required.

Grignard transmetalation (organotin synthesis) reaction; phenylmagnesium bromide transfers phenyl groups to tin(IV) bromide forming tetraphenyltin and magnesium bromide; key transformation is replacement of bromide ligands on Sn by phenyl groups; conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen or argon; excess Grignard reagent ensures complete substitution; no additional catalyst.

Oxidation reaction; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the sulfide group of 4‑methylbenzenethiol to the sulfonic acid functionality, converting –SH to –SO3H; typically performed in aqueous medium with excess H2O2 at ambient to mild elevated temperature (0–60 °C); often acid or neutral pH; no special catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Redox reduction (metal precipitation) reaction; sodium dithionite reduces chloroplatinic acid (hexachloroplatinate) to elemental platinum while being oxidized to sulfate; HCl is liberated as a by‑product; carried out in aqueous solution, usually under inert atmosphere, at room temperature to 80 °C; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst, using water as solvent.

Dehydrative chlorination of an aryl alcohol using thionyl chloride; a phenol is converted to the corresponding aryl chloride (3‑methoxychlorobenzene). Reaction proceeds via formation of an alkoxy‑sulfonium intermediate and loss of SO₂ and HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, pyridine or triethylamine as acid scavenger, in dichloromethane or chloroform. No additional catalyst required.

Chloramine generation (halogen transfer) reaction; dichloroisocyanuric acid reacts with ammonia to transfer one chlorine to ammonia, forming monochloramine (NH2Cl) and converting the cyanuric acid ring to cyanuric acid; performed in aqueous solution, typically at pH 8–9 to keep ammonia predominantly as NH3, at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C); no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Redox/sulfur oxidation reaction; elemental iodine oxidizes sulfide ion in silver sulfide to elemental sulfur while iodine is reduced iodide, precipitating as silver iodide; usually conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium, often with gentle heating to promote solid‑ diffusion; no catalyst needed, water (or dilute acid) serves as solvent.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (alkaline cleavage of an aryl methyl ether). Hydroxide attacks the electron‑deficient 2,4‑dinitro‑anisole, displacing the methoxy group as sodium methoxide and forming 2,4‑dinitrophenolate, which protonates to 2,4‑dinitrophenol. Purpose: depro of an anisole to phenol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 80–120 °C, water or water/ethanol solvent. No catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrodefluorination (reductive defluorination) reaction; hydrogen gas adds to 1,1,1,2,2,3,3,3‑octafluoropropane, cleaving a C‑F bond to give hydrogen fluoride and the less‑fluorinated 1,1,1,2,3,3,3‑heptafluoropropane; performed under H2 pressure (1–10 atm) using a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Ni, or Ru on carbon, in an inert organic solvent like THF or toluene, at elevated temperature (50–150 °C).

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to produce lithium hydroxide from inexpensive salts. Aqueous solution of Li2CO3 and Ca(OH)2 is mixed, often warmed; LiOH remains dissolved while CaCO3 precipitates. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkylation) cyclization forming an eight‑membered heterocycle (1,5‑diazacyclooctane). Ethylenediamine attacks the two bromomethylene groups of 1,4‑dibromobutane in an intramolecular SN2 process, releasing two equivalents of HBr. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, usually with a base (e.g., Na2CO3) to trap HBr, under reflux.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification converting dimethyl terephthalate to diethyl terephthalate. Ethanol acts as nucleophile, displacing methanol from the methyl ester groups. Typical conditions: excess ethanol, reflux (≈78 °C), catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or sodium methoxide, removal of methanol to drive equilibrium. Solvent may be ethanol itself.

Carbonyldiimidazole‑mediated coupling (condensation) to form the carbamate Felbamate. 2‑Fluorophenylacetic acid is activated by CDI, generating an imidazolide intermediate that reacts with 2‑oxazolidinone, giving Felbamate and releasing imidazole. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acidic redox disproportionation of potassium manganate (Mn(VI)). In concentrated H2SO4, MnO4²⁻ is oxidized to permanganate (Mn(VII)) and reduced to manganese dioxide (Mn(IV)), with water formed. Reaction proceeds in aqueous acidic medium, often with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion; no external catalyst is required.

Hydrolytic ring‑opening of ethylene imine (aziridine) to give ethanolamine. Water attacks the strained three‑membered ring under acidic or basic conditions, yielding 2‑aminoethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous solution with dilute HCl or NaOH, ambient to moderate temperature (≤50 °C). No special catalyst beyond the acid/base; water is both reactant and solvent.

Oxidation of a primary bromohydrin to a bromo‑carboxylic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). Chromic acid (often generated from Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) converts 1‑bromoethanol into bromoacetic acid, producing water as the only organic by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium, acetone as co‑solvent, 0 °C to reflux.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of phenyl 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate with ethanol. Ethanol attacks the phenyl ester, displacing phenol and forming ethyl 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate. Usually catalyzed by acid (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOEt) under reflux in excess ethanol; the reaction is driven to completion by removal of phenol or by using excess ethanol.

Preparation of trifluoroacetyl chloride from trifluoroacetic acid using oxalyl chloride. Oxalyl chloride activates the carboxylic acid, releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl and yielding the acid chloride. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate acyl‑chloride formation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of a secondary alkyl bromide with aqueous NaOH, replacing the bromine with a hydroxyl group to give 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol and sodium bromide. Typically performed in aqueous solution at reflux temperature. Purpose: conversion of a good leaving group (Br) into an alcohol while retaining the chlorine substituent.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of dimethyl 3‑aminophthalate to 3‑aminophthalic acid. Two equivalents of NaOH (or KOH) in aqueous–ethanol at reflux cleave the methyl esters, giving methanol and the di‑acid after acid work‑up. Typical solvent: MeOH/H₂O, temperature reflux, followed by acidification to pH 2–3.

Staudinger reduction of phenyl azide with triphenylphosphine in the presence of water to give aniline, triphenylphosphine oxide, and nitrogen gas; Ph‑N₃ reacts with Ph₃P forming an iminophosphorane intermediate, which is hydrolyzed by water to release the amine and Ph₃P=O, liberating N₂. Typical conditions: THF or toluene as solvent, 0 °C to rt; 1.2 equiv Ph₃P, then addition of water (or aqueous work‑up) after completion; reaction proceeds under nitrogen atmosphere.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis. Elemental tungsten and tellurium powders are mixed and heated to ~800–1000 °C in an inert (argon) atmosphere or sealed quartz tube, forming tungsten telluride (WTe₂). No solvent or catalyst.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; EuCl₃ solution reacts with NaOH to precipitate Eu(OH)₃ (insoluble) and form NaCl in solution. Usually performed in water at room temperature; slight heating may improve yield; no catalyst needed.

Hydration reaction; converts anhydrous NiCl₂ to the crystalline hexahydrate NiCl₂·6H₂O by dissolution in water; typically performed at room temperature with stirring; water acts as both solvent and ligand, and the hydrate precipitates upon evaporation.

Hydroboration‑oxidation of a terminal alkyne (1‑heptyne) to the aldehyde (heptanal). Diborane (BH₃·THF) adds anti‑Markovnikov across the triple bond to give a vinyl‑borane intermediate; subsequent oxidation with H₂O₂/NaOH converts the C‑B bond to a carbonyl, affording the aldehyde. Performed in THF under inert atmosphere, BH₃ addition at 0 °C → rt, then aqueous H₂O₂/NaOH at 0–25 °C.

Metathesis (halide‑oxide exchange); synthesis of Ta2O5 using lithium oxide. Key transformation: chloride ions are replaced by oxide, affording tantalum(V) oxide and lithium chloride. Reaction carried out by blending TaCl5 with Li2O and heating at 750–950 °C under N₂ or Ar; no solvent or catalyst required.

Amide‑bond formation (peptide coupling) between p‑aminobenzoic acid (or its activated derivative) and glycine to give p‑aminohippuric acid. Commonly the acid is converted to the acid chloride (using oxalyl chloride or thionyl chloride) or activated with a carbodiimide (DCC/EDC) in the presence of a base (DIPEA) in dichloromethane or DMF; the glycine amine attacks, forming the benzoyl‑glycine amide. Reaction carried out at 0 °C to rt under anhydrous conditions.

Acid–base neutralization; lead(II) oxide reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid to give lead(II) sulfate precipitate and water; performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst needed.

Syn‑dihydroxylation (oxidation) of the C9‑C10 double bond of oleic acid using osmium tetroxide; converts the alkene to a vicinal 9,10‑diol. Typically performed with catalytic OsO4 and a co‑oxidant such as N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) or H2O2 in a t‑BuOH/H2O mixture at 0 °C to room temperature; work‑up with aqueous NaHSO3 gives 9,10‑dihydroxy octadecanoic acid.
