Acid–base neutralization of a carbonate; magnesium carbonate reacts with aqueous hydrogen chloride, releasing carbon dioxide gas and forming magnesium chloride and water; usually performed in aqueous HCl at ambient temperature or with gentle heating, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) between the basic oxide Li2O and hydroiodic acid; produces lithium iodide and water. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Bulky‑base induced elimination (E2): potassium tert‑butoxide in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or DMSO) abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 2‑chloro‑2‑methylheptane, yielding 2‑methyl‑2‑heptene, potassium chloride, and tert‑butanol; the strong, sterically hindered base favors a concerted anti‑periplanar elimination pathway.

Williamson ether synthesis; nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allyl chloride by phenoxide ion to form allyl phenyl ether; purpose is to construct an aryl ether linkage; key transformation is O‑alkylation of phenoxide with allyl halide; typically carried out in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0–50 °C; sodium chloride precipitates as by‑product.

Acid‑base neutralization; barium hydroxide dihydrate neutralizes phosphoric acid to give barium dihydrogen phosphate and water; carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature, stoichiometric amounts, no catalyst needed.

Intramolecular condensation (dehydrative cyclization) of two glycolic acid molecules to give the cyclic dimer glycolide with loss of two water molecules. Conducted at elevated temperature (≈180–200 °C) under reduced pressure or in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., p‑TsOH, Zn(OAc)2) often in bulk or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Protonolysis (acidic cleavage) of a triethylaluminum Al–C bond by HCl, generating ethane gas and the diethylaluminum chloride species. Reaction is performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at 0 °C to –20 °C in a non‑coordinating solvent such as hexanes or toluene; no additional catalyst is required.

Thermal or photochemical decomposition of butyl nitrite (R‑ONO) to give n‑butanol and nitric oxide. The reaction proceeds via homolytic O–N bond cleavage; typically carried out by heating (≈80–120 °C) or irradiating the neat nitrite or a dilute solution in an inert organic solvent (e.g., benzene, CCl4). No catalyst is needed; NO is released as a gas.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methanol replaces the butoxy group of butyl lactate to afford methyl lactate and 1‑butanol; catalyst can be acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe, KOH); excess methanol drives equilibrium; reflux at 60‑80 °C; solvent methanol; purpose: synthesis of the methyl ester.

Alkylation of sodium 2‑chloropropanoate with ethyl bromide to afford ethyl 2‑chloropropionate; performed in DMF, acetone, or DMSO, often under reflux; ethyl bromide serves as the electrophile in an SN2 process; sodium bromide is generated as the inorganic by‑product.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde; 1‑hexanol is converted to hexanal while preserving the carbon skeleton. Common reagents include pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), Dess‑Martin periodinane, or Swern oxidation (oxalyl chloride/DMSO, TEA). These are carried out under anhydrous conditions in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no metal catalyst is required.

Swern oxidation of 4‑methoxyphenethyl alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde. Dimethyl sulfoxide is activated by oxalyl chloride at –78 °C to form a chlorodimethylsulfonium intermediate; the alcohol adds, and triethylamine effect deprotonation, yielding 4‑methoxyphenylacetaldehyde, dimethyl sulfide, CO2, CO, and triethylammonium chloride. Conducted in dry CH2Cl2 (or THF) under inert atmosphere, maintaining –78 °C to 0 °C throughout the addition steps.

Reductive amination of butanal with 2‑phenylethylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride; purpose is to form a secondary amine in a single step; key transformations are condensation of the aldehyde and amine to an imine/iminium ion followed by selective hydride reduction to the amine, releasing water; performed in a mild acidic medium (pH 5‑6) in methanol or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C, with NaCNBH₃ as the reducing agent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid–base neutralization (carbonate protonation) that converts potassium carbonate and hexafluorophosphoric acid into carbon dioxide, water and the non‑coordinating salt potassium hexafluorophosphate; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no special catalyst required.

Metal‑acid redox reaction; produces lutetium(III) fluoride and hydrogen gas; key transformation: elemental lutetium reacts with hydrofluoric acid to give lutetium fluoride and H₂; typically carried out in aqueous or anhydrous HF under gentle heating; HF serves as both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis; employed to produce boric acid and sodium sulfate from metaborate; H₂SO₄ protonates the metaborate to H₃BO₃ and Na⁺ combines with SO₄²⁻ to give Na₂SO₄ (or NaHSO₄ depending on stoichiometry); carried out in aqueous solution, often with mild heating to ensure complete reaction; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation; the carbon‑carbon double bond of oleyl alcohol is reduced to give saturated stearyl alcohol. The reaction employs hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) over 10 % Pd on carbon in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, typically at 25–60 °C. Reaction time ranges from 1 to several hours until complete consumption of the olefin.

Metal reduction (redox) of a high‑valent fluoride; produces titanium(III) fluoride from the higher‑valent titanium(IV) fluoride using elemental titanium as a reductant; TiF4 + Ti → 2 TiF3; carried out in sealed quartz tube or stainless‑steel vessel under argon at 500–700 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Transmetalation of vinyllithium to zinc chloride forming vinylzinc chloride and lithium chloride; provides a vinyl‑zinc reagent useful for Negishi coupling. Reaction performed in dry THF at –78 °C to room temperature under inert gas; ZnCl2 used as a solution or as ZnCl2·LiCl complex; no external catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of an aromatic amine) where p‑nitroaniline attacks acetyl chloride; pyridine acts as a base and HCl scavenger, yielding 4‑nitroacetanilide and pyridinium chloride; carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, often at 0 °C to room temperature, with pyridine in excess.

Anhydride hydrolysis; converts malonic anhydride to malonic acid by cleavage of the cyclic anhydride ring with water; generally performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) at reflux; solvent can be water or a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF); after work‑up the diacid is isolated.

Acid–base metathesis with sulfuric acid; aqueous lead(II) formate reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, forming insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and liberating formic acid; typically conducted at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) between cadmium iodide and tetrafluoroboric acid to give cadmium tetrafluoroborate and hydrogen iodide; conducted in aqueous or polar aprotic media (e.g., water or acetonitrile) at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Redox reduction of chromium(III) bromide to chromium(II) bromide by molecular hydrogen, with concomitant formation of hydrogen bromide; generally requires elevated temperature (150–300 °C) and a metallic catalyst such as Pt or Pd to activate H₂; performed in the gas phase or in high‑boiling inert solvent.

Coordination/complexation reaction forming a dinuclear lanthanum(III) oxalate complex. Oxalate ions from ammonium oxalate ligate two La³⁺ centers to give Tri[oxalato(2‑)]dilanthanum, while ammonium nitrate remains in solution. Purpose: preparation of a lanthanum oxalate chelate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric amounts, gentle heating (50–80 °C) to ensure complete complexation, water as solvent. No additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acyl chloride by cyanide ion; generates an acyl cyanide (benzoyl cyanide) and potassium chloride; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature; cyanide source (KCN) is used in stoichiometric amount; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone (Jones oxidation): 5‑methyl‑2‑hexanol is oxidized by chromic acid generated in situ from sodium dichromate and sulfuric acid, producing 5‑methyl‑2‑hexanone and water; reaction is performed in a mixture of acetone (or dichloromethane) and aqueous H₂SO₄ at 0–25 °C, with the chromium(VI) species acting as the oxidant.

Enzymatic hydrolysis of prothoate by esterase; enzyme‑catalyzed ester (phosphorothioate) cleavage yielding p‑nitrophenol and O,O‑diethyl phosphorothioate. Purpose: detoxification/deactivation of organophosphate pesticide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the phosphorus‑oxygen bond, release of phenolate. Conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8), 20‑40 °C, ambient pressure; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2‑nitro‑1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol to 1‑phenyl‑2‑nitropropene. Type: E1 elimination (dehydration). Purpose: preparation of a nitroalkene intermediate. Key transformation: protonation of the hydroxyl by p‑toluenesulfonic acid, loss of water to generate a carbocation, followed by deprotonation to form the C=C bond adjacent to the nitro group. Conditions: catalytic p‑TsOH (≈5 mol %), non‑polar solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, reflux or gentle heating (~80 °C) until water evolution stops.

Oxidative conversion of 3,5‑dichlorophenol to 3,5‑dichlorobenzoic acid using potassium permanganate in acidic medium. The phenolic ring is oxidized, breaking the C‑C bond adjacent to the hydroxyl and forming a carboxylic acid; MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate. Purpose: preparation of a dichlorobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ (conc. or 1–2 M), KMnO₄ added portionwise, reflux 80–120 °C until color change, then filtration to remove MnO₂. No additional catalyst.

Redox dissolution of lead(IV) oxide in concentrated nitric acid; PbO₂ is reduced to Pb²⁺ forming lead(II) nitrate, while nitrate is reduced to NO₂ gas and water is produced; performed in aqueous conc. HNO₃, often with heating/reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal dehydration of dysprosium(III) hydroxide to dysprosium(III) oxide; heating drives loss of water (→ oxide + H₂O). Typically performed by heating the solid in air at 300‑400 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Redox reaction between nitrogen dioxide and sodium nitrite forming sodium nitrate and nitric oxide. Type: comproportionation/redox. Purpose: in‑situ generation of NO gas and nitrate. Key transformation: NO₂ oxidizes nitrite ion (NO₂⁻) to nitrate (NO₃⁻) while being reduced to NO. Conditions: aqueous solution at 0‑25 °C, neutral to slightly acidic pH; stoichiometric mixing; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidation of hydroquinone to 1,4‑benzoquinone with sodium periodate. Type: periodate oxidation (two‑electron oxidation). Purpose: conversion of a catechol to its quinone form for synthetic or analytical use. Key transformation: removal of two electrons from hydroquinone, formation of the conjugated carbonyl system; periodate reduced to iodate (IO₃⁻). Conditions: aqueous NaIO₄ (0.1‑0.2 M), ambient temperature, pH 7‑8 (often buffered), reaction completes in minutes to an hour; water is the solvent, no additional reagents required.

Oxidation of a thiol to a sulfonic acid using hypochlorite; sodium hypochlorite serves as the oxidant in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature, producing water and sodium chloride as by‑products.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between calcium carbonate and lithium chloride; in aqueous medium the carbonate ion swaps partners to give lithium carbonate (which can precipitate) and soluble calcium chloride, often carried out with heating to improve solubility and drive the equilibrium.

Diazomethane methylation of a carboxylate (diazomethane esterification); purpose is to convert the sodium salt to the methyl ester; the carboxylate attacks the electrophilic carbon of diazomethane, releasing N₂ and forming methyl 3‑methylbutanoate; performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dry ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Acid decomposition of a metal selenide; aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates the selenide anion releasing toxic hydrogen selenide gas while forming soluble beryllium chloride, usually performed under reflux with proper ventilation.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide across an internal alkene; HBr adds Markovnikov‑wise to cis‑2‑hexene to afford 2‑bromohexane, carried out in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or in aqueous HBr at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Hydrolysis of an ester to the corresponding alcohol and acid; aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) or base catalyzes the cleavage of 1‑phenylethyl acetate, yielding phenylethanol and acetic acid, typically refluxed in a water‑ethanol mixture.

Acid‑base metathesis between nitric acid and a metal acetate; in aqueous solution the acetate ions are protonated to give acetic acid while nitrate replaces acetate as the counter‑ion to form manganese(II) nitrate, often performed with slight heating to ensure complete exchange.

Halogen exchange/oxidative fluorination of carbon tetrabromide with fluorine to form dibromodifluoromethane and bromine; purpose is to replace two bromine atoms with fluorine. Fluorine acts as a strong oxidant, abstracting Br atoms and forming Br₂ while inserting F atoms into the carbon centre. Typically conducted at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible vessel, often in liquid HF or a perfluorinated solvent; stringent safety measures and inert (e.g., argon) atmosphere are required.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann coupling of phenol (as phenoxide) with phenyl diazonium chloride to give 4‑phenylphenol, liberating N₂ and forming HCl; usually run in a biphasic system (water/MeCN) at 0‑5 °C for diazonium formation, then warmed with CuI and a base such as NaOH.

Double‑displacement metathesis; purpose is to obtain zinc thiocyanate; key transformation: K⁺ and Zn²⁺ exchange forming Zn(SCN)₂ (often precipitates) and KNO₃ in solution; typical conditions: aqueous mixing at room temperature; no catalyst.

Metal‑acid redox reaction; dissolves neodymium metal as its perchlorate salt with evolution of hydrogen gas; key transformation: 2 Nd + 6 HClO4 → 2 Nd(ClO4)3 + 3 H2; typical conditions: dilute aqueous perchloric acid, temperature from 0 °C to reflux as needed; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 2-bromopyrimidine with ammonia to afford pyrimidin‑2‑amine; analogous to reaction 0 but the bromide is a better leaving group, allowing milder conditions. Key transformation: C–Br bond replaced by C–NH2. Typical conditions: excess NH3 (gas or aqueous) in ethanol or DMF, heated at 60‑100 °C; sometimes a base (e.g., Na2CO3) is added to neutralize HBr formed. No metal catalyst needed.

Reductive amination of indole‑3‑carbaldehyde with N‑ethyl‑N‑methylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride. The aldehyde condenses with the secondary amine to form an iminium ion, which is reduced in situ by NaBH₃CN to give N‑ethyl‑N‑methyl‑1H‑indole‑3‑ethanamine. Purpose: formation of a side‑chain amine on the indole scaffold. Typical conditions: methanol or MeCN solvent, mild acidic buffer (AcOH or NaAc) to promote iminium formation, 0 °C to rt, NaBH₃CN (1.2 eq), reaction time 1–4 h. Catalyst is the hydride donor NaBH₃CN.

Redox decomposition of hydrazine sulfate with formic acid. Hydrazine reduces formic acid, being oxidized to N₂ while formic acid is oxidized to CO₂; water is generated and the sulfate component is protonated to sulfuric acid. Purpose: generation of gaseous CO₂ and N₂ (often used as a safe gas‑generating system). Typical conditions: aqueous mixture, gradual addition of formic acid to a suspension of hydrazine sulfate, gentle heating (50–80 °C) to control gas evolution. No external catalyst.

Type: high‑temperature reduction (hydrogenation). Purpose: preparation of stibine gas (SbH₃). Key transformation: antimony trisulfide (Sb₂S₃) is reduced by H₂ to SbH₃ while sulfur is reduced to H₂S. Typical conditions: dry hydrogen gas passed over solid Sb₂S₃ at 500–800 °C in a quartz tube or furnace; inert carrier gas (Ar or N₂) may be used to avoid oxidation. No solvent; reaction performed in the gas phase; often a metal catalyst (e.g., Ni) can be employed to improve rate.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of copper(I) sulfide; purpose is to exchange anions and form the black Cu2S solid; key transformation: CuI reacts with Na2S to give Cu2S precipitate and NaI in solution; performed in aqueous solution, usually at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature, under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of Cu(I); no catalyst, the product is filtered and washed.

Nickel arsenide (NiAs) undergoes oxidation with oxygen (4 equivalents) to form arsenic trioxide and nickel(II) oxide. This combustion-type reaction occurs under high-temperature conditions, typical of sulfide or arsenide ore roasting.

Beryllium sulfate reacts with sodium azide in a double displacement reaction to form beryllium azide and sodium sulfate. The reaction likely occurs in aqueous solution, driven by solubility differences of the products.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with hydroxide; purpose is to form a primary alcohol while retaining the chloro substituent. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the carbon bearing Br, displacing Br⁻ to give 3‑chloropropanol and NaBr. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux or gentle heating, polar protic solvent (water or water/ethanol mixture); reaction proceeds readily at moderate temperature.

N-chlorosuccinimide chlorinates 2-methyl-4-isothiazolin-3-one at the 5-position via electrophilic substitution. The reaction typically uses a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF) and occurs under mild temperatures without a catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis; base‑catalyzed O‑alkylation of 1,5‑pentanediol with methyl iodide to give the dimethyl ether. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the two hydroxyl groups, generating alkoxides that undergo SN2 attack on MeI. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (DMF, acet or DMSO), ambient to reflux temperature, inert atmosphere; by‑product KI is removed by aqueous work‑up.

Ester hydrolysis (transesterification) of methyl stearate; purpose is to convert the methyl ester into stearic acid while releasing methanol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of the ester and formation of a carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH) often with a co‑solvent such as methanol or ethanol; reaction time several hours.

Transacetalization (acetal formation) of benzaldehyde; dimethoxymethane reacts under acid catalysis to give benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal and formaldehyde; typical conditions mirror reaction 4: catalytic p‑TsOH or HCl in dichloromethane or toluene, ambient to gentle reflux, and azeotropic removal of formaldehyde to shift the reaction forward.

Oxidative cleavage/oxidation of a primary alcohol to a dicarboxylic acid using potassium permanganate. KMnO₄ in aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or KOH) at reflux oxidizes the terminal –CH₂OH of 6‑hydroxyhexanoic acid to –COOH, giving adipic acid; the reaction is usually worked up by acidification and extraction.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of 5‑bromophthalazine; purpose is dehalogenation to obtain the parent phthalazine heterocycle. Key transformation: replacement of the aryl‑Br bond by hydrogen (C–Br → C–H). Typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 % w/w) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature from ambient to reflux.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction between cadmium bromide and sodium hydroxide in water; insoluble cadmium hydroxide precipitates, while sodium bromide remains in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; filtration isolates the Cd(OH)₂ precipitate.

Reductive dehalogenation; purpose is to replace benzylic dibromomethyl groups with methyl groups to afford ortho‑xylene. Key transformation is the reduction of two C–Br bonds to C–H bonds. Typical conditions: zinc metal in glacial acetic acid, reflux for 1–3 h. Acetic acid serves as solvent and proton source; zinc bromide precipitates as by‑product.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between antimony(III) iodide and hydrogen fluoride; purpose is to prepare antimony(III) fluoride and generate hydroiodic acid. Key transformation: exchange of I⁻ for F⁻ (SbI₃ + 3 HF → SbF₃ + 3 HI). Typical conditions: anhydrous HF or aqueous HF solution, low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) in a fluorinated‑compatible vessel; no catalyst required.

Nitrosothiol decomposition of S‑nitroso‑N‑acetylpenicillamine; purpose is controlled release of nitric oxide. Key transformation: cleavage of the S–N=O bond to yield N‑acetylpenicillamine and NO (NO·). Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 20–37 °C; reaction can be accelerated by Cu⁺ ions, light, or mild reducing agents (e.g., ascorbate).

Oxidative combustion of an intermetallic; thorium silicide is exposed to oxygen (air) at elevated temperature, producing thorium dioxide and silicon dioxide as solid oxides; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds readily above ~800 °C; performed in a furnace or flow reactor; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of ammonium formate; purpose: synthesis of formamide; key transformation: loss of water from ammonium formate to produce formamide; typical conditions: heating neat ammonium formate at 150‑200 °C (often under reflux or in a sealed tube); no solvent or catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution of a benzylic bromide; type: SN2 substitution (hydrolysis of alkyl halide); purpose: convert the benzylic bromide to the corresponding benzyl alcohol; key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing bromide to give 4‑chlorobenzyl alcohol and NaBr; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) or NaOH in ethanol/water mixture, temperature ranging from 50 °C to reflux, reaction time of 1–4 h; product isolated by extraction and purification.

Condensation/cyclization of ethylenediamine with cyanogen chloride to form 2‑imidazoline; purpose is heterocycle synthesis. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the diamine on CNCl, intramolecular cyclization, and loss of HCl to give the imidazoline ring. Typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base (triethylamine) to trap the liberated HCl.

Acid‑metal redox reaction producing hydrogen and ammonium aluminum sulfate (alum); is hydrogen gas generation and formation of an alum salt. Key transformation: oxidation of aluminum by sulfuric acid (and reduction of protons and ammonia) to give H₂, while NH₃ is protonated and coordinated to Al³⁺ forming (NH₄)Al(SO₄)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous mixture of concentrated H₂SO₄ and excess NH₃, addition of Al filings or powder, heating under reflux; evolution of H₂ gas is collected, solid alum precipitates on cooling.

Thionation of benzoic acid with Lawesson’s reagent. Lawesson’s reagent (2,4‑bis‑(dimethylamino)‑phosphorodithioic thione) converts the carboxylic carbonyl into a thiocarbonyl, producing thiobenzoic acid and 2,4,6‑trimethylpyridine (collidine) as the organic by‑product from the reagent. Conducted by refluxing benzoic acid with 0.5‑1 equiv Lawesson’s reagent in dry toluene or THF (80‑110 °C) under nitrogen; reaction is typically monitored by TLC and the product isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic substitution (Si–X exchange) used to prepare trimethylsilyl azide; azide anion from potassium azide attacks Me3Si‑Br displacing bromide. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (THF, DMF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; potassium bromide precipitates.

SN2 substitution of 1‑bromohexadecane with ammonia to afford hexadecylamine; usually carried out in liquid ammonia or in a sealed tube with aqueous or alcoholic NH3 at elevated temperature (80–120 °C); the by‑product is ammonium bromide.

Reaction type: Double displacement. Purpose: Precipitation of bismuth carbonate analogously to reaction 3. Key transformations: Bismuth nitrate exchanges ions with potassium carbonate, yielding bismuth carbonate and potassium nitrate. Conditions: Dilute aqueous solution. Solvents: Water.

Redox (reducing) reaction where L‑ascorbic acid reduces ferric chloride to ferrous chloride while being oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid; chloride ions are protonated to give HCl. Usually performed in aqueous solution, ambient temperature, no special catalyst; pH buffered if needed.

Hydride reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol. Acetophenone receives a hydride from KBH₄, affording 1‑phenylethanol while potassium borate is formed as the waste. Conducted in ethanol, methanol, or THF/water mixtures at 0 °C to rt, often under nitrogen; no added catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization; forms neodymium phosphate precipitate and water; commonly executed by adding phosphoric acid to an aqueous suspension of neodymium hydroxide at room temperature, adjusting pH to ~7–8 to promote precipitation; no special catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed Claisen‑type condensation (acylation) of acetone with acetic anhydride to give 2,3‑pentanedione (acetoacetone) and acetic acid as by‑product. Commonly carried out with a weak base such as NaOAc or pyridine, refluxing in pyridine or dry ether, 50–80 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of the diethyl ester back to the dihydroxy dicarboxylic acid; aqueous hydrochloric acid, heating/reflux in a water‑ethanol mixture, liberates ethanol and regenerates the diacid.

Simple acid‑base neutralization; potassium hydroxide deprotonates the hydrochloride salt of urea, releasing free urea, water, and forming potassium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Syn‑dihydroxylation with cold, dilute potassium permanganate; KMnO₄ adds two hydroxyl groups syn to give meso‑2,3‑butanediol; reaction is run in aqueous or acetone/water solution at 0‑5 °C with a low KMnO₄ concentration (≤0.05 M) and neutral or slightly basic pH, stopped as soon as diol forms to avoid over‑oxidation.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide; trimethylamine is converted to trimethylamine N‑oxide. In practice, oxidation is carried out with oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide or peracids (m‑CPBA) in a miscible solvent (e.g., methanol, dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt; molecular oxygen alone is very slow and typically requires a catalyst (e.g., transition‑metal complex) to be effective.

Combustion (oxidation) of 2,2-dimethylheptane; purpose is to convert the hydrocarbon to CO2 and H2O releasing heat. Key transformation: C–H and C–C bonds broken, forming carbonyl carbon in CO2 and oxhydryl groups in H2O. Typical conditions: excess O2, ignition source, flame temperature 800–1500 °C. No solvent or catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation) of phenol with methyl p‑toluenesulfonate; purpose is to form anisole (methyl phenyl ether). Key transformation: phenoxide ion displaces tosylate, producing anisole and p‑toluenesulfonic acid. Typical conditions: phenol deprotonated with base (NaOH, K2CO3), polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF), reflux or gentle heating; reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Metathesis (anion exchange) reaction; used to convert bismuth nitrate to bismuth trichloride; nitrate ions are replaced by chloride, producing nitric acid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, mixing aqueous Bi(NO₃)₃ with conc. HCl; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

The reaction involves a nucleophilic substitution where the phenyl group from phenylmagnesium bromide attacks tributyltin chloride, displacing chloride to form tributyl(phenyl)stannane and magnesium bromide. It occurs under anhydrous conditions with ether solvents (e.g., THF) to stabilize the Grignard reagent.

O‑Methylation (alkylation) of phenol using dimethyl sulfate; 4‑tert‑butylphenol is methylated to 4‑tert‑butyl anisole, producing methyl hydrogen sulfate as by‑product. Typical procedure employs anhydrous pyridine or NaOH as base, dimethyl sulfate added dropwise at 0 °C to rt, in a solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone; reaction is conducted under nitrogen due to the toxic and moisture‑sensitive nature of the methylating agent.

Carbonation of a basic oxide. Lithium oxide reacts with carbon dioxide gas to produce lithium carbonate solid. Conducted at elevated temperatures (200–400 °C) in a flow of CO₂ or under pressure; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis of potassium tartrate with hydrochloric acid to produce tartaric acid and potassium chloride. Type: acid‑base (salt‑acid) reaction. Purpose: liberate tartaric acid. Key transformation: K2C4H4O6 + 2 HCl → C4H6O6 + 2 KCl. Typical conditions: aqueous mixture at ambient temperature, add dilute HCl to a solution of potassium tartrate, stir until pH drops to acidic range. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl chloroacetate with sodium azide; purpose is to install an azido group, yielding ethyl azidoacetate. Key transformation: azide ion replaces chloride. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO), ambient to 50 °C, reaction performed under dry, inert atmosphere; product isolated by aqueous work‑up and extraction.

Grignard addition to a ketone (nucleophilic addition) using methylmagnesium chloride; purpose is to synthesize the tertiary alcohol 2‑phenyl‑2‑propanol. Key transformation: methyl carbanion adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that is protonated on work‑up. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethyl ether or THF, temperature –20 °C to 0 °C during addition, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), followed by aqueous NH4Cl quench.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (chromium(VI) oxidation, Jones oxidation); purpose is to convert acetaldehyde to acetic acid. Key transformation: acetaldehyde is oxidized, chromium reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Typical conditions: aqueous solution of Na2Cr2O7·2H2O with concentrated H2SO4, temperature 0–25 °C, stirring under acidic conditions; reaction quenched with water and extracted.

Acid‑base neutralization (soap formation) of stearic acid with calcium oxide; purpose is to produce calcium stearate, a metal soap. Key transformation: deprotonation of the carboxylic acid and formation of calcium carboxylate, releasing water. Typical conditions: melt or heat mixture (≈150–200 °C) to melt stearic acid, solid CaO added, stirring until a homogeneous molten phase forms; reaction proceeds without solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro‑substituted benzylic alcohol to a β‑amino alcohol. H2 gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO2) in an alcoholic solvent (EtOH or MeOH) at 1–5 atm and 25–50 °C reduces the nitro group to an amine, delivering DL‑phenylalaninol. The reaction is used to prepare chiral amino‑alcohol building blocks.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of arsine; on heating (≈250–300 °C) arsine disproportionates to elemental arsenic and hydrogen gas. Performed in the gas phase by passing arsine over a heated tube in an inert carrier gas; no solvent or catalyst required, although metal surfaces can accelerate the process.

Oxidative deamination/oxidative cleavage of adrenalone with aqueous sodium hypochlorite (bleach). Under basic to neutral pH (pH ≈ 9) at 0 °C to room temperature, NaOCl oxidizes the catecholamine to release ammonia, water, phenylacetaldehyde, and NaCl. The transformation converts the amine functionality into an aldehyde, useful for degrading catecholamines or generating aromatic aldehydes.

Acid‑base salt metathesis to liberate free hydrazine. Sodium carbonate reacts with hydrazine dihydrochloride in water, neutralizing the two HCl equivalents, producing CO₂ gas, H₂O, NaCl and free hydrazine (NH₂NH₂). The reaction is typically performed at ambient temperature with gentle heating to drive off CO₂; no special catalyst is required.

Jones oxidation (chromium(VI) oxidation) of a secondary allylic alcohol to the corresponding α,β‑unsaturated ketone. CrO₃ in aqueous H₂SO₄ (Jones reagent) is added to 1‑hexen‑3‑ol in acetone at 0 °C to rt. The secondary alcohol is oxidized to 1‑hexen‑3‑one with loss of water. This method is a classic protocol for converting secondary alcohols to ketones under mild conditions.

Ester reduction with lithium aluminum hydride; LiAlH4 cleaves the phenyl ester to give phenol and reduces the carbonyl to a primary alcohol, forming 1,2-propanediol. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of melamine with methyl iodide to give altretamine (trimethyl‑melamine) and HI; purpose is synthesis of the anticancer agent altretamine; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) at reflux with a base such as K₂CO₃ or NaH to scavenge HI.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using an acyl chloride. Benzylamine attacks benzoyl chloride in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often in the presence of a base (triethylamine, pyridine) to trap the generated HCl. The reaction affords N‑benzoyl‑benzylamine (an amide) and HCl (neutralized by the base). It is a standard route for preparing secondary amides.

SN2 amination of a primary halide. 2‑Chloroethanol reacts with excess aqueous ammonia (or NH₃ in ethanol) under reflux, giving 2‑aminoethanol (ethanolamine) and HCl. The substitution proceeds with inversion of configuration (not relevant for a primary substrate) and may be facilitated by adding a base (e.g., NaOH) to capture the HCl. Typical solvents are water or ethanol, temperature 80–100 °C.

Halogen exchange (ligand metathesis) of a organotin chloride; used to prepare triphenyl‑tin acetate, a more soluble tin reagent. Sodium acetate displaces chloride, forming NaCl precipitate. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, THF or toluene) with gentle heating (reflux) under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Esterification via acyl‑chloride substitution; conversion of 1‑propanol to propyl butyrate. The alcohol attacks butyryl chloride, releasing HCl which is usually trapped by a base (pyridine or triethylamine). Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an dichloromethane or THF; base acts as both solvent and HCl scavenger.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of an acyl chloride; potassium fluoride supplies fluoride ion that substitutes the chloride of trifluoroacetyl chloride, producing trifluoroacetyl fluoride and potassium chloride. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., 18‑crown‑6) to enhance KF solubility; mild heating (40–80 °C) is typical.

Oxidation – strong oxidant converts the aldehyde group of 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzaldehyde to a carboxylic acid, yielding 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (often in alkaline medium), warm reflux (60‑80 °C) for 1‑3 h; acidic work‑up (HCl) isolates the acid. No special catalyst needed; water or aqueous acetone serves as solvent.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a saturated alkane; n‑hexadecane is converted to 1‑hexadecene with simultaneous release of hydrogen gas. Requires a high‑temperature (≈500–600 °C) flow reactor with Pt/Al₂O₃ as the solid catalyst; inert carrier gas (e.g., N₂ or He) is used and no liquid solvent is involved.

Carbamoylation (acylation) of a phenolic alcohol; chlorphenesin reacts with carbamoyl chloride to form a chlorphenesin carbamate, releasing HCl. The reaction is performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to capture the generated HCl.

SN1 hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl bromide; aqueous NaOH attacks 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpentane, yielding the tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑pentanol and NaBr. The mixture is refluxed in water (or water/ethanol) to ensure complete conversion; the reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate and does not require a catalyst.

Oxidative deamination by monoamine oxidase (MAO); serotonin reacts with molecular oxygen and water, the amine is removed as ammonia, producing 5‑hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde and hydrogen peroxide; the reaction proceeds in aqueous buffer (pH 7.4) with MAO enzyme, typically at 37 °C; no organic solvent needed.

Base‑promoted alkylation/condensation of chloral (trichloroacetaldehyde) with 4‑chlorobenzyl chloride in the presence of potassium carbonate to afford Dicofol, a chlorinated pesticide. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, solid K₂CO₃ as base; work‑up removes inorganic salts and isolates Dicofol.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate) with water to give glycerol and three equivalents of nitric acid. Usually performed by heating an aqueous solution of nitroglycerin with dilute acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH) at 80‑100 °C, followed by neutralisation.

BBr₃‑mediated demethylation of the 6‑methoxy group of Oroxylin A to produce Baicalein, converting an aryl‑methyl ether into a phenol. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; excess BBr₃ is quenched with methanol after the reaction.

Thermal (or acid‑catalyzed) decarboxylation of L‑malic acid to give L‑lactic acid plus CO₂. Typically heated neat or in aqueous sulfuric acid at 150‑200 °C; the reaction proceeds via loss of the β‑carboxyl group.

Cesium hydride reacts violently with water in a redox reaction, producing cesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Hydride ions reduce water molecules, generating hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. This exothermic reaction occurs spontaneously at room temperature and is typically used for hydrogen gas generation. No catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,8‑nonadiene to nonane. Performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney nickel catalyst in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 50 °C; both double bonds are reduced to give the saturated alkane.

Nucleophilic addition (hydration) of water to ketene producing acetic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous solution or by passing ketene gas into water at 0–25 °C; acid or base catalysis can accelerate the reaction but is not required.

Esterification (acylation) of phenol using trifluoroacetic anhydride; purpose is to protect the phenolic hydroxyl as a trifluoroacetate ester. The phenolic O–H attacks the anhydride, forming phenyl trifluoroacetate and releasing one equivalent of trifluoroacetic acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the liberated acid.

Doubledisplacement/neutralization; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes beryllium chloride, precipitating beryllium hydroxide and forming soluble sodium chloride; performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich coupling) of p‑aminobenzoic acid with 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol to afford Meprylcaine. Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group, forming an O‑acyl‑isourea intermediate that reacts with the alcohol to give the ester and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Conducted in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration of glycerol to acrolein. Key transformation: elimination of two water molecules from glycerol. Conditions: concentrated sulfuric acid, high temperature (>280°C).

Neutralization with potassium carbonate; analogous to reaction 3 but using K2CO3; purpose and key transformation are octan‑1‑amine·HCl + K2CO3 → octan‑1‑amine + KCl + CO2↑ + H2O; performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle warming to promote CO2 release; potassium carbonate serves as the base and provides KCl as by‑product.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (benzyne mechanism) converting bromobenzene phenol. Strong base (aqueous NaOH) abstracts a proton adjacent to the bromine, generating benzyne intermediate, which is trapped by hydroxide to give phenoxide that protonates to phenol. Requires high temperature (≈250–300 °C) and often a high‑boiling polar solvent such as ethylene glycol or molten NaOH; sometimes a copper catalyst (Ullmann‑type) is employed to lower temperature.

Phosphorus pentoxide dehydration of pentanamide to pentanenitrile; an amide‑to‑nitrile conversion via removal of water; carried out by heating the amide with excess P2O5, often neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent such as toluene, under anhydrous conditions.

Cyclocondensation of hydrazine with acetylacetone to form 3,5‑dimethylpyrazole. Each carbonyl of the 1,3‑diketone condenses with one –NH₂ of hydrazine, followed by loss of two water molecules and ring closure to give the pyrazole. Typically refluxed in ethanol or methanol (or a mixture with water) for 1–3 h; mild acid (acetic acid) may be added to promote condensation but is not essential.

Azo coupling (diazotization–coupling) to produce 2‑((4‑(dimethylamino)phenyl)diazenyl)benzoic acid. 2‑Aminobenzoic acid is converted in situ to its diazonium salt using Chloramine‑T (N‑chlorosulfonyl‑p‑toluenesulfonamide) under cold acidic conditions (0–5 °C). The diazonium electrophile then undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with N,N‑dimethylaniline, yielding the azo dye. Reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium (HCl or acetate buffer) with the dimethylaniline dissolved in a small amount of a miscible organic solvent (e.g., acetone), maintaining pH ≈ 5–6.

Type: In situ peracid generation (oxidation). Purpose: Produce peracetic acid as an oxidizing agent. Key transformation: Transfer of a peroxide moiety from urea‑hydrogen peroxide to acetic acid, yielding peracetic acid (CH₃COOOH), water, and urea. Typical conditions: Mix acetic acid (often as both reactant and solvent) with solid UHP at 0 – 25 °C under stirring; reaction proceeds without added catalyst, though a trace of mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) can accelerate the rate. Common solvents: neat acetic acid or a mixture of acetic acid with a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane; moisture must be controlled.

Type: Halogen exchange (nucleophilic fluorination). Purpose: Convert a phosphonic dichloride to the corresponding difluoride, a key intermediate for fluorinated phosphonates. Key transformation: Two fluoride ions from potassium fluoride substitute for the two chloride ligands on methylphosphonic dichloride, producing methylphosphonic difluoride and potassium chloride. Typical conditions: Anhydrous, aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, DMF, or THF) under inert atmosphere; KF is used in excess, often with 18‑crown‑6 or a phase‑transfer catalyst to solubilize fluoride; temperature 80–120 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst is required beyond the crown ether/phase‑transfer agent.

Type: Strong nucleophilic reduction of an ester. Purpose: Convert an ester to the corresponding primary alcohol(s). Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of ethyl acetate; subsequent collapse of the alkoxide releases theoxy group as ethanol, and the acyl fragment is reduced to ethanol as well, overall giving two equivalents of ethanol. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF), addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C followed by reflux for 1–3 h under nitrogen. Reaction is quenched carefully with water or diluted acid. No additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution and cyclization leading to imidacloprid; sodium ethoxide deprotonates nitroguanidine, generating a nucleophilic nitrogen that displaces the chloride of 6‑chloro‑3‑pyridylmethyl chloride. Intramolecular condensation then forms the imidazolidine ring, giving the neonicotinoid insecticide imidacloprid. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous ethanol (solvent and base), reflux for several hours under nitrogen; the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up and chromatography.

Type: Acid‑base metathesis (salt formation). Purpose: Convert neodymium triacetate to neodymium chloride, often as a precursor for other neodymium salts. Key transformation: Three equivalents of hydrochloric acid protonate the acetate ligands, releasing acetic acid and forming NdCl₃. Typical conditions: Dissolve neodymium triacetate in minimal water or a polar organic solvent (e.g., methanol), add aqueous HCl dropwise at ambient temperature with stirring; gentle heating (40–60 °C) may be applied to drive off the liberated acetic acid. No catalyst is required.

Type: Photochemical sulfur insertion (radical polysulfide formation). Purpose: Lengthen the sulfur chain on a thioether to give a trisulfide. Key transformation: UV irradiation homolytically cleaves S₈ to generate sulfur radicals; these radicals insert into the C–S bond of methyl‑propyl sulfide, forming a C–S–S–S–CH₃‑propyl trisulfide. Typical conditions: Dissolve the sulfide in an inert, low‑boiling non‑polar solvent (e.g., carbon disulfide, toluene, or hexane), add elemental sulfur (often 2 equiv), purge with nitrogen, and irradiate with UV light (λ ≈ 254 nm) at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20–40 °C) for several hours. No additional catalyst is required.

Salt metathesis/acid–base reaction; converts scandium nitrate to scandium fluoride while generating nitric acid; performed by treating anhydrous scandium nitrate with liquid or gaseous HF, typically at 0–25 °C under anhydrous conditions; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition; used to generate sulfur trioxide gas and solid aluminum oxide from aluminum sulfate by; key transformation breakdown of Al2(SO4)3 into Al2O3 and SO3; typically carried out at temperatures above 600 °C in a furnace under dry air; no solvent required, reaction proceeds in the solid state.

High‑temperature chlorination of a metal carbide; employed to convert tungsten carbide into volatile tungsten hexachloride and carbon tetrachloride; the carbon atom of WC is fully chlorinated to CCl4 while tungsten is oxidized to WCl6; performed by passing dry chlorine gas over WC at 400–600 °C in a quartz or nickel reactor; inert atmosphere (argon) may be used; no liquid solvent, but the products are collected by condensation.

Fluorine‑transfer redox reaction; xenon difluoride oxidizes antimony trifluoride to antimony pentafluoride, releasing elemental xenon; key transformation is increase of Sb oxidation state from +3 to +5 and reduction of XeF2 to Xe; carried out under anhydrous conditions at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in a non‑coordinating solvent such as dry acetonitrile or liquid HF; inert atmosphere required; no additional catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein-type halide exchange); iodide ion displaces chloride in 2‑chloroethanol to give 2‑iodoethanol and sodium chloride; reaction proceeds best in a polar aprotic solvent that precipitates NaCl, most commonly acetone; reflux or gentle heating may be used to accelerate; inert atmosphere is optional.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis/decomposition of N‑nitrosoguanidine; hydroxide attacks the nitroso‑guanidine moiety, yielding hydroxyguanidine and nitrite ion while consuming one water molecule; typically performed in aqueous NaOH solution at 0–25 °C to avoid excessive decomposition; water is the solvent; reaction is used in analytical chemistry to break down nitrosamines for quantification.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of difluoroacetic acid with sodium carbonate, producing sodium difluoroacetate, carbon dioxide and water; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of thorium nitrate to thorium dioxide; a solid‑phase decomposition where Th(NO₃)₄ yields ThO₂ solid, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas; performed by heating the nitrate to 700‑900 °C in an open furnace; no solvent or catalyst.

Halogenation/redox reaction; conversion of zinc phosphide to zinc chloride and phosphorus trichloride; zinc phosphide is exposed to dry chlorine gas, often under reflux, to replace phosphide with chloride and generate PCl3; requires anhydrous conditions and heating (typically 200–300 °C); reactions are carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor without solvent or catalyst.

Reductive amination of pentanal with ammonia (often supplied as NH3·HCl) followed by protonation to give pentylamine hydrochloride; typically catalyzed by a heterogeneous metal (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or Pt) under hydrogen pressure (1–5 atm) in ethanol or methanol at 50–100 °C; after reduction excess HCl is added to form the hydrochloride salt.

Oxidation of a phenol to a quinone using periodic acid; purpose is to produce p‑benzoquinone from hydroquinone; key transformation: HIO4 oxidizes the two hydroxy groups to a conjugated diketone, yielding iodic acid and water; typical conditions: aqueous medium at room temperature, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as acetone; no external catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between aqueous zinc sulfate and barium nitrate, yielding insoluble barium sulfate solid and soluble zinc nitrate; performed in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a hydrazo compound to an azo compound; purpose is to convert hydrazobenzene to azobenzene by removal of two hydrogen atoms; sodium hypochlorite acts as oxidant, converting the –NH–NH– linkage to an –N=N– double bond; reaction is usually performed in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, with pH buffered mildly basic; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of N‑(4‑chlorobenzyl)piperazine with 2‑pyridylmethyl chloride followed by salt formation with hydrogen chloride to afford chlorcyclizine hydrochloride; generally conducted in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane, acetonitrile or THF with a base (e.g., triethylamine) at 0 °C to rt, then HCl gas or aqueous HCl is introduced to produce the hydrochloride salt.

Halide exchange/metathesis between mercuric chloride and calcium diiodide, giving mercuric iodide (sparingly soluble) and calcium chloride; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium, often with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed Knoevenagel/aldol condensation of acetaldehyde with 3,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde in the presence of NaOH, forming the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde (2E‑3‑(3,4‑dihydroxyphenyl)prop‑2‑enal) and water; typical conditions use ethanol/water as solvent, catalytic NaOH (≈10 % of aldehyde), temperature from 0 °C to reflux, followed by acid work‑up; no additional catalyst needed.

Reduction (hydrogen reduction) of zinc oxide to metallic zinc. Purpose: extract zinc metal from its oxide. Key transformation: ZnO + H2 → Zn(s) + H2O; Zn(II) reduced to 0, H2 oxidized to +1. Typical conditions: high temperature (400–500 °C) under a flow of dry hydrogen gas; sometimes a small amount of carbon or a metallic catalyst (e.g., Cu) is used to enhance reduction. No solvent.

Metal‑water reaction (hydrogen evolution); thorium metal reacts with hot water or steam to give thorium(IV) hydroxide (Th(OH)4) and hydrogen gas. Reaction proceeds under reflux or with steam at temperatures above 100 °C; typically performed in aqueous medium without added catalysts.

Radical hydrogen‑atom transfer (propagation): the ethynyl radical reacts with molecular hydrogen, abstracting a hydrogen atom to regenerate acetylene and produce a new hydrogen atom radical. This step closes the radical chain and occurs under the same high‑temperature or photolytic conditions as the previous step; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation); chromic acid (generated from CrO3 and conc. H2SO4) oxidizes 4‑methylbenzaldehyde to 4‑methylbenzoic acid. Conditions: Jones reagent prepared fresh in acetone, reaction temperature 0 °C to rt, reaction time 30 min–1 h, followed by quenching with isopropanol or aqueous sodium bisulfite. Solvent: dry acetone; acidic medium is essential.

Electrophilic sulfonation of camphor using fuming sulfuric acid (oleum) to afford dl‑10‑camphorsulfonic acid and water; performed neat or with excess oleum, typically refluxing at 100‑150 °C under anhydrous conditions; no additional solvent or catalyst required, the reaction proceeds via electrophilic attack of the SO₃ component on the camphor framework.

Hydrolysis of chlorotrifluorosilane (SiClF₃) with water to give hydrochloric acid, hydrofluoric acid and silicic acid (Si(OH)₄); a straightforward aqueous hydrolysis carried out at ambient temperature or mild heating; water acts as both solvent and reactant, no catalyst needed.

Diazotization of 3‑ethyl aniline with sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid followed by hydrolysis of the resulting diazonium salt to 3‑ethyl phenol, releasing nitrogen gas; low temperature (0‑5 °C) is required for formation of the diazonium intermediate, then warming to 25‑40 °C for hydrolysis; aqueous acidic medium is used, sodium nitrite provides the nitrosating agent.

Acid‑base neutralization of barium carbonate with hydrochloric acid forming barium chloride and carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to carbon dioxide and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without catalyst, the evolution of CO₂ drives it to completion.

Metathesis (anion exchange) between hydrochloric acid and methylamine nitrate yielding methylammonium chloride and nitric acid; a simple acid–base salt swap carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; mixing the two aqueous solutions effect the exchange, no additional reagents required.

Esterification (Fischer esterification) of phenol with furan‑2‑carboxylic acid to give phenyl furan‑2‑carboxylate and water; typically performed under reflux with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) in a non‑aqueous solvent such as toluene or benzene, often using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water and drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Metathesis (acid‑base salt exchange) in which nitrate ions replace acetate ions on chromium(III); aqueous mixing of Cr(OAc)3 with excess HNO3 yields Cr(NO3)3 in solution and liberates acetic acid; carried out at ambient temperature in water, no special catalyst required.

Silyl exchange (trans‑silylation) reaction; purpose is to redistribute trimethylsilyl groups between a disilylated alkyne and a terminal alkyne to obtain monosilylated acetylene derivatives. Key transformation: one TMS group is transferred from bis(trimethylsilyl)acetylene to phenylacetylene, yielding trimethylsilylacetylene and phenyl(trimethylsilyl)acetylene. Typical conditions: strong base such as n‑BuLi or NaNH₂ in THF at –78 °C to 0 °C, or catalytic fluoride (TBAF) in THF; inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required beyond the base.

Double‑replacement precipitation reaction forming insoluble antimony(III) selenide; aqueous antimony nitrate reacts with sodium selenide to precipitate Sb2Se3 while sodium nitrate remains in solution; typically performed in water under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of Se2‑, with vigorous stirring and filtration of the black precipitate.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the amide N‑acetylglycine to regenerate glycine and acetic acid; heated aqueous HCl (or alternative acid) at reflux, sometimes with a small amount of inorganic catalyst such as NaCl to enhance ionic strength; the reaction proceeds to completion with removal of the volatile acetic acid if desired.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of N‑methylcarbamic acid to methyl isocyanate and water; achieved by heating the carbamic acid (often in the gas phase or in a sealed tube) above its decomposition temperature (~150 °C), no solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction is rapid and exothermic, producing methyl isocyanate gas.

Hydrolysis of zirconium tetraiodide to zirconium dioxide and hydrogen iodide; zirconium(IV) iodide is reacted with excess water (often under reflux) in a sealed vessel, producing solid ZrO2 and gaseous HI; the reaction is generally carried out in an inert atmosphere to avoid unwanted side reactions, and the HI can be trapped in an alkaline solution.

Redox (acidic reduction) reaction; cobalt(III) oxide is reduced by hydrochloric acid, yielding cobalt(II) chloride, chlorine gas, and water. Performed in aqueous HCl, often warmed to accelerate; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base decomposition of sulfite; aqueous ammonium sulfite is protonated by sulfuric acid, yielding ammonium sulfate, water, and gaseous sulfur dioxide; carried out at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to control SO₂ evolution; water is the solvent; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary chloroacetate by hydroxylamine; purpose is synthesis of aminooxyacetic acid. The chlorine atom is displaced by the N‑O‑H group of hydroxylamine, giving aminooxyacetic acid and releasing HCl. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol/water) at reflux or room temperature in the presence of a base such as Na2CO3 or pyridine to neutralize HCl; no catalyst required.

Redox acid‑mediated decomposition of sodium chlorite with concentrated sulfuric acid; purpose is generation of chlorine dioxide gas for bleaching or disinfection. Chlorite (Cl+3) is oxidized to ClO2 (+4) while a portion is reduced to chloride (Cl‑). The overall stoichiometry yields chlorine dioxide, sodium chloride, sodium bisulfate and water. Conducted in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) with careful, slow addition of acid to control gas evolution; no additional catalyst, water is the solvent.

Hydrolysis of tris(trimethylsilyl)phosphine; water cleaves the Si‑P bonds to release phosphine (PH3) and forms three equivalents of trimethylsilanol (Me3SiOH); reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; usually carried out in aqueous or mixed organic‑aqueous solvent.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation) of guaiacol with methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate. K2CO3 deprotonates the phenolic OH to give the phenoxide, which attacks CH3I to form a second methoxy group, delivering veratrole (1,2‑dimethoxybenzene) and potassium iodide as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux (~80 °C), under nitrogen; base is K2CO3, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution on phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3) by dimethylamine, with pyridine acting as an HCl scavenger. Dimethylamine attacks the phosphorus center, displacing one chloride and forming N,N‑dimethylaminophosphoryl dichloride; the liberated HCl protonates pyridine to give pyridinium chloride. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere; excess pyridine is used as base, no external catalyst.

Combustion reaction; oxidizes hydrogen selenide with oxygen to form selenium dioxide and water; involves complete oxidation of H2Se to SeO2 under flame or elevated temperature conditions; oxygen serves as the oxidizing agent; non-aqueous environment.

Oxidation‑reduction (redox) reaction; periodate oxidizes bromide to molecular bromine while being reduced to iodate (often not shown). Purpose: in‑situ generation of Br2. Key transformation: Br⁻ → Br₂; IO₄⁻ → IO₃⁻. Typically carried out in aqueous solution containing excess HCl, at room temperature or with mild heating. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature combustion (incomplete oxidation) of elemental carbon with oxygen to produce carbon monoxide. Two moles of carbon react with one mole of O2 to give two moles of CO, a redox process where carbon is oxidized from 0 to +2 and oxygen reduced from 0 to –2. Industrially performed in a furnace or gasifier at temperatures above 700 °C with limited oxygen to avoid full oxidation to CO2; may be catalyzed by iron or other metal surfaces; no solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed ester cleavage (hydrohalogenolysis) with hydrogen bromide; purpose is to convert the alkyl acetate into the corresponding alkyl bromide while generating acetic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of bromide on the carbonyl carbon of cyclopropyl acetate, followed by C–O bond cleavage to give cyclopropyl bromide and acetate. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous HBr, reflux temperature (≈80‑100 °C). Common solvent: neat HBr or a polar protic solvent such as glacial acetic acid; reaction performed in sealed tube or under reflux.

Halogen exchange (radical substitution) reaction; dichlorofluoromethane reacts with iodine monochloride to replace a chlorine atom by iodine, producing chlorofluoroiodomethane and liberating chlorine gas. Usually performed under UV irradiation or photochemical conditions in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dry dichloromethane, with the reaction mixture kept cold to collect Cl₂ gas.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction forming a metal acrylate salt. Purpose is to exchange the nitrate anion of zinc nitrate for the acrylate anion, producing zinc acrylate and sodium nitrate. Key transformation: Zn²⁺ pairs with two acrylate anions while Na⁺ pairs with nitrate. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water, stir at room temperature or mild heating (≤50 °C); no special catalyst required. The product zinc acrylate may precipitate and is isolated by filtration, while the sodium nitrate remains in solution.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification with ethanol: 2‑ethylhexyl acetate reacts with excess ethanol to afford ethyl acetate and 2‑ethylhexanol. Similar mechanism to reaction 1, using ethanol as solvent and reactant. Typical conditions are refluxing ethanol (78 °C) with catalytic NaOEt or KOH (1–5 mol %). Reaction time ranges from 1–6 h depending on temperature.

Palladium‑catalyzed Hiyama cross‑coupling of an aryl bromide with an aryl trimethylsilane to form a tri‑aryl (p‑terphenyl). is the construction of a C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond between 4‑bromobiphenyl and phenyltrimethylsilane. Key transformations: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into the C–Br bond, transmetalation activated by fluoride (PdF₂ supplies fluoride), and reductive elimination to give the biaryl product. Typical conditions: Pd(II) source (e.g., PdCl₂, Pd(OAc)₂) with a fluoride activator (CsF or KF), polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, THF, or dioxane, temperature 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere. No additional ligands are strictly required, but phosphine ligands are often employed to improve yields.

Strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄). Purpose is to convert oleic acid (a long‑chain unsaturated fatty acid) into oleyl alcohol. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming an aldehyde intermediate that is further reduced to the alcohol. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C followed by reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours under nitrogen. Reaction is quenched cautiously with water, then aqueous work‑up to isolate the oil‑like oleyl alcohol.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation forming thallium(I) sulfide. Purpose is to generate the insoluble thallium sulfide salt while producing sodium acetate as a soluble by‑product. Key transformation: Tl⁺ ions exchange acetate for sulfide ions, yielding Tl₂S solid. Typical conditions: dissolve thallium(I) acetate and sodium sulfide separately in water, mix at ambient temperature or mild heating (≤40 °C) with vigorous stirring; the black Tl₂S precipitates and is filtered. Because thallium compounds are highly toxic, the reaction is performed in a fume hood with appropriate protective equipment.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange cations to obtain magnesium lactate and sodium chloride. Typically performed by dissolving MgCl2 and sodium lactate in water and mixing at room temperature with stirring; both products remain soluble, no precipitation, and the reaction proceeds without a catalyst.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; calcium hydroxide displaces silver from silver sulfate, forming insoluble calcium sulfate and silver oxide with water as a by‑product. Usually carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating (30–60 °C) to improve solubility of the reactants; the mixture is filtered to isolate the solid Ag2O and CaSO4 precipitates.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of neodymium(III) sulfate; heating decomposes the sulfate to neodymium(III) oxide while releasing sulfur trioxide gas. Conducted at high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) in a furnace under an inert or oxidizing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation acid‑base reaction; oxalic acid reacts with beryllium nitrate to precipitate beryllium oxalate and liberate nitric acid. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the insoluble BeC2O4 is filtered off, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; aqueous hydrogen chloride protonates melperone to give melperone hydrochloride (the pharmaceutically useful salt). Conducted in water with dilute to concentrated HCl at 0–25 °C; stirring ensures complete conversion, no additional reagents required.

Type: formation of a metal carbonyl (coordination complex). Purpose: generate volatile nickel carbonyl for purification, transport, or further processing. Key transformation: elemental nickel reacts with carbon monoxide gas to form Ni(CO)4, nickel remains in oxidation state zero coordinated by four CO ligands. Typical conditions: 50‑150 °C, 1‑5 atm CO, inert atmosphere, gas‑phase in a sealed steel vessel. Common solvents/catalysts: none required.

Redox (reduction‑oxidation) reaction; concentrated hydrochloric acid reduces vanadium(V) oxide to vanadium(III) chloride while chloride ions are oxidized to chlorine gas, with water formed as a by‑product. Typically carried out by heating V2O5 in excess HCl (often reflux) in a glass reactor; the reaction is vigorous and evolves Cl2 gas; no external catalyst is needed.

Redox oxidation of 2,6-dimethoxyhydroquinone to 2,6-dimethoxy-1,4-benzoquinone using ferric chloride as oxidant; ferric (Fe III) is reduced to ferrous chloride (Fe II) and HCl is liberated. Typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium, often water or water/ethanol at ambient temperature, without additional catalysts. Purpose: preparation of a quinone from a hydroquinone.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of the primary alcohol group in 2‑ethoxyethanol with chloride to afford 2‑chloroethyl ethyl ether (Lucas‑type reaction). Conducted with concentrated HCl (sometimes with ZnCl₂ as a Lewis acid) at 50‑80 °C in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane. Purpose: synthesis of a chloro‑alkyl ether from an alcohol.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of 3‑methylbutanamide to the primary amine 3‑methylbutylamine. Performed in dry diethyl ether or THF under inert atmosphere, refluxed, then carefully quenched with water or dilute acid. Purpose: conversion of an amide functional group to an amine.

Acid‑catalyzed Boc deprotection; purpose is to regenerate the free amine. Trifluoroacetic acid protonates the carbamate, causing loss of CO₂ and isobutene (isobutylene) and yielding pyrrolidine. Usually performed at rt in neat TFA or TFA/DCM (1–5 equiv) for 0.5–2 h.

Salt metathesis (acidification); potassium tetrachloroaurate(III) dissolved in aqueous hydrochloric acid yields tetrachloroauric acid (HAuCl₄) and potassium chloride; essentially an ion‑exchange reaction; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination (using I3⁻). Purpose: introduce an iodine ortho to the hydroxyl group of phenol. Key transformation: transfer of an iodine atom from the triiodide ion to the aromatic ring, giving 2‑iodophenol; the remaining iodide combines with tetrabutylammonium to form the salt, and elemental iodine is liberated. Typical conditions: room‑temperature stirring in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane; stoichiometric TBAT (tetrabutylammonium triiodide) is used, no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of imidazole to give 4‑nitroimidazole Carried out in a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 0‑5 °C, then gently warmed; sulfuric acid serves as a dehydrating and protonating medium. Purpose: introduction of a nitro substituent onto the imidazole ring.

Nucleophilic aromatic of 9‑chloroacridine by aqueous ammonia to generate 9‑aminoacridine, followed by protonation with hydrochloric acid to afford the hydrochloride salt. Typical conditions: reflux aqueous NH₃ (or NH₄OH) for several hours, then addition of conc. HCl and cooling to precipitate 9‑aminoacridine hydrochloride. Solvent: water or ethanol. Purpose: synthesis of the pharmacologically useful amine salt.

Simple acid‑base salt formation between dazoxiben (a basic amine) and hydrochloric acid to produce dazoxiben hydrochloride. Usually executed by dissolving dazoxiben in methanol or ethanol and adding aqueous HCl at room temperature, followed by evaporation or crystallization of the salt. Purpose: preparation of the pharmaceutical hydrochloride salt.

(nucleophilic substitution) Reaction to form tetra-n-butylstannane; chloride substitution with n-butyl lithiation. Involves replacement of chloride by n-butyl groups. Typically conducted in ether solvents (e.g., THF) at low temperatures.

Carbonylative esterification (Pd‑catalyzed carbonylation). An aryl iodide undergoes oxidative addition to Pd(0) generated from Pd(OAc)₂, inserts CO, and is methanolated to give the methyl ester. Typical conditions: 5–10 bar CO, Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), phosphine ligand (e.g., PPh₃), triethylamine base, methanol as solvent, 80–120 °C, 4–12 h.

Double‑displacement precipitation. Zinc chloride reacts with sodium chromate to exchange anions, forming sodium chloride in solution and a yellow precipitate of zinc chromate. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to aid crystallisation; no catalyst needed.

Amide‑formation (Weinreb amide synthesis) using carbonyldiimidazole activation. Acetic acid is first activated by CDI to give an acyl‑imidazole intermediate, which then couples with N‑O‑dimethylhydroxylamine to afford N‑methoxy‑N‑methyl acetamide (a Weinreb amide) while releasing imidazole. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; CDI serves as the coupling reagent, no external catalyst required.

Combined azide and ester reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH4 reduces the azide to an amine and the methyl ester to an alcohol, yielding 2‑amino‑1‑propanol (a β‑amino alcohol). Reaction is run in dry ether (THF or Et2O) under inert atmosphere, at 0 °C then reflux for 1–3 h; quenched cautiously with water then acid.

Acid–base protonation (salt metathesis); HCl protonates the sulfide ion of sodium methyl sulfide, converting the –SCH3⁻ anion to methyl mercaptan (CH₃SH) and forming NaCl; typically performed in aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C, often with ice cooling to control odor; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base gas‑generation (dry HCl production). Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates chloride from lithium chloride, displacing HCl gas and forming lithium sulfate. The reaction is done without solvent in a dry glass apparatus, often with gentle heating to drive off HCl; no catalyst is employed.

Direct synthesis of terbium phosphide; combination reaction for preparing the binary phosphide. Key transformation: 2 Tb + P₄ → 2 TbP (or Tb + P → TbP). Performed by heating elemental terbium and phosphorus vapor together at 600–900 °C in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Hydrolytic decomposition of an aryl chloroformate back to the phenol; water attacks the carbonyl of 3‑methylphenyl chloroformate, releasing CO₂ and HCl and regenerating 3‑methylphenol; usually performed at 0 °C to rt in a biphasic water/organic mixture (e.g., aqueous NaHCO₃ or Na₂CO₃ buffer with ether or acetone) to capture the acid byproduct; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) methylation of a carboxylate (Williamson‑type esterification). Sodium 2‑methylbutanoate attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give methyl 2‑methylbutanoate and sodium iodide. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetone at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base displacement (precipitation) reaction; solid barium peroxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, forming insoluble barium sulfate and liberating hydrogen peroxide in solution; laboratory preparation of H₂O₂; carried out at 0–25 °C in aqueous medium; stoichiometric sulfuric acid, water as solvent.

Oxidative conversion of TEMPO‑hydroxy precursor to the TEMPO radical. Two equivalents of 4‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine are oxidized by one equivalent of sodium percarbonate (a solid source of hydrogen peroxide) to generate the stable nitroxyl radical (TEMPO), with water and sodium carbonate as by‑products. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic media at ambient to slightly elevated temperature, under basic conditions; the peroxide acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–carbonate neutralization; thallium carbonate reacts with aqueous hydrobromic acid to afford thallium(I) bromide, carbon dioxide, and water; typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst; carbon dioxide evolves as gas.

Acid digestion and double displacement; used in the chromyl chloride test to detect chromate ions. Concentrated HCl reacts with solid barium chromate on heating, forming water, soluble barium chloride and volatile chromyl chloride (CrO2Cl2) which condenses as a red fume. Typically performed in a dry test tube with excess conc. HCl, no additional solvent, and gentle heat.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal acetate; employed to generate metallic platinum from platinum(II) acetate. Under a flow of H2 gas at 200–300 °C (often in a sealed tube or refluxing solvent such as ethanol or acetic acid), Pt(OAc)2 is reduced to platinum metal while the acetate ligands are protonated to give acetic acid. No external catalyst beyond the Pt precursor is required.

Aqueous metathesis (double‑replacement) precipitation; used to isolate cadmium as an insoluble oxalate. Solutions of ammonium oxalate and cadmium chloride are mixed at ambient temperature, yielding soluble ammonium chloride and a pale‑yellow precipitate of cadmium oxalate. The reaction proceeds in water with stirring; no heating or catalyst is needed.

Redox reaction between permanganate and hydrochloric acid; a classical method for generating chlorine gas while converting Mn(VII) to manganese dioxide. Concentrated HCl (typically 6 M or higher) is added to an aqueous solution of sodium permanganate at room temperature or with mild heating. The mixture produces MnO2 as a brown solid, water, sodium chloride, and Cl2 gas that evolves from the solution. The reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium; no additional catalyst is required.

Aqueous precipitation (metathesis) forming silver oxide; used to separate silver ions from a basic solution. Mixing aqueous silver nitrate with barium hydroxide at room temperature gives water, soluble barium nitrate and a brown precipitate of Ag2O. The reaction occurs in water under neutral to mildly alkaline conditions; no heating or catalyst is necessary.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; converts 1,2‑dichloroethyl acetate to acetic acid and 1,2‑dichloroethanol. The ester is treated with water (often with a catalytic amount of mineral acid such as H2SO4) and heated under reflux. The carbonyl carbon is attacked by water, leading to cleavage of the acetate group and formation of the corresponding alcohol and acetic acid. Typical solvent is the aqueous acidic medium; no special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Acid–base neutralization; ammonia (base) reacts with lactic acid (acid) to form the ammonium salt ammonium lactate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid–base metathesis; hydrobromic acid protonates acetate ions of nickel(II) acetate, yielding acetic acid and nickel(II) bromide Conducted in water, often with gentle heating or reflux; no additional reagents needed.

Combustion‑type solid‑state synthesis (glycine‑fuelled redox); glycine acts as a reducing fuel while barium nitrate and iron(III) nitrate serve as oxidizers, producing gaseous CO₂, N₂, H₂O and solid barium ferrite (BaFe₁₂O₁₉). Carried out by thoroughly mixing the powders and heating to 800–1000 °C in a furnace under air; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Metathesis/precipitation to afford a metal selenide; chromium(III) chloride for side ions from sodium selenide, forming NaCl and chromium selenide (e.g.,₂Se₃). Usually performed under inert atmosphere in dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or liquid ammonia at elevated temperature; moisture must be excluded.

Lactone aminolysis (ring‑opening amidation); γ‑butyrolactone reacts with cyclohexylamine, the amine attacks the carbonyl, opening the lactone ring and forming N‑cyclohexyl‑2‑pyrrolidone with loss of water. Conducted at 150–200 °C, often solvent‑free or in toluene, with water removed by a Dean‑Stark trap; no catalyst is generally required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification. Purpose: produce methyl formate from propyl formate while liberating 1‑propanol. Key transformation: methoxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release propoxide and give methyl formate. Typical conditions: sodium methoxide (1–2 equiv) in dry methanol, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen. Reaction often performed neat or in MeOH as solvent; work‑up involves aqueous quench and removal of 1‑propanol.

Acid–base neutralization reaction; hydrochloric acid protonates ammonium oxalate, converting the oxalate ion to oxalic acid while forming ammonium chloride salts. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the oxalic acid can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization, and the ammonium chloride remains dissolved.

Imine hydrolysis; converts 2‑propanimine (an imine) into the carbonyl compound propan‑2‑one (acetone) and ammonia; key transformation is addition of water across the C=N bond followed by cleavage to give a ketone and NH₃; typically performed in aqueous solution under mild acidic (e.g., HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) catalysis at ambient temperature.
