Performed in dilute aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C to limit HCN loss; no catalyst required, but the reaction is often quenched with a weak base to neutralize HOBr.

Oxidative conversion of elemental rhenium to perrhenate (redox reaction). Purpose is to generate sodium perrhenate (NaReO₄). Key transformation: Re⁰ is oxidized by H₂O₂ in basic medium (NaOH) to Re(VII) as the perrhenate anion, with simultaneous reduction of H₂O₂ to water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, gradual addition of H₂O₂ (30 % w/w) to a suspension of finely powdered Re metal, temperature maintained 25–60 °C, stirring until gas evolution ceases. No external catalyst; peroxide acts as oxidant.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer ether synthesis; purpose is to form hexafluoroisopropyl methyl ether. Key transformation: protonation of hexafluoroisopropanol by H₂SO₄ creates a good leaving group (water), allowing nucleophilic attack by methanol and loss of water to give the ether. Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ (≈10–20 % v/v) as catalyst, HFIP serving as both reactant and solvent, reaction temperature 0–40 °C to avoid side reactions, short reaction time (minutes to an hour). Water is generated as the sole by‑product; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation (esterification) of ethanol with ethyl hydrogen sulfate to form diethyl sulfate and water. The reaction proceeds by nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the sulfonyl group, displacing a proton. Conducted at 80–120 °C under reflux, often with excess ethyl hydrogen sulfate to drive equilibrium; no additional catalyst required, and the reaction mixture can be azeotropically distilled to remove water.

Nucleophilic substitution (al to alkyl bromide) using phosphorus tribromide; converts 2‑methylpentan‑2‑ol into 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpentane while generating phosphorous acid; typically performed under anhydrous conditions, 0 °C to room temperature, in inert organic solvents such as dry dichloromethane or diethyl ether; no external catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (hydration) of a primary isocyanide to a formamide; water adds across the C≡N bond of n‑butyl isocyanide yielding n‑butylformamide; generally carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute HCl) with gentle heating (≈50–80 °C).

The reaction is a hydrogenation where the (E)-hex-3-enal functionality is reduced using hydrogen gas. Palladium on carbon acts as a catalyst, converting the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde into the fully saturated aldehyde (hexanal). Reaction conditions typically involve hydrogen gas under atmospheric pressure in solvents like ethanol or ethyl acetate at moderate temperatures.

Acid–base double‑displacement/decomposition reaction; boric acid reacts with potassium carbonate to produce potassium borate, carbon dioxide, and water; carried out by heating a solid mixture or suspending the reagents in water and gently warming to drive off CO₂.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an aryl bromide; 4‑bromoanisole is reduced with H₂ in the presence of palladium on carbon to give anisole, removing the bromine atom; performed at ambient to 50 °C under 1–5 atm H₂ in solvents such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate.

Amide hydrolysis (deacetylation): 2‑[acetyl(methyl)amino]acetic acid is hydrolyzed with water (often under acidic or basic aqueous conditions and heat) to regenerate 2‑(methylamino)acetic acid and produce acetic acid as by‑product.

Free‑radical autoxidation (air oxidation) of isopropylbenzene; molecular oxygen adds to the benzylic position forming cumene hydroperoxide via a radical chain mechanism; conducted at elevated temperature (≈120–150 °C) under O₂ or air, often without solvent or in a hydrocarbon medium, sometimes initiated by a radical initiator.

Hydrolysis of methylazoxymethanol acetate to methylazoxymethanol. Purpose: deprotect the acetate protecting group to liberate the free hydroxyl functionality. Key transformation: acetate ester → primary alcohol, producing acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature or mild heating; can be performed under neutral, mildly acidic (e.g., dilute HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions; water serves as the solvent; no special catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction; ammonium sulfide reacts with thallium(I) bromide in aqueous solution to precipitate thallium(I) sulfide (Tl₂S) and form soluble ammonium bromide; carried out at room temperature with stirring, water as the solvent.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose: exchange of counter‑ion to generate the ionic liquid acetate; key transformation: proton transfer from acetic acid to the imidazolium hydroxide, yielding water and 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium acetate; typical conditions: room temperature, often performed neat or in a minimal amount of inert solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) under an inert atmosphere; common solvents/catalysts: none required, the ionic liquid itself serves as both reactant and medium.

Neutralization of a carboxylic acid: 2‑methylbutanoic acid is dissolved in water and treated with aqueous NaOH at 0 °C to room temperature, forming sodium 2‑methylbutanoate and water; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds to completion.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: preparation of insoluble magnesium carbonate and soluble cesium chloride; key transformation: exchange of carbonate and chloride ligands between cesium carbonate and magnesium chloride; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature; common solvents/catalysts: water as solvent, no catalyst needed; the precipitated MgCO₃ is filtered and washed.

Zinc/ammonium chloride reduction of a nitroarene (Bechamp‑type reduction); purpose: convert the nitro group of 1‑nitroanthracene to an amino group; key transformation: nitro → amine via electron transfer from Zn metal in the presence of NH₄Cl, generating Zn²⁺ and NH₃; typical conditions: reflux in ethanol‑water mixture (1:1) or ethanol alone, 1–3 h, under nitrogen; common solvents/catalysts: ethanol (or ethanol/water), ammonium chloride acts as a proton source and facilitator of Zn reduction.

Acidification/precipitation of silicate; purpose: isolate silica from sodium silicate solution; key transformation: protonation of silicate species by H₂SO₄, forming SiO₂ solid and sodium sulfate; typical conditions: aqueous medium, gradual addition of concentrated H₂SO₄ at 0–25 °C followed by heating to 60–80 °C to promote silica gel formation; common solvents/catalysts: water as solvent, no catalyst.

Reaction type: alcoholysis (transesterification). Purpose: exchange the butyl ester for a methyl ester, a common step in biodiesel synthesis or flavor ester preparation. Key transformation: methanol attacks the carbonyl of butyl octanoate under catalytic conditions, forming methyl octanoate and releasing butan‑1‑ol. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol (10–20 equiv) with 0.5–1 wt % acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, at 60–70 °C for 2–4 h; removal of butanol (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) drives the equilibrium forward. Methanol serves as both reactant and solvent; acid catalyst is required.

Gas‑solid redox (chalcogenide synthesis); used to prepare molybdenum diselenide (MoSe2), a layered transition‑metal dichalcogenide. Mo(VI) in MoO3 is reduced by H2Se, oxygen is displaced as water and excess selenium is oxidized to SeO2. Typical conditions: pass H2Se gas over MoO3 at 400–600 °C in a sealed quartz tube or tube furnace under inert gas (Ar or N2). No solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidative digestion with concentrated nitric acid; purpose: oxidize iron(II) selenide to soluble iron(III) nitrate and volatile selenium dioxide while generating nitrogen oxides; key transformation: nitrate ion acts as oxidant, converting Se²⁻ to SeO₂ and Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, with reduction of HNO₃ to NO₂ and water; typical conditions: excess conc. HNO₃, reflux 1–2 h, in a glass‑lined vessel, with careful temperature control (≈80–120 °C); common solvents/catalysts: nitric acid itself serves as solvent and oxidant; NO₂ is evolved as a gas.

Dehydrative conversion of an amide to a nitrile with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). Transforms propanamide into propionitrile while evolving HCl and SO₂ gases. Conducted in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, often with excess SOCl₂ and a base (e.g., pyridine) to trap HCl; reaction temperature ranges from 0 °C to reflux (≈70 °C).

Double‑replacement precipitation of a rare‑earth oxalate; purpose: prepare insoluble gadolinium oxalate for further processing (e.g., calcination to Gd₂O₃); key transformation: exchange of oxalate and chloride ions between ammonium oxalate and GdCl₃, forming Gd₂(C₂O₄)₃ precipitate and soluble NH₄Cl; typical conditions: aqueous solution, heating to 60–80 °C with stirring to enhance precipitation; common solvents/catalysts: water as solvent, no catalyst needed; the solid is filtered, washed, and dried.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol; purpose is to oxidize ethanol to acetic acid (industrial route to acetate). Ethanol reacts with molecular oxygen in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu‑based, Pd‑based, or Au‑supported) to give acetic acid and water, proceeding via dehydrogenation and further oxidation steps. Conducted in the gas phase or in a reactor at 150–300 °C and 1–10 atm O₂; catalyst is essential, and solvents are generally not used in the gas‑phase process.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (alkoxide‑mediated esterification); purpose is to form isopropyl benzoate from benzoyl chloride. Sodium isopropoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the ester and NaCl as by‑product. Performed in an aprotic aprotic solvent such as THF or dry ether at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Dehydrative condensation (acid anhydride formation). Phosphorus pentoxide acts as a strong dehydrating agent to remove water from two molecules of methacrylic acid, yielding methacrylic anhydride. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions, often solvent‑free or in a non‑reactive solvent such as toluene, with gentle heating (0–50 °C) and a stream of inert gas to remove generated water.

Reductive amination. The secondary amine N,N‑dimethyl‑1,3‑propanediamine condenses with the ketone 10,11‑dihydro‑5H‑dibenzo[a,d]cyclohepten‑5‑one to form an imine, which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give the tricyclic secondary amine amitriptyline. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., methanol, ethanol, or dichloromethane) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature, often with a weak acid buffer (pH 5–6) to promote imine formation while keeping cyanoborohydride stable.

Grignard addition to an ester. One equivalent of methylmagnesium bromide adds to the carbonyl of isoamyl formate to give a tetrahedral alkoxide; a second equivalent adds to the resulting aldehyde intermediate, affording a secondary alkoxide that upon aqueous work‑up yields isopropyl alcohol. Simultaneously, the original isoamyl alkoxy group is liberated as isoamyl alcohol. The reaction is carried out in anhydrous ether solvents (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux, followed by protonation with dilute acid or NH₄Cl solution.

Friedel‑Crafts methylation (alkylation). Dimethyl serves as a methylating electrophile in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst, AlCl₃, which generates the CH₃⁺ species that attacks the aromatic ring of para‑xylene. Methylation occurs at the two unsubstituted ortho/para positions, converting para‑xylene to 1,2,4,5‑tetramethylbenzene. Reaction is performed in anhydrous, non‑protic solvents such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen, and the mixture is quenched carefully to destroy excess AlCl₃ and dimethyl sulfate.

Synthesis (direct combination) reaction; cesium metal reacts violently with iodine vapor to form the ionic salt cesium iodide (CsI). No catalyst required; typically performed in a dry, inert atmosphere, often with gentle heating to generate iodine vapour and to ensure complete reaction.

Ligand exchange (acid–base) reaction; phenoxide ligands of titanium tetraphenoxide are protonated by acetic acid, releasing phenol and forming titanium(IV) acetate. Typically performed by refluxing Ti(OPh)4 with excess acetic acid in a non‑coordinating solvent such as toluene or xylene under an inert atmosphere; phenol is distilled off or extracted during work‑up.

Metal‑boride synthesis (boriding). Diborane gas reacts with solid manganese(II) chloride at high temperature (typically 600–900 °C) in an inert atmosphere, reducing the chloride and forming manganese boride (MnB) while generating hydrogen chloride as the volatile by‑product. The process is carried out in a sealed tube or furnace, often without a solvent, and the resulting MnB is recovered as a fine powder after cooling and removal of gaseous HCl.

Condensation (hydrazone formation); converts benzaldehyde to its hydrazone by nucleophilic addition of hydrazine to the carbonyl followed by loss of water; typically carried out in ethanol or methanol under reflux; the hydrochloride salt provides the acidic medium and ammonium chloride is formed as a by‑product.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox synthesis of lead telluride; tellurium dioxide oxidizes sulfide in PbS to sulfur dioxide while the lead combines with reduced tellurium to give PbTe. Conducted in sealed quartz tubes or tube furnaces at 800–1000 °C in an inert (argon) atmosphere; the gaseous SO₂ is vented or trapped, and the PbTe product is recovered as a black crystalline solid.

Redox reduction of Ag⁺ to metallic silver by NaBH₄; sodium borohydride donates hydride to Ag⁺, precipitating silver and oxidizing to metaborate while nitrate forms sodium nitrate. Carried out in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) or mixed water/ethanol, often under ice‑bath conditions; the reaction is rapid, produces fine silver particles (or a mirror) and evolves H₂ gas; pH is usually kept neutral to slightly basic to prevent borohydride decomposition.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑bromoethylbenzene by dimethylamine to afford N,N‑dimethylphenethylamine and HBr. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile at 50–80 °C; an excess of dimethylamine (often as a gas or in aqueous solution) is used, and a base (e.g., triethylamine) may be added to scavenge the generated HBr and drive the reaction to completion.

Type: acid‑base/precipitation reaction. Purpose: preparation of indium(III) phosphate as an insoluble solid. Key transformation: indium(III) oxide reacts with phosphoric acid to form InPO₄ and water. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of In₂O₃ is treated with stoichiometric H₃PO₄ and heated to 80–120 °C with stirring until the oxide dissolves, then the mixture is cooled to precipitate the phosphate. Common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; phosphoric acid reacts with basic silver oxide to form insoluble silver phosphate and water. Executed in aqueous medium with gentle heating to dissolve Ag₂O, then cooling to precipitate Ag₃PO₄; the solid is filtered, washed, and dried. No special catalysts are required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an N‑alkylformamide; water attacks the carbonyl of N‑isopropylformamide, cleaving the C‑N bond to give formic acid and isopropylamine; typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., HCl) at reflux temperatures.

This is a thermal decomposition reaction, used to produce yttrium oxide from its nitrate salt. Key transformation: Decomposition of yttrium nitrate to yttrium oxide, releasing nitrogen dioxide and oxygen gases. Typical reaction conditions: Heating to temperatures around 500-800°C in air or an inert atmosphere, with no solvents or catalysts required.

Double displacement (acid‑salt) reaction; purpose is to convert barium selenite into soluble barium nitrate while generating selenous acid in solution; key transformation: BaSeO3 + 2 HNO3 → Ba(NO3)2 + H2SeO3; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid–base neutralization/complex‑formation reaction; fluorosilicic acid (H₂SiF₆) protonates barium carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while the Ba²⁺ combines with SiF₆²⁻ to form soluble barium hexafluorosilicate; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating.

Ammonolysis (amide‑formation) of a carboxylic acid; aqueous ammonia reacts with cyclohexaneacetic acid, removing water to give cyclohexaneacetamide and H₂O; usually requires heating (≈100 °C) or a coupling agent to drive off water, performed in aqueous or alcoholic solvent.

Double displacement (acid‑base) reaction; calcium tellurate reacts with sulfuric acid in aqueous solution to exchange ions, yielding insoluble calcium sulfate precipitate and soluble telluric acid; performed in water at moderate temperature, no catalyst.

Electrophilic bromination of a heteroaromatic xanthine; bromine in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) adds to the 8‑position of theophylline, producing 8‑bromotheophylline and hydrogen bromide; reaction is run at 0 °C to room temperature in DMSO, often under inert atmosphere.

Oxidative deamination of pyridoxamine; molecular oxygen oxidizes the primary amine side chain to an aldehyde, producing pyridoxal and hydrogen peroxide as by‑product. Usually carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at ambient temperature in the presence of a mild metal catalyst (e.g., Cu²⁺ or Fe²⁺) or enzyme mimic to accelerate O₂ activation; no additional reagents required.

Double‑displacement metathesis in aqueous solution; potassium carbonate exchanges anions with lead(II) metavanadate, precipitating insoluble lead(II) carbonate while forming soluble potassium metavanadate; performed at ambient temperature with stirring.

This reaction is a nucleophilic substitution where the fluoride ion displaces the chloride ion in a silyl chloride group. The purpose is anion exchange to generate silyl fluorides. Key transformation involves replacing the chlorine atom bonded to silicon with fluorine. Typical conditions include polar aprotic solvents like THF or HMPA at moderate temperatures. No catalyst is required.

Simple salt metathesis (double‑displacement). In aqueous solution, mercury(II) nitrate reacts with solid silver chloride, exchanging the anions to give soluble silver nitrate and mercury(II) chloride. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature, typically with stirring of the aqueous nitrate solution over the AgCl solid, and no special catalysts or solvents beyond water are required.

Double‑displacement metathesis forming mercury(II) acetate; mercury(II) bromide reacts with sodium acetate to give soluble mercury(II) acetate and sodium bromide; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Enzymatic oxidative decarboxylation of an α‑ketoacid (3‑methyl‑2‑oxopentanoic acid) catalyzed by a CoA‑dependent dehydrogenase complex (similar to pyruvate dehydrogenase). The ketoacid, Coenzyme A and NAD⁺ are converted to the corresponding acyl‑CoA (2‑methylbutyryl‑CoA), NADH, and CO₂ (often written as CO in simplified schemes). Requires thiamine‑pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, Mg²⁺, and occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (~7.4) and temperature (30–37 °C).

Type: Reductive dehalogenation (hydride reduction). Purpose: Convert an alkyl iodide to the corresponding alkane by removing the iodine. Key transformation: Lithium aluminum hydride donates hydride to the carbon bearing iodine, displacing iodide and forming a C–H bond; lithium iodide precipitates and aluminum is converted to aluminum hydroxide upon aqueous work‑up. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether (ethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful quench with water or dilute acid.
Double displacement/cation exchange reaction; forms insoluble calcium chromate precipitate. Reactants dissolved in water, occurring at room temperature.

Acid-base reaction; calcium carbonate neutralizes sulfur dioxide to form calcium sulfite. Used industrially for flue gas desulfurization. Typically operates under dry conditions at elevated temperatures (e.g., 100-150°C).

Epoxidation; meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid oxidizes hexafluoropropylene to form an epoxide. Progresses in non-aqueous solvents (e.g., CH2Cl2) at room temperature, yielding m-chlorobenzoic acid as a byproduct.
Urea condensation; isocyanate reacts with aniline to form triclocarban. Typically carried out under heat or in solvents (e.g., toluene) to facilitate bond formation without catalysts.

Free‑radical α‑bromination of an ester; purpose is to introduce a bromine at the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl for further functionalization; key transformation replaces one α‑hydrogen of ethyl acetate with bromine, producing ethyl bromoacetate and HBr; typical conditions involve photochemical initiation (UV or visible light) or a peroxide initiator, carried out in an inert non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0–25 °C; no additional catalyst is required.

Preparation of nitronium tetrafluoroborate via acid‑base and salt metathesis; purpose is to generate a strong nitrating reagent containing the nitronium ion; key transformation combines nitrate with BF₄⁻ generated in‑situ from BF₃ and HF, yielding NO₂⁺BF₄⁻ and water while Na⁺ pairs with F⁻ to give NaF; typical conditions use anhydrous HF/BF₃ mixture at low temperature (‑20 to 0 °C) under an inert atmosphere, with the liquid HF serving as solvent; no separate catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide with cyanide; purpose is to synthesize pentanenitrile from 1‑chloropentane; key transformation displaces Cl⁻ by CN⁻, forming potassium chloride and pentanenitrile; typical conditions employ a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or dry acetonitrile, heated to 50–80 °C; the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts.

Secondary alcohol oxidation (1‑phenylethanol → acetophenone) using TBHP as oxidant; typical conditions involve a Cu(II)‑ or Fe(II)‑based catalyst (e.g., CuBr₂, FeSO₄) with a ligand such as bipyridine, in acetonitrile or toluene at 40–80 °C; the secondary alcohol is converted to the corresponding ketone while TBHP furnishes tert‑butanol.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) between copper(II) perchlorate and potassium thiocyanate; purpose is to exchange anions and isolate copper(II) thiocyanate; key transformation forms potassium perchlorate in solution and copper(II) thiocyanate as a blue solid precipitate; the reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base proton transfer (salt metathesis) of potassium iodoacetate with sulfuric acid; purpose is to liberate iodoacetic acid from its potassium salt; key transformation protonates the acetate ion, producing iodoacetic acid and potassium hydrogen sulfate; typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑organic medium, often with mild heating if needed; no catalyst is involved.

Base‑mediated saponification with potassium hydroxide: analogous to reaction 2, propyl 2‑methylpropanoate reacts with KOH to afford potassium 2‑methylpropanoate and 1‑propanol. Conducted in aqueous or aqueous‑alcoholic medium under heating.

Double‑displacement precipitation between lead(II) acetate and sodium chromate; purpose is to form insoluble lead(II) chromate for analytical or synthetic use; key transformation exchanges acetate for chromate, yielding a yellow PbCrO₄ precipitate and sodium acetate in solution; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no catalyst is required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (double SN2 substitution) of 1,3‑dichloropropane with aqueous NaOH to afford 1,3‑propanediol; the reaction proceeds by nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on each primary chloride, displacing Cl⁻ as NaCl. Typically performed by refluxing the dihalide in a water/ethanol mixture with excess NaOH; no catalyst is required and the by‑product is sodium chloride.

Oxidation of sulfide to sulfoxide; MnO₂ oxidizes dimethyl sulfide to dimethyl sulfoxide, yielding MnO and water. Typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0‑25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation to the sulfone; stoichiometric MnO₂ is employed. Purpose is preparation of the sulfoxide.

Acid–base metathesis (neutralization) of ammonium tungstate with aqueous KOH producing potassium tungstate, ammonia gas, and water. The ammonium ion is deprotonated by the strong base, releasing NH₃, while the tungstate anion pairs with K⁺ to give soluble K₂WO₄. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off ammonia; no special catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of p‑coumaryl alcohol with aqueous potassium permanganate to give p‑coumaric acid; KMnO₄ oxidizes the primary allylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid while MnO₂ precipitates; carried out in dilute KMnO₄ solution, neutral to slightly alkaline pH, 0‑25 °C, aqueous medium, no additional catalyst required.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation of 3‑chloropropionic acid with KOH to give acrylic acid, potassium chloride and water. Hydroxide abstracts the β‑hydrogen, and chloride leaves in an E2 elimination, forming the C=C double bond of acrylic acid. The reaction is carried out in aqueous KOH under reflux or heating; the process is simply a thermal elimination, no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of indole to 2‑oxindole using peracetic acid (a peracid). The peracid delivers an electrophilic oxygen to the C2‑C3 double bond of indole, forming a cyclic iminium oxide that rearranges to the lactam (oxindole) while releasing acetic acid. Usually performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or glacial acetic acid at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric peracid acts as both oxidant and acid, no metal catalyst is needed.

Kumada‑type copper‑catalyzed cross‑coupling (alkyl‑alkyl coupling). MeMgBr reacts with ethyl 2‑chloropropanoate in the presence of CuI to replace the chloride with a methyl group, yielding ethyl 2‑methylpropanoate. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in THF or diethyl ether, at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; CuI acts as catalyst, generating CuCl and MgBrCl as by‑products.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of acetic anhydride with lithium hydroxide, yielding lithium acetate and acetic acid. Hydroxide attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, opening the anhydride to form the acetate salt and a free carboxylic acid. The reaction is carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic solvent at ambient temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst is required.

Cleavage of diethyl sulfide by hydrogen bromide (HX cleavage) to afford ethyl bromide and ethanethiol. HBr protonates the sulfide, generating a good leaving group (‑S⁺H‑), followed by nucleophilic attack of bromide at the more substituted carbon, producing ethyl bromide and releasing ethanethiol. Conducted in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at low to moderate temperature; the reaction relies solely on the strong acid, no catalyst is necessary.

Hydrolysis and subsequent condensation (sol‑gel) of niobium(V) ethoxide. Water replaces ethoxy groups, producing ethanol and niobium hydroxide that condenses to niobium(V) oxide (Nb2O5). Typically carried out by adding controlled amounts of water to a solution of Nb(OC2H5)5 in ethanol or another alcohol at 0–25 °C, followed by aging or mild heating. No catalyst is needed; the solvent is the alcohol medium.

General type: high‑temperature solid‑state oxidation (redox). Purpose: convert chromium nitride into a more stable oxide and release nitrogen gas. Key transformation: O₂ oxidizes Cr³⁺ in CrN to Cr³⁺ in Cr₂O₃ while N⁻ is oxidized to N₂. Typical conditions: heated to 800–1000 °C in a stream of dry O₂ or air, often in a tube furnace. No solvent; the reactants are solid powders; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; iron(III) nitrate and ammonium chloride exchange anions to give ammonium nitrate and iron(III) chloride. Often carried out by dissolving the salts in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction proceeds spontaneously, no catalyst required. The products remain in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Partial reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). DIBAL‑H delivers a hydride to the nitrile carbon, forming an imine‑aluminum intermediate that hydrolyzes on work‑up to give benzaldehyde while preserving the aldehyde oxidation state. Conducted at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar); typically 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H are used, followed by quench with methanol or aqueous acid. No additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (heterocycle reduction); fully saturates the selenophene aromatic system to give tetrahydroselenophene. Conducted under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) with 5–10 wt % Pd/C in ethanol, methanol or THF at 25–80 °C. The reaction consumes one equivalent of H2 per double bond (four equivalents total) and provides the saturated heterocycle.

Dehydrative condensation using acetic anhydride as activating agent to form a phosphonic anhydride (propylphosphonic anhydride) from propylphosphonic acid. Acetic anhydride acylates the phosphonic acid hydroxyl groups, releasing acetic acid and generating the mixed anhydride linkage. Typically performed neat or in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., toluene, pyridine) at 60–80 °C under nitrogen; a base such as pyridine can be added to scavenge the generated acetic acid. No metal catalyst is required.

SN2 amination of ethyl methanesulfonate with ammonia; ammonia (often as aqueous NH₃ or gaseous NH₃ in excess) displaces methanesulfonate to give ethylamine and methanesulfonic acid; carried out in ethanol or in a sealed tube under pressure at reflux (60‑80 °C); no catalyst required.

Benzylic oxidation of 4‑methylpyridine to 4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde using selenium dioxide. SeO2 selectively oxidizes the methyl group adjacent to the aromatic nitrogen to the aldehyde, proceeding via a selenite ester intermediate. Reaction is usually refluxed in a high‑boiling non‑polar solvent such as 1,4‑dioxane or 1,2‑dichloroethane (100–130 °C) with stoichiometric SeO2; sometimes a co‑oxidant (e.g., tert‑butyl hydroperoxide) is added to improve yield. No metal catalyst, but the reaction is sensitive to moisture.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous medium; ammonium hydroxide reacts with lead chromate to exchange ions, forming soluble ammonium chromate and insoluble lead(II (hydroxide) precipitate; typically performed at room temperature in water.

Generation of a Vilsmeier–Haack reagent (chloro‑N,N‑dimethylformiminium chloride) from DMF and POCl₃; anhydrous activation reaction; POCl₃ chlorinates DMF while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl, giving triethylammonium chloride as by‑product; carried out under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to rt in dry DMF (or other aprotic solvent).

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of benzyl thioacetate with methanol, exchanging the benzyl alkoxy group for a methyl group to give methyl thioacetate and benzyl alcohol. Conducted by refluxing the thioacetate in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of sodium methoxide or dilute acid (e.g., H₂SO₄). Reaction proceeds in methanol solvent; water is removed to drive equilibrium to products.

Reaction between strontium hydroxide and oxalic acid: Neutralization (acid-base double displacement). Produces strontium oxalate and water. Purpose: neutralizing oxalic acid. Key transformation: H+ (from H2C2O4) reacts with OH- (from Sr(OH)2) to form H2O; Sr²+ combines with C2O4^2- to form SrC2O4 (a water-insoluble precipitate). Typically occurs in aqueous solution at room temperature, no catalyst.

Type: conversion of carboxylate to acid chloride using thionyl chloride. Purpose: obtain butanoyl chloride for acylation chemistry. Key transformation: the butanoate oxygen attacks SOCl₂, displacing chloride and generating the acid chloride while releasing SO₂ gas and LiCl as by‑product. Conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, reaction performed at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; a base such as pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMF may be added to scavenge HCl. By‑products: gaseous SO₂ and solid LiCl.

Thermite‑type redox (magnesiothermic reduction); used to produce elemental silicon and magnesium oxide; magnesium metal donates electrons to silicon dioxide, yielding MgO solid and Si metal; performed at very high temperature (typically >1000 °C) in a furnace or sealed crucible, often under inert gas (argon) to avoid oxidation; solid‑state reaction, no solvent required.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of an alkyne; O₃ adds across the triple bond of 1‑ethynylcyclohexene, and oxidative work‑up (e.g., H₂O₂) converts the ozonide to a carboxylic acid, yielding cyclohexene‑1‑carboxylic acid; performed at –78 °C to 0 °C in CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Base‑promoted intramolecular cyclization (dehydrohalogenation) to form an epoxide; sodium carbonate deprotonates the β‑chloro‑like alcohol, displacing chloride intramolecularly to give glycidol; water or ethanol as solvent, reflux (~60–80 °C) under atmospheric pressure; CO₂ and NaCl are by‑products.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction; tin(II) iodide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid upon heating, oxidizing iodide to iodine, reducing sulfate to sulfur dioxide, and forming tin(II) sulfate; overall: SnI₂ + 2 H₂SO₄ → SnSO₄ + I₂ + SO₂ + 2 H₂O; performed with conc. H₂SO₄, heat, typically in a glass vessel; no added catalyst.

Hydrolytic decarboxylation of a carbamate (urethane) to the corresponding amine and alcohol; water attacks the carbonyl, releasing CO₂ and splitting the molecule into 1‑propanol and 3‑(dimethylamino)propylamine; typically heated (80–100 °C) in aqueous medium, optionally under mild acidic or basic catalysis.

Acid‑base neutralization (protonation of a carboxylate); purpose is to regenerate the free carboxylic acid; Na⁺ 3‑methylbutanoate is protonated by HCl to give 3‑methylbutanoic acid and NaCl; usually done by adding aqueous HCl to the aqueous salt solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of fumaric acid with methanol to form methyl fumarate (mono‑ester) and water; the carboxyl group is converted to a methyl ester by nucleophilic attack of methanol under acid catalysis. Typical conditions: excess MeOH, catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, reflux 60–80 °C; removal of water by Dean‑Stark trap or molecular sieves; solvent is the methanol itself.

Reduction of an oxime (N‑benzylidenehydroxylamine) to the primary amine benzylamine with sodium borohydride; purpose is to generate the amine from the oxime intermediate; key transformation is hydride delivery to the C=N bond giving –CH2NH2; carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; by‑products are sodium borate and water, removed during aqueous work‑up.

Reaction type: SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (ester synthesis). Purpose: synthesis of propyl octanoate. Key transformation: nucleophilic substitution of propyl chloride by the octanoate anion, forming the propyl ester and sodium chloride. Typical conditions: because chloride is less reactive, higher temperature (80–110 °C) in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO) or use of a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) to enhance the rate.

Type: double‑displacement/precipitation metathesis. Purpose: synthesize insoluble lanthanum oxalate and recover HCl. Key transformation: oxalic acid protonates the coordinated chloride, forming La2(C2O4)3 precipitate while chloride ions combine with protons to give HCl (and water from the hydrate). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating (20‑60 °C); the reaction proceeds spontaneously, often with stirring. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation of cumyl hydroperoxide to a diperoxide; sulfuric acid protonates the hydroperoxide, facilitating radical coupling to form dicumyl peroxide with loss of water; carried out at 0–25 °C in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetic acid to control exotherm.

Wolff–Kishner-type reduction; purpose is removal of the carbonyl group from tropone to give an all‑carbon cycloheptatriene. Key transformation: C=O of tropone is converted to CH2 via formation of a hydrazone with hydrazine, followed by base‑induced elimination. Typical conditions: excess hydrazine hydrate, KOH (or NaOH) in high‑boiling solvent (e.g., ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol) heated to reflux for several hours. No special catalyst; water is generated.

Ester reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH4 in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux reduces the benzoate ester to two primary alcohols, converting the carbonyl carbon of the benzoate into benzyl alcohol while the original 4‑bromobenzyl alkoxy group becomes 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol; work‑up with water and dilute acid yields the alcohol products.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkyl halide hydrolysis); converts a primary alkyl iodide to the corresponding primary alcohol. Hydroxide ion replaces iodide, forming 1‑propanol and NaI. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol solution, often refluxed to ensure complete reaction; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis in aqueous solution; mixing aqueous phosphoric acid with sodium silicate (Na2SiO3) results in proton transfer to generate silicic acid (H4SiO4) and sodium phosphate (Na3PO4); the reaction proceeds at room temperature in water, often with gentle heating to dissolve the silicate, and the products remain in solution or precipitate depending on concentration and pH.

Conjugate (Michael) addition of a primary amine to an α,β‑unsaturated nitrile; methylamine adds to acrylonitrile to give 3‑(methylamino)propanenitrile; typical conditions involve mixing the reagents in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water at ambient temperature, occasionally with a mild base to neutralize the generated acid; no catalyst is required.

General type: deoxy‑fluorination / redox fluorination using sulfur tetrafluoride. Purpose: convert oxalic acid into the acyl fluoride oxalyl difluoride while oxidizing sulfur from +4 to +6 (SO₂) and generating HF. Key transformation: SF₄ replaces the two hydroxyl groups of oxalic acid with fluorine atoms, yielding oxalyl difluoride, while the sulfur center is oxidized to SO₂ and releases HF. Typical conditions: low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No catalyst; reaction is quenched carefully with ice/water to absorb HF.

Enzyme‑catalyzed substitution of the acetyl group of O‑acetyl‑L‑serine by hydrogen sulfide to form L‑cysteine; PLP‑dependent cysteine synthase mediates nucleophilic attack of HS⁻ on the β‑carbon, releasing acetate; carried out in aqueous buffer at pH 7–8, ambient temperature, often with Mg²⁺ as cofactor.

Condensation (amide formation) of a carboxylic acid with an aniline; salicylic acid reacts with aniline to produce salicylanilide and water; because direct amidation is sluggish, the reaction is usually conducted with a dehydrating agent (e.g., acetic anhydride, DCC, or POCl₃) or under high‑temperature reflux in a nondipolar solvent such as toluene or xylene with azeotropic removal of water; the result is the formation of the aryl amide (salicylanilide).

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges anions between sodium fluoride and barium nitrate to form soluble sodium nitrate and insoluble barium fluoride, which precipitates. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; fluorides replace chlorides on thorium tetrachloride yielding thorium tetrafluoride and gaseous hydrogen chloride. Conducted by passing dry HF gas over solid or melted ThCl4, typically at 200‑300 °C in a sealed reactor; inert atmosphere often used, no additional solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) fluorination of an alcohol; methanol reacts with anhydrous HF to replace the hydroxyl hydrogen with fluorine, producing methyl fluoride and water. Carried out in liquid HF or HF/pyridine (70‑90 % HF) at 0‑25 °C; often uses a superacidic medium (e.g., HF/SbF₅) to promote substitution, no external catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; lead nitrate and lithium sulfate exchange anions to give insoluble lead sulfate and soluble lithium nitrate. Executed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride by ammonia. Purpose: prepare the diamine N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine from 2‑chloro‑N,N‑ethylethylamine. Key transformation: lone pair on NH₃ attacks the carbon bearing Cl, displacing Cl⁻ and forming a new C–N bond; the by‑product is HCl, which is neutralized by the excess ammonia. Typical conditions: excess aqueous or alcoholic NH₃ (30–30 % aq) at reflux (≈80–100 °C) for several hours; sometimes a base such as Na₂CO₃ is added to trap HCl. No metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic halide exchange on phosphorus; phosphorus trichloride reacts with sodium cyanide, where three cyanide ions replace the three chlorides to afford tricyanophosphine (P(CN)₃) and sodium chloride. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or dimethylformamide at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric NaCN acts as nucleophile, no catalyst required.

Type: Acid chloride synthesis (chlorination of a carboxylic acid). Purpose: Convert heptafluorobutyric acid into the corresponding acid chloride for further acylation reactions. Key transformation: R‑COOH + PCl5 → R‑COCl + POCl3 + HCl. Conditions: Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions, 0 °C to room temperature, in inert non‑protic solvents such as dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride or chloroform. By‑products (HCl, POCl3) are removed by gas‑flow or trapped with base.

Type: Redox oxidation (metal oxidation). Purpose: Regenerate the higher oxidation state Rh(III) from Rh(II) in catalytic cycles. Key transformation: Rh2(OAc)4 + H2O2 → 2 Rh(OAc)3 + 2 H2O (overall stoichiometry may vary). Conditions: Aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium, ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation. No special solvent required; dilute H2O2 (30 %) is common.

Type: Base‑mediated hydrolysis (halide exchange). Purpose: Produce soluble potassium silicate and bromide salts from silicon tetrabromide. Key transformation: SiBr4 + 6 KOH → K2SiO3 + 4 KBr + 3 H2O. Conditions: Aqueous KOH solution, vigorous stirring, mild heating (room temperature to 80 °C). Reaction is fast; the silicate precipitates or stays dissolved depending on concentration.

Type: Alcohol to alkyl chloride conversion (Appel‑type substitution). Purpose: Prepare 1‑chloropropane from 1‑propanol for further substitution or elimination reactions. Key transformation: CH3CH2CH2OH + PCl5 → CH3CH2CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl. Conditions: Anhydrous, dry solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2, CCl4), temperature 0 °C to rt, under inert gas. Reaction is typically performed in a sealed flask to contain corrosive HCl gas.

Type: Nitration of an alcohol (formation of alkyl nitrate). Purpose: Synthesize amyl nitrate, a volatile nitrate ester used as a fuel additive or in organic synthesis. Key transformation: C5H11OH + HNO3 → C5H11ONO2 + H2O. Conditions: Concentrated nitric acid (often 70 %–95 %), low temperature (0–5 °C) to control exotherm, sometimes in the presence of a non‑nucleophilic acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid. Reaction is usually performed in an ice bath with careful addition of alcohol to acid.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction; used to exchange the oxalate and acetate anions to obtain copper(II) acetate from the oxalate salt. The copper(II) oxalate solid is mixed with aqueous ammonium acetate; the exchange produces soluble copper(II) acetate and ammonium oxalate. Typical conditions are aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature with stirring; no catalyst required. Water is the solvent.
Fischer esterification; acetylation of rhodinol’s hydroxyl group; acid-catalyzed (often with sulfuric acid) and heated to drive water formation; glacial acetic acid is both reactant and solvent.

Oxidative decomposition of arsine with concentrated nitric acid; arsenic is oxidized to arsenic trioxide while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water. Conducted by bubbling arsine into cold concentrated HNO₃ (0–25 °C) under a fume hood; no added catalyst, the acid acts as both solvent and oxidant.

Base‑mediated N‑alkylation (SN2) of imidazole; purpose is to install a benzyl group on the nitrogen to give 1‑benzylimidazole. Potassium carbonate deprotonates imidazole, generating the nucleophilic imidazolide which attacks benzyl methanesulfonate, displacing methanesulfonate (mesylate) as potassium methanesulfonate. Reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile, generally at 80–120 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst is needed.

Benzylic chloride hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution); purpose is to convert the chloromethyl substituent to a hydroxymethyl group, yielding 2‑nitrobenzyl alcohol; water attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing chloride as HCl; commonly performed in aqueous acidic or neutral medium, often with reflux in a mixture of water and a co‑solvent such as ethanol or THF; the reaction may be accelerated by a small amount of acid or base catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a methyl ether; converts furfuryl methyl ether to furfuryl alcohol and methanol. Water attacks the ether carbon under acidic conditions (e.g., dilute HCl or H₂SO₄) with heating ( reflux or 80–120 °C). The reaction proceeds via protonation of the ether oxygen followed by cleavage of the C–O bond. Solvent is aqueous acidic medium; no metal catalyst required.

Alcoholysis of an acyl fluoride to form an ester; ethanol reacts with acetyl fluoride to afford ethyl acetate and HF; performed in anhydrous solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) at 0–25 °C, often with a stoichiometric base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HF.

Gas‑solid precipitation (sulfide precipitation); synthesis of Ga2S3 from GaCl3. Hydrogen sulfide gas displaces chloride, precipitating gallium(III) sulfide and releasing HCl gas. Typically performed by bubbling H2S through an aqueous solution of GaCl3 at 80‑120 °C under inert gas; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Acylation (esterification) of an allylic alcohol using acetic anhydride; but‑3‑en‑2‑ol is converted to the acetate ester but‑3‑en‑2‑yl acetate with formation of one equivalent of acetic acid. Usually carried out in the presence of a base (pyridine or DMAP) to scavenge the generated acid, at 0 °C to rt in a solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine itself. Reaction is rapid and often driven to completion by removal of acetic acid (e.g., azeotropic distillation).

Hydrolysis of cyanogen bromide (BrCN); yields hydrobromic acid and isocyanic acid (HNCO). Water adds across the C–Br bond, producing HBr and HNCO. The reaction occurs readily in aqueous solution at room temperature or with mild heating; it can be accelerated by slight acid or base catalysis. No special solvent beyond water; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base metathesis followed by carbonate decomposition; ammonium fluoride reacts with strontium carbonate to give strontium fluoride and ammonium carbonate, the latter decomposes on heating to ammonia, carbon dioxide and water. Typically performed in aqueous suspension with gentle heating (50–100 °C) to drive off the gases. No catalyst required; water is the reaction medium.

Basic hydrolysis (saponification) of an ester by ammonium hydroxide; ethyl linoleate is cleaved to ethanol and the ammonium salt of linoleic acid (ammonium linoleate). The reaction is performed in aqueous ammonium hydroxide, often with heating (reflux, 80–100 °C) to complete conversion. No metal catalyst is needed; water/ammonium hydroxide serves as both solvent and base.

General type: formation of a Vilsmeier‑Haack reagent (electrophilic activation). Purpose: to generate the chloroiminium salt used for formylation of activated aromatic rings. Key transformation: dimethylformamide reacts with POCl₃, producing the iminium chloride ([(CH₃)₂N=CHCl]⁺) and HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, POCl₃ added dropwise to dry DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert gas; reaction usually performed neat (DMF serves as solvent). No additional catalyst required.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (heterogeneous reduction). Purpose: to reduce the pyrimidine ring of uridine, yielding tetrahydro‑uridine (tetrahydrouridine). Key transformation: hydrogen adds across the C=C and C=N bonds of the nucleobase, converting unsaturated heterocycle to a saturated analogue. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 30–100 atm, PtO₂ (Adams’ catalyst) 5–10 % wt, aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., water/tert‑butanol), temperature 25–50 °C, stirring under an inert atmosphere.

General type: redox displacement (single‑electron transfer) between a metal and a metal halide. Purpose: to produce elemental copper and antimony(III) chloride. Key transformation: antimony metal reduces Cu(II) to Cu⁰ while being oxidized to SbCl₃. Typical conditions: solid‑state reaction heated to 200–300 °C in a sealed tube or under inert gas; no solvent, often carried out in a graphite or quartz crucible. No catalyst required.

Catalytic partial oxidation; purpose is to convert a long‑chain alkane to the corresponding aldehyde while generating water as the only co‑product. The reaction proceeds via activation of O2 on a solid metal‑oxide or noble‑metal catalyst (e.g., Mo‑V‑Nb oxide, Pt‑Sn/Al2O3) in the gas phase at 300–450 °C under a dilute O2/He mixture. Key transformation is selective removal of two hydrogen atoms from hexadecane to give hexadecanal and water. No additional solvent; the reactants are introduced as vapors.

General type: nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr). Purpose: to replace the fluorine atom on 2‑fluoropyridine with an amino group, giving 2‑aminopyridine. Key transformation: NH₃ attacks the activated pyridine ring, displacing F⁻ which is trapped by Na₂CO₃ as NaF, while carbonate generates CO₂ and water. Typical conditions: excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃, Na₂CO₃ as base, polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO, DMF, or ethanol), reflux 80–120 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous metathesis of CdCl2 with Na2CO3 yielding cadmium(II) carbonate precipitate and soluble NaCl; performed at room temperature in water with stirring; filtration isolates the carbonate; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis in super‑acid medium; purpose is to generate nitronium tetrafluoroborate, a powerful nitrating agent. Anhydrous BF3 reacts with HF to form the fluoroboric acid system, which then protonates cobalt nitrate; subsequent exchange gives CoF2, water and the nitronium salt (NO2+ BF4−). Typical conditions are anhydrous HF or a HF–BF3 mixture at –10 °C to 0 °C in a sealed PTFE vessel, with careful exclusion of moisture. No organic solvent is used; the reaction relies on the super‑acidic environment.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by hydroxylamine; O‑alkylation produces O‑ethylhydroxylamine while HBr is generated as a by‑product. Typically carried out in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or aqueous ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (e.g., NaOH or Na₂CO₃) is often added to neutralize the HBr and suppress N‑alkylation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 3-iodopentane with sodium azide to afford 3-azidopentane. Type: halide‑to‑azide exchange. Purpose: install an azide functionality for subsequent click chemistry or reduction. Key transformation: C‑I → C‑N₃. Typical conditions: NaN₃ (1.5–2 eq) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 50–80 °C under inert atmosphere. By‑product: NaI.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation) where the phenolic carboxylic acid of salicylic acid is deprotonated by sodium ethoxide, yielding sodium salicylate and ethanol. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol, often under reflux to ensure complete deprotonation; the reaction proceeds at ambient pressure without additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between phenylmercuric bromide and silver nitrate, exchanging the bromide for nitrate and precipitating insoluble silver bromide. Performed in aqueous solution (or dilute aqueous ethanol) at room temperature; the silver bromide precipitate is filtered off, leaving phenylmercuric nitrate in solution.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed lactone hydrolysis; water attacks the carbonyl of γ‑valerolactone, opening the ring to give γ‑hydroxyvaleric acid. Commonly conducted in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) or with aqueous NaOH under reflux; after hydrolysis the mixture is neutralized to isolate the hydroxy acid. Solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction) of the basic amine Labetalol with hydrochloric acid to afford Labetalol hydrochloride, the pharmaceutically used salt. Labetalol is dissolved in anhydrous ethanol or methanol, HCl gas or aqueous HCl is added at 0 °C to room temperature, and the mixture is stirred until the salt precipitates; no catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; cobalt(II) bromide reacts with sodium sulfide to produce black cobalt(II) sulfide solid and sodium bromide in solution; conducted in aqueous medium, usually under inert atmosphere to avoid sulfide oxidation; no catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic substitution/organometallic coupling where phenyl lithium attacks phenyl selenyl bromide, forming a C–Se bond to give diphenyl selenide and lithium bromide. Conducted under inert atmosphere in dry THF at low temperature (−78 °C to −20 °C); the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, and the lithium bromide by‑product remains in solution.

Type: Esterification via diazomethane (methylation of a carboxylic acid). Purpose: Convert trichloroacetic acid to its methyl ester. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate on diazomethane forming methyl trichloroacetate and releasing nitrogen gas. Typical conditions: Reaction performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic ether (e.g., diethyl ether) under an inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration isobutanol to isobutene; an E1 elimination that removes water to form the alkene. Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates the hydroxyl group, yielding a carbocation that loses a proton to give the double bond. Reaction is carried out neat with the acid, heated to 140–180 °C, often under reflux with a distillation setup to collect the volatile isobutene.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑catalyzed); used to deprotect the acetate protecting group and obtain cinnamyl alcohol; water attacks the carbonyl of cinnamyl acetate, cleaving the C–O bond to give cinnamyl alcohol and acetic acid; typically performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl or dilute H₂SO₄) at reflux temperature; water or aqueous ethanol serves as the solvent.

Type: Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling. Purpose: Form a C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond to synthesize 3‑phenylpyridine. Key transformation: Transmetalation of phenylboronic acid to palladium, followed by reductive elimination with the aryl‑bromide partner. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %), PPh₃ (10 mol %), K₂CO₃ as base, solvent mixture of toluene/ethanol/water (or dioxane/water), heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen for several hours.

Acid‑base neutralization/absorption of sulfur dioxide by aqueous sodium hydroxide; SO2 reacts with OH‑ to form sodium sulfite and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent, reaction is exothermic but proceeds without additional catalysts.

Type: Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation). Purpose: Prepare ethylene glycol mono‑ethyl ether. Key transformation: Deprotonation of ethylene glycol by NaOH to give alkoxide, which attacks ethyl chloride in an SN2 step yielding the mono‑ether, NaCl and water. Typical conditions: Reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or THF; excess NaOH, often with a phase‑transfer catalyst; temperature 60–80 °C.

Type: Phenol sulfate ester formation (reaction with chlorosulfonic acid). Purpose: Convert quinoline‑8‑ol into its hydrogen sulfate ester. Key transformation: The phenolic OH attacks chlorosulfonic acid, displacing chloride to give quinolin‑8‑yl hydrogen sulfate and HCl. Typical conditions: Addition of chlorosulfonic acid to a cooled (0 °C) solution of quinoline‑8‑ol in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, then gradual warming to ambient temperature; gas‑evolved HCl is vented.

Type: Oxidative acid digestion of a metal phosphide. Purpose: Convert chromium phosphide to soluble inorganic salts for analysis or further processing. Key transformation: Nitric acid oxidizes the phosphide to phosphate (forming phosphoric acid) while simultaneously oxidizing chromium to Cr³⁺, which complexes as chromium(III) nitrate. Typical conditions: Reflux of the solid in dilute (≈4 M) nitric acid, often in a glass vessel, with gradual addition to control temperature (80–120 °C) until gas evolution ceases.

Type: Nucleophilic epoxide ring opening (thiolysis). Purpose: Synthesize 2‑(tert‑butylthio)ethanol. Key transformation: The thiolate generated from tert‑butylthiol attacks the less‑ hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the ring to give a β‑hydroxy thioether. Typical conditions: Reaction performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; optionally a mild base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to generate the thiolate; reaction completes within 1–3 h.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; sodium hexafluorosilicate exchanges its sodium ions with magnesium chloride to give sodium chloride and magnesium hexafluorosilicate. Typically carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required; the products remain in solution and may be isolated by evaporation or cooling.

Oxidative dissolution (redox) of tin metal in aqua regia (a 3:1 mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO₃). Tin is oxidized to Sn⁴⁺ forming tin(IV) chloride, while chloride is oxidized to chlorine gas and nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide; water is formed as a by‑product. The reaction is performed under reflux or gentle heating; the acidic medium itself provides the oxidizing power, no additional catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of tribromoiodomethane in water; the C–I bond is cleaved by water to give tribromomethanol and hydrogen iodide. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to accelerate the reaction; the process may be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed, but no specific catalyst is essential.

Acid–base/salt formation reaction between lanthanum oxide and ammonium bromide upon heating; the oxide is protonated by ammonium ions, releasing ammonia gas and water while forming lanthanum bromide. Conducted by heating a solid mixture (≈300 °C) in a sealed vessel or under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of 3‑methylpent‑2‑ene to give ethanal and butan‑2‑one; purpose is cleavage of the C=C bond into carbonyl fragments; key transformations involve addition of O3 to the double bond forming an ozonide, followed by reductive workup with water (or H2O2) to afford aldehyde and ketone; typical conditions are O3 in dichloromethane at –78 °C, then quench with aqueous workup; common solvent is CH2Cl2, workup uses water (often with H2O2).

N‑alkylation of adenine with epichlorohydrin under basic conditions (NaOH); the deprotonated N9 of adenine attacks the epoxide, opening the ring to afford 9-(2,3-dihydroxypropyl)adenine. Performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑ethanol medium at 0–50 °C; NaOH acts as base and promoter; no additional catalyst is needed.

Hydrolysis and condensation of titanium butoxide (Ti(OC₄H₉)₄) with water, a sol‑gel process that converts the alkoxide to titanium dioxide while liberating n‑butanol. Typically conducted in an alcoholic or aqueous medium, often with acidic or basic catalyst (e.g., HCl or NH₄OH) at ambient to moderate temperature; the reaction yields TiO₂ precipitate and four equivalents of n‑butanol.

SN2 substitution of a primary alcohol with PBr3; converts hexadecan‑1‑ol to the corresponding alkyl bromide (1‑bromohexadecane) while generating phosphorous acid; typically performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux, using a stoichiometric amount of PBr3.

Base‑mediated deprotonation (salt hydrolysis); dimethylammonium chloride is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, liberating dimethylamine, producing sodium chloride and water. Performed at room temperature or with mild heating in water or a water‑ethanol mixture; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; exchanges anions between potassium dichromate and silver sulfate to form soluble potassium sulfate and insoluble silver dichromate precipitate; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of a carboxylate) that converts sodium prop‑2‑ynoate into benzyl prop‑2‑ynoate while generating sodium bromide; key step is displacement of bromide by the carboxylate oxygen; usually carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, THF or acetone at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Aqueous alkaline hydrolysis of chlorotrifluorosilane; hydroxide attacks silicon, displacing chloride and fluoride and ultimately yielding sodium silicate, sodium chloride, sodium fluoride and water; performed in aqueous NaOH solution, often at 0–25 °C or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no extra catalyst is required.

Metal–alkoxide formation (single‑displacement acid–base reaction) in dry methanol; produces calcium methoxide and evolves hydrogen gas; key transformation: Ca + 2 CH₃OH → Ca(OCH₃)₂ + H₂↑; usually carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at reflux temperature (≈65 °C) to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst required.

Oxidative cyclization of o‑phenylenediamine to phenazine using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid; dichromate oxidizes the diamine, forming the heterocyclic phenazine ring and reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) sulfate; typically conducted in concentrated H₂SO₄, heated to 80–120 °C; the acid medium serves as solvent and dichromate acts as oxidant, no separate catalyst.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling. 4‑Bromoanisole couples with phenylboronic acid in the presence of tetrakis(triphenylphosphine)palladium(0) and potassium carbonate as base, using tetrahydrofuran (often with a small amount of water) as solvent, heated to reflux (80–100 °C). The reaction forms the biaryl 4‑methoxybiphenyl. Purpose: construction of a C–C bond between two aryl fragments.

Acidification of sodium sorbate with aqueous hydrochloric acid; simple acid–base neutralization that converts the sodium salt of sorbic acid to the free carboxylic acid; carried out in water at ambient temperature; products are sorbic acid and NaCl in solution.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification exchanging the propyl ester for a methyl ester. Propyl 5‑hydroxyhexanoate reacts with excess MeOH to give methyl 5‑hydroxyhexanoate and propanol. Catalysts: p‑TsOH (≈0.1 eq) or NaOMe (≈0.05 eq); reflux MeOH (or toluene with azeotropic removal of propanol) for several hours.

Cyclocondensation of ethane‑1,2‑diamine with ethanedial (glyoxal) to give an imidazoline ring; each amine adds to an aldehyde carbonyl followed by dehydration to close the five‑membered heterocycle; usually refluxed in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid or a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water; ethanol is the common solvent; mild acid may be used as catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of di‑isobutyl phthalate with 1‑butanol; the n‑butanol attacks a carbonyl ester, displacing isobutyl alcohol (2‑methyl‑1‑propanol) and forming butyl‑isobutyl phthalate; carried out with excess 1‑butanol as solvent, using a strong acid such as sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid as catalyst, under reflux (~120 °C) until equilibrium is reached.

N‑alkylation of a β‑keto amine (cathinone) – ethyl bromide undergoes SN2 substitution on the cathinone nitrogen in the presence of potassium carbonate, producing N‑ethylcathinone and KBr. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone, at ambient temperature or gentle heating; K₂CO₃ acts as base to deprotonate the amine and scavenge HBr.

Acid‑base/precipitation reaction to prepare gadolinium trifluoride. Gadolinium carbonate reacts with hydrofluoric acid; the carbonate is protonated and decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O while fluoride ions coordinate Gd³⁺, precipitating GdF₃. Typically carried out in aqueous HF (≈40 % w/w) at room temperature to 80 °C with stirring; the insoluble GdF₃ is filtered off.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of acridine with chlorine; electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) to introduce chlorine at the 9‑position, yielding 9‑chloroacridine. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often with a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃ or AlCl₃) at 50‑100 °C.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) of diethylene glycol using boron trifluoride etherate, producing 1,4‑dioxane and water. Reaction is performed in a dry non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or toluene) with BF₃·OEt₂ (1‑2 equiv) at 0‑25 °C followed by heating (reflux) to promote cyclization.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation between copper(II) acetate and ammonium carbonate, forming insoluble copper(II) carbonate and soluble ammonium acetate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; copper carbonate precipitates and is isolated by filtration. No special solvent or catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction where diphenylcarbazide is oxidized by potassium ferricyanide to 1,5‑diphenylcarbazone while ferricyanide is reduced to ferrocyanide. Typically carried out in an aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 5‑7) at room temperature; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst and is used in colorimetric assays.

Acyl‑transfer (esterification) of methanol with acetic‑formic anhydride, giving methyl acetate and formic acid. Nucleophilic attack of methanol on the acetyl carbonyl displaces formic acid. Reaction is usually performed at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, often in the presence of a base like pyridine to neutralize the liberated acid.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of an acrylate ester); purpose is regeneration of acrylic acid and recovery of the alcohol. Water adds to the carbonyl of 2‑ethylhexyl acrylate, cleaving the ester bond to give acrylic acid and 2‑ethylhexanol, with H⁺ as catalyst. Conducted in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) at 80–120 °C; mixed solvent systems such as water/acetone are common to improve miscibility.

Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride) using thionyl chloride; the primary alcohol of 4‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine is converted to 4‑(chloromethyl)pyridine via an intermediate chlorosulfite; reaction usually run neat or in dichloromethane with excess SOCl₂, reflux or room temperature, often with pyridine as base; by‑products are SO₂ and HCl.

Grignard addition of 2‑pyridylmagnesium bromide to dimethylformamide followed by acidic work‑up, affording 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde, dimethylamine, and magnesium bromide. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, temperatures from –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, then quenched with dilute acid to release the aldehyde. No additional catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction; aqueous acid–base exchange to generate chloric acid in situ from barium chlorate and hydrochloric acid, yielding barium chloride as by‑product; performed in water at ambient or cooled temperature to limit decomposition of HClO3; no catalyst required.

Sodium borohydride reduction of 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑one to 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol; general type: selective hydride reduction of a ketone; purpose: convert carbonyl to secondary alcohol; key transformation: C=O → C‑OH; typical conditions: NaBH4 (1–1.5 equiv) in protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol or aqueous THF at 0 °C to room temperature; by‑product sodium metaborate (NaBO2); no catalyst required.

Combustion/oxidation reaction; complete oxidation of formaldehyde to carbon dioxide and water; typically carried out in the gas phase with excess oxygen at elevated temperature (300–500 °C) often over a metal‑oxide catalyst such as CuO or Pt; no solvent.

Acid–base neutralisation (salt‑to‑free‑base conversion); sodium carbonate deprotonates methylphenidate hydrochloride releasing carbon dioxide and water and forming the free‑base methylphenidate and sodium chloride; conducted in aqueous suspension at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 substitution); sodium ethoxide acts as nucleophile displacing chloride of 1‑chloropropane to give ethyl propyl ether and sodium chloride; carried out in anhydrous ethanol (or dry THF) under reflux; inert atmosphere often used; no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; the terminal double bond of dodec‑1‑ene is reduced to a saturated C–C single bond, yielding dodecane. Typical conditions use H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni) in ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate at 25–80 °C.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of an alkyl sulfonate; water attacks the pentan‑3‑yl 4‑methylbenzenesulfonate, displacing the sulfonate group to afford 4‑methylbenzenesulfonic acid and pentan‑3‑ol; performed in aqueous (or aqueous‑ethanol) medium, typically heated mildly (50–80 °C); can be acid or base catalysed, but often proceeds uncatalysed.

Oxidative acid dissolution of a metal oxide; fuming nitric acid reacts with gadolinium oxide to form gadolinium nitrate, water and nitrogen dioxide gas; reaction is conducted by refluxing the oxide in concentrated HNO₃ (often 90 % or higher) at 80–120 °C; the acid serves both as proton donor and oxidising agent; no external catalyst.

Combination (solid‑state synthesis); purpose: preparation of a tin‑phosphide binary compound; key transformation: Sn metal reacts with red P to form Sn‑P phosphide; typical conditions: intimate mixing of powdered Sn and red P followed by heating to 600‑800 °C in an inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst required.

Type: Strong oxidative degradation (redox) of a nitrogen‑containing organic compound. Purpose: Completely mineralize methylhydrazine to innocuous gases while reducing permanganate. Key transformation: Potassium permanganate in acidic (H₂SO₄) medium is reduced to MnO₂; methylhydrazine is oxidized, its carbon skeleton to CO₂ and nitrogen atoms to N₂, with water produced from proton transfers. Typical conditions: Aqueous sulfuric acid (1–5 M), excess KMnO₄, temperature 80–150 °C,; proceeds without added catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed Knoevenagel/condensation followed by decarboxylative cyclization; purpose: synthesis of anisindione from diethyl oxalate and 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde; key steps: NaOEt deprotonates diethyl oxalate, forming a benzylidene malonate intermediate that cyclizes intramolecularly, losing CO₂ and ethanol to give anisindione; typical conditions: ethanol solvent, NaOEt (≈10 % mol) as base, reflux 60‑80 °C, then aqueous HCl work‑up; no metal catalyst required.

Aqueous redox (oxidation of nit by hypochlorite); purpose: conversion of nitrite to nitrate while reducing hypochlorite to chloride; key transformation: NO₂⁻+ OCl⁻ → NO₃⁻ + Cl⁻; typical conditions: dilute aqueous solution, ambient temperature, pH near neutral to slightly alkaline, rapid mixing; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base precipitation; formation of barium arsenate (Ba3(AsO4)2). As2O5 is dissolved in hot water to give H3AsO4, then reacted with Ba(OH)2 (3 mol Ba(OH)2 per mol As2O5) to precipitate Ba3(AsO4)2 and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at 60–80 °C with stirring; the white precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a metal nitride; purpose: generate ammonia and the corresponding oxide from erbium nitride; key transformation (overall): 2 ErN + 3 H₂O → Er₂O₃ + 2 NH₃; typical conditions: steam or boiling water at 400‑800 °C, solid‑state reaction under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of Er; no solvent or catalyst required.

Para‑hydroxylation of norephedrine to give p‑hydroxynorephedrine; general type is oxidative aromatic hydroxylation (often catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 enzyme or by chemical oxidants such as peracids); purpose is to introduce a hydroxyl group at the para position of the phenyl ring; key transformation is insertion of an oxygen atom onto the aromatic carbon para to the existing substituent; typical conditions for a biotransformation involve an aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8), NADPH‑regenerating system, and incubation with a recombinant P450 enzyme at 30 °C; chemical routes use a stoichiometric oxidant (e.g., mCPBA) in an organic solvent at low temperature.

Redox oxidation of elemental selenium by dilute nitric acid; purpose is to dissolve selenium to give selenous acid while reducing nitrate to monoxide. Selenium is added to cold (0–5 °C) dilute HNO3, producing H2SeO3 and NO gas; a small amount of water is consumed in the overall stoichiometry. The reaction is conducted in aqueous solution under mild stirring, typically at temperatures below 10 °C to limit side reactions. No special catalyst; the acid itself provides the oxidizing power.

Acyl‑chloride esterification; pyridine acts as base/HCl scavenger to convert salicyloyl chloride and isopropanol into isopropyl 2‑hydroxybenzoate (isopropyl salicylate) with release of HCl. Key transformation is nucleophilic acyl substitution on the acyl chloride. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dry dichloromethane or THF as solvent; pyridine (or triethylamine) present in stoichiometric amount.

Acid‑base/neutralization reaction between a basic carbonate and an acidic oxide. Sodium carbonate reacts with arsenic pentoxide to yield carbon dioxide gas and sodium arsenate. Usually performed in aqueous medium with gentle heating to evolve CO₂; water is the solvent and no special catalyst is required.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HCl to 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to give the tertiary chloride 2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane. ZnCl₂ acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst (Lucas conditions) to increase H⁺ electrophilicity. Conducted at 0 °C to reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or diethyl ether.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt reaction. Aqueous sodium sulfate exchanges anions with tin(II) chloride to afford sodium chloride and soluble stannous sulfate. Reaction proceeds readily at room temperature in water; no catalyst is required.

Reaction type: base‑mediated hydrolysis (saponification) of an acyl chloride; purpose: generate (E)‑cinnamic acid from the corresponding chloride; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the carbonyl carbon of (E)‑3‑phenylprop‑2‑enoyl chloride, yielding the carboxylate which is protonated on work‑up to give the acid and chloride is expelled as NaCl; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M) added to a solution of the acyl chloride in a biphasic system (e.g., EtOAc/H2O) at 0 °C to avoid side reactions, then warmed to rt; the product is isolated after acidification.

Dehydrative conversion of an amide to a nitrile (Vilsmeier‑type dehydration). Phosphorus oxychloride dehydrates 2,6‑dichlorobenzamide, producing the nitrile dichlobenil (2,6‑dichlorobenzonitrile) and phosphoric acid as by‑product. Typically carried out under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine, which also buffers the released acid) with POCl₃ added dropwise.

Acid–base reaction of beryllium carbonate with hydrogen bromide; carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming beryllium bromide. Conducted in aqueous HBr (conc. or 1–2 M) at 50–100 °C to ensure complete gas evolution; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation of 2‑methylthiophene; introduces a sulfonic acid group at the 5‑position to afford 2‑methylthiophene‑5‑sulfonic acid; typically carried out with concentrated H₂SO₄ (or fuming H₂SO₄) at 50–80 °C, the acid acts as both solvent and reagent; no additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: introduce an acetyl group para to the methyl substituent of toluene. Key transformation: generation of the acetyl cation from acetyl chloride and a Lewis acid, which then attacks the aromatic ring to give 1‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanone; HCl is released as by‑product. Typical conditions: AlCl3 (1.0–1.5 equiv) as catalyst, anhydrous CH2Cl2 or carbon disulfide as solvent, reaction started at 0 °C then warmed to reflux (40‑80 °C) under inert atmosphere.

Oxidative decomposition (acid oxidation) of carbohydrazide by conc. nitric acid; nitrogen gas and CO₂ are generated while water is formed; performed by adding solid carbohydrazide to cold, concentrated HNO₃ and allowing the mixture to warm (0–25 °C initially, then to reflux); the reaction proceeds without added catalyst; HNO₃ serves as both oxidant and solvent.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts a primary alkyl bromide to a thiol; purpose is synthesis of 3‑pentanethiol; key transformation is replacement of Br by –SH (from H2S) and generation of HBr in solution; usually carried out by bubbling H2S gas through aqueous solution of 3‑bromopentane or by adding aqueous NaSH, heated under reflux; aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent; HBr formed stays in aqueous phase.

Nucleophilic aromatic of 2‑chloropyridine with methylamine, yielding 2‑(methylamino)pyridine and HCl; generally conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 100–130 °C; a base (e.g., triethylamine or NaHCO₃) is added to trap HCl and drive the reaction; no metal catalyst is required.

Reduction of a disulfide bond: dibenzyl disulfide is reduced by sodium borohydride to give benzyl mercaptan; carried out in protic solvents like methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₄ supplies hydride to cleave the S–S bond; no additional catalyst needed.
Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); hydroxide replaces iodine on 2‑iodopropan‑1‑ol to generate 1,2‑propanediol (propylene glycol); generally conducted in aqueous NaOH, heated under reflux.

Kolbe‑Schmitt carboxylation of o‑cresol (2‑methylphenol) using sodium hydroxide and carbon dioxide to afford 6‑methylsalicylic acid after acid work‑up; reaction performed in aqueous NaOH solution under CO₂ pressure (~100 atm) at 120–130 °C; followed by acidification to precipitate the acid; no external catalyst required.
