Thermal pyrolysis of cellulose; high‑temperature (≈400–600 °C) inert‑atmosphere degradation of the polymer produces gases CO₂, CO, H₂O and ethylene; no solvent or catalyst is employed, the process relies solely on heat‑induced bond scission.

Nucleophilic addition of sulfite to formaldehyde (bisulfite adduct formation). Sodium sulfite adds to polymeric formaldehyde (paraformaldehyde) in aqueous solution, yielding the water‑soluble sodium hydroxymethanesulfonate (formal­dehyde sulfoxylate). Purpose: to trap formaldehyde, improve safety, or use the adduct as a reducing agent. Performed at room temperature in water; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Cesium phosphate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid in aqueous medium to give phosphoric acid and soluble cesium chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring; no special reagents needed.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation of 2‑naphthol; purpose is to introduce a sulfonic acid group at the 6‑position to afford 2‑naphthol‑6‑sulfonic acid, useful as a dye intermediate. The substrate is treated with fuming sulfuric acid (oleum, ≥20 % free SO3) at 80–120 °C for 1–2 h. The sulfonic acid group is installed via an SEAr mechanism, and water is liberated. No additional solvent; the reaction medium is the sulfonating mixture itself.

Oxidation of chloride by manganese(III) oxide in hydrochloric acid: redox reaction in which Mn₂O₃ oxidizes chloride ions to chlorine gas while being reduced to MnCl₂; water is formed as by‑product. Typically carried out by adding solid Mn₂O₃ to concentrated aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C; the evolution of Cl₂ gas is observed. No catalyst needed; aqueous solution acts as medium.

Acid‑base exchange (salt formation). Caesium oxalate is protonated by nitric acid, producing oxalic acid and cesium nitrate. Reaction carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst required.

Redox reaction of a metal with water. Aluminum metal reacts with water (typically hot water or in the presence of a base to remove the protective oxide layer) to generate hydrogen gas and aluminum hydroxide. Conditions: elevated temperature or alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH solution) to overcome passivation; the process oxidizes Al to Al(III) and reduces water to H₂.

Esterification via thionyl chloride activation. Oleic acid is first converted to the corresponding acyl chloride by thionyl chloride, then reacts with ethanol to give ethyl oleate while releasing sulfur dioxide and two equivalents of hydrogen chloride. The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in dry dichloromethane or pyridine at reflux, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization forming sodium arsenite; As2O3 + Na2CO3 + H2O → 2 NaAsO2 + CO2 + H2O (often written As2O3 + Na2CO3 → 2 NaAsO2 + CO2); carried out in aqueous solution at moderate temperature with stirring; no special catalyst.

Amide hydrolysis of 3‑hydroxypentanamide back to 3‑hydroxyvaleric acid and ammonia; acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis; commonly reflux in aqueous HCl (6 M) or NaOH (1 M) at 100–150 °C, then neutralize to isolate the acid and release NH3; solvent is water or water/MeOH; no extra catalyst required.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); purpose is to couple acetic acid with sec‑butanol to give sec‑butyl acetate under mild, non‑acidic conditions. DCC activates the carboxylic acid to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by the alcohol; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Commonly carried out in dry dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP; no metal catalyst needed.

Metal‑acid reduction producing phosphine; purpose: generate PH₃ gas from phosphinic acid; key transformation: Zn metal reduces H₃PO₂ in hydrochloric acid to phosphine, Zn²⁺ (as ZnCl₂) and water; typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M) with excess Zn at room temperature or gentle reflux, gas collected over water; no special catalyst needed.

Metal‑hydride reduction of an ester; purpose is complete reduction of methyl propionate to the corresponding primary alcohols, 1‑propanol and methanol. LiAlH4 transfers hydride to the carbonyl, generating an alkoxide that is hydrolyzed on work‑up. Reaction is performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, initially at 0 °C warmed to reflux; quenched carefully with water or dilute acid.

Radical halogenation of a group‑14 hydride; purpose is substitution of a hydrogen atom in germane (GeH4) by bromine to afford bromogermane (GeH3Br) and hydrogen bromide. Requires initiation by UV light or heat to generate Br· radicals; typically carried out in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform under reflux; no added catalyst.

Single‑displacement redox reaction with copper(I) chloride; purpose is to obtain copper metal from CuCl; key transformation: Zn oxidized to Zn²⁺ while Cu⁺ reduced to Cu(s); typical conditions: aqueous suspension of CuCl, often heated or performed in excess chloride (e.g., dilute HCl) to improve solubility; solvent: water (or aqueous HCl); no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization with a metal carbonate; purpose is to convert acetic acid into silver acetate while releasing carbon dioxide and water. Silver carbonate reacts with two equivalents of acetic acid, forming soluble silver acetate and evolving CO2 gas. Usually performed at room temperature in a non‑coordinating solvent such as ether or directly in the solid state; no additional catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 nucleophilic substitution); ethoxide ion attacks ethyl chloride to form diethyl ether and potassium chloride. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol or THF under inert atmosphere, typically at 0–80 °C; no catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of ferrocene; AlCl₃ generates the benzoyl acylium ion from benzoyl chloride, which electrophilically attacks the cyclopentadienyl ring to give benzoyl‑ferrocene with HCl as by‑product. Performed in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; excess AlCl₃ is used as Lewis acid catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester; purpose is to reduce the C=C double bond to give the saturated ester propyl propanoate. Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–5 atm), 0 °C to reflux, catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni; solvent often ethanol, ethyl acetate or THF.

Acylation of the primary alcohol of 2‑mercaptoethanol with acetic anhydride to give 2‑acetoxyethanethiol (O‑acetylation) and one equivalent of acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: catalytic pyridine or DMAP as base, 0 °C to room temperature, dichloromethane or THF as solvent; the reaction proceeds rapidly (≤1 h) and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; barium acetate exchanges anions with lead(II) sulfate, precipitating insoluble BaSO₄ and leaving soluble lead(II) acetate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Copper‑catalyzed alkynylation (SN2-type C‑C bond formation); terminal acetylene is deprotonated by triethylamine to give the acetylide, which, in the presence of CuI, couples with cyclopropyl bromide to afford cyclopropylacetylene. Reaction carried out in dry THF or DMF under nitrogen, typically at 0–25 °C; CuI functions as the catalyst and TEA as base.

Double‑displacement precipitation of a lanthanide fluoride; Lu(NO₃)₃ reacts with NH₄F, exchanging anions to form insoluble LuF₃ (which can be filtered) and soluble NH₄NO₃. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution, then cooling to isolate the fluoride precipitate; no catalyst required.

Reduction; conversion of a nitro phenol to an amino phenol using zinc dust and ammonium chloride (a mild acidic medium). Purpose: synthesis of p‑aminophenol, a key intermediate for pharmaceuticals such as paracetamol. Key transformation: –NO2 group is reduced to –NH2 while the phenolic OH remains unchanged. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic solution, zinc dust added to a suspension of p‑nitrophenol and NH4Cl, heated to reflux (≈80–100 °C) for several hours. No special catalyst beyond the Zn/NH4Cl system; filtration removes excess zinc after completion.

Synthesis of benzoyl azide from benzoyl chloride and azidotrimethylsilane: same class as reaction 2, nucleophilic acyl substitution; purpose is to generate benzoyl azide for Curtius rearrangement; key transformation is displacement of chloride by the azide moiety, forming benzoyl azide and trimethylsilyl chloride; usually performed in dry dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to rt with pyridine or triethylamine as HCl scavenger; no catalyst required.

Chemical ester hydrolysis of a phosphate ester; purpose is dealkylation to afford a mono‑phosphate and an alcohol; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the dimethyl phenyl phosphate producing phenyl hydrogen phosphate and methanol; typically performed in aqueous solution, often with mild acid (e.g., dilute HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) as catalyst, at room temperature to 80 °C; no special organic solvent required.

Double‑displacement (acid–base) reaction; exchange of the acetate anion of cobalt(II) acetate with the sulfate anion of sulfuric acid to give cobalt(II) sulfate and acetic acid. Purpose: preparation of soluble cobalt(II) sulfate or removal of acetate ligands. Key transformation: Co(OAc)2 + H2SO4 → CoSO4 + 2 HOAc. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20–60 °C) with stirring until all solids dissolve. No catalyst required; the reaction proceeds spontaneously in water.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; chlorine oxidizes the peroxide oxygen in barium peroxide, liberating molecular oxygen and forming barium chloride. Purpose: laboratory generation of O2 (historically the Brayton process). Key transformation: BaO2 + Cl2 → BaCl2 + O2. Typical conditions: solid‑gas contact at high temperature (≈400–600 °C) in a sealed furnace or reactor; no solvent. No catalyst; the reaction is driven by the thermodynamic favorability of Cl2 reduction to Cl− and O2 release.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the ammonium salt of picolinic acid (ammonium picolinate). Ammonia deprotonates the carboxylic acid of picolinic acid, giving water and the ionic salt. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst or solvent needed beyond water.

Metathesis/acid–base reaction; sulfuric acid protonates dipotassium selenite, exchanging potassium for hydrogen to generate selenous acid and potassium sulfate. Purpose: preparation of H2SeO3 in aqueous media or conversion of selenite salts to the corresponding acid. Key transformation: H2SO4 + K2SeO3 → H2SeO3 + K2SO4. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, moderate heating (≈50–80 °C) to aid dissolution; reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature as well. No catalyst required.

Transetherification (ether exchange) between ethanol and furfuryl methyl ether, yielding ethyl furfuryl ether and methanol. Purpose: synthesis of the ethyl ether derivative of furfuryl alcohol; also a method to recycle methanol. Key transformation: CH3CH2OH + CH3O‑C4H3O‑CH2‑ → CH3OH + CH3CH2O‑C4H3O‑CH2‑. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert solvent (toluene or xylene) with removal of the formed methanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium to the right; acid catalyst such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or Lewis acid (e.g., BF3·OEt2) is commonly employed. Reaction temperature 80–120 °C; reaction time 2–6 h.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Purpose: reduce the carbonyl of 2,2,2‑tribromoacetaldehyde to give 2,2,2‑tribromoethanol. Key transformation: H₂ adds across the C=O bond, converting –CHO to –CH₂OH. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–3 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst, in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, at room temperature to reflux for 1–4 h. No additional reagents needed.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (Fischer ether synthesis) yielding 2‑methoxypropane; purpose is to prepare the methyl‑isopropyl ether; key transformation CH3OH + (CH3)2CHOH → (CH3)2CHOCH3 + H2O; carried out with a strong acid (concentrated H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) at 130‑150 °C, often using excess alcohol and azeotropic removal of water; the acid acts as the catalyst.

Thermal cracking (propane pyrolysis); propane heated to ~800 °C, often over a zeolite or metal‑oxide catalyst, causing C‑C bond cleavage to give ethylene and methane; provides ethylene as a petrochemical feedstock.

Type: N‑alkylation (SN2) of imidazole using a strong base. Purpose: attach a benzyl group to the nitrogen of imidazole to form 1‑benzylimidazole. Key transformation: NaH deprotonates imidazole to generate the imidazolide anion, which displaces chloride from benzyl chloride. By‑products are NaCl and H₂ from NaH protonation. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (DMF, THF, or DMSO), NaH (1.1 eq) added at 0 °C, then benzyl chloride (1.0 eq) added, reaction stirred at rt to 40 °C for 2–12 h under inert N₂ atmosphere.

Type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive cleavage) of a disulfide to a thiol. Purpose: convert benzyl disulfide into benzyl mercaptan. Key transformation: H₂ reduces the S–S bond, yielding two equivalents of benzyl‑SH. Typical conditions: H₂ (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5 % loading) or Raney Ni, in ethanol methanol solvent, at rt to reflux for 1–3 h. Reaction is usually performed under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Halogenation (free‑radical substitution); purpose is to fully brominate tribromomethane to carbon tetrabromide, releasing HBr; key transformation CHBr3 + Br2 → CBr4 + HBr; carried out under UV irradiation or thermal initiation, usually in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl4) with excess Br2; no special catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (amination); transforms a secondary bromide into the corresponding secondary amine (pentan‑2‑amine). Ammonia serves as nucleophile; ammonium bromide precipitates. Often performed in liquid NH₃ or ethanol under reflux; excess NH₃ drives the reaction.

Type: thermal decomposition (redox) of a metal cyanide. Purpose: generate cyanogen gas and elemental silver. Key transformation: heating AgCN causes electron transfer, producing Ag⁰ and (CN)₂. Typical conditions: solid AgCN heated to 200–300 °C in a sealed quartz tube or under a flow of inert gas; no solvent or catalyst is required. The reaction is conducted in a well‑ventilated hood due to toxic cyanogen.

Acylation of 1H‑tetrazol‑5‑amine with acetic anhydride; type: amide formation (acetylation of an amine); purpose: protect the tetrazolyl nitrogen as an N‑acetyl derivative; key transformation: the amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride, releasing acetic acid and forming N‑(2H‑tetrazol‑5‑yl)acetamide; typical conditions: neat acetic anhydride or in pyridine as solvent, heating to 50‑80 °C for 1–2 h; catalytic DMAP can be used to accelerate the reaction.

Thermal dehydration of chromium(III) hydroxide to chromium(III) oxide; upon strong heating (≈300–500 °C) the hydroxide loses water, yielding Cr₂O₃ (green solid) and water vapor; performed in a furnace or heat gun under air or inert atmosphere.

Type: acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: prepare the sodium salt of fluoroacetic acid. Key transformation: deprotonation of fluoroacetic acid by NaOH gives water and sodium fluoroacetate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric NaOH (1 eq) added to fluoroacetic acid at 0–25 °C, stirring until dissolution; reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature.

Type: alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: convert methyl 3‑nitrobenzoate to 3‑nitrobenzoic acid, releasing methanol. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give the carboxylate and methanol; subsequent acid work‑up yields the free acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1.5–2 eq) in water/ethanol (1:1) mixture, reflux (80–100 °C) for 2– h. After completion, the mixture is acidified (e.g., with dilute HCl) to precipitate 3‑nitrobenzoic acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; reduces the C=C bond of but‑2‑en‑1‑ol to give the saturated primary alcohol butan‑1‑ol. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni, in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol, methanol) at room temperature to 100 °C.

Free‑radical chlorination (substitution) of 1,2‑dichloropropane with chlorine to afford 1,2,3‑trichloropropane; purpose is further chlorination to a fully chlorinated three‑carbon chain; typically carried out under UV irradiation in CCl₄ or similar inert solvent; chlorine gas is the only reagent.

Oxid of phenylacetaldehyde to phenylacetic acid using potassium permanganate under basic conditions. KMnO₄ oxidizes the aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid, generating MnO₂ precipitate, KOH, and water. Carried out in aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or KOH) at reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours; the reaction is quenched byification and filtration removes MnO₂.

Neutralization of hexanoic acid with hexylammonium hydroxide to afford hexylammonium hexanoate and water; purpose is to generate an ammonium carboxylate salt, useful as an ionic liquid or surfactant; key step is proton transfer from the acid to the ammonium base; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature with gentle stirring.

Double‑replacement/precipitation reaction in which aqueous ammonia neutralizes indium(III nitrate, producing insoluble indium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate. Conducted in water at room temperature; the mixture is stirred until the white indium hydroxide precipitate forms, then filtered and washed. No additional reagents required.

Type: alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an amide. Purpose: cleave the amide bond to form the corresponding carboxylic acid and release ammonia. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, followed by elimination of NH₃ to give the carboxylate, which upon acid work‑up affords 4‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (5–10 M, 1.5–2 equiv) heated to reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours. The reaction mixture is cooled, acidified with dilute HCl to precipitate the acid, and the product is filtered and purified. Solvent is water or a water/ethanol mixture.

Strong oxidative conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; potassium permanganate oxidizes 4‑(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde to 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoic acid. The aldehyde is oxidized to the acid while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II). Conducted in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or KOH), KMnO₄ added portionwise at 0–25 °C, often followed by reflux. Water (or water/acetone) is the solvent; permanganate itself acts as the oxidant, no separate catalyst needed.

Free‑radical chlorination of pentane; UV light or thermal initiation leads to hydrogen abstraction at a secondary carbon, affording 2‑chloropentane and HCl; performed in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl4) or neat gas; no catalyst; used to generate a secondary alkyl chloride.

Direct combination (synthesis) of a metal and halogen; purpose is preparation of zirconium tetrachloride, a Lewis‑acid precursor. Key transformation: Zr(s) + Cl₂(g) → ZrCl₄(s). Typical conditions: heated to 400–500 °C in a sealed tube or flow reactor under an inert atmosphere; excess chlorine drives the reaction. No solvent required.
Dehydration (thermal condensation) of gold(III) hydroxide to give gold(III) oxide and water; typically achieved by heating the hydroxide solid, often in a dry atmosphere, no solvent required.

N‑alkylation via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; purpose is synthesis of N‑methylethanolamine, a building block for surfactants and chelating agents. Key transformation: the nitrogen lone pair of ethanolamine attacks methyl iodide, displacing I⁻ to give N‑methylethanolamine and HI. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, acetonitrile or THF, 0 °C to room temperature; excess amine or a base (e.g., NaHCO₃, triethylamine) is used to neutralize the generated HI.

Reaction type: redox. Purpose: reduction of platinum(IV) to platinum(II). Key transformation: hydrogen gas reduces platinum tetrachloride (Pt⁴⁺) to platinum dichloride (Pt²⁺), generating hydrogen chloride. Conditions: likely heating and acidic environment. No specific catalyst mentioned.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation/acid‑base reaction; purpose is generation of chloric acid in solution while removing lead as insoluble sulfate. Key transformation: H₂SO₄ + Pb(ClO₃)₂ → HClO₃ + PbSO₄↓. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, temperature kept below 50 °C to avoid decomposition of chloric acid; the lead(II) sulfate precipitates and is filtered. No catalyst required.

Base‑promoted O‑demethylation (nucleophilic aromatic substitution); purpose is conversion ofxetin (6‑methoxy‑7,8‑dihydroxy‑coumarin) to esculetin (6,7‑dihydroxy‑coumarin). Key transformation: NaOH attacks the methyl group of the aryl‑O‑Me, cleaving the C‑O bond to give methanol and the phenolic esculetin. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; reaction can be carried out in water or water/ethanol mixture. After cooling, the mixture is neutralized and the product isolated by filtration or extraction.

Dehydrative anhydride formation; used to convert a dicarboxylic acid into its cyclic anhydride. The carbonyl oxygen of acetic anhydride activates the carboxyl groups of naphthalene‑1,8‑dicarboxylic acid, promoting intramolecular condensation and loss of one equivalent of acetic acid to give naphthalic anhydride. Typically performed by heating the acid with excess acetic anhydride at 100‑130 °C, often under nitrogen. Solvent may be none (neat) or a high‑boiling inert liquid such as toluene; a catalytic amount of pyridine can be added to scavenge liberated HCl.

Ozonolysis of an alkene; employed to cleave the C=C bond of 1,1,3‑trichloropropene and generate aldehyde fragments. Ozone adds across the double bond forming a molozonide that rearranges to an ozonide; reductive work‑up (Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) yields chloroacetaldehyde and 2,2‑dichloroacetaldehyde. Conducted at –78 °C to 0 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, under an inert atmosphere; the reaction is quenched after complete ozone consumption.

High‑temperature redox reduction; carbon (often as charcoal or coke) serves as a reducing agent for mixed‑valent terbium oxide (Tb4O7). Carbon is oxidized to CO2 while Tb4O7 is reduced to Tb2O3 (indium‑type Tb(III) oxide). The solid‑state reaction is carried out in a furnace at 800‑1000 °C in a flowing inert gas or air, with intimate mixing of carbon and oxide powders; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of an aryl chloride to form an aryl ether (often Cu‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type); purpose is synthesis of 2‑methoxypyridine, a useful heteroaryl ether. Key transformation: the chloride on 2‑chloropyridine is displaced by methoxide (generated from methanol and a base), yielding 2‑methoxypyridine and HCl. Typical conditions: generation of methoxide with NaH, NaOMe or K₂CO₃ in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 100–150 °C; copper(I) iodide (5–10 mol %) with a nitrogen ligand (e.g., 1,10‑phenanthroline) is common; the acidic by‑product (HCl) is scavenged by the base.

Gas‑phase reduction of vanadium(V) oxide by carbon monoxide; CO acts as a reducing agent converting V2O5 to VO2 while being oxidized to CO2; carried out at 300–600 °C under a flow of CO (often diluted with inert gas); solid V2O5 is reduced on a hot surface; CO2 is the gaseous by‑product; no additional catalyst needed.

Direct synthesis/oxidation reaction; manganese metal reacts with fluorine gas to form manganese(II) fluoride (MnF₂); manganese is oxidized to +2, fluorine reduced to –1; performed at moderate temperature (200–300 °C) under controlled F₂ flow, often in a fluorine‑compatible reactor; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Metathesis/acid‑base precipitation; phosphoric acid protonates the acetate ligands of indium(III) acetate, generating acetic acid and forming insoluble indium(III) phosphate. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient to mildly elevated temperature (20‑60 °C) with vigorous stirring; the precipitated InPO4 is filtered off. No special catalyst is required; dilute acid medium assists dissolution of the indium salt.

Epoxide ring‑opening addition; the secondary amine of piperazine attacks ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring and installing a 2‑hydroxyethyl substituent on one nitrogen, yielding N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)piperazine. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (water, ethanol) at 50‑80 °C under nitrogen; a base such as NaHCO3 or K2CO3 is often added to deprotonate the amine and accelerate the nucleophilic attack. The reaction may be catalyzed by a phase‑transfer catalyst for improved rate.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation of an aromatic amine with thiocyanate (generated in situ from NH4SCN and HCl) to give an aryl‑thiourea; purpose is preparation of α‑naphthylthiourea as a reagent or precursor; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the protonated amine on isothiocyanic acid followed by tautomerisation to the thiocarbonyl; typical conditions are aqueous HCl, temperature 0–50 °C, stirring until completion; no special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl iodide with fluoride ion to afford a primary alkyl fluoride; purpose is halogen exchange to install a fluorine atom; key transformation is attack of F⁻ on the electrophilic carbon displacing I⁻; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or NMP, often with 18‑crown‑6 or tetra‑n‑butylammonium fluoride to increase KF solubility; reflux temperature for several hours; KI precipitates and is removed.

Base‑catalysed bis‑alkylation of barbituric acid at the C‑5 active methylene to give the barbiturate butobarbital; purpose is synthesis of a sedative‑hypnotic barbiturate; key transformation is deprotonation of barbituric acid (often with NaH, K2CO3 or NaOEt) followed by SN2 attack of ethyl chloride and 1‑methyl‑butyl chloride; ultrasound irradiation enhances mixing and reaction rate; typical conditions: reflux in dry THF or acetonitrile under nitrogen, 30–60 min ultrasonic bath, then work‑up and purification.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using Dess‑Martin periodinane (DMP); purpose is conversion of 1‑methyl‑4‑piperidinol to 1‑methyl‑4‑piperidone, a key intermediate in pharmaceutical synthesis. Key transformation: DMP transfers an oxygen atom to the alcohol, forming the carbonyl and producing iodobenzene diacetate as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, 1–1.5 equiv DMP, with a mild base such as pyridine or NaHCO₃ to neutralize acidic by‑products; reaction completes in 0.5–2 h, followed by aqueous work‑up with sodium thiosulfate.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis; zirconium dioxide reacts with sodium carbonate upon heating (≈800–1000 °C) to yield sodium zirconate (Na2ZrO3) and release carbon dioxide gas; performed in a crucible or furnace under dry conditions, no solvent or catalyst.

The acid-sulfite reaction between strontium sulfite and sulfuric acid produces strontium sulfate, sulfur dioxide gas, and water. It is used to generate SO₂ gas or convert sulfite to sulfate. Key transformations include sulfite reacting with acid to release SO₂. Conditions are aqueous solution at room temperature, with water as the solvent. No catalysts are required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of strontium oxalate from aqueous sodium oxalate and strontium chloride; purpose is isolation of the insoluble strontium salt; key transformation is exchange of cations, forming NaCl (soluble) and SrC₂O₄ (sparingly soluble) which precipitates; performed at room temperature or slight heating in water with vigorous stirring; the solid is filtered, washed, and dried; no catalyst required.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of a metal and a metalloid to form an intermetallic compound, manganese arsenide. Elements are intimately mixed and heated under inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) at 600‑800 °C to promote diffusion and reaction; no solvent, catalyst, or additional reagents.

Single displacement/redox reaction; halogen replacement where Br₂ oxidizes I⁻ to form I₂. Br₂ acts as a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂. Occurs in aqueous or non-polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄) at ambient conditions. No catalyst.

Oxidation of a primary neopentyl alcohol to the corresponding carboxylic acid (2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid). The alcohol is first oxidized to the aldehyde and then to the acid using a strong oxidant such as potassium permanganate in alkaline medium, Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄), or NaClO₂ with NaH₂PO₄ (Pinnick oxidation). Reactions are performed at 0 °C to rt, aqueous or biphasic organic/aqueous media, and the acid is isolated by acidification and extraction.

Intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) of succinic acid to succinic anhydride; purpose is preparation of the cyclic anhydride for further acylation chemistry; key transformation is loss of water from the dicarboxylic acid to form a five‑membered anhydride ring; commonly carried out by heating succinic acid with a strong dehydrating agent such as acetic anhydride, propionic anhydride, or excess P₂O₅, or by flash vacuum pyrolysis at 200–250 °C; reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in a dry solvent (toluene) or neat, and the anhydride is distilled or sublimed away.

Dehydrative condensation of orthophosphoric acid; two molecules of H₃PO₄ lose water to form pyrophosphoric acid (diphosphoric acid). This condensation requires elevated temperature (200–300 °C) under reduced pressure or with a dehydrating agent (e.g., P₂O₅) to drive off water. The reaction is used to generate polyphosphate intermediates.

Double displacement/redox synthesis of a metal chalcogenide; hydrogen telluride (acid) reacts with tin(II) chloride to precipitate tin(II) telluride and release hydrogen chloride gas. Typically performed in aqueous solution under inert atmosphere, often at 0–25 °C, with stirring and removal of HCl gas.

TEMPO‑mediated aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde (oxidative dehydrogenation). The oxoammonium species derived from TEMPO oxidizes the benzylic –CH₂OH to –CHO, while NaOCl serves as the terminal oxidant and NaBr accelerates the catalytic cycle. Reaction is performed at ambient temperature in a biphasic mixture (e.g., CH₂Cl₂/H₂O or MeCN/H₂O) buffered to pH 8–9 (often with NaHCO₃). Catalytic amount of TEMPO (≈5 mol %) and stoichiometric NaOCl are used; NaBr (≈10 mol %) acts as co‑catalyst.

Pinnick oxidation of an aldehyde; 2‑nonenal is oxidized to 2‑nonenoic acid using sodium chlorite in the presence of catalytic hydrogen peroxide (or sodium chlorite alone) in a buffered aqueous medium (often phosphate buffer) with a co‑solvent such as tert‑butanol. Reaction carried out at 0 °C to room temperature, pH 3–5, to avoid over‑oxidation.

Redox reduction of tin(IV) oxide using carbon monoxide; SnO₂ reduced to SnO and CO oxidized to CO₂; performed at elevated temperatures (≈500–700 °C) in a CO stream or CO/air mixture; solid–gas reaction, no solvent.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of allyl bromide with cesium acetate to afford allyl acetate and cesium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, or acetone) at ambient temperature; cesium ion enhances acetate nucleophilicity and improves yields.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using Diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to obtain benzaldehyde from ethyl benzoate; key transformation is hydride addition to the carbonyl forming an alkoxyaluminium intermediate which on low‑temperature work‑up gives the aldehyde while ethanol is released; typical conditions: 0 °C to –78 °C, dry THF as solvent, 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H, inert atmosphere; quench with methanol or aqueous ammonium chloride.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal oxide. Hydrogen bromide gas reacts with solid beryllium oxide, protonating the oxide to give soluble beryllium bromide and water. Usually carried out by passing dry HBr gas over heated BeO or by dissolving BeO in aqueous HBr at reflux; the reaction proceeds quantitatively.

Fischer esterification of tartaric acid with ethanol to produce ethyl tartrate (mono‑ester) and water; catalyzed by concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, refluxing ethanol (≈78 °C) with removal of water (Dean–Stark) or using excess ethanol; typical reaction time 4–12 h.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a lactam;4‑piperidone is reduced with H₂ over palladium on carbon to give piperidine and water. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, room temperature to 50 °C, with reaction monitored until gas uptake ceases.

Reaction type: acid–base neutralization with gas evolution; Purpose: convert calcium carbonate to soluble calcium acetate while liberating CO₂; Key transformation: carbonate reacts with acetic acid to give Ca²⁺ acetate, water and CO₂ gas; Typical conditions: aqueous or glacial acetic acid at room temperature, excess acid, stirring; Common solvent/catalyst: water/acetic acid mixture, no catalyst.

Oxime formation (condensation); converts 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde to its oxime for protection or further functionalization; the aldehyde carbonyl reacts with hydroxylamine (from hydroxylamine hydrochloride) to give a C=N‑OH group; typically performed in ethanol or methanol with sodium acetate as buffer (pH ~5) under reflux for 1–2 h.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of 3‑chloropropan‑1‑ol with alcoholic KOH to give allyl alcohol; purpose is synthesis of the allylic alcohol. Key transformation is removal of a β‑hydrogen and chloride to form a C=C double bond while retaining the primary alcohol. Typical conditions: refluxing KOH in ethanol or isopropanol (alcoholic medium), often 60–80 °C, aqueous KOH solution with excess alcohol as solvent.

Oxidation of an α‑hydroxy aldehyde to an α‑hydroxy acid; glycolaldehyde is converted to glycolic acid using oxidants such as sodium chlorite (Pinnick oxidation), NaClO₂ with a buffer, or mild aerobic oxidation catalysts. Usually performed in aqueous buffer (pH 3–5) at 0–25 °C; the reaction proceeds via aldehyde → carboxylic acid without affecting the adjacent hydroxyl group.

Same reaction type as #2 but using potassium phosphate; lead nitrate and potassium phosphate in aqueous solution give a lead(II) phosphate precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate; ambient conditions, water solvent, no catalyst.

Ethanolysis (transesterification) of benzyl acetate; ethanol replaces the acetate group, producing ethyl acetate and benzyl alcohol; conducted with excess ethanol, catalyzed by a mineral acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or a base (NaOEt) at 70–90 °C.

Acid–base neutralization; metal oxide reacts with strong acid to give a soluble metal salt and water. Scandium oxide is dissolved in aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically with gentle heating and stirring, yielding scandium chloride in solution and water as by‑product. No catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Acid‑metal displacement (single‑displacement) reaction; elemental lithium reacts with hydrochloric acid to generate hydrogen gas and lithium chloride. Typically carried out by adding lithium metal to aqueous HCl (or dry HCl gas in an ether/THF solvent) at 0 °C to control vigorous hydrogen evolution; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds rapidly.

Strong‑base induced E2 dehydrohalogenation of 3‑iodopentane. Purpose: formation of an internal alkene by elimination of HX. Key transformation: potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, the C–I bond breaks, yielding 2‑pentene and potassium iodide. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (THF, DME) at 0‑25 °C to 60 °C under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst needed.

Double displacement (precipitation) between sodium formate and silver nitrate; purpose is to prepare silver formate from readily available salts; the reaction swaps Na⁺ and Ag⁺ to yield solid AgCOO and soluble NaNO₃; usually performed in water, optionally with mild heating to improve crystal formation; no catalyst is employed.

Acid–base reaction; carbonate reacts with a carboxylic acid to release CO₂ and form the corresponding acetate salt. Typically carried out in aqueous solution or dilute acetic acid; gentle heating may be applied to drive off CO₂. No special catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Acid–base metathesis between sulfuric acid and silver cyanide. Purpose: generation of hydrogen cyanide gas and precipitation of silver sulfate. Key transformation: protonation of cyanide anion releases HCN, while Ag⁺ combines with SO₄²⁻ to form insoluble Ag₂SO₄. Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄, low temperature (0‑25 °C) in aqueous suspension, performed in a fume hood due to toxic HCN. No catalyst.

Reductive cleavage of an azo bond using sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄). Purpose: conversion of 4‑aminoazobenzene to the corresponding aromatic amines. Key transformation: dithionite reduces the N=N linkage, splitting the molecule into aniline and p‑phenylenediamine while being oxidized to sulfite/bisulfite. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH ~7‑9 (often with NaOH to maintain dithionite stability), ambient temperature, excess Na₂S₂O₄. No metal catalyst.

Acid‑base reaction of hydrofluoric acid with sodium metasilicate. Purpose: conversion of silicate to silica and fluoride salts. Key transformation: protonation of silicate anion yields SiO₂ precipitate and water; Na⁺ pairs with F⁻ to give NaF. Typical conditions: aqueous HF (conc. ~10‑20 %), ambient to mild heating, vigorous stirring. No catalyst required.

Oxidation (aldehyde to carboxylic acid) – Pinnick oxidation. Sodium chlorite (NaClO2) converts the aldehyde group of 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde into a carboxyl group, yielding 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid. Typically performed in a buffered aqueous medium (e.g., NaH2PO4, pH 4–5) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often with a scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to suppress side‑reactions. Solvent mixture of water/t‑butanol is common; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution; calcium tartrate precipitates while potassium chloride remains dissolved; performed at room temperature or with mild heating; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (ammonium salt hydrolysis). Aqueous NaOH deproton the ammonium ions of zinc ammonium sulfate, producing ammonia gas, water, sodium sulfate and zinc hydroxide precipitate. Reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; vigorous stirring may be used to keep solids suspended. No special catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base salt formation (ammonium tetrafluoroborate). Purpose: generate a stable diammonium tetrafluoroborate salt. Key transformation: protonation of both amine groups of ethylenediamine by HBF₄ to give ethylenediammonium dication paired with two BF₄⁻ anions. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium, addition of cold 48 % HBF₄ to ethylenediamine solution at 0 °C, stirring, followed by crystallization from ethanol or ether.

Base‑catalysed etherification (phenol‑epichlorohydrin condensation) to form resorcinol diglycidyl ether. The phenolic OH of resorcinol attacks epichlorohydrin in the presence of calcium hydroxide, producing glycidyl ether linkages and water, while calcium chloride precipitates. Conducted at 60–80 °C in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or THF) under nitrogen; purpose is preparation of a bis‑epoxy resin monomer.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Sodium carbonate exchanges anions with calcium hypochlorite, precipitating calcium carbonate and generating sodium hypochlorite in solution. Performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent. Used to produce sodium hypochlorite (bleach) while removing calcium as solid.

Acid–base neutralization; lead(II) oxide reacts with aqueous nitric acid to produce soluble lead(II) nitrate and water; usually conducted in aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst required.

Reductive amination of a ketone with ammonia. 2‑Chloroacetophenone condenses with ammonia to form an imine (or iminium) intermediate, which is reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to give 1‑(2‑chlorophenyl)propan‑2‑amine. The reaction is typically run in methanol or ethanol at pH 5–6, at room temperature or mild heating, under nitrogen. NaCNBH₃ serves as the mild, chemoselective reducing agent.

Reductive de‑nitroation of 2,5‑dichloronitrobenzene to 2,5‑dichloroaniline using stannous chloride in hydrochloric acid. SnCl₂ reduces the nitro group to an amino group under acidic conditions, typically refluxing at 60–100 °C in aqueous HCl. The reaction yields the desired aniline and tin chlorides as by‑products; purpose is synthesis of a dichloro‑aniline intermediate.

Disproportionation (redox) of iodous acid (HIO₂) in aqueous solution, producing elemental iodine (I₂), water, and iodic acid (HIO₃). The reaction proceeds upon heating or in the presence of acid/base and requires no external catalyst. It converts iodine in the +3 oxidation state to a mixture of 0 and +5 states.

Dehydration (elimination) reaction catalyzed by enolase; purpose is generation of the high‑energy enol‑phosphate phosphoenolpyruvate in glycolysis; key transformation: removal of water from 2‑phosphoglycerate to form phosphoenolpyruvate; requires divalent metal ion cofactor (Mg²⁺) and occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH and temperature (≈ 37 °C); reaction is reversible.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of 2,2‑dichlorobutane over palladium on carbon. Molecular hydrogen reduces the C–Cl bonds, releasing hydrogen chloride and forming n‑butane. Typically carried out at 1–5 atm H₂, 20–50 °C, in a solvent such as ethanol or methanol. Purpose is dehalogenation to obtain the saturated alkane.

Oxidation reaction; converts the benzylic double bond of acenaphthene to a 1,2-diketone (acenaphthene‑1,2‑dione). Performed with aqueous potassium permanganate in concentrated sulfuric acid under reflux; KMnO4 serves as oxidant and MnSO4 is reduced to Mn(II). Typical solvent is water/H2SO4 mixture; reaction proceeds at 80‑100 °C.

Reaction type: alkaline hydrolysis combined with β‑elimination (E2) of an α‑bromo ester. Purpose: converts methyl 2‑bromobutanoate into the unsaturated carboxylic acid (crotonic acid) and methanol, while eliminating bromide as NaBr. Key transformation: NaOH hydrolyzes the ester to the carboxylate, then intramolecular elimination of HBr yields the α,β‑unsaturated acid; methanol is released from the ester moiety. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (excess) heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) for 2–4 h; after reaction, acidify with dilute HCl to precipitate the acid. Solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Alkoxide exchange (transesterification) of a metal alkoxide with an alcohol; titanium(IV) isopropoxide reacts with ethanol to afford titanium(IV) ethoxide and isopropanol; commonly performed under reflux in excess ethanol, sometimes with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove the isopropanol; inert atmosphere and anhydrous conditions are typical; no catalyst required.

Transesterification between a primary alcohol (butan‑1‑ol) and titanium tetraisopropoxide; purpose is to exchange alkoxy ligands and generate titanium tetrabutoxide while releasing isopropanol. The reaction is conducted under anhydrous conditions, often with azeotropic removal of the liberated isopropanol to drive equilibrium forward. Typical conditions: reflux in a dry, aprotic solvent (toluene, benzene, or xylene), inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), and removal isopropanol by Dean‑Stark apparatus.

Gas‑phase oxidation reaction; nitrate radical (NO3•) oxidizes carbon monoxide (CO) yielding nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and carbon dioxide (CO2); takes place in the nighttime atmosphere; proceeds without solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation; methoxide ion deprotonates chloroacetic acid, yielding sodium chloroacetate and methanol. No redox change occurs. Typical conditions: stir chloroacetic acid with sodium methoxide in anhydrous methanol or a mixed methanol/water solvent at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is usually complete within minutes.

Acyl exchange (mixed anhydride formation) using potassium 2‑methylpropanoate and acetic anhydride; purpose is to synthesize isobutyric anhydride; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate on acetic anhydride giving 2‑methylpropanoic anhydride and potassium acetate; typical conditions: dry aprotic solvent (THF or dichloromethane), 0 °C to rt, often with pyridine or triethylamine as base to scavenge generated acid; no metal catalyst required.

Reductive amination of a ketone. 4‑Phenylbutan‑2‑one reacts with ammonium acetate as the nitrogen source; NaCNBH₃ reduces the intermediate imine to afford 4‑phenylbutan‑2‑amine. The reaction is carried out in methanol or ethanol (often with a small amount of water) at 20‑50 °C, under mildly acidic to neutral conditions (pH 5‑6). NaCNBH₃ acts as the selective reducing agent; no metal catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using an anhydride; methylamine attacks one carbonyl of propionic anhydride, opening the anhydride to give N‑methylpropanamide and liberating propionic acid as the by‑product. Typical conditions: dilute solution of methylamine in a solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, temperature controlled at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize the released acid, reaction time 1–2 h.

E2 elimination reaction. Potassium hydroxide in ethanol induces dehydrohalogenation, removing β-hydrogens and bromide to form 3-methyl-1-heptene. Follows anti-periplanar transition state without carbocation.

Nitrosation of a urea derivative; nitrosyl sulfate (NO+ source) reacts with N‑propylurea to introduce a nitroso group on the nitrogen, forming N‑nitroso‑N‑propylurea while generating sulfuric acid as the acidic by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (often cooled to 0–5 °C) to control the highly electrophilic NO+, slow addition of nitrosyl sulfate, stirring until completion; the reaction is usually performed under inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation; electrophilic aromatic substitution used to introduce a trifluoroacetyl group onto the aromatic ring of toluene. The group directs the acylation predominantly to the para position, giving 4‑(trifluoroacetyl)‑toluene and HCl as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–1.5 equiv) as Lewis‑acid catalyst, inert atmosphere, dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride as solvent, 0 °C to ambient, followed by aqueous work‑up to remove HCl and AlCl₃ residues.

Halide metathesis (halogen exchange); used to prepare trimethylsilyl iodide from the bromide. Lithium iodide swaps its iodide for the bromide of bromotrimethylsilane, yielding LiBr and Me3SiI. Typically carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Redox (single‑displacement) reduction of nickel(II) iodide by zinc metal, wherein zinc is oxidized to Zn²⁺ and Ni²⁺ is reduced to elemental nickel; usually conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol or water) with heating; no external catalyst.

SN2 substitution of ethyl iodide with aqueous ammonia to give ethylamine and ammonium iodide. Reaction is carried out in aqueous NH₃ (often concentrated, ~25 % w/w) at room temperature or mild reflux (30–50 °C). Excess ammonia drives the reaction to completion; no catalyst needed. This method provides a straightforward preparation of primary amines.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Sodium azide reacts with copper(I) bromide to afford copper(I azide precipitate and NaBr. Performed in aqueous or mixed water/ethanol medium at low temperature, protected from light; product isolated by filtration.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic aromatic alkylation (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation) of 2‑tert‑butylphenol with isobutylene to introduce a second tert‑butyl group at the para position, affording 2,4‑di‑tert‑butylphenol. Performed in concentrated H2SO4 (or other strong protic acid) at 60–100 °C; the acid acts as both catalyst and proton source, often without additional solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; sodium carbonate reacts with nickel(II) sulfate in aqueous solution to exchange the cations, precipitating nickel(II) carbonate and leaving sodium sulfate in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts a primary alkyl chloride to the corresponding primary alcohol. Hydroxide ion attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacements yields 2‑methylsulfinylethanol and NaCl. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux temperature; water or water‑mixed organic solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) is used as the reaction medium.

High‑temperature carbothermic reduction (redox) of vanadium(V) oxide by carbon, producing metallic vanadium and carbon monoxide. Reaction carried out in a furnace at >1300 °C under an inert (e.g., argon) or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reactants are mixed and heated, no solvent or catalyst.

Reductive dehalogenation of bromocyclopentane using zinc metal in acetic acid; zinc donates electrons to the carbon–bromine bond, generating cyclopentane and ZnBr2. Reaction performed in glacial acetic acid as solvent, typically refluxed for several hours; zinc dust acts as the reductant, no additional catalyst.

Grignard addition to a ketone; methylmagnesium bromide adds to 3‑octanone to form a tertiary alkoxide which on aqueous work‑up yields 3‑methyl‑3‑octanol. Conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; the Grignard reagent is the nucleophile, no external catalyst.

Esterification (anhydride methanolysis): methanol attacks the carbonyl of 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic anhydride, yielding one equivalent of 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid and one equivalent of methyl 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate; typically carried out at reflux in an inert solvent (e.g., toluene or dichloromethane) with a catalytic amount of acid or base, and the reaction mixture is worked up by aqueous extraction.

Electrophilic aromatic α‑chlorination of a ketone: chlorine gas in the presence of FeCl₃ generates electrophilic Cl⁺ which attacks the α‑methylene of acetophenone to give 2‑chloroacetophenone; the reaction is done at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often under an inert atmosphere.

Acid‑catalyzed cyclization (dehydrative cyclization) of cannabidiol to Δ⁹‑tetrahydrocannabinol: p‑toluenesulfonic acid protonates the phenolic hydroxyl, promoting intramolecular electrophilic attack to form the closed pyran ring of THC with loss of water; usually performed in toluene or benzene under reflux with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH and removal of water (Dean–Stark).

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation: aqueous potassium permanganate oxidizes the 2‑methyl substituent of 2‑methylpyrazine to a carboxyl group, producing pyrazine‑2‑carboxylic acid, while MnO₂ and KOH are generated; the reaction is carried out in warm water under basic conditions, often with excess KMnO₄ and stirring until the purple color fades.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion) of a nitrile to a primary amine; hydrogen gas (1–5 atm) is passed over a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or PtO₂ in ethanol or methanol at 50–100 °C, reducing 3‑methoxypropanenitrile to 3‑methoxypropylamine.

Acetylation (ester formation) of a diol: triethylene glycol reacts with two equivalents of acetic anhydride to give the diacetate and two equivalents of acetic acid; the reaction proceeds at 0 – 25 °C in a solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, sometimes catalyzed by DMAP, and the acid by‑product is removed by washing.

Reduction of an N‑oxide: sodium borohydride reduces the N‑oxide group of 2,6‑dimethylpyridine N‑oxide to the corresponding pyridine, producing sodium metaborate as a by‑product; the reaction is performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, often under nitrogen, and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; Raney nickel under H₂ (1–5 atm) reduces 4‑aminobenzonitrile to the primary amine 4‑(aminomethyl)aniline. Typical solvent is ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux; the reaction converts a –C≡N group to –CH₂NH₂.

Carbothermic reduction (redox) of iron(II) oxide by elemental carbon to give iron and carbon monoxide. Important step in blast‑furnace ironmaking. FeO + C → Fe + CO. Conducted at very high temperature (≈1400–1500 °C) in a reducing furnace; solid‑solid/gas system; no solvent or catalyst.

Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis; formation of iridium(III) chloride by oxidative chlorination of elemental iridium. Conducted by passing dry Cl2 gas over finely divided iridium metal at elevated temperature (≈250‑300 °C) in a quartz or alumina tube; no solvent required. Typical inert‐gas atmosphere, optional slight excess chlorine to ensure complete conversion.

N‑acylation (amidation) of cyclohexylamine with acetic anhydride; the amine attacks the anhydride carbonyl, displacing acetate to give N‑cyclohexyl‑acetamide and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt, often without added catalyst.

Formation of a secondary amide from diethylamine and 2‑hydroxypropanoyl chloride; the acid chloride reacts with the amine to give N,N‑diethyl‑2‑hydroxypropanamide while releasing HCl. The reaction is carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF, typically in the presence of a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to rt.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) in aqueous solution; arsenic acid reacts with three equivalents of silver nitrate to form insoluble silver arsenate precipitate and liberates three equivalents of nitric acid. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Strong reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ (in dry THF or diethyl ether, under inert atmosphere) reduces ethylparaben (ethyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate) to 4‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol, generating ethanol as a by‑product. The reaction is usually initiated at 0 °C and then refluxed until completion, followed by careful aqueous work‑up.

Oxidative coupling of a thiol using iodine; I₂ oxidizes two molecules of 2‑mercaptoethanol to the corresponding disulfide bis(2‑mercaptoethyl) sulfide, producing hydrogen iodide. The reaction proceeds at room temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or Et₂O, often with the iodine added portionwise; no additional catalyst is needed.

Grignard alkylation of a silicon halide; nucleophilic substitution (Si‑Cl replacement) that converts trichlorosilane into triethylsilane. Three equivalents of ethylmagnesium chloride attack the Si‑Cl bonds, forming Si–C bonds and precipitating MgCl₂. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; excess Grignard reagent is often used to drive the reaction to completion. The product is isolated after aqueous quench and distillation.

Oxidative fluorination (redox) of plutonium(III) fluoride to plutonium(V) fluoride. Molecular fluorine acts as a strong oxidizing agent, raising the oxidation state of Pu from +3 to +5 while being reduced to fluoride ion. Conducted in the gas phase or in a fluorine‑compatible vessel (e.g., nickel or steel) at elevated temperatures (300–600 °C) with a flow of dry F₂; no solvent is used. The solid PuF₅ is collected after cooling, and excess fluorine is vented through scrubbers.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). The 3‑azidopropan‑1‑ol is converted to 3‑azidopropanal while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) oxide and pyridine is regenerated. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional base is required.

Halogenation of a metal carbonyl; oxidative chlorination of diiron nonacarbonyl (Fe₂(CO)₉) with Cl₂. Chlorine attacks the Fe‑CO framework, converting the metal centers to FeCl₂ and liberating carbon monoxide gas. The reaction is carried out in a dry, inert solvent such as THF, toluene, or pentane at 0°C to room temperature, with a slow feed of Cl₂ gas under a nitrogen blanket. CO is evolved and can be trapped; the solid FeCl₂ is isolated after solvent removal.

Acid‑base precipitation (double‑displacement) in aqueous solution; ammonia neutralizes zirconium nitrate, forming soluble ammonium nitrate and insoluble zirconium hydroxide. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water: Zr(NO₃)₄ + 4 NH₃·H₂O → Zr(OH)₄↓ + 4 NH₄NO₃. The zirconium hydroxide precipitate is filtered, washed, and can be dried or calcined; the filtrate contains the ammonium nitrate.

Reduction (deoxygenation) of ethanol by hydroiodic acid; primary alcohol is reduced to ethane while iodide is oxidized to iodine, water is formed. Typically performed with excess conc. HI, often with catalytic red phosphorus to regenerate HI; reflux in aqueous or neat HI at 80‑120 °C.

Acid–base neutralization forming lithium succinate; succinic dicarboxylic acid reacts with lithium oxide to give the lithium salt and water. Usually carried out in aqueous medium or by heating solid reagents together (≈200 °C) to promote salt formation.

Oxidative cyclization of 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole to benzothiazolin‑2‑one using hydrogen peroxide; the thiol is oxidized to a carbonyl and the ring closes, producing water as by‑product. Conducted in mild aqueous or alcoholic solution at 0–50 °C, often under neutral or slightly basic conditions; no additional catalyst required.

Neutralization of phosphomolybdic acid with sodium hydroxide to give sodium phosphomolybdate; acid‑base reaction forming the salt and water; performed in aqueous solution with controlled addition of NaOH at ambient temperature; pH adjusted to neutral/alkaline; water is the only by‑product.

Reaction type: acid-mediated silyl halide exchange (desilylation). Purpose: replace the trimethylsilyl group with chloride, generating chlorotrimethylsilane and releasing isothiocyanic acid. Key transformation: Si–N=C=S bond is cleaved, Si–Cl formed, N=C=S liberated as HN=C=S. Typical conditions: treat isothiocyanatotrimethylsilane with gaseous or aqueous HCl (1–2 equiv) at 0 °C to room temperature. Common solvent: anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform; reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Acid–base reaction between sodium ethoxide and L‑ascorbic acid; the ethoxide deprotonates the phenolic acid, yielding ethanol and sodium ascorbate (the sodium salt of ascorbic acid). Typically performed in anhydrous ethanol at room temperature; the reaction is rapid and quantitative.

Fischer esterification of cyclohexanol with acetic acid catalyzed by sulfuric acid; cyclohexanol is converted to cyclohexyl acetate with water released. Reaction run under reflux (≈100 °C) in excess acetic acid, using catalytic H₂SO₄ (≈5 %); removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation.

High‑temperature redox synthesis of diboron tetrachloride; hydrogen gas reduces two equivalents of boron trichloride to give B₂Cl₄ and generates hydrogen chloride. Conducted in the gas phase at elevated temperature (≈300‑500 °C) in an inert (e.g., nitrogen) atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Halogen exchange/oxidative halogenation of titanium diselenide with iodine. I₂ reacts with TiSe₂, replacing the chalcogenide ligands to give a volatile titanium tetra‑iodide (TiI₄) and elemental selenium as a solid/by‑product. The key transformation is Ti–Se bond cleavage and formation of Ti–I bonds, with Se liberated. Conducted under anhydrous, inert conditions (dry‑tube or sealed ampoule) at 200–400 °C to promote vapor‑phase reaction; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Alcoholysis of a silyl acetate; converts the acetoxy group of dimethylacetoxysilane to a methoxy group via reaction with methanol, producing dimethylmethoxysilane and acetic acid; typically performed under reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or THF, often with a base catalyst (e.g., pyridine) or by azeotropic removal of the acetic acid.

Aqueous alkaline nucleophilic substitution; 3‑bromopentane reacts with NaOH aqueous solution to give 3‑pentanol and NaBr; typically reflux in water or water/ethanol mixture, SN2 on the secondary carbon or SN1 under heated conditions.

Redox nitrosylation (biological S‑nitrosylation); O₂ oxidizes NO to N₂O₃ which nitrosates reduced glutathione, converting four GSH molecules into four S‑nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) and producing two H₂O; occurs in aqueous physiological buffer (pH ≈ 7.4) at ambient temperature; no added solvent or catalyst required, reaction proceeds spontaneously in the presence of O₂ and NO.
Acid‑base neutralisation; aqueous sulfuric acid reacts with nickel(II) hydroxide to produce nickel(II) sulfate solution and water; performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide replaces chloride on 1‑chloropiperidine to give 1‑cyanopiperidine; typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile at 50‑100 °C; potassium chloride precipitates as by‑product.

Metathesis (ligand substitution) reaction; chromium(III) picolinate reacts with sulfuric acid, the picolinate ligands are protonated to give picolinic acid while sulfate ions replace them to form chromium(III) sulfate; performed in aqueous sulfuric acid, often with heating (50‑80 °C) to improve solubility and shift equilibrium; water is the solvent and excess acid ensures complete ligand exchange.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride). Purpose: convert a tertiary alcohol into the corresponding tertiary chloride. Key transformation: the hydroxyl group of 2‑phenyl‑2‑propanol is replaced by a chlorine atom, generating 2‑chloro‑2‑phenylpropane with evolution of SO₂ and HCl. Typical conditions: add thionyl chloride (1–1.5 equiv) to the alcohol at 0 °C, then stir at room temperature or gentle reflux under anhydrous conditions. Common solvent/base: dry dichloromethane or pyridine (pyridine scavenges HCl); sometimes triethylamine is used. No additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis; boron triiodide reacts violently with water, a typical halide hydrolysis. The B–I bonds are cleaved, forming boric acid (B(OH)3) and releasing hydroiodic acid (HI). Usually performed at 0 °C to control exotherm, in aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; melamine hydrochloride is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide to afford free melamine, sodium chloride, and water. The hydroxide ion abstracts the proton from the melamine‑HCl salt, regenerating the neutral melamine base. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; stoichiometric NaOH is used and no special solvent or catalyst is required.

Sulfurization (oxidation) of trimethylphosphine; elemental sulfur inserts to form trimethylphosphine sulfide (P=S bond); usually carried out at room temperature in anhydrous THF or toluene under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of iodine(III) to iodine(V). Iodosylbenzene (PhIO) is oxidized by peracetic acid to iodylbenzene (PhIO₂), with acetic acid formed as a by‑product. Conducted in glacial acetic acid or a mixture of acetic acid and dichloromethane at 0–25 °C; stoichiometric amount of peracetic acid is added slowly under stirring. No additional catalyst is required; the peracid acts as the oxidant.

Halide metathesis (double displacement); KI exchanges chloride for iodide on nickel(II) chloride yielding nickel(II) iodide and potassium chloride; conducted in aqueous or ethanolic solution with gentle heating or reflux; often performed without additional reagents.

SN2 alkylation of dimethylamine with 1‑chloropentane; the amine attacks the primary carbon, displacing chloride to afford N,N‑dimethyl‑1‑pentylamine while HCl is generated and typically scavenged by a base (excess amine or K2CO3); reaction run in aprotic solvents such as THF or acetonitrile at 0 °C to reflux.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; nitronium tetrafluoroborate delivers NO2⁺ which substitutes at the 3‑position of 1,2,4,5‑tetrachlorobenzene giving 1,2,4,5‑tetrachloro‑3‑nitrobenzene and HBF₄; performed at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C) in non‑protic solvents like nitromethane or CH₂Cl₂; no additional catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (salt metathesis) between phenylmercury chloride and potassium iodide to give phenylmercury iodide and potassium chloride. The reaction proceeds by simple double‑displacement of the halide ion in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often at room temperature, and does not require additional catalysts. The mixture is generally stirred in water or a water‑methanol blend until complete exchange is observed.

Ester aminolysis (amide formation); ammonia attacks ethyl butyrate, displacing ethanol and forming butyramide; usually carried out in excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) in a sealed vessel or in ethanol solvent; no catalyst required.

Alcoholysis of hexamethyldisiloxane with ethanol to afford trimethyl ethoxysilane and trimethylsilanol; ethanol serves as the nucleophile opening the Si–O–Si bond. Conducted under reflux in ethanol, typically with a catalytic acid (e.g., HCl) or Lewis acid catalyst.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert salicylic acid into the more lipophilic isopropyl salicylate ester used in fragrances or prodrugs; key transformation is replacement of the carboxylic‑OH by an O‑iPr group with loss of water; typically performed by refluxing salicylic acid in excess isopropanol with catalytic concentrated H2SO4 (1–2 equiv) at 80–85 °C; the alcohol serves as solvent, sometimes toluene is added to azeotropically remove water.

Oxidative thiol coupling (disulfide formation); purpose is to synthesize diphenyl disulfide from phenyl mercaptan; key transformation is two Ph‑SH molecules oxidized to a Ph‑S‑S‑Ph bond while water and Na2SO4 are generated; usually carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous/acetone solution at 60–80 °C using Na2S2O8 (sodium persulfate) as the oxidant; no additional catalyst is required.

SN2 displacement of bromide by cyanide ion on 2‑bromoacetamide producing 2‑cyanoacetamide and NaBr. Reaction usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution of NaCN at 0–60 °C; no catalyst required.

Chemoselective reduction of an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde; purpose is to obtain the allylic alcohol trans‑2‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol while preserving the C=C bond; key transformation is reduction of the aldehydic carbonyl to a primary alcohol; typical conditions are NaBH4 (1–1.5 equiv) in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere; the solvent is protic and the reaction is quenched with water after completion.

Hydrogen reduction (metal halide to metal) reaction; used to obtain metallic molybdenum; MoBr₃ is reduced by H₂ gas, producing Mo metal and HBr gas; performed in the solid state at high temperature (≈500‑800 °C) under a flow of H₂; no solvent, inert atmosphere often employed, no catalyst.

Acid–base halogenation (metal oxide + hydrogen halide); purpose is to convert lutetium oxide to lutetium triiodide; Lu₂O₃ reacts with HI, producing LuI₃ and H₂O; usually performed by refluxing the oxide in concentrated aqueous hydrogen iodide at 200–250 °C; water serves as the reaction medium.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of a methyl ester; purpose is to produce the sodium salt of benzoic acid (sodium benzoate) and methanol. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the ester carbonyl, leading to cleavage of the C–OCH₃ bond and formation of the carboxylate anion, which is subsequently protonated by water to give methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating at reflux (≈80 °C) for 30 min to 2 h. Solvent: water; reaction may be performed in aqueous methanol or ethanol to improve solubility. No additional catalyst needed.

SN2 alkylation of a thiolate to form a thioether; purpose is to prepare cyclopentyl‑methyl sulfide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the deprotonated cyclopentanethiolate on methyl bromide with loss of bromide as HBr; commonly performed by first generating the thiolate with a base such as NaH, K2CO3 or NaOH in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, acetone) at 0 °C to 25 °C; no metal catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (protonation of sulfide); purpose is to convert potassium sulfide to the more soluble hydrosulfide salt; key transformation is proton transfer from HCl to S²⁻ forming KHS and KCl; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometry is 1 equiv HCl per mole K2S, giving one mole KCl and one mole KHS.

Leuckart‑Wallach reductive amination; purpose is the synthesis of 3‑methyl‑amphetamine from 3‑methyl‑phenylacetone; key transformation is simultaneous amination and reduction of the ketone carbonyl using ammonium formate/formic acid to give the primary amine with evolution of CO2 and H2O; typically performed by heating the ketone with excess ammonium formate (or a 1:1 mixture of formic acid and ammonia) in a sealed tube at 150–200 °C for several hours; the reaction medium is usually neat formic acid or a formic acid/water mixture, no external catalyst required.

In‑situ peracid epoxidation; formic acid reacts with hydrogen peroxide to generate performic acid, a peracid that transfers an oxygen atom to the C9‑C10 double bond of oleic acid, yielding 9,10‑epoxy‑octadecanoic acid and water; typically carried out at 0–5 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, with slow addition of H₂O₂ to control exotherm; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (Friedel‑Crafts bromination); AlBr₃ coordinates to Br₂ generating the electrophilic Br⁺ that attacks the anisole ring, methoxy group directing substitution para to itself; produces para‑bromoanisole and HBr as by‑product; performed in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; AlBr₃ is the Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride; water attacks the carbonyl carbon of 2‑naphthoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming 2‑naphthoic acid while releasing HCl; usually conducted in a biphasic system (e.g., THF/water) or directly in aqueous medium at 0 °C to reflux; no external catalyst required, though a base (NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize the liberated HCl.

Acid‑metal displacement (redox) reaction; elemental potassium reduces phosphoric acid, producing hydrogen gas and the fully deprotonated potassium phosphate (K₃PO₄); highly exothermic and performed under inert atmosphere (argon) with dry potassium metal, often in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or under liquid ammonia to moderate reactivity; no catalyst used.

Acid dissolution of tin(IV) sulfide in concentrated sulfuric acid, producing soluble tin(IV) sulfate and evolving hydrogen sulfide gas. Conducted by heating SnS₂ in conc. H₂SO₄ (often reflux) to promote protonation of the sulfide and release of H₂S, while the tin is converted to Sn(SO₄)₂.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (halide exchange); iodide ion from KI displaces the methanesulfonate leaving group on isopropyl methanesulfonate, yielding isopropyl iodide and potassium methanesulfonate; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent like acetone or DMF, often with reflux and optionally 18‑crown‑6 to increase KI solubility; reaction proceeds via a concerted backside attack (inversion of configuration).

Steglich esterification (carbodiimide‑mediated ester formation). Purpose: synthesis of the ester monobenzone from para‑hydroxybenzoic acid and p‑tert‑butyl phenol. Key transformation: activation of the carboxylic acid by DCC to form an O‑acyl‑urea intermediate, DMAP catalyzes nucleophilic attack by the phenol, yielding the ester and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to ambient temperature, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane or THF as solvent, stoichiometric DCC and catalytic DMAP; reaction run 2–12 h, work‑up removes precipitated DCU.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: conversion of the methyl ester of Nω‑nitro‑L‑arginine to the free amino acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the ester carbonyl, formation of a tetrahedral intermediate, collapse to release methanol and generate the carboxylate, which after acid work‑up furnishes Nω‑nitro‑L‑arginine. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux or 50–80 °C for 1–4 h, followed by acidification (e.g., HCl) to precipitate the product; water is the solvent.

Redox oxidation of tetraethyllead with concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: destruction of organolead compounds and formation of ethyl nitrate as a by‑product. Key transformation: nitric acid oxidizes the Pb–C bonds, yielding lead(II) nitrate, ethyl nitrate from the ethyl groups, nitrogen dioxide gas, and water. Typical conditions: excess 70–98 % HNO₃, temperature maintained below 50 °C to control vigorous gas evolution; reaction performed in a fume hood, no additional catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide (saponification): 3‑methoxybenzamide is treated with aqueous NaOH, cleaving the amide to give 3‑methoxybenzoic acid and ammonia. Conditions typically involve refluxing in water or aqueous ethanol with excess NaOH (1.5–2 equiv) for several hours; work‑up acidifies the reaction mixture to liberate the free acid.

Alkaline hydrogen‑peroxide oxidation of a α‑hydroxy‑ketone. Dihydroxyacetone is oxidized by excess H₂O₂ under basic conditions (e.g., NaOH) to tartronic acid (hydroxymalonic acid) with concom formation of water. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; the base facilitates peroxide decomposition to the reactive perhydroxyl anion. No additional catalyst is required.

Thermal decarboxylation (hydrodecarboxylation) of stearic acid. Purpose: shortening of the fatty‑acid carbon chain to produce heptadecane and CO₂. Key transformation: cleavage of the C‑C bond adjacent to the carboxyl group, releasing CO₂ and reducing the remaining chain to an alkane. Typical conditions: high temperature (300–400 °C) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), often with a metal catalyst such as Cu, Ni, or Pd on carbon; reaction carried out in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or a high‑boiling hydrocarbon can be used as medium.

Halogen exchange forming interhalogen iodine monochloride. Purpose: preparation of ICl, a useful electrophilic halogenating reagent. Key transformation: simultaneous oxidation–reduction where iodine is oxidized from 0 to +1 and chlorine reduced from 0 to –1, resulting in two equivalents of ICl. Typical conditions: gaseous I₂ and Cl₂ mixed in a dry, inert container, often at 0–25 °C; reaction can be performed in a non‑reactive solvent such as CCl₄ or directly in the gas phase; no catalyst is required.

Azo coupling (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of phenyl diazonium tetrafluoroborate with 2‑naphthol under alkaline aqueous conditions (often NaOH, 0‑5 °C) to form the azo dye 1‑(phenylazo)‑2‑naphthol; HBF₄ is generated as a by‑product. Typical solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Hydroiodic acid protonates ammonium hydroxide, yielding water and the ammonium salt (NH4I). Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst required; water serves as the solvent.

Tertiary amine N‑oxidation with a peracid; oxidizes the nitrogen of N,N‑dimethyltryptamine to the N‑oxide while reducing m‑chloroperbenzoic acid to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; the peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the lone pair on nitrogen; commonly carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, using 1.1–1.5 equiv m‑CPBA under inert atmosphere; work‑up involves aqueous sodium bicarbonate to neutralize the benzoic acid.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation; mercury(II) chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide to produce mercury(II) hydroxide solid and sodium chloride in solution; carried out in water at ambient temperature, simple mixing suffices, no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis. The acetate ester of fenchol is cleaved by water to give acetic acid and the corresponding alcohol, fenchol. Common conditions: reflux in a mixture of water and a protic acid (e.g., 1 M H2SO4 or HCl) or under basic conditions (NaOH) followed by acid work‑up. Solvents such as THF or dioxane are often used to aid mixing of the organic ester with water.

Halide exchange (nucleophilic substitution, SN2). Bromide ion displaces chloride on the α‑chloroacetophenone to afford phenacyl bromide, with precipitation of NaCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent like acetone or DMF, usually under reflux; the insoluble NaCl drives the reaction forward. No catalyst is needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Thorium nitrate reacts with potassium hydroxide to form soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble thorium hydroxide, which precipitates out. Performed in water at ambient temperature or with mild heating to ensure complete dissolution of the reactants. No catalyst required.

Condensation to form a sulfonamide (sulfanilamide). The sulfonic acid group of p‑aminobenzenesulfonic acid reacts with ammonia, eliminating water and creating the sulfonamide bond of sulfanilamide. Typical procedure involves heating an aqueous or ethanolic solution of the sulfonic acid with excess ammonia (often under reflux) and removing water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation). No external catalyst is necessary.

Oxidation of an aniline to a nitro compound (peracid oxidation). Peracetic acid oxidizes 2‑methoxyaniline, converting the amino group to a nitro group and producing 2‑nitroanisole, along with acetic acid and water as by‑products. Reactions are usually run in glacial acetic acid or a mixture of acetic acid and water at 0 °C to room temperature to control exotherm; excess peracetic acid (often 3 equiv) ensures full conversion. No additional catalyst is required.

Transmetallation (metal exchange) between methylmagnesium bromide (Grignard reagent) and indium trichloride to afford trimethylindium and magnesium bromide/chloride salts. Conducted in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to room temperature.
Hydrogen reduction of zinc chromite; solid‑state reduction to separate zinc metal and chromium(III) oxide; high temperature (~1000 °C) under a flow of H₂ gas; no solvent, inert atmosphere optional.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; employed to convert soluble mercuric chloride to mercury(II) cyanide for waste treatment or isolation of the cyanide complex; HgCl2 reacts with NaCN in water, forming soluble NaCl and precipitating Hg(CN)2; usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with excess NaCN; no special catalyst.
