Transesterification. Purpose is exchanging alkoxy groups between esters. Key transformation: Methanol displaces butanol from butyl acetate via nucleophilic attack, catalyzed by acid or base. Typically uses sodium methoxide (NaOCH3) or concentrated H2SO4 in refluxing methanol. Reversible reaction driven forward using excess methanol.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; reduces methyl 2‑anilinoacetate to 2‑(phenylamino)ethanol by converting the carbonyl carbon to a primary alcohol. Carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful quench with water/alcohol.

Conversion of an ester to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride (dealkylative chlorination); the methyl ester is transformed into pyridine‑4‑carbonyl chloride, with methyl chloride and SO₂ as volatile by‑products. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to reflux for 1–2 h under nitrogen.

Mild acid‑base reaction with a carbonate/bicarbonate buffer; sodium bicarbonate reacts with heptanoic acid, yielding sodium heptanoate, carbon dioxide, and water; the reaction proceeds in water at room temperature or with gentle heating, providing a gentle neutralization that evolves CO2 gas.

Acidic oxidation of 3‑phenyl‑1‑propanol to 3‑phenylpropionic acid using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid (chromic acid oxidation). Performed in aqueous sulfuric acid, heated under reflux; the reaction converts the primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid and reduces Cr(VI) to Cr(III).

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) of magnesium iodide with ammonium carbonate, producing insoluble magnesium carbonate and soluble ammonium iodide. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the precipitate is filtered and washed.

Acid–base neutralization; the strong acid perchloric acid reacts with the strong base sodium hydroxide to give the salt sodium perchlorate and water. Reaction proceeds readily in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst is required. Stirring the two aqueous solutions together yields the neutralization.

Electrophilic addition of bromine across a double bond (anti‑addition); Br2 reacts with 1‑methylcyclopentene via a bromonium‑ion intermediate, followed by nucleophilic opening to give trans‑1,2‑dibromo‑1‑methylcyclopentane; performed in an inert solvent such as CCl4 or CH2Cl2, often at 0 °C to rt and in the dark; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of p‑benzoquinone to hydroquinone using H₂ gas with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt, or Raney Ni in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or methanol). Reaction is performed under moderate H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to50 °C.

Precipitation (double displacement) reaction used to synthesize the pigment malachite (basic copper carbonate). Copper(II) acetate reacts with sodium carbonate and sodium hydroxide in aqueous solution, forming a bright blue Cu2CO3(OH)2 solid precipitate and sodium acetate as by‑product. Typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no special catalyst is required.

N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of allyl‑barbituric acid to produce the barbiturate drug aprobarbital. The deprotonated barbituric acid (generated by NaOH) attacks 1‑methylbutyl bromide in an SN2 step, giving the bis‑alkylated barbiturate. Conducted in polar protic solvent (ethanol or water/ethanol mixture) under reflux; NaOH serves as base, no additional catalyst required.

Gas‑phase reduction of germanium tetrafluoride with hydrogen; converts GeF₄ to germanium(II) fluoride (GeF₂) and produces HF; performed at elevated temperature (300–400 °C) in a sealed quartz tube or flow reactor; no solvent required.

Fenton‑type oxidative conversion of phenanthrene to 9,10‑phenanthrenedione (phenanthrene‑9,10‑dione). Hydrogen peroxide in the presence of Fe(III) chloride generates hydroxyl radicals that attack the aromatic rings, leading to oxidation and formation of the quinone. Carried out in aqueous acidic medium (≈pH 3) at room temperature or slightly warmed; FeCl3 acts as catalyst, H2O2 is the oxidant, and water is the solvent.

Acid‑base salt formation yielding butamirate citrate. Citric acid is neutralized by the basic amine butamirate in aqueous solution, producing the corresponding citrate salt upon evaporation or cooling. Usually performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction where sulfuric acid reacts with barium chromate to give chromium trioxide (as chromic acid that dehydrates to CrO3) and insoluble barium sulfate. The process occurs in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to promote dissolution of BaCrO4 and precipitation of BaSO4. No catalyst is needed; water is the reaction medium.

Gas‑phase reduction of vanadium(V) oxide to vanadium(IV) oxide; hydrogen gas reduces V2O5 to VO2 with formation of water vapor; typical conditions are flowing H2 (5–10 % in inert carrier) at 300–500 °C, often in a tubular furnace; solid V2O5 is the reactant, water is the only by‑product; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to convert soluble sulfide into insoluble zinc sulfide; K2S + ZnCl2 → ZnS(s) + 2 KCl; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Precipitation/sulfidation reaction; converts soluble ferrous hydroxide to insoluble ferrous sulfide, releasing water; useful for qualitative detection of Fe2+ or sulfide precipitation; carried out in aqueous solution by bubbling H2S gas through a Fe(II) hydroxide suspension at ambient temperature; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Solid‑state decomposition; generates silicon tetrafluoride gas and sodium fluoride. Typically performed by heating sodium hexafluorosilicate (Na2SiF6) at 200–300 °C in a dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Fischer esterification; 5‑aminolevulinic acid reacts with methanol under acidic conditions (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) to form methyl aminolevulinate and water. Conducted by refluxing ALA in excess methanol with a few drops of acid, removing water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium; used to synthesize the more lipophilic prodrug methyl aminolevulinate.

Acid‑base neutralization; hydrobromic acid protonates iron(III) hydroxide to give water and the iron(III) bromide salt. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stoichiometric quantities.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; converts pyrrole‑2‑carbonyl chloride to pyrrole‑2‑carboxylic acid by nucleophilic acyl substitution; typically carried out in aqueous solvent (water or water/organic mixture) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a mild base such as NaHCO₃ to neutralize the released HCl.

Catalytic dehydrogenation; cyclododecane loses molecular hydrogen to form cyclododecene (an internal alkene). Carried out at elevated temperatures (300–500 °C) over transition‑metal catalysts such as Pt, Pd or Cr₂O₃ on alumina, often under an inert gas flow.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous metathesis of Er(NO3)3 with HF to produce insoluble erbium(III) fluoride and nitric acid; carried out in dilute HF solution at low to ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; safety precautions for HF are essential; no catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to an ester; methylmagnesium bromide adds twice to ethyl butyrate, first forming a ketone intermediate that is further attacked, giving after aqueous work‑up the tertiary alcohol 3‑methyl‑3‑pentanol and ethanol as the leaving‑group by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, followed by acid work‑up.

Lewis‑acid fluoride transfer reaction forming silver hexafluoroantimonate from silver fluoride and antimony pentafluoride; carried out in anhydrous liquid HF, SO₂ClF, or other dry non‑protic solvents at low temperature under inert atmosphere; no external catalyst; produces AgSbF6, a highly soluble silver salt with weakly coordinating SbF₆⁻ anion.

High‑temperature solid‑state nitridation (carbothermal synthesis); silicon carbide reacts with nitrogen gas to produce silicon nitride and carbon. Performed in a furnace at 1300–1500 °C under flowing N₂, often in a sealed graphite crucible to contain the solid products.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (elimination): 1‑propanol reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to eliminate water and form propene. The purpose is to generate the alkene from the primary alcohol. Key transformation is removal of a water molecule (E1 mechanism) producing the C=C bond. Typical conditions are heating the alcohol with 95–98 % H2SO4 at 140–180 °C, often in a distillation apparatus to continuously remove propene. No solvent beyond the sulfuric acid is required; the acid itself acts as the medium.

Reductive conversion of a seleninic acid to a selenol; methylseleninic acid is reduced by sodium borohydride to give methylselenol, with water formed and sodium borate as the oxidized borohydride. Typically carried out in dry methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the reaction is quenched carefully with water.

Esterification of a carboxylate with diazomethane (methylation). Sodium 4‑fluorobenzoate is suspended in dry diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C under nitrogen; a solution of diazomethane is added dropwise. The diazomethane reacts to give methyl 4‑fluorobenzoate and nitrogen gas. The reaction is performed in the dark, at low temperature, and the product is isolated by evaporation and chromatography if needed.

Alkoxide‑acid metathesis yielding aluminum sulfate; used to prepare Al₂(SO₄)₃ from organometallic precursor. Aluminum isopropoxide reacts with H₂SO₄, protons convert isopropoxide groups to isopropanol and the sulfate anion binds Al³⁺ to give Al₂(SO₄)₃. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (e.g., water/acetone) at ambient to modestly elevated temperature (20‑60 °C); vigorous stirring facilitates removal of isopropanol; no extra catalyst required.

Redox (metal‑oxide reduction) reaction; elemental aluminum reduces sulfur trioxide to sulfur dioxide while being oxidized to aluminium oxide. Conducted at high temperature (≈800–1200 °C) in a furnace, often in a flowing N₂ or inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions; no solvent is used.

Redox dissolution of a metal in an oxidizing acid; purpose is to convert elemental gall into soluble gall nitrate while reducing nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide. Key transformation: Ga metal is oxidized from 0 to +3 oxidation state, nitrate ions become coordinated to Ga³⁺, andNO₃ is reduced to NO₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: concentrated (≈68 %) nitric acid, reflux or gentle heating (50‑80 °C) in a glass flask, with vigorous stirring; reaction evolves brown NO₂ gas. No additional catalyst; aqueous acidic medium serves as both solvent and reactant.

Oxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; purpose is to obtain 5‑carboxyresorcinol from orcinol. Key transformation: the methyl substituent on the aromatic ring is oxidized to –CO₂H, while KMnO₄ is reduced to insoluble MnO₂; water is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline or neutral KMnO₄ solution, heating under reflux (often 80‑100 °C) until the purple color fades, followed by filtration to remove MnO₂ precipitate. No special catalyst; the reaction proceeds in water or aqueous alkaline medium.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification) of 4‑aminosalicylic acid with phenol; purpose is to form phenyl 4‑aminosalicylate ester. Key transformation: the carboxyl group of the acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which then reacts with phenol to give the ester and releases dicyclohexylurea as a solid by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) under nitrogen, 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer; reaction mixture is stirred 12‑24 h, then filtered to remove dicyclohexylurea and purified.

Selective reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to obtain the corresponding aldehyde (2‑ethylhexanal) without over‑reduction to the alcohol. Key transformation: the C≡N triple bond is partially reduced to a C=O aldehyde, with DIBAL‑H delivering a hydride to the carbon of the nitrile; the aluminium alkoxide intermediate is hydrolyzed on work‑up. Typical conditions: dry THF (or toluene) at –78 °C (dry‑ice/acetone bath) under inert atmosphere; 1‑1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H is added dropwise, then the reaction is quenched with aqueous NaOH or dilute acid at low temperature, followed by extraction.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of phosphorus pentachloride with hydrogen fluoride; purpose is to generate phosphorus pentafluoride and hydrogen chloride gas. Key transformation: the five chlorine ligands on PCl₅ are replaced by fluorine atoms from HF, producing PF₅ and HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous HF (excess) in a sealed, pressure‑rated vessel, often at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature (20‑50 °C); the reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to avoid moisture; PF₅ is collected as a gas or condensed under cold conditions. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal acetate salt; purpose is to prepare soluble magnesium acetate from magnesium hydroxide and acetic acid. Key transformation: two equivalents of acetic acid donate protons to the two hydroxide ions of Mg(OH)₂, yielding water and the magnesium acetate salt (Mg(CH₃COO)₂). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until complete dissolution; excess acetic can be used to ensure full conversion, and the product may be isolated by evaporation or crystallization. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; dysprosium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous nitric acid, being protonated and dissolved to give dysprosium(III) nitrate hydrate and water; heating is usually applied to accelerate dissolution; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst needed.

Carbothermic reduction (solid‑state redox) of nickel(III) oxide; purpose is to reduce higher‑valent nickel oxide to NiO while oxidizing carbon to CO. At high temperatures (≈800–1000 °C) carbon reacts with Ni₂O₃ (or NiO) to produce NiO and carbon monoxide gas. Conducted in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

Electrophilic nitrosation of a secondary urea; converts N‑methylurea into the N‑nitroso derivative (N‑methyl‑N‑nitrosourea). Conducted in aqueous solution at 0–5 °C, using nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO2 and HCl (pH 2–4). Water is the only by‑product.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt displacement); protonates the sulfate of ammonium sulfate with hydriodic acid to afford sulfuric acid and ammonium iodide. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts of HI and (NH4)2SO4 are mixed, no catalyst required.

Enzymatic S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine‑dependent methyl transfer; transfers a methyl group from SAM to protopine to form allocryptopine, producing S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Typically performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7.5) with Mg²⁺ cofactor at 25–35 °C, using the purified methyltransferase enzyme; no synthetic catalyst needed.

synthesis and oxidation-reduction reaction; production of cadmium fluoride through oxidation of Cd metal by fluorine gas; reaction proceeds vigorously upon heating cadmium in fluorine flow; high-temperature solid-gas interaction (e.g., >300°C); no solvent or catalyst.

Oxidative roasting (solid‑state oxidation) of tantalum telluride in excess oxygen at high temperature (typically 600–900 °C) to convert Ta from a lower oxidation state to Ta(V) oxide (Ta2O5) and Te from -II to Te(IV) dioxide (TeO2); purpose is to obtain separable oxide products for further processing; no solvent or catalyst is required, the reaction is conducted in a furnace with a flow of dry air or pure O2.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑pling; couples 2‑bromophenol with phenylboronic acid to give (1,1′‑biphenyl)-2‑ol. Reaction mixture contains Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %), PPh₃ (10 mol %), K₂CO₃ as base, and a polar aprotic solvent such as THF, dioxane or toluene with a small amount of water. Heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen for several hours.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; cleaves N‑(3‑phenylpropyl)acetamide to give acetic acid and 3‑phenylpropylamine (released as its free base after work‑up). Performed in aqueous HCl (≈ 6 M) at reflux (≈ 100 °C) for several hours; water or aqueous ethanol serves as solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (deacetylation). Purpose: remove the N‑acetyl protecting group from the lactam to give the free 2‑piperidone. Key transformation: cleavage of the N‑acetyl amide bond, producing 2‑piperidone and acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–6 M), reflux 80–100 °C for several hours. Solvent is water or water‑methanol mixture; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative acid dissolution (redox); copper phosphide (Cu3P) reacts with concentrated nitric acid, yielding copper(II) nitrate (Cu(NO3)2), phosphoric acid (H3PO4), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) gas. Performed at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) with careful venting of NO2; aqueous medium, no additional catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic hydride reduction of an aldehyde. Purpose: convert cyclopentanecarbaldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol (cyclopentylmethanol). Key transformation: transfer of a hydride from NaBH₄ to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that is protonated to give the alcohol; H₂ gas is not involved. Typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1–2 equiv) added to a solution of the aldehyde in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction completes within minutes to an hour. No additional catalyst required; work‑up often involves aqueous quench and extraction.

Type: SN2 N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of a primary amine. Purpose: generate 1,1‑dimethylhydrazine (unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine) while releasing HBr. Key transformation: the lone pair on the nitrogen of methylhydrazine attacks the electrophilic carbon of methyl bromide, displacing bromide and forming a new N–C bond; the bromide abstracts a proton from the hydrazine nitrogen to give HBr. Typical conditions: methylhydrazine (often as an aqueous or alcoholic solution) mixed with methyl bromide (often as a solution in acetone or MeCN) at 0 °C to reflux; excess amine can be used to trap the HBr. A base such as Na₂CO₃ or NaHCO₃ is sometimes added to neutralize the acid and improve yield.

Acid‑mediated protonolysis of a magnesium benzoate salt; purpose is to liberate the free 2‑hydroxybenzoic acid from its magnesium salt; the key step is protonation of the Mg–O bond by HCl yielding MgCl₂ and the carboxylic acid; performed by treating the solid magnesium salt with aqueous HCl at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20–40 °C); solvent is water (or dilute aqueous HCl); no additional catalyst needed.

Base‑promoted nucleophilic substitution (SN2/SN1) of a secondary alkyl bromide; purpose is to synthesize 2‑hexanol from 2‑bromohexane; key transformation is hydroxide ion attack on the carbon bearing bromine, yielding 2‑hexanol and NaBr; typical conditions are aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) heated under reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture (e.g., ethanol‑water), no additional catalyst is needed.

(transesterification) Nucleophilic substitution of methyl ester with ethanol to yield ethyl ester. Catalyzed by acids (e.g., H2SO4) or bases (e.g., NaOEt). Typically requires heating under reflux in ethanol.

Type: acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification followed by salt formation (hydrochloride). Purpose: prepare Meclofenoxate hydrochloride (centrophenoxine·HCl), a pro‑drug ester of 4‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid and 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol. Key transformation: the carboxyl group of 4‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid reacts with the hydroxyl of 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol, losing water to form the ester linkage; concurrent protonation by HCl/p‑toluenesulfonic acid generates the hydrochloride salt of the tertiary amine. Typical conditions: equimolar amounts of acid and alcohol combined with catalytic p‑TsOH (≈5 mol %) and excess conc. HCl; reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or benzene with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water, temperature 80–120 °C for several hours. The final product is isolated as the hydrochloride salt after cooling and solvent removal.

Type: Rosenmund reduction (catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride to an aldehyde). Purpose: convert pyridine‑2‑carbonyl chloride to 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde. Key transformation: hydrogen (H₂) adds across the C=O bond of the acyl chloride on the surface of a poisoned palladium catalyst (Pd/BaSO₄), producing the aldehyde and liberating HCl as the by‑product. Typical conditions: Pd on BaSO₄ (often poisoned with quinoline or sulfur) under low‑pressure H₂ (1–5 atm), temperature 0–50 °C, in a dry, inert solvent such asene, toluene, or diethyl ether. Reaction time ranges from 30 min to several hours; the mixture is filtered to remove catalyst, and the aldehyde is purified by distillation or chromatography.

Alkoxide exchange (transalkoxylation); purpose: replace the methoxy group on calcium with an ethoxy group, generating methanol; key transformation: methoxide ligand is displaced by ethoxide via equilibrium exchange, producing calcium ethoxide and methanol; typical conditions: anhydrous environment, reflux in a dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or toluene); no additional catalyst needed.

Type: combustion/oxidation (complete oxidation) of a diarsane (As₂H₄). Purpose: convert arsenic‑hydrogen species to the thermodynamically stable oxide, arsenic trioxide (As₂O₃), while generating water. Key transformation: molecular oxygen abstracts hydrogen from the As–H bonds, forming H₂O, and simultaneously oxidizes arsenic from the –III to the +III oxidation state, yielding As₂O₃. Typical conditions: exposure of gaseous or liquid diarsane to excess O₂ at elevated temperature (often flame or furnace, >400 °C). No solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds explosively under dry, well‑ventilated conditions. The products are collected as solid As₂O₃ and water vapor.

Type: SN2 alkyl substitution between a secondary alkyl chloride and a tertiary amine (dimethylamine) to form a chelating diamine (TMEDA). Purpose: synthesize N,N,N′,N′‑tetramethylethylenediamine (EDA), a common ligand, while generating HCl. Key transformation: the nitrogen lone pair of dimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the chlorine in 2‑chloro‑N,N‑dimethylethylamine, displacing chloride and forming a new N–C bond; the liberated chloride abstracts a proton from the amine, giving HCl. Typical conditions: dimethylamine (often as a gas or 2 M solution in THF) added to a solution of theoroamine in anhydrous THF, diethyl ether or MeCN at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is usually performed under nitrogen to avoid moisture. A base (e.g., triethylamine) may be added to scavenge the HCl if desired, but the stoichiometric equation includes HCl as a product. After completion, the mixture is filtered or washed to remove salts, and TMEDA is isolated by distillation.

Salt metathesis (acid–base exchange) between europium(III) phosphate and acetic acid; the phosphate anion is protonated to phosphoric acid and the europium cation is transferred to acetate, yielding europium(III) acetate in solution. Carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating (reflux) to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base precipitation; isolates basic bismuth nitrate (bismuth subnitrate) by adding excess KOH to aqueous Bi(NO₃)₃; K⁺ replaces Bi³⁺ forming soluble KNO₃ while insoluble basic bismuth nitrate precipitates; performed in water at ambient to mild heating with stirring; no catalyst required.

Ligand exchange/metathesis acid‑base reaction; converts InCl₃ to indium acetate; chloride ions are swapped for acetate, producing HCl (often as gas) and soluble In(OAc)₃; typically carried out by refluxing InCl₃ in glacial acetic acid or an AcOH/MeCN mixture under nitrogen; no catalyst needed.

Appel‑type bromination of a secondary alcohol; purpose is to produce 2‑bromopropane from isopropanol. Key transformation analogous to (2): formation of a bromosulfite intermediate from thionyl bromide and the alcohol, then SN2 inversion to give the secondary bromide, with release of SO₂ and HBr. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, base (pyridine or TEA) to neutralize HBr; inert atmosphere required.

Halide metathesis/precipitation; exchanges chloride for bromide on tetramethylammonium ion while precipitating AgCl; Ag⁺ abstracts Cl⁻ from NMe₄Cl, forming solid AgCl and soluble NMe₄Br; carried out in aqueous or ethanolic solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Oxidative combustion (solid‑state oxidation); converts yttrium sulfide to yttrium oxide and sulfur dioxide; sulfide is oxidized by O₂ to SO₂, yttrium forms Y₂O₃; performed in a high‑temperature furnace (≈800‑1200 °C) under flowing O₂ or air; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Alkaline disproportionation (redox) of iodine; hot aqueous potassium hydroxide similarly converts iodine to potassium iodide and potassium iodate; overall: 3 I₂ + 6 KOH → 5 KI + KIO₃ + 3 H₂O; analogous to the sodium system, employed for iodide/iodate preparation; conducted in water with KOH under reflux; no catalyst.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type aryl amination (Goldberg coupling) of 1‑iodo‑4‑bromobenzene with ammonia; PPh₃ acts as ligand, NaOtBu as base; converts the aryl iodide to 4‑bromoaniline with NaI as by‑product; typical conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), PPh₃ (10–20 mol %), NaOtBu (1.5 equiv), DMF or dioxane, 100–120 °C under N₂; no additional catalyst needed beyond CuI.

Nitrosation reaction used to synthesize nitrosourea anticancer agents; nitrous acid electrophilically attacks the urea nitrogen of N,N'-bis(2-chloroethyl)urea forming a N‑nitroso group and releasing water. Typically performed in cold aqueous acid (HCl/NaNO2) at 0–5 °C, often in water or mixed aqueous–organic solvent.

Acylation (acetylation) of a primary amine; 2‑aminoethanethiol reacts with acetic anhydride, the amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl, displacing acetate and forming N‑(2‑sulfanylethyl)acetamide with acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, often at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; produces aluminum phosphate and potassium nitrate; aqueous aluminum nitrate reacts with potassium phosphate, precipitating AlPO4 while KNO3 remains in solution; carried out in water, usually at room temperature or with mild heating; stirring ensures thorough mixing; no catalyst needed.

SN2 substitution of benzyl chloride with the azide from azidotrimethylsilane, giving benzyl azide; typically performed in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, MeCN) at room temperature; no catalyst needed; trimethylsilyl chloride is generated as by‑product.

Halogenolysis of a disilane to generate trimethylsilyl iodide; iodine cleaves the Si–Si bond of hexamethyldisilane, each silicon receives an iodide to afford two equivalents of Me₃SiI. Usually carried out in dry THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Reaction type: base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: convert the amide to the sodium salt of nicotinic acid while liberating free diethylamine. Key transformations: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the amide carbonyl, cleavage to give sodium nicotinate and diethylamine. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–5 M), heating (reflux or 80–100 °C) for several hours. Common solvents/catalysts: water or water/ethanol mixture; excess NaOH ensures complete conversion.

Formation a methyl lithium organometallic reagent by reduction of iodomethane with lithium metal; two lithium atoms insert into the C–I bond, giving LiI and CH₃Li. Performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen or argon.

Acidic hydrolysis of a metal carbide; magnesium carbide reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce soluble magnesium chloride and acetylene gas; performed in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating or reflux to evolve the gas, no catalyst needed.

Halide metathesis (double‑displacement) between AgCl and phenyltrimethylammonium iodide; exchanges anions to give insoluble AgI precipitate and phenyltrimethylammonium chloride in solution; carried out in water or aqueous methanol at ambient temperature; simple precipitation work‑up isolates AgI.

Reduction/halogenation of arsenic trioxide by hydroiodic acid to give arsenic triiodide; HI supplies both iodide and protons, converting As₂O₃ to AsI₃ while water is formed. Conducted by refluxing As₂O₃ in concentrated HI (often 57 % aqueous) at elevated temperature (≈100 °C) under inert atmosphere.

This is an acid-base neutralization reaction. The purpose is to form sodium oxalate and water. The hydrogen oxalate ion (HC2O4^-) donates a proton to hydroxide, neutralizing the acid and forming the oxalate dianion. The reaction occurs under standard conditions without catalysts.

This is a condensation reaction forming dipyrromethane through the acid-catalyzed electrophilic substitution of pyrrole with acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde acts as an electrophilic carbon source, attacking the activated positions on the pyrrole ring. Typically requires mild acidic conditions (e.g., acetic acid catalyst) and elevated temperature for ring coupling.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of ethyl iodide by thiocyanate ion to afford ethyl thiocyanate. Key transformation: C₂H₅I + SCN⁻ → C₂H₅SCN + I⁻. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMF, DMSO) under reflux; excess NaSCN drives the reaction; no catalyst required.

This is a redox reaction where hydrofluoric acid (HF) oxidizes elemental boron. The purpose is to produce tetrafluoroboric acid (HBF4) and hydrogen gas as a byproduct. The reaction occurs at elevated temperatures, with HF serving as both acid and oxidant.

Ether synthesis via nucleophilic substitution of tert‑butyl bromide with sodium methoxide (Williamson/SN1 pathway); produces tert‑butyl methyl ether and NaBr; typically performed in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, or directly in methanol, at reflux (≈65 °C) under inert atmosphere; excess NaOMe drives reaction to completion.

This is an ester hydrolysis reaction, yielding acetic acid and allyl alcohol. Water cleaves the ester bond in allyl acetate via acid- or base-catalyzed hydrolysis. In acidic conditions, it follows a nucleophilic acyl substitution mechanism, typically using aqueous acid (e.g., H2SO4) and heat.

This is a redox reaction involving sulfur and potassium hydroxide. Elemental sulfur disproportionate into sulfide (S^2-) and thiosulfate (S2O3^2-). The reaction requires heat in aqueous potassium hydroxide to drive sulfur oxidation and reduction, with no external catalysts needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated dicarboxylic acid; the carbon–carbon double bond of (E)-2‑decenedioic acid is reduced to give the fully saturated decanedioic acid. Typically carried out with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 25–80 °C.

Cyanate addition (urea formation) with potassium cyanate; tert‑butylamine attacks the carbon of the cyanate ion to give tert‑butylurea and potassium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at 50–80 °C; no additional catalyst is needed.

High‑temperature reduction of a metal oxide by carbon monoxide; ZnO is reduced by CO to metallic zinc while CO is oxidized to CO₂. Conducted in a furnace at ≈900–1100 °C under a flow of CO (or CO/H₂ mixture); no solvent or catalyst is required besides the solid ZnO.

Free‑radical anti‑Markovnikov hydrohalogenation of styrene (peroxide effect). Benzoyl peroxide initiates radical addition of HBr across the C=C bond of styrene, furnishing phenethyl bromide (2‑phenylethyl bromide). Usually performed at ambient temperature in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, with excess HBr gas or aqueous HBr solution.

Acidic hydrolysis of N‑methyl‑2‑phenylacetamide; an amide cleavage that yields phenylacetic acid and methylammonium chloride. Performed in aqueous hydrochloric acid (1–6 M) at reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours; the reaction is driven to completion by excess acid and water, and the product acid is isolated after neutralization or extraction.

esterification of cyclopentanecarboxylic acid with methanol to give methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate. The reaction is acid‑catalyzed (commonly conc. H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), refluxing methanol (often used in excess) to drive equilibrium toward ester formation; water formed is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to improve yield.

Deacon oxidation of hydrogen chloride to chlorine gas. Gaseous HCl reacts with O₂ at high temperature (≈350–450 °C) over a copper(II) chloride/alumina catalyst to produce Cl₂ and H₂O. This gas‑phase process is employed industrially for chlorine recovery from HCl streams.

Acid‑base displacement forming nitrous acid; aqueous potassium nitrite is protonated by nitric acid, yielding potassium nitrate and nitrous acid (HNO₂). Performed in dilute aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to minimize decomposition of the unstable HNO₂; no special catalyst is required.

Condensation (amide formation): A carboxylic acid reacts with ammonia to give the corresponding primary amide and water. The key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the carbonyl carbon followed by loss of water. Usually carried out under heating (150‑200 °C) with a dehydrating agent (e.g., thionyl chloride, oxalyl chloride, or by azeotropic removal of water) or under high‑pressure conditions. Solvent may be an inert high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or dimethylformamide; catalyst is not required beyond the dehydrating reagent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: primary amine synthesis. Key transformation: ammonia acts as nucleophile replacing bromide in 1-bromo-3-methylbutane. Conditions: aqueous ammonia, elevated temperature. Excess ammonia prevents further alkylation.

Metal‑ammonia reduction / generation of organolithium reagent: Lithium metal dissolves in liquid ammonia to give solvated electrons which reduce naphthalene to the radical anion lithium naphthalenide. This is a single‑electron transfer process used as a strong nucleophilic base or electron donor. Typical conditions: dry liquid NH₃ at –78 °C to –33 °C under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen). No additional solvent; the reaction medium is liquid ammonia itself.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (combustion) reaction; metallic magnesium reduces ammonium perchlorate (NH4ClO4) upon ignition, yielding magnesium chloride (MgCl2), magnesium oxide (MgO), nitrogen gas (N2) and water (H2O). Used as an energetic component in propellant formulations. Performed as a mixed solid, ignited by heat; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Eschweiler–Clark reductive methylation of an N‑heterocycle; pyrrole reacts with formaldehyde and formic acid, forming an iminium intermediate that is reduced by formic acid to give N‑methylpyrrole, with water and CO2 as by‑products; typically refluxed in an aqueous or alcoholic solution of formic acid (often 95 % formic acid) at 100 °C; no external catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). The reaction proceeds in anhydrous dichloromethane at ambient temperature, delivering cinnamyl aldehyde without over‑oxidation to the acid.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ring‑opening hydrolysis of a cyclic enol ether: 2,5‑Dihydrofuran reacts with water to afford γ‑hydroxybutyraldehyde by protonation of the enol ether, nucleophilic attack of water, and subsequent tautomerization/cleavage of the C–O bond. Usually performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1  HCl) at ambient temperature or mild heating (30‑60 °C). Water is the solvent; acid acts as catalyst.

Alcohol to alkyl bromide substitution (SN2) using hydrogen bromide: Propargyl alcohol is protonated by HBr, the bromide ion displaces water to give propargyl bromide and water. Acetic acid serves as a solvent and may help generate a more acidic medium. Reaction is typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature to avoid side reactions, in excess HBr (often generated in situ from NaBr/H₂SO₄). No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide with hydroxide: Phenethyl bromide reacts with aqueous or alcoholic KOH, where hydroxide attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing bromide to form phenethyl alcohol and potassium bromide. Conducted under reflux (≈80 °C) in water or ethanol. No special catalyst; the base (KOH) drives the reaction.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification (methanolysis). Exchanges the 2‑hydroxyethyl group for a methoxy group, yielding methyl octanoate and ethylene glycol. Commonly performed with catalytic NaOMe or a catalytic amount of H₂SO₄ in excess methanol, refluxing (≈65 °C) for 2–6 h. Methanol acts as both solvent and reactant.

Acid–base equilibrium forming bicarbonate: Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) reacts with lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃) in aqueous solution to produce two equivalents of lithium bicarbonate (LiHCO₃). This is a neutralization/solubility‑driven reaction often used to generate bicarbonate buffers. Performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Type: Sandmeyer chlorination (aryl diazonium to aryl chloride). Purpose: Introduce a chloro substituent at the para position of a methoxy‑substituted aromatic ring. Key transformation: replacement of the diazonium group by Cl, generating 4‑methoxychlorobenzene, N₂, and Cu(II) chloride. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–2 M), CuCl (0.1–0.2 eq) as catalyst, temperature 0–25 °C; reaction often performed under inert atmosphere.

Halide metathesis (salt exchange); replaces bromide ligands on Pt(II) with iodide, yielding platinum(II) iodide and potassium bromide; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation); potassium carbonate deprotonates cyclopentyl alcohol to the alkoxide, which attacks methyl iodide to form methyl cyclopentyl ether and KI; carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or DMF, often under reflux; base serves as the only catalyst.

Zinc/ammonium chloride reduction of a nitro group; zinc dust in the presence of NH₄Cl reduces 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine, generating Zn²⁺, NH₄Cl, and water; usually conducted in aqueous ethanol or methanol under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization; trifluoroacetic acid reacts with potassium carbonate to form potassium trifluoroacetate salt and carbonic acid, which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Organometallic acyl substitution (nucleophilic acyl addition); dimethylcadmium transfers a methyl group to benzoyl chloride, producing acetophenone and cadmium(II) chloride; conducted under inert atmosphere in ether solvents (e.g., THF) at low temperature; dimethylcadmium serves as the nucleophilic methyl source.

Metal‑halogen exchange to generate ethyl lithium; ethyl iodide reacts with elemental lithium to give organolithium reagent; performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to –78 °C under nitrogen or argon; lithium iodide forms as by‑product.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of an alkyl bromide with nitrate ion; silver nitrate provides nitrate nucleophile and precipitates AgBr, converting 2‑bromopropane to propan‑2‑yl nitrate. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or acetonitrile under reflux, protected from light; AgBr removal drives the reaction forward.

Halogenation/oxidation. Used to synthesize titanium tetrachloride and boron trichloride. Key transformations: Cl₂ oxidizes Ti and B. Conditions: high temperature, direct reaction with gaseous Cl₂ (no solvent or catalyst required).

Swern oxidation. Purpose: oxidize primary alcohols to aldehydes. Key transformations: activation of DMSO with oxalyl chloride forms an intermediate, which oxidizes 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol to 3,3-dimethylbutanal. Conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane at low temperature (-78°C), followed by triethylamine base.
Oxidation. Converts methanol to formaldehyde. Key transformations: hypochlorite oxidizes alcohol. Conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature. Possible catalyst: TEMPO (if used).
Nucleophilic reduction. Reduces ketones to secondary alcohols. Key transformation: NaBH₄ donates hydride to carbonyl carbon. Conditions: protic solvents (e.g., methanol, ethanol), room temperature.

Nitrile reduction to diamine. LAH reduces 3-aminopropionitrile’s nitrile group (-CN) to a primary amine (-CH₂NH₂). Key transformation: selective reduction of nitrile. Conditions: LAH in anhydrous THF, followed by acidic workup (e.g., aqueous HCl). Solvent: THF.

Acidic ester hydrolysis; deprotects an acetate protecting group on a benzylic alcohol. The acetate carbonyl C–O bond is cleaved by aqueous HCl (often heated under reflux), yielding furan‑2‑ylmethanol and acetic acid; water serves as solvent.

Single‑displacement redox (halogen exchange); fluorine oxidizes iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to fluoride, yielding KF. Typically carried out in a dry, inert fluorinated solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or liquid HF) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; the reaction is highly exothermic and requires careful gas handling.

Type: Acid‑base/neutralization (salt metathesis). Purpose: Convert a metal hydroxide into its soluble chloride while liberating ammonia gas. Key transformation: NH4Cl reacts with Sc(OH)3 to exchange ions, producing ScCl3, NH3 (g) and H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, often heated to 60–80 °C to drive off NH3; the reaction is vigorous and may be performed in a reflux setup. Common solvents/catalysts: water; no catalyst required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Purpose: Replace a chlorine atom on a secondary alkyl halide with hydrogen to form the corresponding secondary alcohol. Key transformation: 1‑chlorobutan‑2‑ol + H2 → 2‑butanol + HCl (the HCl is neutralized by the base or catalyst surface). Typical conditions: H2 pressure of 1–5 atm, 25–100 °C, using a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO2. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol, methanol or THF as solvent; palladium on carbon or Raney nickel as catalyst.

Type: Direct fluorination (oxidative fluorination). Purpose: Synthesize volatile tungsten hexafluoride, a valuable precursor for tungsten processing and organometallic chemistry. Key transformation: WO3 + F2 → WF6 + O2, with simultaneous oxidation of tungsten from +6 in the oxide to +6 in the fluoride and reduction of fluorine to fluoride ligands. Typical conditions: High temperature (200–450 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (nickel or Monel), under excess F2 gas flow. Common solvents/catalysts: No solvent; reaction is gas‑phase; reactor materials act as inert surfaces.

Type: Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed). Purpose: Cleave the benzyl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate ester to recover benzyl alcohol and generate trifluoroacetic acid. Key transformation: Benzyl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate + H2O → benzyl alcohol + 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetic acid. Typical conditions: Reflux in a mixed organic/water solvent (e.g., TH/H2O or MeOH/H2O) with a catalytic amount of HCl (or NaOH for alkaline hydrolysis) for 2–6 h; reaction may be neutralized after completion. Common solvents/catalysts: dilute HCl or NaOH as catalyst; THF, methanol, or acetonitrile as co‑solvent.

Type: Salt dissociation (acid‑base equilibrium in water). Purpose: Generate free semicarbazide base and release hydrochloric acid from its hydrochloride salt. Key transformation: Semicarbazide·HCl + H2O ⇌ semicarbazide + HCl (aq). Typical conditions: Dissolution in water at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be used to accelerate dissolution. Common solvents/catalysts: Water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbonate formation) between methyl chloroformate and phenol producing methyl phenyl carbonate and hydrogen chloride; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to trap HCl; purpose is preparation of a phenyl carbonate ester.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation): phosphorus pentabromide decomposes upon heating to give phosphorus tribromide and bromine vapor. The reaction is typically carried out in the solid state or in an inert, non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride under reflux; temperatures around 100‑150 °C promote the equilibrium shift toward PBr₃ and Br₂.

Double‑replacement/precipitation reaction of silver fluoride with hydrochloric acid; the fluoride is displaced by chloride, yielding insoluble silver chloride (AgCl) as a white precipitate and hydrofluoric acid (HF) in solution. Carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed.

Type: Double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis). Purpose: Prepare insoluble mercury(II) sulfide (HgS) by exchanging anions between sodium sulfide and mercuric acetate. Key transformation: Na2S + Hg(OAc)2 → HgS (solid) + 2 NaOAc (aqueous). Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly warmed, rapid stirring to promote precipitation of HgS. Common solvents/catalysts: Water; sometimes a small amount of ethanol to improve solubility, but no catalyst is needed.

Prilezhaev epoxidation; perbenzoic acid epoxidizes cyclooctene to cyclooctene oxide, generating benzoic acid as by‑product. Standard protocol uses 1.2 eq perbenzoic acid, 0 °C to ambient temperature, in dichloromethane or chloroform, with slow addition of the peracid to control exotherm; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Halogen addition to an alkyne; Cl₂ adds across the triple bond of 2‑butyne in two successive steps, giving first a 1,2‑dichloro‑alkene intermediate that further reacts to the fully saturated 2,2,3,3‑tetrachlorobutane. Conducted in a non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, often at 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light to avoid radical side reactions.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (hydrolysis) of cyanuric chloride; water attacks the electron‑deficient triazine ring, displacing three chloride ions and forming cyanuric acid while liberating three equivalents of HCl. Performed in aqueous media (sometimes with a small amount of organic co‑solvent) and heated (50–100 °C) to accelerate the reaction; the resulting mixture is acidified to precipitate cyanuric acid.

Oxidation (redox) of sodium dithionite by molecular oxygen; S₂O₄²⁻ is oxidized to sulfate (SO₄²⁻) while O₂ is reduced to water, producing sodium sulfate in aqueous solution. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature under air or oxygen sparging; no catalyst is required, though stirring and slightly basic pH (maintained by excess dithionite) improve rate.

High‑temperature chlorination (redox) of chromium carbide; Cl₂ oxidizes the carbide to generate carbon tetrachloride and converts chromium to CrCl₃. Conducted in the gas phase or in a sealed quartz tube at elevated temperatures (≈500–800 °C) with excess chlorine; no solvent is used, and the solid products are collected after cooling.

Azo coupling (aryl‑aryl coupling) – The diazonium salt couples with aniline under mildly basic aqueous conditions, forming the azo bond (‑N=N‑) to give azobenzene and releasing HCl. This is a key step in the synthesis of azo dyes and pigments. Typical procedure uses a buffered aqueous solution (pH ≈ 8–9) with sodium acetate or carbonate, temperature kept below 5 °C during addition and then allowed to reach ambient temperature; no metal catalyst is required.

Selective reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); the hydride adds to the carbon of the nitrile, forming an imine‑aluminum complex that on work‑up furnishes chloroacetaldehyde. Reaction is performed in dry THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, using exactly 1 equiv of DIBAL‑H; quench with methanol or aqueous ammonium chloride at low temperature to prevent over‑reduction.

Metallothermic reduction; lithium metal reduces zirconium tetrabromide to elemental zirconium while forming lithium bromide; typically performed under inert atmosphere at elevated temperatures (200‑400 °C) in a dry hydrocarbon or ether.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange counter‑ions and obtain potassium hexafluorostannate. In aqueous solution the fluoride salts exchange cations: Na2SnF6 + 2 KF → K2SnF6 + 2 NaF. Usually performed at room temperature or with gentle heating in water; no catalyst required; water acts as solvent.

Acidic oxidative oxidation; potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid oxidizes the primary alcohol of 3‑hydroxymethylpyridine to the corresponding carboxylic acid (nicotinic acid); reaction is carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid under reflux, often with vigorous stirring; water serves as solvent.

Transmetallation (organometallic exchange); used to synthesize diphenylmercury from phenylmercuric chloride. The phenyl group of phenylmagnesium chloride transfers to mercury, displacing chloride as magnesium chloride. Typically performed under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑base reaction (metal carbonate neutralization). Lead(II) carbonate reacts with glacial acetic acid, producing lead(II) acetate, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Conducted under reflux in excess acetic acid; no catalyst.

Chlorination/formation of sulfonyl chloride; phosphorus pentachloride converts sodium p‑toluenesulfonate into p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride while generating sodium chloride and phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃) as by‑products; usually conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

Reaction type: dehydration of a carboxylic acid to the corresponding anhydride using a strong dehydrating agent. Purpose: preparation of isobutyric anhydride from the acid. Key transformation: phosphorus pentoxide removes water from two equivalents of isobutyric acid, linking them via an anhydride bond and forming phosphoric acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: mix isobutyric acid (2 equiv) with P2O5 (≈0.5‑1 equiv) under inert atmosphere; gently heat (80‑120 °C) in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dry toluene, xylene, or under solvent‑free conditions in a Dean‑Stark apparatus. Reaction proceeds until gas evolution ceases; the product is distilled under reduced pressure to separate the anhydride from phosphoric acid residues.

Acidic/neutral hydrolysis of an anhydride. Water attacks one carbonyl of succinic anhydride, opening the ring and ultimately yielding succinic acid after proton transfer. Usually performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or mild heating (50–80 °C); no catalyst required. Purpose: convert the anhydride to the corresponding dicarboxylic acid.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); provides butanal while retaining the tert‑butyl group as tert‑butyl alcohol. DIBAL‑H adds a single hydride to the carbonyl at low temperature, forming an alkoxide that, on work‑up, gives the aldehyde. Typical conditions: DIBAL‑H (1 equiv) in dry toluene or CH₂Cl₂, –78 °C under inert atmosphere, addition over 15–30 min, stir 30 min–1 h, then quench with methanol at –78 °C followed by aqueous work‑up. Aldehyde is isolated by distillation.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamoylation). Sodium methoxide acts as a nucleophile and base, attacking the carbonyl carbon of N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride to give methyl N‑methylcarbamate and precipitate NaCl. Typically carried out in anhydrous methanol or dry THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric NaOMe is used, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalysed hydrolysis of a methyl ester. Purpose: produce 2‑aminoacetic acid from methyl 2‑aminoacetate using acid conditions. Key transformation: protonated water attacks the carbonyl of the ester, breaking the C–O bond and giving 2‑aminoacetic acid and methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (conc. or 1 M), reflux for several hours; alternatively, prolonged stirring at room temperature can work. Solvent: aqueous HCl (water).

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous potassium carbonate reacts with strontium chromate, exchanging the cations to precipitate sparingly soluble strontium carbonate while keeping potassium chromate in solution; performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring.

Microbial biotransformation of a plant lignan; gut bacteria reduce and dehydroxylate secoisolariciresinol to produce the mammalian lignan enterodiol; the reaction occurs anaerobically in the intestinal tract via enzymatic hydrogenation and involves cleavage of the benzylic ether linkage.

Base‑catalyzed condensation of 4‑chlorophenylacetyl chloride with 4‑hydroxycoumarin to form the anticoagulant diphacinone (a bis‑coumarin). Sodium ethoxide deprotonates the phenolic OH and facilitates acyl transfer; NaCl is formed as by‑product. Usually carried out in dry ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, with anhydrous conditions to prevent hydrolysis of the acyl chloride.

S‑alkylation (methylation) of thioacetic acid with methyl triflate to give methyl thioacetate; purpose: preparation of a thioester; key transformation: transfer of a methyl group to sulfur, generating triflic acid as by‑product; typical conditions: anhydrous non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; no catalyst required, by‑product often neutralized.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus (salt metathesis); phenyl‑Li attacks the P–Cl bond of chlorodiphenylphosphine, forming a new P‑C bond and giving triphenylphosphine with LiCl as by‑product. Conducted under dry, oxygen‑free conditions in an ether solvent (THF or Et₂O) at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to room temperature; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) required.

Redox halogenation of a metal oxide; purpose is to convert uranium(IV) oxide into a volatile metal bromide and liberate oxygen. The reaction oxidizes Br2 while reducing the oxide lattice, forming UBr4 and O2. Typically performed by grinding solid UO2 with excess Br2 and heating in a sealed tube at 200‑300 °C. No solvent; the reaction proceeds in the melt of bromine under inert atmosphere.

Acylation (esterification) of 2,4‑dichlorophenol with 3,5‑dinitrobenzoyl chloride to afford the pesticide tetradifon, releasing hydrogen chloride. The reaction is typically performed in pyridine or triethylamine as an HCl scavenger, at 0 °C to ambient temperature, under an inert atmosphere to avoid moisture‑induced hydrolysis.

Acid‑base neutralization (phenol deprotonation). p‑Cresol donates a proton to NaOH, generating water and the sodium phenoxide (sodium p‑cresolate). The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature with vigorous stirring. No additional catalysts are required.

Metathesis/precipitation in acidic medium; silver nitrate and hydroiodic acid exchange ions to form insoluble silver iodide (AgI) precipitate and nitric acid (HNO₃) in solution; typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C to minimize side reactions; water is the solvent.

Chan–Lam copper‑catalyzed C‑N cross‑coupling. Phenylboronic acid and aniline are coupled in the presence of Cu(OAc)2 and pyridine to furnish diphenylamine, with water as the only by‑product and reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I) acetate. The reaction is usually performed in a mixed solvent such as MeOH/H2O or CH2Cl2 under air, at 25‑60 °C. Pyridine acts both as ligand and base; Cu(OAc)2 is the catalyst.

Base‑promoted ether cleavage (hydrolysis of an ethoxymethyl ether); NaOH attacks the ethoxymethyl group of 4‑(ethoxymethyl)phenol, yielding 4‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol and ethanol; used for deprotecting EOM protecting groups; generally carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) with reflux, sometimes in a mixed solvent such as THF/H₂O.

Quaternary ammonium formation via SN2 alkylation (methylation) of dimethylinoethanol with methyl chloride. The tertiary amine attacks methyl chloride, producing choline chloride as a quaternary ammonium salt. The reaction is carried out in an aqueous or polar protic solvent (e.g.,anol or ethanol) at reflux temperature (60‑80 °C) under an inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions. No catalyst is required; excess methyl chloride drives completion.

Copper‑catalyzed direct aryl carboxylation of an aryl iod with carbon dioxide. 2‑Iodonaphthalene reacts with CO2 in the presence of CuI (often with a base such as Cs2CO3 or K3PO4) to give 2‑naphthoic acid. The transformation proceeds under CO2 pressure (1–5 atm) in a polar aprotic solvent like DMF or DMSO at 100‑150 °C. CuI serves as the catalytic species that mediates oxidative addition of the aryl iodide and subsequent insertion of CO2.

This is a hydrolysis/precipitation (metathesis reaction in which aqueous potassium hydroxide hydrolyzes titanium tetrachloride to give titanium dioxide solid and potassium chloride, with water formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH solution, 0–25 °C or gentle reflux, vigorous stirring; product TiO₂ precipitates and is filtered. No special catalyst is required; water is the solvent.

Radical dehalogenation (reductive) of an alkyl iodide with tributyltin hydride. A tributyltin radical abstracts the iodine, forming a carbon‑centered radical that abstracts hydrogen from Bu₃SnH to give butane and tributyltin iodide. Typical conditions: reflux in toluene or benzene, catalytic amount of AIBN (or another radical initiator), under nitrogen.

This is an oxidative conversion of a primary benzylic alcohol to the correspondinghyde using sodium hypochlorite (bleach) in the presence of acetic acid as a buffer. It is a mild, selective oxidation (hypochlorite oxidation). Common conditions: aqueous NaOCl (10–15 % w/v), pH adjusted to ~5–6 with acetic acid, ambient temperature (0–25 °C) or gentle warming; often performed in a biphasic mixture with dichloromethane or chloroform as an organic co‑sol to extract the aldehyde. No additional catalyst is needed.

This is a peroxide oxidation of a sulfide to the sulfoxide using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant. The reaction selectively forms the sulfoxide without over‑oxidation to the sulfone when controlled. Typical conditions: dilute H₂O₂ (30 % w/w) added dropwise to a solution of dibutyl sulfide in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, acetonitrile, or THF; temperature low (0–5 °C) initially then allowed to rise to 20–25 °C; a weak acid catalyst (e.g., glacial acetic acid) or a phase‑transfer catalyst may be used to accelerate the reaction. No metal catalyst is required.

Allylic bromination; radical substitution to install a bromine atom at the allylic position of 1-pentene, giving 3-bromo-1-pentene. Typically carried out with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in carbon tetrachloride or CCl4 under reflux and light or a radical initiator (AIBN). Purpose: selective functionalization of the double bond without adding across it.

General type: acid–base metathesis (anion exchange). Purpose: replace acetate ligands with chloride to obtain bismuth(III) chloride. Key transformation: Bi³⁺ trades acetate for chloride ions, producing BiCl₃ and liberating acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, often with excess HCl; mild heating (≈40‑60 °C) may be used to increase solubility. Solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of 5‑methoxytryptamine using formaldehyde and formic acid; the amine is first formylated then reduced in situ, yielding 5‑methoxy‑N‑methyltryptamine. Conducted in aqueous formic acid (excess) with formaldehyde at 80–100 °C for several hours; no external reducing metal catalyst is required, and carbon dioxide is evolved as the only gaseous by‑product.

This is a Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 nucleophilic substitution) where sodium methoxide attacks each carbon of 1,2‑dichloroethane, displacing chloride to afford 1,2‑dimethoxyethane and sodium chloride. Standard conditions: anhydrous methanol (or dry THF) as solvent, excess sodium methoxide, reflux temperature (≈65 °C for methanol) under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. Reaction proceeds smoothly without added catalyst; the salt precipitates and can be filtered off.

This is a trans‑vinyl ester exchange (acyl transfer) in which ethanol attacks vinyl propanoate, displacing the vinyl group as acetaldehyde and forming ethyl propanoate. The vinyl group serves as a good leaving group because its elimination yields the thermodynamically favorable acetaldehyde. Typical conditions: catalytic amounts of a base (e.g., triethylamine) or a Lewis acid (e.g., Ti(OiPr)₄) in an inert solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, temperature 40–80 °C, and removal of acetaldehyde (by distillation) to drive the reaction to completion. No stoichiometric catalyst is required.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification of triethylsilanol with benzoic acid in the presence of dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC). This is a Steglich‑type coupling that forms a silyl benzoate ester without using an acid chloride. Purpose: mild esterification when acid chlorides are undesired; produces dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Key transformation: Si–OH + PhCOOH → Si–O–COPh, with DCC activating the carboxyl group. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, catalytic DMAP often added to accelerate acyl transfer; by‑product (dicyclohexylurea) is filtered off after reaction.

E2 elimination (base‑induced dehydrohalogenation); tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 2‑bromopropane, generating propylene and tert‑butanol while forming NaBr. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g THF or DMSO) at ambient to reflux temperature; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base reaction; purpose is to convert insoluble thulium oxide into soluble thulium nitrate; key transformation: Tm2O3 + 6 HNO3 → 2 Tm(NO3)3 + 3 H2O; carried out in aqueous nitric acid, usually with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Ligand‑exchange/complexation; platinum(II) acetate reacts with acetylacetone, displacing acetate ligands to give platinum(II) acetylacetonate and releasing acetic acid. Typically refluxed in a high‑boiling non‑coordinating solvent (toluene, benzene or xylene) under nitrogen; no external catalyst.

Acid‑base metathesis/precipitation; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes cadmium phosphate, producing soluble sodium phosphate and precipitating cadmium hydroxide. Performed in water at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no catalyst.

Thiocarbamoylation of an amine; 2‑methylaniline nucleophilically attacks thiophosgene to form a thiocarbamoyl chloride intermediate, which is hydrolyzed by water to give N‑(2‑methylphenyl)thiourea and HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often in the presence of a base (e.g triethylamine) to scavenge HCl; inert atmosphere is common.

Enzymatic cleavage of S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) by ACC synthase; purpose is biosynthetic production of the ethylene precursor 1‑aminocyclopropane‑1‑carboxylic acid (ACC) and the by‑product 5′‑methylthioadenosine (MTA). The reaction is a lyase‑type transformation that removes the methylthioadenosine moiety and generates the cyclopropane ring of ACC. Occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.5) with the enzyme; no synthetic solvent or catalyst is used.

The reaction is an acid-base protonation. Purpose: to regenerate octanoic acid from its carboxylate salt. Key transformation: potassium octanoate is protonated by HCl to form octanoic acid. Conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature.

Double displacement/acid‑base metathesis; sulfuric acid protonates bismuth chloride and swaps anions to give insoluble bismuth(III) sulfate liberating hydrogen chloride gas. Typically performed in aqueous solution with heating (80‑100 °C) to drive off HCl; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Condensation (amidation) of a carboxylic acid with a secondary amine to form a secondary amide; the carbonyl carbon is activated and bonds to the nitrogen, releasing water. In practice the acid is often first converted to its acid chloride (using SOCl₂ or oxalyl chloride) or coupled with reagents such as DCC/EDC in dichloromethane or DMF, then treated with diethylamine at 0 °C to rt. The purpose is synthesis of N,N‑diethyldodecanamide.

Combustion/oxidation reaction; purpose is to oxidize elemental phosphorus to its anhydride; phosphorus is burned in excess oxygen, yielding phosphorus pentoxide (P4O10); requires high temperature (often >400 °C) under a stream of dry O2; no solvent, solid product collected as white powder.

Metal‑mediated reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; sodium amalgam delivers electrons to perillaldehyde, converting the carbonyl to a hydroxyl group and giving perillyl alcohol. Conducted in an alcoholic or aqueous medium (often ethanol) at 0‑25 °C under inert atmosphere; Na/Hg is the reducing agent, no additional catalyst needed.

Selective carbonyl reduction; sodium borohydride transfers hydride to the ketone of carvone, reducing it to the allylic secondary alcohol carveol without affecting the conjugated double bond. Typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1–2 eq) in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature for 1–2 h; reaction quenched with water; no catalyst required.

Strong hydride reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine; lithium aluminiumride adds two hydride equivalents to the nitrile carbon of 3‑methylphenylacetonitrile, forming the imine intermediate that is further reduced to 2‑(3‑methylphenyl)ethan‑1‑amine. Conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen at reflux (≈70 °C) for 2–4 h; excess LiAlH₄ is used; reaction is quenched carefully with water then dilute acid. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; the ester ethyl acetate exchanges its ethoxy group with the hydroxyl of 2‑methoxy‑1‑propanol, producing ethanol and propylene glycol methyl ether acetate (PGMEA); typically run under reflux with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) in an inert solvent such as toluene or xylene; removal of the volatile ethanol drives the equilibrium forward.

Carbothermic reduction: indium(III) oxide is reduced by carbon to produce metallic indium and carbon monoxide. Carried out at very high temperature (typically >1300 °C) in a furnace under an inert or reducing atmosphere; the solid carbon acts as both reductant and heat source, no catalyst is used.

Catalytic hydrogenation () of a nitro‑adamantane derivative; the nitro group of 1‑nitroadamantane is reduced to a primary amine to give 1‑aminoadamantane; performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 5–10 % Pd/C at room temperature to 50 °C in a protic solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate; the reaction is selective for the nitro group and does not affect the adamantane cage.

Acid–base double‑displacement (metathesis) forming a rare‑earth phosphate; trichloroneodymium reacts with phosphoric acid to precipitate neodymium phosphate while liberating three equivalents of hydrochloric acid (which may evolve as HCl gas or remain in solution); carried out in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating improve dissolution and precipitation; the solid phosphate is typically isolated by filtration and washing with water.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; phenylboronic acid couples with 5‑bromopyrimidine to afford 5‑phenylpyrimidine via palladium‑catalyzed C–C bond formation; standard conditions use a Pd(0) source (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂), a base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, and a solvent system (toluene/water, dioxane/water, or DMF) under inert atmosphere at 80–110 °C; the reaction tolerates the heteroaryl bromide and delivers the arylated product in good yield.

Selective reduction of an aromatic aldehyde; sodium borohydride reduces the aldehyde function of 4‑iodobenzhyde to the corresponding primary alcohol, (4‑iodophenyl)methanol, without affecting the aryl iodide; typically performed at0 °C to room temperature in methanol, ethanol, or a mixture of THF/water; the reaction is quenched with dilute acid after completion and the product isolated by extraction or chromatography.

Hydrolysis (solvolysis) of a secondary alkyl bromide with water to give the corresponding alcohol and hydrobromic acid; purpose is preparation of cyclohexanol from bromocyclohexane. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation (or SN2) displacing bromide. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at elevated temperature (reflux), sometimes acid or base catalysis; common solvent is water or dilute aqueous ethanol.

Acid‑base neutralization and gas evolution; magnesium carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid to form magnesium sulfate, carbonic acid, and water; the unstable carbonic acid immediately decomposes to CO₂ gas and H₂O; common practice is to add solid MgCO₃ slowly to aqueous HSO₄ (often diluted, 1 M) stirring at ambient temperature, allowing CO₂ to escape; the resulting aqueous MgSO₄ solution can be concentrated or the solid salt crystallized.

Double‑displacement precipitation of silver(I) iodide from aqueous silver nitrate and potassium iodide; produces insoluble AgI and soluble potassium nitrate; performed in water at room temperature, often with gentle agitation.

Acid‑base neutralization; carbonate anion is protonated by nitric acid yielding carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂/H₂O) and forming cesium nitrate salt; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Reductive cleavage of a disulfide; sodium borohydride reduces bis(2‑pyridyl) disulfide to two equivalents of 2‑mercaptopyridine while being oxidized to sodium borate; typically carried out in protic solvents such as ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature, excess NaBH₄, no additional catalyst.

Acyl‑halide esterification; acetyl bromide acylates isobutanol to give isobutyl acetate with concurrent formation of hydrogen bromide; usually conducted in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to capture HBr.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of a transition metal with a metalloid to afford an intermetallic compound, chromium arsenide; requires high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) under inert atmosphere (argon) in a sealed tube or furnace, no catalyst.

Acidic halogenation of a ceramic nitride; concentrated hydrochloric acid reacts with silicon nitride to generate volatile silicon tetrachloride and ammonium chloride; performed by refluxing Si₃N₄ in aqueous HCl at elevated temperature (≈100 °C), water as solvent, no catalyst.

Methylation of 2‑aminobenzoic acid with diazomethane (diazomethane esterification); purpose is to protect the carboxyl group as a methyl ester without acidic conditions; key step is nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate on diazomethane, loss of N₂, forming methyl 2‑aminobenzoate; performed at 0 °C to rt in dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required, but the reaction is quenched with acetic acid after completion.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution to form a thioester; methanethiol attacks acetyl chloride producing S‑methyl thioacetate and hydrogen chloride; carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl; no catalyst needed.

Type: N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of barbituric acid; purpose: synthesis of the sedative barbital (diethyl‑barbituric acid). Key transformation: deprotonated barbituric acid nitrogen attacks ethyl bromide twice, forming two N‑ethyl bonds while HBr is trapped by triethylamine to give triethylammonium bromide. Typical conditions: reflux in a dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF, or THF) with excess triethylamine under nitrogen; reaction time 2–12 h. Common reagents: triethylamine as base, ethyl bromide as alkylating agent.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of chromic acid; purpose: preparation of sodium chromate solution. Key transformation: two hydroxide ions neutralize the acidic protons of H2CrO4, producing water and the chromate anion, which pairs with sodium cations. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts of NaOH added slowly to a solution of chromic acid with stirring. No special catalysts required; water is the solvent.

Type: Metathesis / acid‑base displacement (fluorination) reaction; purpose: conversion of scandium phosphate to soluble scandium fluoride while liberating phosphoric acid. Key transformation: fluoride ions from HF replace phosphate ligands on Sc^3+, forming ScF3 (insoluble) and generating H3PO4. Typical conditions: aqueous hydrofluoric acid (excess) at room or mild heating; performed in PTFE‑lined equipment due to HF corrosion. No catalyst; HF serves both acid and fluoride source.

Type: Fischer esterification; purpose: preparation of ethyl phenoxyacetateester) from phenoxyacetic acid. Key transformation: the carboxylic acid carbonyl is protonated, ethanol attacks to form a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by loss of water and regeneration of the acid catalyst, yielding the ester. Typical conditions: reflux in excess anhydrous ethanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid); removal of water by Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic distillation drives the equilibrium. Common solvents: ethanol itself acts as solvent; sometimes toluene is used as co‑solvent.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; purpose: generation of ammonia gas and formation of sodium iodate. Key transformation: hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium ion to give NH3 (released) and water; the iodate anion pairs with Na^+ to give NaIO3. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; NaOH added to a cold solution of ammonium iodate with vigorous stirring. No catalyst needed; water is solvent.

Type: Halide exchange (ligand substitution) on a metal carbonyl complex; purpose: preparation of bromopentacarbonylrhenium by swapping the chloride ligand for bromide. Key transformation: a bromide ion from HBr displaces the chloride ligand coordinated to Re(CO)5Cl, forming Re(CO)5Br and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane, chloroform, or THF; reaction performed at 0 °C to room temperature, often with slight excess HBr. No external catalyst required; the process relies on the nucleophilic nature of bromide.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic nitro group while retaining the aryl bromide; purpose is conversion of the nitro to an amine to afford 4‑bromoaniline. Conditions: H₂ gas (1‑3 atm), 5‑10 % Pd/C, protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25‑80 °C. Water is produced as the only by‑product.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of hydrogen chloride to the carbon‑carbon double bond of allyl chloride giving Markovnikov addition to afford 1,2‑dichloropropane. Typically performed by bubbling HCl gas through the allyl chloride or using aqueous HCl, often at reflux; no special solvent is required, though a polar solvent such as ethanol can be used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl chloride by sodium ethanethiolate, a Williamson‑type thioether synthesis, producing diethyl sulfide and sodium chloride. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) between sodium oxalate and thorium nitrate in aqueous solution; purpose: isolation of thorium oxalate as an insoluble precipitate; key transformation: exchange of Na⁺ and Th⁴⁺ ions forming solid Th(C2O4)2 and soluble NaNO3; conditions: aqueous medium, stirring at rt or mild heating, no catalyst; solid filtered and washed.

Reaction type: cyclocondensation forming a 1,2,4‑dithiazolidine dione. Purpose: construct a heterocyclic dithiazolidinone ring. Key transformation: nucleophilic substitution of the chloride of monochloroacetic acid by the sulfur of ammonium dithiocarbamate, followed by intramolecular cyclization and oxidation to give 1,2,4‑dithiazolidine‑3,5‑dione, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, mild heating (50‑80 °C), often with a base (NaOH) to deprotonate the dithiocarbamate; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralisation reaction between hydrobromic acid and thallium(I) hydroxide, forming thallium bromide salt and water. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds readily without additional reagents.

Protonation (acid–base salt formation) of piperidolate (the conjugate base of piperidine) with hydrochloric acid, yielding piperidinium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous or ethanolic solution at 0–25 °C; the product precipitates or remains in solution as the hydrochloride salt.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous nickel nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate to precipitate nickel(II) carbonate while sodium nitrate remains in solution; typically done by adding aqueous Na₂CO₃ to Ni(NO₃)₂ solution under stirring, optionally at low temperature to improve crystal formation; water solvent; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between aqueous sodium chromate and cadmium bromide, exchanging anions to give soluble sodium bromide and insoluble cadmium chromate precipitate. Reaction is carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the cadmium chromate precipitate is filtered off.

Acid‑catalysed O‑methylation (Fischer‑type esterification) of picric acid with methanol in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid, producing methyl picrate and water. The mixture is refluxed in excess methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄, and removal of water drives the reaction to completion.
Hydrolysis of anhydride; formic anhydride reacts with water to produce two equivalents of formic acid; can be run at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

SN2 methylation (O‑alkylation) of N‑methylhydroxylamine with methyl iodide in basic aqueous/acetone medium; NaOH deprotonates the hydroxyl group, which attacks CH3I to give N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine, NaI and water; performed at 0‑25 °C, no catalyst required.

Amidation of 2,6‑dimethylaniline using acetyl chloride to give N‑(2,6‑dimethylphenyl)acetamide; the amine attacks the acyl chloride, generating HCl which is scavenged by a base (pyridine, triethylamine). Reaction carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane or chloroform under nitrogen.
